- Consolidation and cohesion of important information - Basic timeline -
Period Timeframe Key Features
Advent of Europeans Portuguese Arrival (1498 CE) Vasco da Gama lands in Calicut, establishes first European trade route with India
Portuguese Expansion (1505–1510 CE) Goa captured by Albuquerque, becomes Portuguese stronghold
Dutch Arrival (1605 CE) Dutch East India Company sets up trading posts in Pulicat, Masulipatnam
English Arrival (1600–1612 CE) East India Company established, first factory at Surat, trade privileges from Jahangir
French Arrival (1664 CE) French East India Company establishes base in Pondicherry, Surat
Rise of British Power Anglo-Dutch Rivalry (1650–1750 CE) British gain dominance over Dutch in Indian trade
Battle of Plassey (1757 CE) Robert Clive defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah, establishes British control over Bengal
Battle of Buxar (1764 CE) British defeat Mughal, Awadh, and Bengal forces, gain Diwani rights (revenue collection)
Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–1799 CE) Conflicts with Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, British annex parts of Mysore
Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818 CE) British defeat Maratha Confederacy, expand control over central and western India
Early Resistance and Reforms Sanyasi-Fakir Rebellion (1760–1800 CE) Monks and peasants resist British revenue policies in Bengal
Revolt of 1857 (1857 CE) First War of Independence, led by sepoys, Mangal Pandey, Rani Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar
British Crown Rule (1858 CE) End of East India Company, Government of India Act, Queen Victoria’s Proclamation
Social Reforms (1820–1880 CE) Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Brahmo Samaj), Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (widow remarriage), abolition of Sati (1829)
Formation of Indian National Congress (1885 CE) Founded by A.O. Hume, early leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji demand self-governance
Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883 CE) Proposed equal treatment for Indian and European judges, opposed by British residents
Freedom Struggle Partition of Bengal (1905 CE) Lord Curzon’s partition fuels Swadeshi and Boycott movements, rise of nationalism
Muslim League Formation (1906 CE) Founded in Dhaka to represent Muslim political interests, led by Aga Khan
Morley-Minto Reforms (1909 CE) Indian Councils Act, introduces separate electorates for Muslims
Gandhian Era Begins (1915 CE) Gandhi returns from South Africa, leads Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918) Satyagrahas
Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh (1919 CE) Repressive laws spark protests, massacre in Amritsar kills hundreds
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922 CE) Gandhi’s call to boycott British goods, schools, courts; Khilafat Movement aligns
Chauri Chaura Incident (1922 CE) Violence leads Gandhi to suspend Non-Cooperation Movement
Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1934 CE) Salt March to Dandi, mass protests, Round Table Conferences in London
Path to Independence Government of India Act (1935 CE) Provisions for provincial autonomy, federal structure, elections in 1937
World War II Impact (1939–1945 CE) Indian soldiers fight, Congress opposes British war effort, Subhas Bose forms INA
Quit India Movement (1942 CE) Gandhi’s “Do or Die” call, mass arrests, widespread protests
INA Trials and Naval Mutiny (1945–1946 CE) Trials of INA leaders, Royal Indian Navy revolt in Bombay fuel unrest
Cabinet Mission and Interim Government (1946 CE) Plans for independence, Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan intensifies
Independence and Partition (1947 CE) India gains independence on August 15, Partition creates India and Pakistan, mass migrations
- Kingdoms/dyansties in chronological order
Kingdom/Empire Dynasty Ruler / Key Figure Period Capital Titles / Notes Key Achievements Policies / Patronage Decline / End Additional Details
Post-Mughal and Regional Powers (1707–1857 CE)
Mughal Empire Timurid Bahadur Shah I 1707–1712 CE Delhi Shah Alam (King of the World) Suppressed Sikh and Rajput rebellions Reconciliation with Rajputs, weak central authority Natural death, succession wars Empire fragmented, regional governors (e.g., Nizam of Hyderabad) gained autonomy
Jahandar Shah 1712–1713 CE Delhi — Brief reign, controlled by Zulfiqar Khan Extravagant spending, noble influence Deposed and killed by Farrukhsiyar Weakened Mughal prestige, noble factions dominant
Farrukhsiyar 1713–1719 CE Delhi — Granted British trade rights (1717 CE) Controlled by Sayyid brothers, weak rule Deposed, blinded, killed Sayyid brothers acted as kingmakers
Rafi-ud-Darajat 1719 CE Delhi — Brief reign, puppet of Sayyid brothers Nominal rule, no significant policies Natural death Shortest-reigning Mughal emperor
Shah Jahan II 1719 CE Delhi — Brief reign, puppet of Sayyid brothers Nominal rule, no significant policies Natural death Installed to replace Rafi-ud-Darajat
Muhammad Shah 1719–1748 CE Delhi Rangila (Colorful) Faced Nadir Shah’s invasion (1739 CE) Patronage of Urdu poetry, music, Mughal painting Natural death, empire weakened Loss of northwest to Nadir Shah, rise of Marathas
Ahmad Shah Bahadur 1748–1754 CE Delhi — Lost to Ahmad Shah Durrani (Second Battle of Panipat) Weak rule, controlled by viziers Deposed, blinded Maratha and Afghan conflicts eroded authority
Alamgir II 1754–1759 CE Delhi — Puppet of Imad-ul-Mulk, faced Maratha expansion Nominal rule, no significant patronage Assassinated Delhi sacked by Durrani (1757 CE)
Shah Alam II 1759–1806 CE Delhi — Battle of Buxar (1764 CE), became British vassal Poetry, granted Diwani rights to British Blinded by Rohillas, died East India Company controlled revenues
Bahadur Shah Zafar 1837–1857 CE Delhi Zafar (Victory), Poet-King Figurehead of 1857 Revolt, composed Urdu ghazals Patronage of Urdu literature, Ghalib’s mentor Exiled to Rangoon (1857 CE) Last Mughal emperor, nominal rule under British
Maratha Empire Bhonsle, Peshwa Shahu I 1707–1749 CE Satara Chhatrapati (Sovereign) Stabilized Maratha Confederacy, appointed Peshwas Delegated power to Peshwas, promoted expansion Natural death, Peshwa dominance Confederacy included Scindias (Gwalior), Holkars (Indore), Gaekwads (Baroda), Bhonsles (Nagpur)
Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 1713–1720 CE Pune Peshwa (Prime Minister) Consolidated Maratha power, treaty with Mughals Administrative reforms, Chauth collection Natural death Strengthened confederacy structure
Peshwa Baji Rao I 1720–1740 CE Pune Peshwa (Prime Minister) Battle of Palkhed (1728 CE), expanded to Malwa Military campaigns, confederacy expansion Natural death Raids into Mughal territories, Delhi (1737 CE)
Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao 1740–1761 CE Pune Peshwa (Prime Minister) Controlled Delhi, peak Maratha power Taxation (Chauth, Sardeshmukhi), centralized rule Third Battle of Panipat (1761 CE) Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani weakened confederacy
Peshwa Baji Rao II 1796–1818 CE Pune Peshwa (Prime Minister) Last Peshwa, fought Third Anglo-Maratha War Weak governance, British alliances Exiled to Bithur (1818 CE) Maratha Confederacy dissolved, princely states emerged
Mysore Kingdom Wodeyar Hyder Ali 1761–1782 CE Seringapatam Nawab (Governor) First Anglo-Mysore War, rocket artillery Military modernization, anti-British alliances Natural death Usurped Wodeyar rule, established military state
Tipu Sultan 1782–1799 CE Seringapatam Sultan, Tiger of Mysore Third Anglo-Mysore War, pioneered war rockets Sericulture, trade with France, Middle East Killed in Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799 CE) Wodeyar rule restored under British after his death
Sikh Empire Khalsa Ranjit Singh 1799–1839 CE Lahore Sher-e-Punjab (Lion of Punjab) Unified 12 Sikh Misls, captured Kashmir, Multan Secular governance, modernized Khalsa army Natural death Misls included Sukerchakia, Ahluwalia, Bhangi
Duleep Singh 1843–1849 CE Lahore Maharaja (Great King) Last Sikh ruler, child during Anglo-Sikh Wars Under British regency, nominal rule Annexed by British (1849 CE) Exiled to England, converted to Christianity
Hyderabad State Asaf Jahi Nizam-ul-Mulk 1724–1748 CE Hyderabad Nizam (Administrator of the Realm) Founded semi-independent state, resisted Marathas Feudal governance, Mughal allegiance Natural death Controlled Deccan, seven Nizams ruled until 1948
Mir Osman Ali Khan 1911–1948 CE Hyderabad Nizam, His Exalted Highness Founded Osmania University, built infrastructure Modernization, loyalty to British Annexed by India (1948 CE) Wealthiest Indian ruler, resisted Indian integration
Awadh Nawabi Shuja-ud-Daula 1754–1775 CE Lucknow Nawab Vazir (Governor Vizier) Developed Lucknow, fought Battle of Buxar Patronage of Shia culture, Urdu poetry Natural death Persian Shia dynasty, semi-independent from Mughals
Wajid Ali Shah 1847–1856 CE Lucknow Nawab, Poet-King Patronized Kathak, Urdu drama Cultural patronage, extravagant lifestyle Annexed by British (1856 CE) Exiled to Calcutta, composed poetry
Bengal Nawabi Siraj-ud-Daula 1756–1757 CE Murshidabad Nawab Nazim (Governor Ruler) Resisted British at Fort William Anti-British policies, centralized rule Defeated at Plassey, executed (1757 CE) Last independent Nawab, British installed Mir Jafar
Rohilkhand Rohilla Hafiz Rahmat Khan 1748–1774 CE Bareilly Nawab (Governor) Resisted Marathas, established Rohilla state Pashtun governance, military focus Killed by Awadh forces (1774 CE) Pashtun settlers, annexed by Awadh and British
Bharatpur State Jat Suraj Mal 1755–1763 CE Bharatpur Maharaja (Great King) Looted Delhi (1757 CE), fortified Bharatpur Jat consolidation, fortifications Killed in ambush Jat agrarian community, resisted Mughals
British Dominance and Princely States (1757–1947 CE)
British India East India Company Robert Clive 1757–1767 CE Calcutta Governor, Baron Clive Battle of Plassey, dual government in Bengal Revenue collection, colonial administration Left India, died by suicide Controlled Bengal, Bihar, Orissa; later Crown rule (1858 CE)
Warren Hastings 1772–1785 CE Calcutta First Governor-General Regulating Act (1773 CE), expanded control Judicial reforms, princely state treaties Resigned, faced impeachment Established British paramountcy
Baroda State Gaekwad Sayaji Rao Gaekwad III 1875–1939 CE Baroda Maharaja (Great King) Modernized Baroda, Baroda College Education, social reforms, British allegiance Acceded to India (1947 CE) Part of Maratha Confederacy, Gaekwad lineage
Gwalior State Scindia Madho Rao Scindia 1886–1925 CE Gwalior Maharaja (Great King) Developed Gwalior Fort, railways Modernization, loyalty to British Acceded to India (1947 CE) Part of Maratha Confederacy, Scindia lineage
Indore State Holkar Tukoji Rao Holkar II 1903–1926 CE Indore Maharaja (Great King) Industrialized Indore Education, infrastructure, British treaties Acceded to India (1947 CE) Part of Maratha Confederacy, Holkar lineage
Jodhpur State Rathore Umaid Singh 1918–1947 CE Jodhpur Maharaja (Great King) Built Umaid Bhawan Palace Urban development, British paramountcy Acceded to India (1947 CE) Rajput state, ruled Marwar region
Travancore State Kulasekhara Chithira Thirunal 1924–1947 CE Trivandrum Maharaja (Great King) Modernized Travancore, Travancore University Social reforms, British allegiance Acceded to India (1947 CE) Malayali state, ruled southern Kerala
Jaipur State Kachwaha Man Singh II 1922–1947 CE Jaipur Maharaja (Great King) Developed Jaipur, patronized arts Modernization, British loyalty Acceded to India (1947 CE) Rajput state, ruled Amber region
- European powers -
European Power Time Period Key Locations Notable Leaders Key Steps (How It Started, First Factory, Deals, Progression) Major Battles/Forts Contemporary Rulers & Relations
Portuguese 1498–17th century CE Goa, Diu, Daman, Bombay, Malabar Vasco da Gama, Afonso de Albuquerque 1. Started with Vasco da Gama’s arrival at Calicut (1498), seeking spice trade.

2. First factory established at Cochin (1503) after deal with local ruler.

3. Secured trade monopoly via naval dominance; captured Goa (1510) as permanent base.

4. Expanded with forts in Diu, Daman; dominated western coast trade. 		Battle of Diu (1509), Fort Aguada (Goa), Diu Fort Vijayanagara Empire (trade initially), Zamorin of Calicut (hostile), Mughals (mixed trade/conflict)
Dutch (VOC) 1605–17th century CE Coromandel Coast, Bengal, Malabar, Gujarat Cornelis de Houtman, Pieter van den Broecke 1. Began with Cornelis de Houtman’s expedition (1595–97), aimed at spices.

2. First factory at Petapuli (1606, Coromandel), followed by Pulicat (1610).

3. Gained trade rights from Mughal Emperor Jahangir (1610s) for Surat.

4. Focused on trade, not conquest; established posts in Bengal (Chinsurah), Gujarat. 		Minor clashes with Portuguese, Fort Geldria (Pulicat) Mughal Empire (trade farman), Vijayanagara remnants (trade), local rulers (competitive)
French 1664–1757 CE Pondicherry, Bengal, Malabar François Caron, François Martin 1. Started with French East India Company’s formation (1664), late entry.

2. First factory at Surat (1668), but Pondicherry (1674) became key base.

3. Deal with Nawab of Carnatic for Pondicherry land; fortified it.

4. Expanded to Chandernagore (Bengal); trade-focused with minor conflicts. 		No major battles pre-1757, Fort Louis (Pondicherry) Mughal Empire (trade under Aurangzeb), Carnatic Nawabs (cooperative initially)
Danes (Danish East India Company) 1616–17th century CE Tranquebar, Bengal Ove Gjedde 1. Initiated with Danish East India Company (1616), seeking trade.

2. First factory and fort at Tranquebar (1620), leased from Nayak of Tanjore.

3. Secured minor trade rights from Mughals for Bengal (Serampore).

4. Small-scale presence; focused on commerce, not expansion. 		No major battles, Fort Dansborg (Tranquebar) Mughal Empire (trade permits), Nayaks of Tanjore (land lease)
East India Company (British) 1600–1757 CE Bengal, Madras, Bombay, Gujarat William Hawkins, Sir Thomas Roe, Robert Clive 1. Started with EIC’s charter (1600), Hawkins’ mission to Mughal court (1608).

2. First factory at Surat (1612) after defeating Portuguese at Swally.

3. Secured trade farman from Jahangir (1615) for broader rights.

4. Expanded with Fort St. George (Madras, 1640), Fort William (Calcutta, 1690s); shifted to territorial control by Plassey (1757). 		Battle of Swally (1612), Battle of Plassey (1757), Fort William Mughal Empire (trade under Jahangir), Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah (hostile by 1757)
- Battles and campaigns -
Conflict / Battle Name Time (Approx.) Location Participants Purpose / Context Outcome Key Commanders / Notes
Maratha-Mughal and Regional Conflicts (1707–1761 CE)
Battle of Jajau 1707 CE Jajau, near Agra Mughal factions (Azam Shah vs. Bahadur Shah I) Succession struggle after Aurangzeb’s death to claim the Mughal throne. Bahadur Shah I’s victory. Azam Shah killed. Bahadur Shah I, Azam Shah (Mughal). Weakened Mughal unity, aided Maratha rise.
Maratha Raids on Delhi 1710–1711 CE Delhi Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Marathas under Shahu I raided to exploit Mughal instability post-Aurangzeb. Maratha success. Plundered Mughal territories. Shahu I (Maratha), Mughal governors. Early Maratha expansion.
Battle of Palkhed 1728 CE Palkhed, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Nizam of Hyderabad Peshwa Baji Rao I aimed to assert Maratha dominance over the Deccan. Maratha victory. Nizam ceded territories. Baji Rao I (Maratha), Nizam-ul-Mulk (Hyderabad). Guerrilla tactics decisive.
Battle of Delhi (1737) 1737 CE Delhi Maratha Empire vs. Mughal Empire Marathas under Baji Rao I raided Delhi to demonstrate Mughal weakness. Maratha victory. Mughal defenses overrun. Baji Rao I (Maratha), Mughal garrison. Exposed Mughal decline.
Battle of Bhopal 1737 CE Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh Maratha Empire vs. Mughal allies & Nizam Marathas aimed to force Nizam to cede Malwa, expanding central India influence. Maratha victory. Treaty of Bhopal (1738); Malwa ceded. Baji Rao I (Maratha), Nizam-ul-Mulk (Hyderabad). Strengthened Maratha confederacy.
Battle of Vasai 1739 CE Vasai, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Portuguese Marathas under Chimaji Appa aimed to expel Portuguese from Konkan coast. Maratha victory. Vasai Fort captured. Chimaji Appa (Maratha), Portuguese garrison. Ended Portuguese regional dominance.
Nadir Shah’s Invasion 1739 CE Delhi, Northwest India Persian Empire vs. Mughal Empire Nadir Shah invaded to plunder Mughal wealth under Muhammad Shah. Persian victory. Delhi sacked; Peacock Throne looted. Nadir Shah (Persia), Muhammad Shah (Mughal). Mughal treasury drained, weakened empire.
Maratha Invasion of Bengal 1741–1744 CE Bengal, Orissa Maratha Empire vs. Nawab of Bengal Marathas under Bhaskar Pandit raided Bengal to extract chauth (tribute). Maratha success. Treaty of 1744; Orissa ceded. Bhaskar Pandit (Maratha), Alivardi Khan (Bengal). Known as Bargi invasions; devastated Bengal.
Battle of Udgir 1760 CE Udgir, Maharashtra Maratha Empire vs. Nizam of Hyderabad Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau aimed to consolidate Deccan control against Nizam’s resistance. Maratha victory. Nizam ceded territories, paid indemnity. Sadashivrao Bhau (Maratha), Nizam Ali Khan (Hyderabad). Strengthened Maratha hold before Panipat.
Third Battle of Panipat 1761 CE Panipat, Haryana Maratha Empire vs. Durrani Empire, with Mughal allies Marathas aimed to dominate North India and install Vishwasrao as Mughal emperor; Ahmad Shah Durrani sought to protect Punjab influence. Durrani victory. Maratha expansion halted; heavy casualties on both sides. Sadashivrao Bhau, Malhar Rao Holkar (Maratha), Ahmad Shah Durrani, Najib-ud-Daula (Durrani). Largest battle of 18th century; Maratha power weakened.
Anglo-French Rivalry (1744–1763 CE)
First Carnatic War 1744–1748 CE Coromandel Coast (Madras, Arcot) British East India Company (Governor Charles Floyer) vs. French East India Company (Governor Joseph François Dupleix) Anglo-French rivalry during War of the Austrian Succession; French aimed to dominate South India trade. Inconclusive. Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748); Madras returned to British. Joseph Dupleix (French), Charles Floyer (British). French captured Madras (1746).
Second Carnatic War 1749–1754 CE Arcot, Trichinopoly, Tamil Nadu British East India Company (Governor Thomas Saunders) vs. French East India Company (Governor Joseph François Dupleix), with Chanda Sahib Anglo-French proxy war over Nawabship of Arcot; British backed Muhammad Ali Khan. British victory. Treaty of Pondicherry (1754); Muhammad Ali Khan confirmed Nawab. Robert Clive, Stringer Lawrence (British), Dupleix, Chanda Sahib (French). Clive’s defense of Arcot pivotal.
Battle of Wandiwash 1760 CE Wandiwash, Tamil Nadu British East India Company (Governor George Pigot) vs. French East India Company (Governor Thomas Lally) Key battle in Third Carnatic War; British aimed to eliminate French influence in South India. British victory. French power in India crippled. Eyre Coote (British), Thomas Lally (French). Paved way for British dominance in South India.
Third Carnatic War 1756–1763 CE Wandiwash, Madras, Pondicherry British East India Company (Governor George Pigot) vs. French East India Company (Governor Thomas Lally) Part of Seven Years’ War; Anglo-French struggle for South India and Bengal trade. British victory. Treaty of Paris (1763); French influence curtailed. Eyre Coote (British), Thomas Lally (French). Wandiwash and Pondicherry sieges decisive.
Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–1799 CE)
First Anglo-Mysore War 1767–1769 CE Mysore, Tamil Nadu British East India Company (Governor Harry Verelst) vs. Mysore Kingdom British aimed to curb Hyder Ali’s power, allied with Nizam and Marathas. Mysore victory. Treaty of Madras (1769); mutual restoration of territories. Hyder Ali (Mysore), Joseph Smith (British). Hyder Ali reached Madras outskirts.
Second Anglo-Mysore War 1780–1784 CE Mysore, Carnatic British East India Company (Governor Warren Hastings) vs. Mysore Kingdom, with French support Hyder Ali, with French allies, sought to expel British from South India. Inconclusive. Treaty of Mangalore (1784); status quo restored. Hyder Ali, Tipu Sultan (Mysore), Eyre Coote (British). Mysore’s rocket artillery effective.
Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790–1792 CE Mysore, Seringapatam British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Cornwallis) vs. Mysore Kingdom British, with Maratha and Nizam allies, aimed to weaken Tipu Sultan’s French ties. British victory. Treaty of Seringapatam (1792); half of Mysore ceded, heavy indemnity. Charles Cornwallis (British), Tipu Sultan (Mysore). Tipu’s capital besieged.
Fourth Anglo-Mysore War 1798–1799 CE Seringapatam, Mysore British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Wellesley) vs. Mysore Kingdom British aimed to eliminate Tipu Sultan’s resistance and French alliance. British victory. Tipu killed; Mysore annexed, Wodeyars restored. Arthur Wellesley, George Harris (British), Tipu Sultan (Mysore). Siege of Seringapatam decisive.
Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818 CE)
First Anglo-Maratha War 1775–1782 CE Maharashtra, Gujarat British East India Company (Governor Warren Hastings) vs. Maratha Empire (Peshwa Madhavrao II) British aimed to install Raghunathrao as Peshwa to control Maratha politics. Maratha victory. Treaty of Salbai (1782); status quo restored. Warren Hastings, John Carnac (British), Mahadji Scindia, Nana Fadnavis (Maratha). Battle of Wadgaon (1779) key.
Second Anglo-Maratha War 1803–1805 CE Central India, Maharashtra British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Wellesley) vs. Maratha Confederacy (Scindias, Holkars, Bhonsles) British aimed to curb Maratha power after Treaty of Bassein (1802). British victory. Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803), Treaty of Rajghat (1805); Maratha autonomy reduced. Arthur Wellesley (British), Daulat Rao Scindia, Yashwantrao Holkar (Maratha). Battles of Assaye, Laswari decisive.
Battle of Assaye 1803 CE Assaye, Maharashtra British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Wellesley) vs. Maratha Confederacy (Scindias) British aimed to defeat Scindia’s forces in Second Anglo-Maratha War to control Deccan. British victory. Maratha forces routed. Arthur Wellesley (British), Daulat Rao Scindia (Maratha). Wellesley’s tactical brilliance; high casualties.
Battle of Laswari 1803 CE Laswari, Rajasthan British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Wellesley) vs. Maratha Confederacy (Scindias) British aimed to crush Scindia’s northern forces in Second Anglo-Maratha War. British victory. Scindia’s power in North India broken. Gerard Lake (British), Daulat Rao Scindia (Maratha). Decisive for British control of Delhi.
Third Anglo-Maratha War 1817–1818 CE Maharashtra, Central India British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Hastings) vs. Maratha Confederacy (Peshwa Baji Rao II, Holkars, Scindias) British sought to annex Maratha territories after Peshwa’s rebellion. British victory. Peshwa deposed; Maratha Empire dissolved. Francis Rawdon-Hastings (British), Baji Rao II, Malhar Rao Holkar (Maratha). Battle of Koregaon symbolic.
Anglo-Nepalese War (1814–1816 CE)
Anglo-Nepalese War 1814–1816 CE Nepal (Nalapani, Jaithak, Malaon) British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Hastings) vs. Kingdom of Nepal British aimed to curb Gurkha expansion into Awadh and Sikkim, secure trade routes. British victory. Treaty of Sugauli (1816); Nepal ceded Kumaon, Garhwal, Sikkim. David Ochterlony (British), Amar Singh Thapa, Bhimsen Thapa (Nepal). Gurkha resistance led to recruitment by British.
Anglo-Burmese Wars (1824–1885 CE)
First Anglo-Burmese War 1824–1826 CE Assam, Manipur, Arakan, Tenasserim British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Amherst) vs. Konbaung Dynasty British aimed to secure northeast frontiers against Burmese expansion. British victory. Treaty of Yandabo (1826); Burma ceded Assam, Manipur, Arakan, Tenasserim. Archibald Campbell (British), Maha Bandula (Burma). High British casualties due to disease.
Ahom Rebellion 1828 CE Assam Ahom rebels vs. British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Amherst) Ahom nobles rebelled against British rule post-First Anglo-Burmese War, aiming to restore monarchy. British victory. Rebellion suppressed; Assam fully annexed. Gomdhar Konwar (Ahom), British garrison. Early anti-colonial uprising in Northeast.
Second Anglo-Burmese War 1852–1853 CE Pegu (Lower Burma) British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Dalhousie) vs. Konbaung Dynasty British sought to annex Pegu after trade disputes and Burmese governor’s actions. British victory. Pegu annexed as Lower Burma; no formal treaty. Henry Godwin (British), Pagan Min (Burma). Provoked by Commodore Lambert.
Third Anglo-Burmese War 1885 CE Mandalay, Upper Burma British Empire (Viceroy Lord Dufferin) vs. Konbaung Dynasty British aimed to annex Upper Burma to secure trade and counter French influence. British victory. Burma fully annexed; King Thibaw exiled. Harry Prendergast (British), Thibaw Min (Burma). Swift campaign; Burma became British province.
Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–1849 CE)
First Anglo-Sikh War 1845–1846 CE Punjab (Mudki, Ferozeshah) British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Hardinge) vs. Sikh Empire British aimed to curb Sikh military power post-Ranjit Singh. British victory. Treaty of Lahore (1846); Kashmir ceded, Sikh army reduced. Hugh Gough, Henry Hardinge (British), Lal Singh, Tej Singh (Sikh). Sikh betrayal key.
Second Anglo-Sikh War 1848–1849 CE Punjab (Chilianwala, Gujrat) British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Dalhousie) vs. Sikh Empire British sought to annex Punjab after Sikh rebellion against Treaty of Lahore. British victory. Punjab annexed (1849); Duleep Singh deposed. Hugh Gough, Charles Napier (British), Sher Singh Attariwala (Sikh). Battle of Gujrat decisive.
Anglo-Afghan Wars (1839–1842 CE)
First Anglo-Afghan War 1839–1842 CE Kabul, Kandahar, Afghanistan British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Auckland) vs. Emirate of Afghanistan British aimed to install Shah Shuja to counter Russian influence (Great Game). Afghan victory. British withdrawal; Shah Shuja killed. William Elphinstone, John Keane (British), Dost Mohammad Khan, Akbar Khan (Afghan). Disastrous British retreat from Kabul.
Indian Revolt of 1857
Indian Revolt of 1857 1857–1858 CE Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi Indian rebels (sepoys, princely states) vs. British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Canning) Sepoys and princely states rebelled against British rule, triggered by greased cartridges. British victory. Mughal Empire ended; British Crown assumed direct rule (1858). Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib (rebels), Colin Campbell, Hugh Rose (British). Sieges of Delhi, Lucknow key.
Other Annexations and Conflicts (1756–1856 CE)
Battle of Plassey 1757 CE Plassey, Bengal British East India Company (Governor Robert Clive) vs. Nawab of Bengal Clive aimed to oust Siraj-ud-Daulah and install Mir Jafar to control Bengal. British victory. Mir Jafar installed; Bengal under EIC control. Robert Clive (British), Siraj-ud-Daulah, Mir Jafar (Bengal). Betrayal by Mir Jafar pivotal.
Battle of Buxar 1764 CE Buxar, Bihar British East India Company (Governor Henry Vansittart) vs. Mughal Empire, Awadh, Bengal British aimed to consolidate control over Bengal against allied Indian forces. British victory. Treaty of Allahabad (1765); EIC gained Diwani rights. Hector Munro (British), Shuja-ud-Daula (Awadh), Mir Qasim (Bengal). EIC became de facto ruler of Bengal.
Vellore Mutiny 1806 CE Vellore, Tamil Nadu Indian sepoys vs. British East India Company (Governor William Bentinck) Sepoys rebelled against British dress code changes and religious insults. British victory. Mutiny suppressed; over 100 sepoys executed. Gillesby Rollo (British), sepoy leaders. Precursor to 1857 Revolt.
Paika Rebellion 1817 CE Khordha, Odisha Paika warriors vs. British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Hastings) Paikas rebelled against British land revenue policies and loss of privileges. British victory. Rebellion crushed; leaders executed. Bakshi Jagabandhu (Paika), British garrison. Early anti-British uprising.
British Conquest of Sindh 1843 CE Sindh (Miani, Hyderabad) British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Ellenborough) vs. Talpur Amirs British aimed to annex Sindh for strategic control of Indus River. British victory. Sindh annexed; Amirs deposed. Charles Napier (British), Mir Sher Muhammad Talpur (Sindh). Napier’s controversial annexation.
Santhal Rebellion 1855–1856 CE Jharkhand, Bengal Santhal tribes vs. British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Dalhousie) Santhals rebelled against British land policies and moneylender exploitation. British victory. Rebellion suppressed; Santhal leaders executed. Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu (Santhal), British garrison. Significant tribal uprising.
Annexation of Awadh 1856 CE Lucknow, Awadh British East India Company (Governor-General Lord Dalhousie) vs. Nawab of Awadh British annexed Awadh citing misgovernance by Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. British annexation. Awadh incorporated into British India. James Outram (British), Wajid Ali Shah (Awadh). Fueled resentment, led to 1857 Revolt.
- British heads of colonial India -
Name Title Time Period Location Governed Additional Title Policies Achievements/Issues
Governors of Bengal (1757–1773 CE)
Roger Drake Governor of Bengal 1757 Bengal Presidency None Strengthened British trade and fortifications in Calcutta post-Plassey. Fled during Nawab’s attack on Calcutta (1756); criticized for mismanagement leading to Black Hole incident.
Robert Clive Governor of Bengal 1757–1760, 1765–1767 Bengal Presidency Architect of British Dominance Introduced Dual Government (1765); secured Diwani rights for EIC; reformed military and revenue systems. Victory at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) established EIC dominance; Dual Government led to exploitation, famine (1770).
Henry Vansittart Governor of Bengal 1760–1765 Bengal Presidency None Attempted to curb corruption in EIC; negotiated with Nawab Mir Qasim. Faced Bengal White Mutiny (1766); conflicts with Mir Qasim led to Battle of Buxar. Although this battle was fought in his reign, but the treaty was signed by Clive as British head in India.
Harry Verelst Governor of Bengal 1767–1769 Bengal Presidency None Focused on stabilizing Bengal post-Buxar; regulated trade. Limited reforms; Bengal Famine (1770) began during tenure, exposing EIC mismanagement.
John Cartier Governor of Bengal 1769–1772 Bengal Presidency None Attempted famine relief; maintained EIC control over Bengal. Bengal Famine (1770) worsened; criticized for inadequate response.
Governors-General of Bengal (1773–1833 CE)
Warren Hastings Governor-General of Bengal 1772–1785 Bengal Presidency (oversaw Madras, Bombay) Pioneer of British India Ended Dual Government (1772); introduced Regulating Act (1773); established revenue and judicial systems; promoted Orientalist studies. Founded Asiatic Society (1784); fought First Anglo-Maratha War (1776–82); faced impeachment for corruption (Chait Singh, Begums of Awadh affairs).
John Macpherson Governor-General of Bengal (Acting) 1785–1786 Bengal Presidency None Maintained stability; continued Hastings’ policies. Interim role; limited impact due to short tenure.
Charles Cornwallis Governor-General of Bengal 1786–1793 Bengal Presidency Father of Civil Services Introduced Permanent Settlement (1793); Cornwallis Code for judicial reforms; restructured civil services; pursued non-intervention policy. Won Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92); Permanent Settlement caused peasant distress; established Sanskrit College (1791).
John Shore Governor-General of Bengal 1793–1798 Bengal Presidency None Continued Permanent Settlement; adhered to non-intervention policy. Stable administration; criticized for inaction during Maratha-Nizam conflicts (Battle of Kharda, 1795).
Richard Wellesley Governor-General of Bengal 1798–1805 Bengal Presidency Architect of British Paramountcy Introduced Subsidiary Alliance (1798); expanded EIC territories; established Fort William College; censored press. Won Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799), Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05); annexed Tanjore, Carnatic; high costs led to recall.
Charles Cornwallis Governor-General of Bengal 1805 Bengal Presidency Father of Civil Services Planned administrative consolidation. Died shortly after arrival; minimal impact in second term.
George Barlow Governor-General of Bengal (Acting) 1805–1807 Bengal Presidency None Focused on financial retrenchment; maintained peace. Faced Vellore Mutiny (1806); criticized for weak foreign policy.
Gilbert Elliot-Murray-Kynynmound (Lord Minto I) Governor-General of Bengal 1807–1813 Bengal Presidency None Strengthened alliances with princely states; suppressed piracy; sent missions to Persia, Sindh. Annexed Amboina, Banda Islands; maintained stability; faced financial strain.
Francis Rawdon-Hastings (Lord Hastings) Governor-General of Bengal 1813–1823 Bengal Presidency None Pursued aggressive expansion; abolished press censorship; reformed education. Won Anglo-Nepalese War (1814–16), Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18); annexed Central India; Paika Rebellion (1817); financial deficits.
John Adam Governor-General of Bengal (Acting) 1823 Bengal Presidency None Maintained existing policies; interim administration. Short tenure; no major achievements or issues.
William Pitt Amherst (Lord Amherst) Governor-General of Bengal 1823–1828 Bengal Presidency None Focused on consolidating territories; pursued cautious foreign policy. Won First Anglo-Burmese War (1824–26); faced Ahom Rebellion (1828); high war costs.
William Butterworth Bayley Governor-General of Bengal (Acting) 1828 Bengal Presidency None Interim administration; continued Amherst’s policies. Short tenure; no significant impact.
Governors-General of India (1833–1858 CE)
William Bentinck Governor-General of India 1828–1835 British India Reformer of British India Abolished Sati (1829); suppressed Thugee; introduced English education (1835); financial reforms; Charter Act (1833). Promoted social reforms; English education sparked debates; reduced EIC deficits.
Charles Metcalfe Governor-General of India (Acting) 1835–1836 British India Liberator of Indian Press Removed press restrictions; continued Bentinck’s reforms. Strengthened press freedom; short tenure limited broader impact.
George Eden (Lord Auckland) Governor-General of India 1836–1842 British India None Pursued forward policy in Afghanistan; promoted education and irrigation. First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42) ended in disaster; improved canal systems.
Edward Law (Lord Ellenborough) Governor-General of India 1842–1844 British India None Annexed Sindh; reorganized military; banned slavery in India (1843). Conquest of Sindh (1843) controversial; recalled for defying EIC directors.
William Wilberforce Bird Governor-General of India (Acting) 1844 British India None Interim administration; maintained stability. Short tenure; no major policies or issues.
Henry Hardinge Governor-General of India 1844–1848 British India None Reformed education; expanded railways; pursued cautious Sikh policy. Won First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46); introduced early railway plans; faced Sikh unrest.
James Andrew Ramsay (Lord Dalhousie) Governor-General of India 1848–1856 British India Founder of Modern India Introduced Doctrine of Lapse; expanded railways, telegraphs; promoted widow remarriage; Wood’s Education Despatch (1854). Annexed Punjab, Satara, Jhansi; built railways; Doctrine of Lapse fueled 1857 Revolt.
Viceroys of India (1858–1947 CE)
Charles Canning (Lord Canning) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1856–1862 British India None Introduced Government of India Act (1858); abolished Doctrine of Lapse; passed Widow Remarriage Act (1856). Managed 1857 Revolt; established universities; criticized for leniency toward rebels. His reign is given as viceroy from 1856 just for transition, because actual viceroy post was introduced after 1857.
John Lawrence Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1864–1869 British India Savior of Punjab Strengthened Punjab administration; pursued non-intervention policy; fought Anglo-Bhutanese War. Established High Courts; faced Wahabi Movement; improved irrigation.
Richard Bourke (Lord Mayo) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1869–1872 British India None Introduced financial decentralization; established Mayo College; conducted first census (1872). Promoted education; assassinated in Andamans (1872).
Thomas Baring (Lord Northbrook) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1872–1876 British India None Focused on famine relief; pursued cautious foreign policy. Mitigated Bihar famine (1874); faced Kuka Movement in Punjab.
Robert Bulwer-Lytton (Lord Lytton) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1876–1880 British India None Introduced Vernacular Press Act (1878); Arms Act; reduced salt tax; pursued forward policy in Afghanistan. Proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India (1877); Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–80); criticized for Delhi Durbar during famine.
George Ripon (Lord Ripon) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1880–1884 British India Father of Local Self-Government Repealed Vernacular Press Act; introduced local self-government; passed Ilbert Bill (1883). Promoted liberal reforms; Ilbert Bill controversy sparked racial tensions.
Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood (Lord Dufferin) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1884–1888 British India None Strengthened northwest frontier defenses; founded Indian National Congress (1885); annexed Upper Burma. Won Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885); INC formation marked political awakening.
Henry Petty-Fitzmaurice (Lord Lansdowne) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1888–1894 British India None Passed Age of Consent Act (1891); reformed army; introduced factory legislation. Stabilized frontier; Age of Consent Act faced backlash from conservatives.
Victor Bruce (Lord Elgin) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1894–1899 British India None Focused on famine relief; maintained frontier stability. Managed plague and famine (1896–97); criticized for slow response to crises.
George Curzon (Lord Curzon) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1899–1905 British India None Partitioned Bengal (1905); created North-West Frontier Province; passed Ancient Monuments Act; reformed education and police. Improved railways, irrigation; Bengal Partition sparked nationalist unrest; resigned after Kitchener dispute.
Gilbert Elliot-Murray-Kynynmound (Lord Minto II) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1905–1910 British India None Introduced Morley-Minto Reforms (1909); promoted Muslim League; maintained law and order. Reforms expanded legislative councils; separate electorate for Muslims sowed communal tensions.
Charles Hardinge (Lord Hardinge) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1910–1916 British India None Reversed Bengal Partition (1911); shifted capital to Delhi; supported Home Rule movement. Hosted Delhi Durbar (1911); survived assassination attempt; faced Ghadar Movement.
Frederic Chelmsford (Lord Chelmsford) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1916–1921 British India None Introduced Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919); passed Rowlatt Act (1919); repressed Jallianwala Bagh protests. Reforms led to Government of India Act (1919); Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) fueled nationalism.
Rufus Isaacs (Lord Reading) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1921–1926 British India None Promoted dyarchy; suppressed Non-Cooperation Movement; certified salt tax. Stabilized administration; faced growing nationalist agitation; Chauri Chaura incident (1922).
Edward Wood (Lord Irwin) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1926–1931 British India None Negotiated Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); appointed Simon Commission; held First Round Table Conference. Pact paused Civil Disobedience; Simon Commission boycotted; faced rising nationalism.
Freeman Freeman-Thomas (Lord Willingdon) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1931–1936 British India None Repressed Civil Disobedience; passed Government of India Act (1935); separated Burma from India. Act laid federal structure; faced communal tensions; suppressed Congress activities.
Victor Hope (Lord Linlithgow) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1936–1943 British India None Implemented Government of India Act (1935); declared India’s WWII entry; repressed Quit India Movement. Faced Cripps Mission failure (1942); Bengal Famine (1943) caused millions of deaths; Quit India Movement suppressed.
Archibald Wavell (Lord Wavell) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1943–1947 British India None Held Simla Conference (1945); conducted INA trials; planned British withdrawal. INA trials fueled nationalism; Simla Conference failed; managed WWII aftermath.
Louis Mountbatten (Lord Mountbatten) Viceroy and Governor-General of India 1947 British India Architect of Indian Independence Formulated Mountbatten Plan; oversaw partition and independence; accelerated British withdrawal. Facilitated independence (1947); partition led to communal violence, mass migration.

Portuguese Administrators (1502–1961 CE)
Francisco de Almeida Viceroy of Portuguese India 1505–1509 Goa, Cochin, other Indian Ocean possessions First Viceroy of Portuguese India Established naval supremacy; promoted trade monopolies; fortified coastal settlements. Victory at Battle of Diu (1509) secured Portuguese naval dominance; faced resistance from Zamorin of Calicut.
Afonso de Albuquerque Governor and Captain-General 1509–1515 Goa, Diu, Bombay Founder of Portuguese India Conquered strategic ports; centralized administration in Goa; promoted Christianization and intermarriage. Captured Goa (1510), establishing Portuguese capital; faced internal dissent and died en route to Portugal.
Lopo Soares de Albergaria Governor of Portuguese India 1515–1518 Goa, Cochin, Diu None Strengthened fortifications; expanded trade routes; maintained naval patrols. Consolidated Goa’s defenses; faced challenges from Ottoman-backed Gujarat forces.
Garcia de Sá Governor of Portuguese India 1548–1549 Goa, Daman, Diu None Promoted trade with Southeast Asia; strengthened Goa’s administration. Short tenure; maintained stability but faced Mughal pressure on Diu.
Constantino de Bragança Viceroy of Portuguese India 1558–1561 Goa, Daman, Diu None Expanded missionary activities; fortified Daman and Diu; pursued anti-piracy campaigns. Strengthened Portuguese defenses; missionary zeal alienated local populations.
António de Noronha Viceroy of Portuguese India 1571–1573 Goa, Daman, Diu None Reformed tax collection; maintained naval supremacy; supported Jesuit missions. Stabilized finances; faced Mughal and Maratha raids on Portuguese territories.
João de Castro Viceroy of Portuguese India 1545–1548 Goa, Daman, Diu Hero of Diu Defended Diu against Gujarat; promoted trade and missionary work; reorganized administration. Victory at Second Siege of Diu (1546); died in office, leaving financial strain.
Manuel de Saldanha Viceroy of Portuguese India 1758–1765 Goa, Daman, Diu None Modernized administration; promoted trade; resisted Maratha incursions. Maintained Portuguese holdings; faced declining influence amid British rise.
José Pedro da Câmara Governor of Portuguese India 1822–1825 Goa, Daman, Diu None Introduced liberal reforms; improved local governance; maintained neutrality in regional conflicts. Stabilized administration; limited impact due to Portuguese decline in India.
José Ferreira Pestana Governor of Portuguese India 1900–1907 Goa, Daman, Diu None Modernized infrastructure; promoted education; maintained colonial status quo. Improved roads and schools in Goa; faced nationalist movements and economic stagnation.
Dutch Administrators (1605–1825 CE)
Pieter de Carpentier Governor-General of Dutch East Indies 1623–1627 Pulicat, Nagapattinam, Cochin Consolidator of Dutch Trade Expanded VOC trade networks; fortified Pulicat; negotiated treaties with local rulers. Established Pulicat as Dutch headquarters (1610); faced Portuguese and British competition.
Jan Pieterszoon Coen Governor-General of Dutch East Indies 1619–1623, 1627–1629 Pulicat, Nagapattinam Founder of Dutch Colonial Empire Established Batavia as VOC capital; monopolized spice trade; pursued aggressive military campaigns. Strengthened Dutch presence in India; brutal policies in Indonesia alienated allies.
Gerard Reynst Governor-General of Dutch East Indies 1613–1615 Pulicat, Coromandel Coast None Initiated trade posts on Coromandel Coast; negotiated with Golconda rulers. Established early Dutch foothold; died in office, limiting impact.
Adriaan van der Dussen Governor of Dutch Malabar 1663–1664 Cochin, Cannanore None Consolidated Dutch control post-Portuguese expulsion; promoted trade in pepper and textiles. Captured Cochin from Portuguese (1663); faced local resistance and British rivalry.
Rijcklof van Goens Governor of Dutch Ceylon and Malabar 1662–1663, 1670–1675 Cochin, Nagapattinam Architect of Dutch Expansion Expanded Dutch territories; fortified Cochin; pursued aggressive anti-Portuguese campaigns. Captured Nagapattinam (1658); overextension strained VOC resources.
Carel Reyniersz Governor-General of Dutch East Indies 1650–1653 Pulicat, Nagapattinam None Streamlined trade operations; maintained peace with local rulers. Stabilized Dutch trade; limited territorial gains due to Portuguese resistance.
Herman van Speult Governor of Dutch Coromandel 1618–1620 Pulicat None Established textile trade; fortified Pulicat; negotiated with Vijayanagara rulers. Laid foundation for Dutch Coromandel trade; faced Portuguese naval threats.
French Administrators (1664–1954 CE)
François Caron Director of French East India Company 1668–1672 Pondicherry, Surat Founder of French India Established Pondicherry as French base; promoted trade with Mughal Empire; fortified settlements. Founded Pondicherry (1674); faced Dutch attacks and Mughal restrictions.
François Martin Governor of French India 1674–1706 Pondicherry, Chandernagore Consolidator of French India Developed Pondicherry’s infrastructure; negotiated with local rulers; promoted Catholic missions. Transformed Pondicherry into a major port; faced Dutch siege (1693) and financial constraints.
Pierre Benoît Dumas Governor-General of French India 1735–1741 Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe None Expanded French territories; strengthened alliances with local rulers; improved fortifications. Acquired Mahe and Karaikal; maintained neutrality in European wars; faced British rivalry.
Joseph François Dupleix Governor-General of French India 1742–1754 Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe, Karaikal Architect of French Ambitions Pursued territorial expansion; allied with Indian princes; promoted French trade and military influence. Captured Madras (1746); lost influence after Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748); recalled due to high costs.
Charles Godeheu Interim Governor of French India 1754–1755 Pondicherry None Negotiated peace with British; reduced military ambitions; focused on trade. Ended Dupleix’s aggressive policies; ceded territories to British, weakening French position.
Thomas Arthur de Lally Governor-General of French India 1758–1761 Pondicherry None Pursued military campaigns against British; attempted to unify French settlements. Initial success at Buxar (1757); lost Pondicherry to British (1761); executed for failure.
Victor Hugues Governor of French India 1816–1822 Pondicherry, Chandernagore None Restored French administration post-Napoleonic Wars; promoted trade and local governance. Reestablished French presence; limited influence due to British dominance.
Henri de Bougainville Governor of French India 1908–1913 Pondicherry, Chandernagore None Modernized administration; improved education and infrastructure; maintained colonial status quo. Enhanced Pondicherry’s infrastructure; faced rising Indian nationalism.
Danish Administrators (1620–1845 CE)
Ove Gjedde Commander and Governor 1620–1621 Tranquebar Founder of Danish India Established Tranquebar as Danish colony; negotiated trade rights with Tanjore rulers. Founded Tranquebar (1620); faced logistical challenges and Portuguese competition.
Roland Crappé Governor of Tranquebar 1621–1636 Tranquebar None Developed trade in textiles and spices; fortified Tranquebar; promoted Lutheran missions. Established stable trade post; faced Dutch and Portuguese rivalry.
Bernt Pessart Governor of Tranquebar 1636–1643 Tranquebar None Expanded trade networks; maintained neutrality in regional conflicts. Strengthened Tranquebar’s economy; faced internal mismanagement issues.
Willem Leyel Governor of Tranquebar 1643–1648 Tranquebar None Reorganized administration; promoted trade with Europe; resisted Dutch encroachments. Maintained Danish presence; limited resources hampered growth.
Peter Anker Governor of Tranquebar 1788–1806 Tranquebar, Serampore None Modernized trade operations; promoted education; maintained neutrality during Napoleonic Wars. Improved Tranquebar’s infrastructure; faced British occupation during wars.
Johan Caspar Richter Governor of Serampore 1829–1836 Serampore None Promoted missionary work; improved local governance; prepared for British transition. Strengthened Serampore’s administration; overseen by British after 1836 treaty.
- British acts and regulations -
Title Time Purpose Details British Officials Involved Outcome
Constitutional Acts
Regulating Act 1773 To regulate EIC governance and curb corruption.
  • Established Governor-General of Bengal with a four-member council.
  • Required EIC to report revenue and administration to Parliament.
  • Set up Supreme Court in Calcutta for British subjects.
  • First attempt to centralize British control in India.
 Warren Hastings (Governor-General), Lord North (Prime Minister)
  • Improved parliamentary oversight of EIC activities.
  • Council disputes often paralyzed decision-making.
  • Corruption persisted, necessitating further reforms.
  • Led to Pitt’s India Act for stronger control.
Pitt’s India Act 1784 To strengthen British government control over EIC.
  • Created Board of Control to oversee EIC’s political affairs.
  • Retained Governor-General’s authority under Board supervision.
  • Separated EIC’s commercial and political functions.
  • Aimed to reduce corruption and mismanagement.
 Warren Hastings (Governor-General), William Pitt (Prime Minister)
  • Enhanced British government control over EIC.
  • Reduced EIC autonomy, aligning with imperial interests.
  • Criticized for not addressing Indian grievances.
  • Set precedent for Crown’s role in India.
Charter Act 1793 To renew EIC’s charter and refine governance.
  • Extended EIC’s trade monopoly for 20 years.
  • Increased Governor-General’s powers over presidencies.
  • Allowed limited Christian missionary activity.
  • Strengthened centralized administrative control.
 Charles Cornwallis (Governor-General), Henry Dundas (Board of Control President)
  • Consolidated EIC’s administrative framework.
  • Restricted missionary activity limited social impact.
  • Trade monopoly faced opposition from merchants.
  • Laid groundwork for future reforms.
Charter Act 1813 To open India to trade and missionaries.
  • Ended EIC’s trade monopoly except for tea and China trade.
  • Allowed unrestricted Christian missionary activity.
  • Allocated 100,000 rupees annually for Indian education.
  • Promoted British commercial and cultural influence.
 Lord Minto (Governor-General), Robert Dundas (Board of Control President)
  • Opened India to British trade, boosting commerce.
  • Missionary influx laid groundwork for cultural changes.
  • Education funding sparked Western vs. Oriental debates.
  • Strengthened British economic foothold.
Charter Act 1833 To centralize governance and promote social reforms.
  • Created Governor-General of India, replacing Bengal title.
  • Ended EIC’s commercial activities, focusing on governance.
  • Added law member to council; promoted Indian civil service entry.
  • Endorsed English education via Macaulay’s Minute.
 William Bentinck (Governor-General), Thomas Babington Macaulay (Law Member)
  • Centralized British rule across presidencies.
  • Advanced English education, shaping modern elite.
  • Limited Indian civil service access caused resentment.
  • EIC’s commercial exit shifted focus to administration.
Charter Act 1853 To reform EIC governance and civil services.
  • Extended EIC rule without fixed term.
  • Separated legislative and executive councils.
  • Introduced open competition for civil services.
  • Empowered Governor-General to annex princely states.
 Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General), Charles Wood (Board of Control President)
  • Improved legislative process and civil service access.
  • Annexation policies fueled unrest (e.g., 1857 Revolt).
  • Last EIC charter before Crown takeover.
  • Criticized for ignoring Indian representation.
Government of India Act 1858 To transfer governance from EIC to British Crown.
  • Abolished EIC rule, establishing direct Crown control.
  • Created Secretary of State for India and India Office.
  • Introduced Viceroy and Governor-General title.
  • Promised non-interference in religious practices.
 Lord Canning (Viceroy), Lord Stanley (Secretary of State)
  • Marked transition to Crown rule post-1857 Revolt.
  • Reassured princely states, stabilizing alliances.
  • Limited Indian governance role fueled nationalist demands.
  • Religious non-interference eased tensions partially.
Indian Councils Act 1861 To expand legislative participation.
  • Allowed Viceroy to nominate Indians to Legislative Council.
  • Restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras.
  • Introduced portfolio system for council members.
  • Aimed to improve governance post-1857.
 Lord Canning (Viceroy), Charles Wood (Secretary of State)
  • Increased Indian elite participation in councils.
  • Limited to non-official roles, restricting influence.
  • Strengthened provincial legislative frameworks.
  • Criticized for minimal Indian empowerment.
Indian Councils Act 1892 To enhance Indian representation in legislatures.
  • Increased non-official members in central/provincial councils.
  • Allowed indirect elections via municipalities, universities.
  • Permitted budget discussions and resolutions.
  • Addressed growing Indian political demands.
 Lord Lansdowne (Viceroy), Lord Cross (Secretary of State)
  • Introduced limited electoral process.
  • Failed to satisfy Indian National Congress demands.
  • Sparked agitation for self-governance.
  • Expanded council roles but retained British control.
Indian Councils Act (Morley-Minto Reforms) 1909 To expand Indian legislative participation and address communal concerns.
  • Increased Legislative Council size (up to 60 members).
  • Introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
  • Allowed Indians in Viceroy’s Executive Council.
  • Permitted budget debates and resolutions.
 Lord Minto (Viceroy), John Morley (Secretary of State)
  • Enabled Indian representation (e.g., Gokhale in council).
  • Separate electorates deepened communal divisions.
  • Failed to satisfy nationalists, fueling extremism.
  • Seen as divide-and-rule tactic by critics.
Government of India Act (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) 1919 To introduce limited self-governance and address nationalist demands.
  • Introduced dyarchy in provinces (transferred/reserved subjects).
  • Established bicameral central legislature.
  • Expanded electorate to 5 million voters.
  • Promised gradual dominion status.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State)
  • Allowed Indian control over education, health in provinces.
  • Disappointed nationalists, sparking Non-Cooperation Movement.
  • Dyarchy criticized for inefficiency and limited scope.
  • Expanded electorate laid groundwork for reforms.
Government of India Act 1935 To establish a federal structure and grant provincial autonomy.
  • Proposed All-India Federation with princely states.
  • Introduced provincial autonomy with elected ministries.
  • Expanded electorate to 35 million voters.
  • Retained Viceroy’s veto and reserved powers.
 Lord Willingdon (Viceroy), Samuel Hoare (Secretary of State)
  • Enabled Congress ministries in provinces (1937).
  • Federation failed due to princely state opposition.
  • Criticized for limited central Indian power.
  • Fueled demands for full independence.
Social Acts
Sati Regulation 1829 To abolish the practice of Sati.
  • Declared Sati (widow burning) illegal and punishable.
  • Applied initially to Bengal, later extended.
  • Supported by Indian reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy.
  • Aimed to eradicate a controversial custom.
 William Bentinck (Governor-General), Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Indian reformer)
  • Significantly reduced Sati practices.
  • Faced resistance from orthodox Hindus.
  • Strengthened Indian reformist movements.
  • Alienated conservatives, escalating tensions.
Widow Remarriage Act 1856 To legalize widow remarriage among Hindus.
  • Permitted Hindu widows to remarry.
  • Removed inheritance barriers for remarried widows.
  • Supported by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
  • Promoted women’s rights and social reform.
 Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General), Lord Canning (Viceroy)
  • Encouraged progressive social change.
  • Limited adoption due to social stigma.
  • Fueled orthodox resentment, aiding 1857 Revolt.
  • Strengthened reformist advocacy in India.
Age of Consent Act 1891 To raise the age of consent for girls.
  • Raised age of consent from 10 to 12 for girls.
  • Applied to married and unmarried girls across India.
  • Aimed to protect girls from early marriage/abuse.
  • Supported by reformers like Behramji Malabari.
 Lord Lansdowne (Viceroy), Andrew Scoble (Legislative Member)
  • Slightly reduced child marriages.
  • Faced opposition from conservatives (e.g., Tilak).
  • Sparked debates on British cultural interference.
  • Limited enforcement weakened impact.
Economic Acts
Permanent Settlement Act 1793 To stabilize land revenue collection.
  • Fixed land revenue in perpetuity for Bengal zamindars.
  • Made zamindars landowners responsible for taxes.
  • Applied to Bengal, Bihar, Orissa.
  • Aimed to create a loyal landlord class.
 Charles Cornwallis (Governor-General), John Shore (Revenue Advisor)
  • Ensured stable revenue for British.
  • Impoverished peasants due to high taxes.
  • Empowered zamindars, causing tenant exploitation.
  • Criticized for long-term agrarian distress.
Bengal Rent Act 1859 To regulate landlord-tenant relations in Bengal.
  • Defined tenancy rights for ryots under zamindars.
  • Limited arbitrary evictions and rent increases.
  • Applied to Bengal Presidency, addressing Permanent Settlement issues.
  • Aimed to protect tenants and stabilize agriculture.
 Lord Canning (Viceroy), James Wilson (Financial Member)
  • Improved tenant security, reducing some exploitation.
  • Implementation was weak, favoring zamindars.
  • Sparked debates on land reforms among elites.
  • Led to further tenancy laws (e.g., 1885 Act).
Factories Act 1881 To regulate working conditions in factories.
  • Limited working hours for children under 12.
  • Mandated safety measures in factories.
  • Applied to factories with 100+ workers.
  • Addressed industrial labor exploitation.
 Lord Ripon (Viceroy), Alexander Kinloch Forbes (Legislative Member)
  • Improved conditions for child laborers.
  • Limited scope due to few factories in India.
  • Weak enforcement reduced effectiveness.
  • Set precedent for future labor laws.
Factories Act 1891 To strengthen factory labor protections.
  • Extended protections to women, limiting work hours.
  • Raised minimum age for child workers to 9.
  • Applied to factories with 50+ workers, expanding scope.
  • Aimed to address growing industrial labor issues.
 Lord Lansdowne (Viceroy), Andrew Scoble (Legislative Member)
  • Improved conditions for women and child workers.
  • Still faced enforcement challenges in small factories.
  • Responded to international labor reform pressures.
  • Prompted further updates in 1911 Act.
Factories Act 1911 To further improve factory working conditions.
  • Restricted adult male work to 12 hours daily.
  • Raised child worker age to 12, banned night work.
  • Introduced mandatory rest intervals for workers.
  • Strengthened safety and inspection regulations.
 Lord Hardinge (Viceroy), Robert Carlyle (Legislative Member)
  • Enhanced worker safety and reduced exploitation.
  • Compliance varied due to limited inspectors.
  • Supported growing industrial workforce needs.
  • Led to comprehensive 1934 Act reforms.
Factories Act 1934 To modernize and expand factory labor regulations.
  • Limited work hours to 10 daily for adults, 5 for children.
  • Introduced factory licensing and regular inspections.
  • Extended protections to smaller factories (20+ workers).
  • Aligned with global labor standards (e.g., ILO).
 Lord Willingdon (Viceroy), J.P. Thompson (Legislative Member)
  • Significantly improved factory conditions.
  • Increased compliance through stricter enforcement.
  • Supported industrial growth with humane standards.
  • Criticized by some employers for raising costs.
Administrative Acts
Indian Penal Code 1860 To establish a uniform criminal law system.
  • Codified criminal offenses and punishments across India.
  • Based on Macaulay’s draft, covering murder, theft, etc.
  • Applied to all residents, replacing local laws.
  • Aimed to standardize justice under British rule.
 Lord Canning (Viceroy), Thomas Babington Macaulay (Drafter)
  • Created consistent legal framework, aiding governance.
  • Ignored customary laws, alienating some communities.
  • Remains basis of Indian criminal law today.
  • Strengthened British judicial control.
Indian Evidence Act 1872 To standardize rules of evidence in courts.
  • Defined admissible evidence, witness testimony rules.
  • Applied to all courts in British India.
  • Based on British legal principles, replacing local practices.
  • Aimed to ensure fair trials and judicial consistency.
 Lord Mayo (Viceroy), James Fitzjames Stephen (Law Member)
  • Improved judicial fairness and trial reliability.
  • Complex rules challenged local legal practitioners.
  • Strengthened British legal administration.
  • Remains influential in Indian evidence law.
Vernacular Press Act 1878 To control Indian-language newspapers.
  • Allowed magistrates to censor vernacular press.
  • Required publishers to submit content for approval.
  • Targeted nationalist publications post-1857.
  • Aimed to suppress anti-British sentiment.
 Lord Lytton (Viceroy), Alexander Arbuthnot (Council Member)
  • Curbed nationalist press temporarily.
  • Sparked protests from leaders like Surendranath Banerjee.
  • Repealed in 1882 by Lord Ripon.
  • Fueled Indian nationalism due to repression.
Ilbert Bill 1883 To allow Indian judges to try Europeans.
  • Proposed equal jurisdiction for Indian/European judges.
  • Applied to mofussil courts outside presidency towns.
  • Aimed to remove racial discrimination in judiciary.
  • Faced European opposition, leading to amendments.
 Lord Ripon (Viceroy), Courtenay Ilbert (Law Member)
  • Passed in diluted form, allowing European judge demands.
  • Exposed British racial biases in administration.
  • Galvanized Indian nationalism and reform demands.
  • Highlighted colonial inequalities.
Press Act 1910 To regulate press and curb seditious content.
  • Empowered authorities to seize seditious publications.
  • Required newspapers to deposit securities.
  • Targeted nationalist press amid revolutionary activities.
  • Aimed to control anti-British propaganda.
 Lord Minto (Viceroy), Herbert Risley (Home Secretary)
  • Suppressed nationalist publications temporarily.
  • Sparked protests from Indian journalists, elites.
  • Repealed in 1922 due to nationalist pressure.
  • Fueled anti-British sentiment and press activism.
Educational Acts
Indian Universities Act 1904 To reform and regulate university education.
  • Empowered universities to appoint professors, set curricula.
  • Introduced stricter affiliation rules for colleges.
  • Applied to universities in Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, etc.
  • Aimed to improve higher education quality post-Curzon reforms.
 Lord Curzon (Viceroy), Thomas Raleigh (Legislative Member)
  • Improved university standards and academic rigor.
  • Criticized for increasing British control over education.
  • Limited access for some colleges, causing resentment.
  • Strengthened higher education framework.
Military/Security Acts
Arms Act 1878 To restrict Indian access to firearms.
  • Prohibited Indians from possessing firearms without licenses.
  • Exempted Europeans and Eurasians from restrictions.
  • Enforced strict penalties for violations.
  • Prevented rebellions post-1857 Revolt.
 Lord Lytton (Viceroy), Alexander Arbuthnot (Council Member)
  • Reduced potential for armed uprisings.
  • Angered Indian elites and nationalists.
  • Seen as discriminatory, fueling anti-British sentiment.
  • Enforcement was uneven across regions.
Rowlatt Act 1919 To curb revolutionary activities.
  • Allowed detention without trial for suspected terrorists.
  • Restricted press and public gatherings.
  • Established special tribunals for trials.
  • Targeted post-WWI nationalist unrest.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Sydney Rowlatt (Committee Chair)
  • Sparked nationwide protests and unrest.
  • Led to Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919).
  • Unified nationalists under Gandhi’s Non-Cooperation.
  • Repealed in 1922 due to backlash.
- British reforms -
Title Time Purpose Details British Officials Involved Outcome
Administrative Reforms
Dual Government Abolition 1772 To end exploitative dual governance in Bengal.
  • Terminated Dual Government system where EIC and Nawab shared power.
  • Placed revenue and judicial administration under EIC control.
  • Aimed to streamline governance and reduce corruption.
  • Applied primarily to Bengal Presidency.
 Warren Hastings (Governor-General)
  • Centralized EIC authority in Bengal.
  • Reduced Nawab’s influence, stabilizing administration.
  • Initial mismanagement led to revenue issues.
  • Laid foundation for British administrative control.
Cornwallis Code 1793 To reform judicial and administrative systems.
  • Introduced judicial regulations for civil, criminal, and revenue cases.
  • Separated revenue and judicial functions to curb corruption.
  • Established district courts under British judges.
  • Promoted merit-based civil service recruitment.
 Charles Cornwallis (Governor-General)
  • Improved judicial fairness and administrative efficiency.
  • Excluded Indians from high posts, causing resentment.
  • Strengthened British control over local governance.
  • Set precedent for professional civil services.
Economic Reforms
Ryotwari System 1820 To reform land revenue collection in South India.
  • Assessed land revenue directly on individual ryots (peasants).
  • Applied in Madras, Bombay, and parts of Assam.
  • Aimed to eliminate intermediaries like zamindars.
  • Introduced periodic revenue settlements.
 Thomas Munro (Governor of Madras), Lord Hastings (Governor-General)
  • Increased revenue flexibility compared to Permanent Settlement.
  • High assessments burdened peasants, causing distress.
  • Empowered ryots but required extensive surveys.
  • Widely adopted in South India, shaping agrarian economy.
Mahalwari System 1833 To streamline land revenue in North India.
  • Assessed revenue on village communities (mahals).
  • Applied in North-West Provinces, Punjab, and parts of Central India.
  • Allowed collective responsibility for tax payment.
  • Aimed to balance revenue stability and local customs.
 William Bentinck (Governor-General), Holt Mackenzie (Revenue Secretary)
  • Simplified revenue collection in fragmented regions.
  • High assessments led to peasant indebtedness.
  • Maintained village autonomy but strained local economies.
  • Adopted widely in North India, complementing Ryotwari.
Social Reforms
Thugee Suppression 1830 To eradicate Thugee (banditry) practices.
  • Launched campaign to suppress Thugee gangs across India.
  • Established special courts and police units under William Sleeman.
  • Used intelligence and informers to capture Thugs.
  • Aimed to enhance public safety and British authority.
 William Bentinck (Governor-General), William Sleeman (Superintendent)
  • Arrested thousands, significantly reducing Thugee activities.
  • Strengthened British law enforcement reputation.
  • Some innocents were targeted, causing local distrust.
  • Model for later anti-crime campaigns.
Educational Reforms
Macaulay’s Minute 1835 To promote English education in India.
  • Advocated English as the medium of higher education.
  • Prioritized Western curriculum over Oriental studies.
  • Allocated Charter Act 1833 funds for English schools.
  • Aimed to create an English-educated Indian elite.
 William Bentinck (Governor-General), Thomas Babington Macaulay (Law Member)
  • Established English education, shaping modern Indian elite.
  • Neglected vernacular and Oriental education, alienating traditionalists.
  • Laid foundation for universities and colleges.
  • Sparked debates on cultural imposition vs. modernization.
Wood’s Education Despatch 1854 To establish a structured education system.
  • Proposed a network of schools, colleges, and universities.
  • Promoted vernacular primary education, English higher education.
  • Established education departments and teacher training.
  • Encouraged grants-in-aid for private schools.
 Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General), Charles Wood (Board of Control President)
  • Founded universities in Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857).
  • Expanded access to education, especially in urban areas.
  • Limited funding and focus on elites hindered mass education.
  • Known as the “Magna Carta” of Indian education.
Constitutional Reforms
Subsidiary Alliance 1798 To expand British influence over princely states.
  • Required Indian states to accept British troops for “protection.”
  • Demanded tribute or territory for military upkeep.
  • Prohibited states from foreign alliances without British approval.
  • Aimed to ensure British paramountcy.
 Richard Wellesley (Governor-General)
  • Extended British control over states like Hyderabad, Mysore.
  • Weakened Indian states’ sovereignty, causing resentment.
  • Facilitated territorial expansion via annexations.
  • Criticized as coercive, fueling anti-British sentiment.
Doctrine of Lapse 1848 To annex princely states without heirs.
  • Allowed British to annex states if rulers died without natural heirs.
  • Denied adoption rights for succession in princely states.
  • Applied to states like Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur.
  • Aimed to consolidate British territory.
 Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General)
  • Annexed key states, expanding British India.
  • Angered Indian rulers and elites, fueling 1857 Revolt.
  • Seen as culturally insensitive, ignoring adoption traditions.
  • Abandoned post-1857 to appease princely states.
Local Self-Government 1882 To introduce local governance in India.
  • Established municipal and district boards with elected members.
  • Granted boards powers over local taxes, roads, sanitation.
  • Encouraged Indian participation in local administration.
  • Aimed to foster political education and loyalty.
 Lord Ripon (Viceroy)
  • Enabled limited Indian involvement in governance.
  • Boards lacked real power, controlled by British officials.
  • Laid foundation for future decentralization.
  • Praised by nationalists but criticized for limited scope.
White Paper on Indian Constitutional Reform 1933 To outline the British government's proposals for constitutional reform based on RTC discussions.
  • Published following the three Round Table Conferences.
  • Summarized the proposed structure: All-India Federation (including Princely States), Provincial Autonomy, safeguards for minorities and British interests.
  • Detailed proposals for federal and provincial legislatures, division of powers, special powers for Governors/Governor-General.
 Samuel Hoare (Secretary of State), Lord Willingdon (Viceroy - context)
  • Formed the basis for the deliberations of a Joint Select Committee of the British Parliament.
  • Led directly to the drafting and enactment of the Government of India Act, 1935.
  • Met with criticism from both conservative British elements (too radical) and Indian nationalists (inadequate).
- British commissions and commitees -
Title Time Purpose Details British Officials Involved Outcome
Economic Commissions
Famine Commission (Campbell Commission) 1866 To investigate causes of famines and recommend relief measures.
  • Formed after Orissa Famine (1866) to study famine causes.
  • Recommended improved irrigation, railways, and relief systems.
  • Proposed permanent famine codes for administration.
  • Focused on Bengal and other famine-prone areas.
 Lord Lawrence (Viceroy), George Campbell (Chair)
  • Led to development of early famine codes.
  • Improved irrigation and transport infrastructure (limited).
  • Set precedent for future famine inquiries.
Famine Commission (Strachey Commission) 1880 To develop a comprehensive famine prevention and relief policy.
  • Formed after Great Famine (1876–78) to assess relief failures.
  • Recommended Famine Code with relief works, food distribution, suspensions of revenue.
  • Proposed agricultural reforms (irrigation) and data collection.
  • Emphasized state responsibility for relief.
 Lord Lytton (Viceroy), Richard Strachey (Chair)
  • Led to adoption of Provincial Famine Code (1883), standardizing relief.
  • Established principles of state intervention during famines.
  • Influenced subsequent famine policies significantly.
Famine Commission (Lyall Commission) 1898 To review famine codes after the famine of 1896-97.
  • Examined the working of the Strachey Commission's codes.
  • Recommended modifications in relief measures, emphasizing flexibility.
  • Suggested inclusion of non-officials in relief work, moral strategy.
  • Advocated for agricultural banks and irrigation expansion.
 Lord Elgin II (Viceroy), James Lyall (Chair)
  • Led to revisions in famine codes, emphasizing more humane approach.
  • Highlighted need for better agricultural credit.
  • Recommendations influenced future relief efforts.
Famine Commission (MacDonnell Commission) 1901 To review famine relief effectiveness after the famine of 1899-1900.
  • Re-evaluated existing famine codes and relief strategies.
  • Stressed early action, better transport, and moral strategy in relief.
  • Recommended appointment of a Famine Commissioner.
  • Emphasized development of agriculture and irrigation as preventative measures.
 Lord Curzon (Viceroy), Anthony MacDonnell (Chair)
  • Led to further refinement of famine codes and administration.
  • Increased focus on preventative measures like irrigation.
  • Considered a comprehensive review leading to improved responses.
Welby Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure) 1895-1900 To investigate the financial administration and expenditure of British India.
  • Examined the apportionment of charges between Britain and India ('Home Charges').
  • Investigated complaints about excessive military spending and 'Drain of Wealth'.
  • Heard testimonies from Indian nationalists like Dadabhai Naoroji, G.K. Gokhale.
  • Analyzed India's financial machinery.
 Lord Elgin II (Viceroy), Lord Welby (Chair)
  • Majority report largely defended existing financial arrangements.
  • Minority report (by Indian members) highlighted financial injustices.
  • Increased awareness in Britain about Indian financial grievances.
  • Limited direct impact on policy change but fueled nationalist economic critique.
Hilton Young Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance) 1926 To examine India's currency and finance system and make recommendations.
  • Studied issues related to the gold exchange standard and rupee ratio.
  • Considered the need for a central banking institution for India.
  • Recommended the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
  • Advised on stabilizing the rupee exchange rate.
 Lord Irwin (Viceroy), Edward Hilton Young (Chair)
  • Led directly to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and establishment of RBI in 1935.
  • Influenced currency policy and stabilization efforts.
  • Key step in modernizing India's financial system.
Educational Commissions
Raleigh Commission (Indian Universities Commission) 1902 To inquire into the condition and prospects of universities in India.
  • Appointed by Lord Curzon to suggest improvements in university education.
  • Recommended stricter control over university affiliation of colleges.
  • Focused on raising standards of teaching and examination.
  • Proposed reorganization of university senates and governance.
 Lord Curzon (Viceroy), Thomas Raleigh (Chair)
  • Led to the Indian Universities Act, 1904.
  • Increased government control over universities, criticized by nationalists.
  • Aimed to improve academic standards but curtailed university autonomy.
Hunter Commission (Indian Education Commission) 1882 To review progress of education since Wood’s Despatch (1854).
  • Examined primary, secondary, and higher education.
  • Recommended expansion and improvement of vernacular primary education under local bodies.
  • Proposed increased grants-in-aid for private (esp. Indian) enterprise in secondary/higher education.
  • Encouraged female education and specific arrangements for Muslim education.
 Lord Ripon (Viceroy), William Hunter (Chair)
  • Boosted primary education, transferring control to local boards.
  • Encouraged growth of private Indian schools and colleges.
  • Limited progress in female education despite recommendations.
  • Led to differentiation between government and private institutions.
Sadler Commission (Calcutta University Commission) 1917-1919 To investigate problems of Calcutta University and reform higher education.
  • Found university overloaded, recommended separating intermediate classes (creating intermediate colleges).
  • Advocated for more residential, unitary universities rather than purely affiliating ones.
  • Proposed secondary education boards and greater focus on vocational training.
  • Emphasized research, teacher training, and university autonomy.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Michael Sadler (Chair)
  • Led to establishment of several new universities (Dacca, Lucknow, etc.) on reformed lines.
  • Influenced creation of Boards of Secondary Education in provinces.
  • Shaped the structure of modern Indian university system significantly.
  • Implementation impacted by financial constraints.
Hartog Committee 1929 To survey the growth of education under dyarchy and suggest improvements.
  • Reviewed primary, secondary, higher education; part of Simon Commission's work.
  • Noted quantitative expansion but qualitative decline, esp. in primary education (wastage/stagnation).
  • Recommended consolidation and improvement of primary education over rapid expansion.
  • Suggested selective admission and better standards for secondary/higher education.
 Lord Irwin (Viceroy), Philip Hartog (Chair)
  • Highlighted problems of quality and dropout rates in primary education.
  • Led to some efforts towards consolidation but less focus on mass expansion.
  • Recommendations influenced policies but limited impact due to depression/political climate.
Social / Police Commissions
Frazer Commission (Police Commission) 1902-1903 To investigate police administration and recommend reforms.
  • Appointed by Lord Curzon; found police force inefficient, corrupt, and unpopular.
  • Recommended better pay, training, strength, and officer recruitment (separate cadres).
  • Proposed establishment of provincial Criminal Investigation Departments (CIDs).
  • Suggested a Central Intelligence Bureau (DIB).
 Lord Curzon (Viceroy), Andrew Frazer (Chair)
  • Led to reorganization and modernization of police forces across India.
  • Established CIDs and the Central Intelligence Bureau.
  • Improved police training and conditions to some extent.
