  • Strengthened state control but public distrust often persisted.
Inquiry Commissions
Hunter Commission (Disorders Inquiry Committee) 1919 To investigate the disturbances in Punjab, Delhi, Bombay (incl. Jallianwala Bagh massacre).
  • Headed by Lord Hunter; included British and Indian members.
  • Examined events leading to martial law in Punjab and the Amritsar massacre.
  • Recorded evidence, including General Dyer's testimony.
  • Produced majority (British) and minority (Indian) reports with differing conclusions.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Lord Hunter (Chair)
  • Majority report condemned Dyer's actions but found imposition of martial law justified.
  • Minority (Indian) report strongly condemned Dyer and martial law administration.
  • Led to Dyer's removal from command but no legal action; public outcry in India.
  • Deepened distrust between Indians and the British government. Congress conducted its own inquiry.
Constitutional & Administrative Commissions
Lee Commission (Royal Commission on Superior Civil Services) 1923-1924 To inquire into organisation/conditions of public services & Indianisation.
  • Examined recruitment, pay, pensions, and pace of Indianisation of superior services (ICS, IPS etc.).
  • Recommended increased rate of Indian recruitment (reaching 50% direct recruits for ICS in 15 years).
  • Advocated establishment of a Public Service Commission.
  • Suggested improved pay/conditions for British officers.
 Lord Reading (Viceroy), Lord Lee of Fareham (Chair)
  • Led to establishment of the Public Service Commission (1926).
  • Accelerated the pace of Indianisation in civil services.
  • Addressed some grievances of British officers but also faced nationalist criticism.
Muddiman Committee (Reforms Enquiry Committee) 1924 To inquire into the working of the 1919 Act (Dyarchy).
  • Assessed functioning of dyarchy in provincial governments.
  • Majority report found dyarchy workable, suggested minor adjustments.
  • Minority report (incl. Jinnah, Sapru) found dyarchy flawed and recommended fundamental changes/review.
  • Aimed partly to respond to Swarajist demands/critiques.
 Lord Reading (Viceroy), Alexander Muddiman (Chair)
  • Majority report recommendations were largely accepted but had limited impact.
  • Highlighted the deep divisions regarding the success/failure of dyarchy.
  • Minority report reflected growing demand for greater provincial autonomy.
  • Contributed to the case for further constitutional review (leading to Simon Commission).
Simon Commission (Indian Statutory Commission) 1927–1930 To review the functioning of the 1919 Act and propose further reforms.
  • All-British commission (no Indian members) to assess Indian governance.
  • Recommended abolition of dyarchy, establishment of representative govt in provinces.
  • Proposed federal structure for India but with safeguards.
  • Suggested continuation of separate electorates.
 Lord Irwin (Viceroy), Sir John Simon (Chair)
  • Widely boycotted by Indians ("Simon Go Back") due to exclusion of Indians.
  • Led to intensified nationalist agitation (e.g., Nehru Report as response, later Civil Disobedience).
  • Its report formed a basis for discussions at Round Table Conferences and influenced GOI Act 1935.
Butler Committee (Indian States Committee) 1927–1929 To investigate relationship between princely states and British paramount power.
  • Examined rights and obligations arising from treaties and paramountcy.
  • Asserted that paramountcy rested with the British Crown, not the Government of India.
  • Stated states should not be transferred without their consent to a new Indian government.
  • Aimed to clarify relationship amidst calls for federation.
 Lord Irwin (Viceroy), Sir Harcourt Butler (Chair)
  • Reaffirmed British paramountcy, disappointing states seeking more autonomy.
  • Its findings influenced discussions on princely states' role in proposed federation.
  • Did little to resolve the complexities of integrating states into a future India.
- British conferences -
Title Time Purpose Details British Officials Involved Outcome
Wartime Sessions
Chelmsford’s War Conference 1918 To secure Indian support for World War I efforts.
  • Held in Delhi to rally Indian leaders for war contributions.
  • Sought increased recruitment, financial aid, and resources.
  • Involved princely states, political leaders, and elites.
  • Aimed to strengthen British war effort amid global conflict.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State)
  • Secured significant Indian troop and financial contributions.
  • Highlighted Indian loyalty but raised reform expectations.
  • Led to Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms as a reward.
  • Nationalist dissatisfaction fueled post-war unrest.
Constitutional Conferences
First Round Table Conference 1930 To discuss constitutional reforms for India.
  • Held in London with Indian and British representatives.
  • Focused on federal structure, provincial autonomy, and safeguards.
  • Excluded Congress, which boycotted due to Simon Commission.
  • Aimed to address Simon Commission recommendations.
 Lord Irwin (Viceroy), Ramsay MacDonald (Prime Minister)
  • Agreed on federal framework and responsible government.
  • Lacked Congress participation, limiting legitimacy.
  • Paved way for Gandhi-Irwin Pact to involve Congress.
  • Highlighted communal tensions over representation.
Second Round Table Conference 1931 To continue constitutional reform discussions with broader representation.
  • Included Congress (Gandhi), Muslim League, and princely states.
  • Discussed federal structure, communal representation, safeguards.
  • Addressed minority rights and princely state integration.
  • Aimed to build consensus post-Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
 Lord Willingdon (Viceroy), Ramsay MacDonald (Prime Minister)
  • Failed to reach consensus due to communal disagreements.
  • Led to Communal Award to resolve representation issues.
  • Gandhi’s participation raised Congress’s profile.
  • Advanced discussions for Government of India Act 1935.
Third Round Table Conference 1932 To finalize constitutional reforms for India.
  • Held in London with limited Indian representation.
  • Focused on federal structure, provincial autonomy, safeguards.
  • Excluded Congress and key Muslim League leaders.
  • Aimed to draft framework for 1935 Act.
 Lord Willingdon (Viceroy), Ramsay MacDonald (Prime Minister)
  • Produced white paper for Government of India Act 1935.
  • Lacked broad Indian support, reducing impact.
  • Confirmed separate electorates, deepening communal divide.
  • Finalized key provisions for provincial autonomy.
Political Conferences
Simla Conference 1945 To form an interim government with Indian leaders.
  • Held in Simla to discuss Wavell Plan for self-governance.
  • Involved Congress, Muslim League, and other parties.
  • Proposed Viceroy’s Executive Council with Indian members.
  • Aimed to bridge Hindu-Muslim divide and advance independence.
 Lord Wavell (Viceroy), Archibald Wavell (Viceroy)
  • Failed due to Muslim League’s demand for parity with Congress.
  • Highlighted irreconcilable communal differences.
  • Paved way for Cabinet Mission as a follow-up.
  • Strengthened British push for negotiated independence.
- British plans, missions and offers -
Title Time Purpose Details British Officials Involved Outcome
Constitutional Offers
Montagu’s Declaration 1917 To promise gradual self-governance to secure Indian war support.
  • Announced “responsible government” as British policy goal.
  • Proposed increased Indian participation in governance.
  • Issued to counter nationalist unrest during World War I.
  • Led to Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms and 1919 Act.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State)
  • Raised Indian expectations for self-rule.
  • Led to Government of India Act 1919, introducing dyarchy.
  • Disappointed nationalists for limited reforms, sparking unrest.
  • Marked shift toward constitutional concessions.
August Offer 1940 To secure Indian support for World War II and address political demands.
  • Proposed dominion status as a post-war goal.
  • Offered expanded Viceroy’s Council with Indian members.
  • Promised no constitutional changes without Indian consent.
  • Aimed to counter Congress’s non-cooperation during WWII.
 Lord Linlithgow (Viceroy), Leo Amery (Secretary of State)
  • Rejected by Congress and Muslim League for vagueness.
  • Failed to secure unified Indian war support.
  • Highlighted British reluctance for immediate reforms.
  • Led to increased nationalist agitation, including Quit India.
Political Pacts
Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931 To end Civil Disobedience Movement and involve Congress in talks.
  • Agreement between Gandhi and Viceroy Irwin to halt protests.
  • British agreed to release political prisoners, lift salt tax bans.
  • Congress committed to join Second Round Table Conference.
  • Aimed to reduce tensions post-Simon Commission boycott.
 Lord Irwin (Viceroy), Mahatma Gandhi (Congress Leader)
  • Ended Civil Disobedience, enabling Congress participation in talks.
  • Prisoner releases boosted nationalist morale.
  • Limited concessions disappointed radical Congress members.
  • Facilitated Second Round Table Conference, though inconclusive.
Communal Awards
Communal Award 1932 To resolve communal representation disputes for constitutional reforms.
  • Allocated separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, others.
  • Reserved seats for depressed classes (Dalits) with separate electorates.
  • Issued after Second Round Table Conference’s failure to agree.
  • Aimed to ensure minority representation in legislatures.
 Lord Willingdon (Viceroy), Ramsay MacDonald (Prime Minister)
  • Accepted by Muslim League but opposed by Congress.
  • Gandhi’s fast led to Poona Pact, merging Dalit-Hindu electorates.
  • Reinforced communal divisions, shaping polarized politics.
  • Influenced Government of India Act 1935 provisions.
Constitutional Proposals and Missions
Cripps Mission 1942 To propose constitutional reforms and gain Indian war support.
  • Offered dominion status post-WWII with right to secede.
  • Proposed Indian-led constituent assembly for constitution.
  • Included provincial opt-out clause, enabling partition.
  • Aimed to counter Japanese threat and Congress demands.
 Lord Linlithgow (Viceroy), Stafford Cripps (Envoy)
  • Rejected by Congress for delayed independence and partition clause.
  • Muslim League opposed for not guaranteeing Pakistan.
  • Led to Quit India Movement due to nationalist frustration.
  • Introduced constituent assembly idea, influencing later plans.
Wavell Plan (Breakdown Plan) 1945 To form an interim government with Indian leaders.
  • Proposed Viceroy’s Executive Council with equal Hindu-Muslim members.
  • Aimed for Indian-led governance except for defense.
  • Discussed at Simla Conference with Congress, Muslim League.
  • Sought to bridge communal divide and prepare for independence.
 Lord Wavell (Viceroy), Archibald Wavell
  • Failed at Simla Conference due to Muslim League’s parity demands.
  • Exposed deepening Hindu-Muslim political rift.
  • Prompted Cabinet Mission as a follow-up effort.
  • Highlighted challenges of unified interim governance.
Cabinet Mission 1946 To propose a plan for Indian independence and unified government.
  • Proposed three-tier federal structure with provinces, groups, and union.
  • Offered constituent assembly to draft constitution.
  • Rejected separate Pakistan but allowed provincial autonomy.
  • Involved Congress, Muslim League, and British negotiators.
 Lord Wavell (Viceroy), Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State), Stafford Cripps
  • Initially accepted by Congress and League, but disputes arose.
  • Failed to prevent partition due to communal disagreements.
  • Formed interim government with Indian leaders (1946).
  • Laid groundwork for Indian Independence Act 1947.
Attlee’s Announcement February 1947 To commit to British withdrawal and self-government.
  • Pledged self-government by June 1948.
  • Appointed Mountbatten as Viceroy to oversee transfer.
  • Addressed princely states’ future post-British rule.
  • Aimed to pressure Indian leaders to negotiate.
 Clement Attlee (Prime Minister), Lord Wavell (Viceroy)
  • Accelerated independence talks, advancing timeline to 1947.
  • Led to Mountbatten Plan and partition agreement.
  • Raised partition inevitability, fueling communal tensions.
  • Signaled British intent to exit, prioritizing swift withdrawal.
Balkan Plan (Dickie Bird/Ismay Plan) May 1947 To propose a fragmented partition of India.
  • Proposed provinces as independent successor states.
  • Allowed provinces, princely states to choose India, Pakistan, or independence.
  • Developed as alternative to Cabinet Mission’s unity plan.
  • Presented to provincial governors in April 1947.
 Lord Mountbatten (Viceroy), Hastings Ismay, George Abell
  • Rejected by Nehru for risking Balkanization of India.
  • Prompted V.P. Menon’s two-nation plan.
  • Influenced Mountbatten Plan’s final partition framework.
  • Criticized for potential to destabilize subcontinent.
V.P. Menon Plan May–June 1947 To propose a two-nation partition as an alternative to Balkan Plan.
  • Proposed partition into India and Pakistan with dominion status.
  • Developed by V.P. Menon, adopted by Mountbatten.
  • Addressed Nehru’s concerns about Balkanization.
  • Formed basis for Mountbatten Plan (June 3 Plan).
 Lord Mountbatten (Viceroy), V.P. Menon (Reforms Commissioner)
  • Accepted as foundation for Mountbatten Plan.
  • Enabled partition and independence in August 1947.
  • Reduced fragmentation risks but fueled communal violence.
  • Shaped Indian Independence Act 1947.
Mountbatten Plan (June 3 Plan) June 1947 To outline partition and independence of India and Pakistan.
  • Proposed partition into India and Pakistan by August 1947.
  • Allowed provinces, princely states to choose dominion.
  • Established Boundary Commission under Cyril Radcliffe.
  • Built on V.P. Menon’s plan, replacing Balkan Plan.
 Lord Mountbatten (Viceroy), Clement Attlee (Prime Minister)
  • Accepted by Congress and Muslim League, enabling partition.
  • Led to Indian Independence Act 1947 and two dominions.
  • Triggered mass migration and communal violence.
  • Marked end of British colonial rule in India.
- British reports and recommendations -
Title Time Purpose Details British Officials Involved Outcome
Key British Reports, Despatches, and Policy Documents Concerning India
Rowlatt Committee Report (Sedition Committee Report) 1918 To investigate 'revolutionary conspiracies' and recommend legislation to deal with them.
  • Chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt, reviewed political terrorism and sedition in India.
  • Assessed links between activities in India and abroad (e.g., Ghadar movement).
  • Recommended extending wartime emergency measures (Defence of India Act 1915) into peacetime.
  • Proposed special powers like detention without trial, juryless trials for specific offenses.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Sir Sidney Rowlatt (Chair)
  • Led directly to the enactment of the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919 (infamously known as the Rowlatt Acts).
  • Granted government extensive powers to suppress dissent, overriding civil liberties.
  • Sparked widespread outrage and protests across India -> Rowlatt Satyagraha led by Gandhi.
  • Contributed significantly to the events leading up to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
Montagu-Chelmsford Report (Report on Indian Constitutional Reforms) 1918 To propose constitutional reforms towards responsible government in India.
  • Outlined principles based on Montagu's 1917 Declaration.
  • Proposed system of 'Dyarchy' in provinces (dividing subjects into Transferred - under Indian ministers, and Reserved - under Governor).
  • Recommended a bicameral legislature at the Centre with expanded representation but limited powers.
  • Suggested gradual increase in self-governing institutions.
  • Advocated for direct elections (though on a limited franchise).
 Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State), Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy)
  • Formed the direct basis for the Government of India Act, 1919.
  • Introduced partial responsible government in provinces but was deemed inadequate by most nationalists ("too little, too late").
  • The reforms were criticized for complexity and limitations, contributing to post-war nationalist movements.
Simon Commission Report 1930 To report on the working of the 1919 Act and suggest further constitutional reforms.
  • Published in two volumes after extensive (though boycotted) tour of India.
  • Recommended abolition of dyarchy and establishment of full responsible government in provinces.
  • Advocated for a federal structure involving British India and potentially Princely States.
  • Recommended continuation of separate electorates and retention of significant powers by the Governor/Governor-General.
  • Did not recommend Dominion Status immediately.
 Sir John Simon (Chair), Lord Irwin (Viceroy - context)
  • The Commission itself was boycotted by major Indian parties due to its all-British composition.
  • The Report's recommendations were seen as conservative by nationalists.
  • It became the basis for discussion at the Round Table Conferences (1930-32).
  • Significantly influenced the framework of the Government of India Act, 1935.
- British important treaties and pacts -
Title Time Purpose Details Key Parties / Signatories Involved Outcome
Treaties with Indian States
Treaty of Allahabad 1765 To settle terms after the Battle of Buxar.
  • Signed between Robert Clive and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, and separately with Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.
  • Granted the Diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the East India Company.
  • Shah Alam II received Allahabad and Kora, resided under Company protection.
  • Awadh paid war indemnity, Allahabad/Kora ceded, but remained a buffer state.
 Robert Clive (EIC), Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor), Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh)
  • Legitimized EIC's control over vast revenues, establishing its financial and political power in Eastern India.
  • Marked the beginning of the Dual Government system in Bengal.
  • Established British influence over the Mughal Emperor.
Treaty of Salbai 1782 To end the First Anglo-Maratha War.
  • Signed between the British EIC (represented by Warren Hastings) and the Maratha Confederacy (represented by Mahadji Scindia).
  • Restored territories conquered since the Treaty of Purandar (1776) to their respective owners.
  • British recognized Madhavrao II as Peshwa; Marathas recognized British possession of Salsette.
  • British agreed not to support Raghunathrao (claimant to Peshwa).
 Warren Hastings (EIC - represented by David Anderson), Mahadji Scindia (Maratha representative)
  • Established peace between the British and Marathas for about 20 years.
  • Increased Mahadji Scindia's influence among Maratha chiefs.
  • Allowed the British to focus on conflicts elsewhere (e.g., Mysore).
Treaty of Bassein 1802 To establish a Subsidiary Alliance between the British EIC and the Maratha Peshwa.
  • Signed by Peshwa Baji Rao II seeking British protection after defeat by Holkar.
  • Peshwa accepted Subsidiary Alliance terms: maintain British troops, cede territory for their upkeep, surrender foreign policy control.
  • Agreed not to employ Europeans hostile to the British.
 Peshwa Baji Rao II, Lord Wellesley (EIC Governor-General - represented locally)
  • Severely undermined Peshwa's authority and Maratha independence.
  • Directly led to the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805) as other Maratha chiefs (Scindia, Bhonsle) resisted the treaty.
  • Marked a significant step in British ascendancy over the Marathas.
Treaty of Amritsar 1809 To define spheres of influence between the British EIC and the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh.
  • Signed between Charles T. Metcalfe (British envoy) and Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
  • Fixed the Sutlej River as the boundary between the Sikh Empire and British territories/protected states.
  • British recognized Ranjit Singh's sovereignty north of the Sutlej.
  • Both parties agreed to mutual non-interference across the river.
 Charles T. Metcalfe (EIC), Maharaja Ranjit Singh (Sikh Empire)
  • Prevented immediate conflict between the British and the Sikh Empire.
  • Allowed Ranjit Singh to consolidate his power north of the Sutlej.
  • Checked Ranjit Singh's ambitions towards Cis-Sutlej states, bringing them under British protection.
  • Maintained stability on the North-West frontier for several decades.
Treaty of Lahore 1846 To end the First Anglo-Sikh War.
  • Signed after British victory over the Sikh army.
  • Sikhs ceded Jullundur Doab (territory between Beas and Sutlej) to the British.
  • Large war indemnity imposed; Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh to meet part of it.
  • Sikh army size limited; British resident appointed at Lahore.
 Sir Henry Hardinge (Governor-General), Maharaja Duleep Singh (represented by Lahore Durbar chiefs)
  • Marked significant weakening of the Sikh Empire.
  • Established strong British influence/control over the Lahore Durbar.
  • Led to further instability and ultimately the Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) and annexation of Punjab.
Inter-European Agreements Concerning India/Asia
Anglo-Dutch Treaty 1824 To resolve territorial and commercial disputes between Britain and the Netherlands in Asia.
  • Defined spheres of influence: Dutch dominance in Indonesian archipelago, British dominance in India/Malaya peninsula.
  • Territorial exchanges: British ceded Bencoolen (Sumatra) to Dutch; Dutch ceded Malacca and possessions in India to British.
  • Regulated trade and navigation rights.
 Representatives of Great Britain, Representatives of the Netherlands
  • Consolidated British control over the Indian mainland and Malacca Straits.
  • Confirmed Dutch control over Indonesia.
  • Reduced Anglo-Dutch friction in the region for a period.
Agreements During the Nationalist Movement
Gandhi-Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact) 1931 (March 5) To suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) and facilitate Congress participation in the Second Round Table Conference (RTC2).
  • Signed between Mahatma Gandhi (on behalf of Congress) and Lord Irwin (Viceroy).
  • British agreed to withdraw ordinances, release political prisoners (not charged with violence).
  • Congress agreed to suspend CDM and participate in RTC2.
  • Allowed peaceful picketing and salt manufacturing for personal use.
 Mahatma Gandhi (INC), Lord Irwin (Viceroy of India)
  • Provided a temporary truce; CDM suspended.
  • Enabled Gandhi's participation in RTC2 in London.
  • Seen by some nationalists as a compromise; raised Congress prestige internationally.
  • Failed to achieve lasting resolution; CDM resumed later.
Poona Pact 1932 (September 24) To resolve the issue of separate electorates for Depressed Classes granted by the British Communal Award.
  • Agreement between Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (representing Depressed Classes) and Madan Mohan Malaviya (representing upper-caste Hindus, following Gandhi's fast unto death).
  • Abandoned separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
  • Instead, reserved nearly double the number of seats (147) for Depressed Classes within the general Hindu electorate in provincial legislatures (compared to 71 under Communal Award).
  • Also ensured representation in Central Legislature.
 Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Madan Mohan Malaviya (Accepted by British Government)
  • Ended Gandhi's fast; averted direct separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
  • Significantly increased reserved seats for Depressed Classes in legislatures.
  • Accepted by the British government as modification to the Communal Award.
  • Remained a point of debate regarding effective representation.
- Important systems in modern India related to economy, polity, administration, etc -
System Time Period Location/Region Purpose Core Features & Details Key Figures & Roles Outcome
Economic Systems
Revenue Farming (Ijaradari) 1765–1793 Bengal, Bihar To maximize short-term revenue collection via intermediaries.
  • Revenue collection rights auctioned to ijaradars for fixed sums.
  • Ijaradars extracted revenue from peasants, often excessively.
  • Short-term contracts prioritized British profits over stability.
  • Precursor to Permanent Settlement, used post-Diwani grant.
 Robert Clive (acquired Diwani, 1765), Warren Hastings (expanded system), Ijaradars (collaborators)
  • Increased British revenue but destabilized rural economy.
  • Exploited peasants, causing famines (e.g., Bengal 1770).
  • Replaced by Permanent Settlement due to inefficiencies.
  • Highlighted early colonial exploitation.
Permanent Settlement 1793–1947 Bengal, Bihar, parts of Odisha To stabilize land revenue and create loyal landlord class.
  • Fixed land revenue permanently, paid by zamindars.
  • Zamindars became hereditary landlords, collecting from peasants.
  • High revenue demand, often 10/11th of rental income.
  • Aimed to incentivize agricultural improvement.
 Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General, introduced), John Shore (revenue expert), Zamindars (collaborators)
  • Created powerful zamindar class, loyal to British.
  • Impoverished peasants via high rents, evictions.
  • Failed to improve agriculture, causing land sales.
  • Persisted until Zamindari Abolition Acts post-1947.
Ryotwari System 1820–1947 Madras, Bombay, parts of Assam To collect revenue directly from cultivators, maximizing income.
  • Peasants (ryots) paid revenue directly to British.
  • Revenue assessed on land quality, revised periodically.
  • Eliminated intermediaries like zamindars.
  • Encouraged peasant proprietorship but with high rates.
 Thomas Munro (introduced in Madras), Alexander Read (early proponent), Lord Elphinstone (expanded in Bombay)
  • Increased British revenue but burdened peasants.
  • Encouraged smallholder farming, unlike zamindari.
  • High assessments led to debt, land loss.
  • Shaped land tenure in South India until 1947.
Mahalwari System 1822–1947 North-West Provinces, Punjab, Central India To collect revenue through village communities, balancing efficiency and tradition.
  • Revenue assessed on village estates (mahals), not individuals.
  • Village leaders or co-sharers responsible for payment.
  • Revenue periodically revised, based on land productivity.
  • Blended zamindari and ryotwari principles.
 Holt Mackenzie (introduced), Lord William Bentinck (expanded), Village headmen (collaborators)
  • Preserved village structures but increased revenue pressure.
  • Caused peasant indebtedness, land transfers.
  • Strengthened British control over North India.
  • Persisted until post-1947 land reforms.
Drain of Wealth 1757–1947 Pan-India To extract economic surplus for British benefit.
  • Transferred wealth via high taxes, trade imbalances.
  • Exported raw materials (e.g., cotton) to Britain, imported finished goods.
  • Home charges (e.g., pensions, debt interest) drained resources.
  • Enforced via revenue systems, trade monopolies.
 Robert Clive (initiated post-Plassey), Dadabhai Naoroji (critic, theorized drain), East India Company (enforcer)
  • Impoverished India, enriching British economy.
  • Fueled nationalist critique (e.g., Naoroji’s “Poverty and Un-British Rule”).
  • Contributed to famines, rural distress.
  • Persisted until independence, shaping economic critique.
Trade Policy 1757–1947 Pan-India, ports (e.g., Calcutta, Bombay) To prioritize British economic interests via trade control.
  • EIC monopoly (pre-1833) controlled exports (e.g., opium, textiles).
  • Free trade post-1833 favored British manufactures.
  • High tariffs on Indian goods, low on British imports.
  • Developed ports, railways to extract resources.
 Warren Hastings (EIC monopoly), Lord Curzon (trade expansion), Indian merchants (affected)
  • Deindustrialized India (e.g., textile decline).
  • Created export economy (e.g., opium to China).
  • Enriched Britain, impoverished Indian artisans.
  • Galvanized Swadeshi Movement post-1905.
Railway Policy 1853–1947 Pan-India (e.g., Bombay-Calcutta, Delhi-Madras) To facilitate trade, military movement, and administration.
  • Private British companies built railways with guaranteed returns.
  • Connected ports to hinterlands for resource extraction.
  • State took over unprofitable lines post-1900.
  • Prioritized colonial needs over Indian mobility.
 Lord Dalhousie (initiated policy), James Andrew (railway engineer), British investors (funders)
  • Built 40,000+ miles of track by 1947.
  • Boosted British trade, military control.
  • High costs drained Indian revenue.
  • Facilitated nationalist mobilization via connectivity.
Administrative Systems
Cornwallis Code 1793–1857 Bengal, later pan-India To establish standardized judicial and administrative governance.
  • Separated revenue and judicial roles to reduce corruption.
  • Introduced British-style courts, civil service rules.
  • Excluded Indians from high administrative posts.
  • Codified land revenue under Permanent Settlement.
 Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General, introduced), John Shore (advisor), District collectors (enforcers)
  • Created centralized British administration.
  • Alienated Indian elites via exclusion.
  • Improved judicial efficiency but ignored local customs.
  • Laid foundation for colonial bureaucracy.
Civil Service System 1853–1947 Pan-India To professionalize administration with loyal British officials.
  • Indian Civil Service (ICS) recruited via competitive exams in London.
  • ICS officers (mostly British) managed districts, provinces.
  • Limited Indian entry until 1920s reforms.
  • Ensured British control over key decisions.
 Lord Macaulay (shaped ICS exams), Lord Curzon (reformed), Satyendranath Tagore (early Indian ICS)
  • Created efficient but elitist bureaucracy.
  • Excluded Indians, fueling nationalist demands.
  • Indianization post-1919 increased Indian ICS officers.
  • Persisted as IAS model post-1947.
Police System 1861–1947 Pan-India, urban and rural To maintain colonial law and order, suppress dissent.
  • Centralized police under Police Act 1861.
  • British officers led, Indian constables enforced.
  • Focused on protecting British interests, quelling protests.
  • Reformed post-1902 (Frazer Commission) for efficiency.
 Lord Canning (introduced Act), Andrew Frazer (reformed), Indian constables (enforcers)
  • Ensured British control over unrest (e.g., 1857, Quit India).
  • Alienated Indians due to brutality, corruption.
  • Strengthened via 1902 reforms but remained unpopular.
  • Formed basis for modern Indian police post-1947.
Political Systems
Subsidiary Alliance 1798–1857 Princely states (e.g., Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh) To secure control over princely states without direct annexation.
  • States maintained British troops, paid subsidies.
  • British resident controlled foreign policy, disputes.
  • Prevented alliances with other powers (e.g., Marathas).
  • Weakened states’ autonomy, preserving nominal rulers.
 Lord Wellesley (introduced), Tipu Sultan (resisted), Nizam of Hyderabad (adopter)
  • Expanded British influence over 100+ states.
  • Enabled annexations (e.g., Awadh 1856).
  • Resentment fueled 1857 Revolt.
  • Shaped paramountcy until 1947.
Doctrine of Lapse 1848–1856 Princely states (e.g., Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur) To annex states without heirs, consolidating territory.
  • Denied adoption of heirs, annexing states.
  • Targeted weak or disputed successions.
  • Justified as enforcing British legal norms.
  • Applied selectively for territorial gains.
 Lord Dalhousie (introduced), Rani Lakshmibai (resisted), Nana Saheb (affected)
  • Annexed 7 states (e.g., Jhansi 1853).
  • Contributed to 1857 Revolt.
  • Discontinued post-1857 to appease states.
  • Increased British control pre-1857.
Dyarchy 1919–1935 Provinces (e.g., Bengal, Madras, Bombay) To introduce limited self-governance while retaining British control.
  • Divided provincial subjects into transferred (Indian ministers) and reserved (British governors).
  • Transferred subjects included education, agriculture.
  • Reserved subjects included finance, police.
  • Based on Government of India Act 1919.
 Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State), Indian ministers (e.g., C.R. Das)
  • Introduced limited Indian participation.
  • Frustrated nationalists due to restricted powers.
  • Led to Non-Cooperation Movement.
  • Evolved into Provincial Autonomy post-1935.
Provincial Autonomy 1935–1947 Provinces (e.g., Punjab, United Provinces) To grant greater self-governance while retaining central control.
  • Provinces gained legislative, financial autonomy.
  • Governors retained veto, emergency powers.
  • Based on Government of India Act 1935.
  • Elected Indian ministries governed provinces.
 Lord Linlithgow (Viceroy), Samuel Hoare (Secretary of State), Congress ministries (e.g., Nehru, Patel)
  • Enabled Congress, Muslim League governance (1937–39).
  • Strengthened Indian political experience.
  • Limited by British veto, communal tensions.
  • Paved way for independence framework.
Educational Systems
Western Education System 1835–1947 Pan-India, urban centers (e.g., Calcutta, Bombay) To create a class of English-educated Indians for administration.
  • Promoted English as medium via Macaulay’s Minute (1835).
  • Established universities (e.g., Calcutta, 1857), colleges.
  • Wood’s Despatch (1854) expanded schools, grants-in-aid.
  • Neglected vernacular, mass education.
 Lord Macaulay (authored Minute), Charles Wood (Despatch), Raja Rammohan Roy (supported)
  • Created educated Indian elite, fueling nationalism.
  • Limited access, reaching <10% of population.
  • Marginalized traditional education systems.
  • Shaped modern Indian education post-1947.
Military Systems
Military Recruitment System 1858–1947 Pan-India, esp. Punjab, United Provinces To ensure loyal, effective army post-1857 Revolt.
  • Recruited from “martial races” (e.g., Sikhs, Gurkhas).
  • Reduced Bengal Army, increased British officers.
  • Used Indian troops for colonial wars (e.g., WWI, WWII).
  • Offered land grants, pensions to ensure loyalty.
 Lord Canning (post-1857 reforms), Lord Kitchener (reorganized), Indian sepoys (recruits)
  • Created loyal army, suppressing unrest (e.g., 1857).
  • Exploited Indian soldiers for global wars.
  • Nationalist infiltration (e.g., INA) by 1940s.
  • Formed basis for Indian Army post-1947.
- Important british revolts, movements, satyagrahas, dacouties, raids, conspiracies, bombings, massacres, etc -
Title Period Location Key Figures (Led by) Details British Reaction (Governor-General/Viceroy) Ending and Outcome
Revolts
Chuar Rebellion 1767–1833 Jungle Mahals, Bengal Jagannath Singh Patar, Durjan Singh
  • Tribal uprising against high revenue demands.
  • Targeted zamindars, British agents.
  • Multiple phases, peaked in 1798–1799.
  • Aimed to restore tribal autonomy.
  • Deployed military to suppress rebels.
  • Offered revenue concessions post-1798.
  • Strengthened police control.
  • Governor-General: Warren Hastings (early), Lord Cornwallis (later).
  • Suppressed by 1833, leaders killed.
  • Limited revenue reforms granted.
  • Inspired later tribal revolts.
  • Highlighted rural exploitation.
Paika Rebellion 1817 Khordha, Odisha Bakshi Jagabandhu
  • Resisted British land revenue policies.
  • Paika warriors attacked British posts.
  • Opposed loss of hereditary privileges.
  • Supported by local zamindars.
  • Military suppression, captured leaders.
  • Restored some Paika privileges.
  • Reinforced revenue systems.
  • Governor-General: Lord Hastings.
  • Suppressed in 1817, Jagabandhu surrendered.
  • Minor land reforms introduced.
  • Recognized as first independence war by Odisha.
  • Inspired regional resistance.
Bhil Revolt 1818–1847 Khandesh, Maharashtra Sewaram, Bhagoji Naik
  • Triggered by British occupation, land loss.
  • Bhils resisted forest right restrictions.
  • Multiple phases (1825, 1831, 1847).
  • Used guerrilla tactics against British.
  • Military suppression, built forts.
  • Conceded forest rights post-1818.
  • Recruited Bhils into hill police.
  • Governor-General: Lord Hastings (1818), Lord Dalhousie (1847).
  • Suppressed by 1847, leaders captured.
  • Partial restoration of forest rights.
  • Strengthened British control.
  • Inspired later Bhil movements.
Kol Uprising 1831–1832 Chotanagpur, Bihar Buddho Bhagat
  • Kols resisted land alienation to outsiders.
  • Opposed high taxes, bonded labor.
  • Attacked moneylenders, zamindars.
  • Joined by Mundas, Oraons.
  • Military campaign to crush rebels.
  • Reinforced revenue systems.
  • Arrested leaders, restored order.
  • Governor-General: Lord William Bentinck.
  • Suppressed in 1832, Buddho killed.
  • Limited land reforms introduced.
  • Increased British tribal control.
  • Legacy of tribal resistance.
Santhal Uprising 1855–1856 Rajmahal Hills, Bengal Sidhu Murmu, Kanhu Murmu
  • Resisted land alienation, high taxes.
  • Attacked moneylenders, British agents.
  • Mobilized 10,000 Santhals for revolt.
  • Aimed to expel “Dikus” (outsiders).
  • Deployed troops, killed ~20,000 Santhals.
  • Created Santhal Parganas district.
  • Arrested leaders, imposed martial law.
  • Governor-General: Lord Dalhousie.
  • Suppressed in 1856, leaders executed.
  • Santhal Parganas formed for governance.
  • Inspired later tribal movements.
  • Celebrated as “Santhal Hul” today.
Indian Rebellion of 1857 1857–1858 North, Central India (Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow) Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Saheb
  • Triggered by Enfield rifle cartridge issue.
  • Sepoy mutiny spread to civilian revolt.
  • Aimed to restore Mughal rule, end EIC.
  • Major centers: Delhi, Kanpur, Jhansi.
  • Military campaign, recaptured Delhi.
  • Harsh reprisals, mass executions.
  • Ended EIC rule, introduced Crown rule.
  • Governor-General: Lord Canning.
  • Suppressed by June 1858, peace by 1859.
  • Government of India Act 1858 enacted.
  • Bahadur Shah exiled, leaders killed.
  • Galvanized nationalist sentiments.
Kuka Revolt 1871–1872 Punjab Ram Singh
  • Namdhari Sikhs opposed British policies.
  • Attacked butcher shops, British posts.
  • Advocated Swadeshi, cow protection.
  • Aimed for Sikh revival, independence.
  • Arrested Ram Singh, exiled to Burma.
  • Executed 65 Kukas without trial.
  • Banned Namdhari gatherings.
  • Viceroy: Lord Mayo.
  • Suppressed in 1872, leaders exiled.
  • Weakened Kuka movement.
  • Inspired Sikh nationalism.
  • Highlighted British brutality.
Moplah Rebellion 1921–1922 Malabar, Kerala Variamkunnath Kunjahammed Haji
  • Muslim peasants resisted landlords, British.
  • Triggered by Khilafat Movement, land issues.
  • Attacked police stations, zamindars.
  • Had communal overtones against Hindus.
  • Imposed martial law, deployed troops.
  • Arrested leaders, killed 2,000+.
  • Wagon Tragedy killed 67 prisoners.
  • Viceroy: Lord Reading.
  • Suppressed in 1922, Haji killed.
  • Exacerbated Hindu-Muslim tensions.
  • Led to land reforms in Malabar.
  • Criticized for communal violence.
Movements
Aligarh Movement 1875–1898 Aligarh, United Provinces Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
  • Promoted Muslim education, modernization.
  • Founded Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College.
  • Advocated loyalty to British rule.
  • Countered Congress’s nationalist agenda.
  • Supported as pro-British initiative.
  • Granted funds for Aligarh College.
  • Encouraged Muslim separatism.
  • Viceroy: Lord Lytton (early), Lord Dufferin (later).
  • Evolved into Aligarh Muslim University (1920).
  • Strengthened Muslim identity, education.
  • Laid groundwork for Muslim League.
  • Criticized for divisive politics.
Swadeshi Movement 1905–1908 Bengal, pan-India Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal
  • Protested Bengal Partition (1905).
  • Promoted Indian goods, boycotted British.
  • Involved students, urban classes.
  • Combined moderate, extremist tactics.
  • Arrested leaders, banned meetings.
  • Reversed Bengal Partition (1911).
  • Repressed extremist publications.
  • Viceroy: Lord Curzon (start), Lord Minto II.
  • Declined by 1908, partition reversed.
  • Boosted Indian industry, nationalism.
  • Strengthened Congress’s mass base.
  • Inspired later boycott movements.
Non-Cooperation Movement 1920–1922 Pan-India Mahatma Gandhi
  • Protested Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh.
  • Boycotted British goods, institutions.
  • Promoted Khadi, self-reliance.
  • Supported Khilafat Movement.
  • Arrested leaders, banned Congress rallies.
  • Used force against protests.
  • Negotiated minor concessions.
  • Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford (start), Lord Reading.
  • Withdrawn in 1922 post-Chauri Chaura.
  • Mobilized millions, rural India.
  • Strengthened Congress organization.
  • Led to Civil Disobedience Movement.
Civil Disobedience Movement 1930–1934 Pan-India Mahatma Gandhi
  • Expanded Salt Satyagraha to broader defiance.
  • Boycotted British goods, institutions.
  • Included tax refusal, picketing.
  • Supported by women, youth.
  • Arrested 100,000+, banned Congress.
  • Used force, seized assets.
  • Negotiated Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Round Table talks.
  • Viceroy: Lord Irwin (start), Lord Willingdon.
  • Withdrawn in 1934, partial reforms.
  • Gained global sympathy, nationalist unity.
  • Led to Government of India Act 1935.
  • Strengthened Congress organization.
Quit India Movement 1942 Pan-India Mahatma Gandhi, Congress leaders
  • Demanded immediate British withdrawal.
  • “Do or Die” call, mass protests.
  • Included strikes, sabotage, underground.
  • Rejected Cripps Mission proposals.
  • Arrested Gandhi, Congress leaders.
  • Suppressed protests, killed 10,000+.
  • Banned Congress, censored media.
  • Viceroy: Lord Linlithgow.
  • Suppressed by 1943, leaders jailed.
  • Showed mass resolve for independence.
  • Weakened British morale, war effort.
  • Accelerated independence talks.
Tebhaga Peasant Movement 1946–1947 Bengal Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha
  • Demanded 2/3rd crop share for sharecroppers.
  • Opposed landlord exploitation.
  • Led by communist-aligned peasants.
  • Spread across North Bengal districts.
  • Deployed police to suppress protests.
  • Arrested leaders, banned rallies.
  • Negotiated partial reforms.
  • Viceroy: Lord Wavell.
  • Ended with independence in 1947.
  • Limited land reforms introduced.
  • Strengthened communist influence.
  • Inspired post-1947 peasant struggles.
Satyagrahas/Campaigns
Champaran Satyagraha 1917 Champaran, Bihar Mahatma Gandhi
  • Protested forced indigo cultivation.
  • Peasants demanded fair treatment.
  • Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India.
  • Used non-violent resistance.
  • Formed Champaran Agrarian Committee.
  • Allowed Gandhi to investigate.
  • Passed Champaran Agrarian Act.
  • Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford.
  • Ended in 1917, reforms granted.
  • Abolished forced indigo system.
  • Boosted Gandhi’s prominence.
  • Inspired future satyagrahas.
Kheda Satyagraha 1918 Kheda, Gujarat Mahatma Gandhi, Vallabhbhai Patel
  • Protested high taxes during famine.
  • Peasants refused revenue payment.
  • Non-violent resistance, boycotts.
  • Supported by local leaders.
  • Negotiated with peasant leaders.
  • Suspended tax collection for two years.
  • Arrested some activists.
  • Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford.
  • Ended in 1918, taxes suspended.
  • Strengthened Congress’s rural base.
  • Enhanced Patel’s leadership role.
  • Proved efficacy of satyagraha.
Rowlatt Satyagraha 1919 Pan-India, esp. Punjab Mahatma Gandhi
  • Opposed Rowlatt Act’s repressive laws.
  • Nationwide hartal, protests called.
  • Non-violent civil disobedience.
  • Triggered Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
  • Imposed martial law in Punjab.
  • Arrested leaders, banned gatherings.
  • Ordered Jallianwala Bagh firing.
  • Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford.
  • Suspended post-massacre, 1919.
  • Rowlatt Act repealed in 1922.
  • Galvanized anti-British sentiment.
  • Led to Non-Cooperation Movement.
Salt Satyagraha 1930 Dandi, Gujarat, pan-India Mahatma Gandhi, Sarojini Naidu
  • Protested British salt monopoly.
  • Gandhi led Dandi Salt March.
  • Mass civil disobedience, salt-making.
  • Attracted global attention.
  • Arrested Gandhi, 60,000+ Indians.
  • Suppressed protests, raided saltworks.
  • Negotiated Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
  • Viceroy: Lord Irwin.
  • Ended with Gandhi-Irwin Pact, 1931.
  • Released prisoners, relaxed salt laws.
  • Boosted Congress’s mass appeal.
  • Strengthened independence movement.
Individual Satyagraha 1940–1941 Pan-India Mahatma Gandhi, Vinoba Bhave, Nehru
  • Protested British war policies.
  • Individuals offered symbolic resistance.
  • Demanded free speech, independence.
  • Rejected August Offer of 1940.
  • Arrested satyagrahis, banned protests.
  • Downplayed movement’s impact.
  • Maintained war-time control.
  • Viceroy: Lord Linlithgow.
  • Ended in 1941, limited impact.
  • Kept nationalist spirit alive.
  • Paved way for Quit India Movement.
  • Highlighted free speech issues.
Mutinies
Vellore Mutiny 1806 Vellore, Madras Presidency Sepoys (no single leader)
  • Triggered by new uniform regulations.
  • Sepoys attacked British officers.
  • Killed 130 British soldiers.
  • Aimed to resist cultural interference.
  • Swift military suppression.
  • Executed 100+ sepoys, punished others.
  • Withdrew uniform regulations.
  • Governor-General: Lord Minto.
  • Suppressed within days, 1806.
  • Restored order, reforms withdrawn.
  • Highlighted sepoy discontent.
  • Precursor to 1857 Revolt.
Great Revolt 1857 1857–1858 North, Central India (Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow) Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope
  • Sepoy mutinies sparked by Enfield rifle cartridges.
  • Mutinies spread to civilian revolt against EIC rule.
  • Aimed to restore Mughal authority, end British control.
  • Major centers included Delhi, Jhansi, Kanpur.
  • Deployed military, recaptured Delhi, Lucknow.
  • Harsh reprisals, mass executions of rebels.
  • Ended EIC rule, introduced Crown rule (1858).
  • Governor-General: Lord Canning.
  • Suppressed by June 1858, peace by 1859.
  • Bahadur Shah exiled, leaders killed or fled.
  • Government of India Act 1858 enacted.
  • Galvanized nationalist sentiments.
Air Force and Army Signals Mutinies January 1946 to Early February 1946 Bombay, Karachi, Madras, Delhi Indian airmen, signal corps (no single leader)
  • Protested poor conditions, racial discrimination.
  • Strikes in Royal Indian Air Force, Army Signals units.
  • Inspired by Royal Indian Navy Mutiny.
  • Demanded better pay, national independence.
  • Negotiated with strikers, promised reforms.
  • Arrested key agitators, court-martialed.
  • Downplayed as labor unrest, suppressed media.
  • Viceroy: Lord Wavell.
  • Ended in February 1946, strikes subsided.
  • Minor concessions on pay, conditions.
  • Highlighted military unrest, nationalist fervor.
  • Contributed to independence momentum.
Royal Indian Navy Mutiny Mid-February 1946 Bombay, Karachi, other ports B.C. Dutt, naval ratings
  • Naval ratings protested poor conditions.
  • Seized ships, raised nationalist flags.
  • Supported by Congress, League.
  • Spread to 78 ships, 20,000 sailors.
  • Deployed troops, negotiated surrender.
  • Arrested leaders, court-martialed.
  • Downplayed as labor dispute.
  • Viceroy: Lord Wavell.
  • Ended with trials, 1946.
  • Released most mutineers under pressure.
  • Accelerated independence talks.
  • Showed military unrest.
Bombings/Conspiracies
Alipore Bomb Case 1908 Manicktolla, Calcutta Khudiram Bose, Prafulla Chaki
  • Attempted to assassinate Douglas Kingsford.
  • Bomb killed two British women.
  • Part of Yugantar group’s activities.
  • Aimed to inspire revolutionary zeal.
  • Arrested conspirators, raided hideouts.
  • Convicted Aurobindo Ghosh, others.
  • Imposed press censorship.
  • Viceroy: Lord Minto II.
  • Khudiram executed, Chaki suicided, 1908.
  • Suppressed Yugantar activities.
  • Inspired further revolutionary acts.
  • Highlighted militant nationalism.
Nasik Conspiracy 1909 Nasik, Bombay Presidency Anant Kanhere, Vinayak Savarkar
  • Assassinated British official A.M.T. Jackson.
  • Planned by Abhinav Bharat Society.
  • Aimed to destabilize British rule.
  • Used arms smuggling, propaganda.
  • Arrested conspirators, executed Kanhere.
  • Banned revolutionary literature.
  • Imprisoned Savarkar for life.
  • Viceroy: Lord Minto II.
  • Suppressed in 1910, leaders convicted.
  • Weakened Abhinav Bharat.
  • Inspired youth radicalization.
  • Strengthened British surveillance.
Delhi Conspiracy 1912 Delhi Rashbehari Bose, Basant Kumar Biswas
  • Attempted to assassinate Viceroy Hardinge.
  • Bomb thrown at Hardinge’s procession.
  • Planned by revolutionary groups.
  • Aimed to strike fear in British.
  • Arrested conspirators, executed Biswas.
  • Increased police surveillance.
  • Banned revolutionary organizations.
  • Viceroy: Lord Hardinge.
  • Suppressed in 1914, leaders convicted.
  • Hardinge survived, tightened security.
  • Fueled revolutionary momentum.
  • Led to Ghadar Movement.
Lahore Conspiracy 1915 Punjab, United Provinces Rashbehari Bose, Sachindra Sanyal
  • Planned military mutiny during WWI.
  • Ghadar Movement coordinated uprisings.
  • Aimed to overthrow British rule.
  • Involved sepoys, revolutionaries.
  • Infiltrated plot, arrested leaders.
  • Executed 42 conspirators.
  • Imposed Defence of India Act.
  • Viceroy: Lord Hardinge.
  • Thwarted in 1915, leaders executed.
  • Weakened Ghadar Movement.
  • Inspired later conspiracies.
  • Strengthened British repression.
Kakori Conspiracy 1925 Kakori, United Provinces Ramprasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan
  • Robbed train to fund HRA activities.
  • Hindustan Republican Association planned.
  • Aimed to finance arms, propaganda.
  • Killed one passenger accidentally.
  • Arrested 40+ conspirators.
  • Executed Bismil, Khan, others.
  • Banned HRA activities.
  • Viceroy: Lord Reading.
  • Suppressed in 1927, leaders executed.
  • Weakened HRA, inspired HSRA.
  • Galvanized youth nationalism.
  • Publicized revolutionary cause.
Dacoities/Raids
Barrah Dacoity 1918 Barrah, Bengal Jatindranath Mukherjee
  • Robbed British funds for arms.
  • Part of Jugantar group’s activities.
  • Used guerrilla tactics, local support.
  • Aimed to finance revolutionary acts.
  • Deployed police, arrested suspects.
  • Increased surveillance in Bengal.
  • Banned Jugantar publications.
  • Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford.
  • Suppressed in 1918, leaders jailed.
  • Limited revolutionary funding.
  • Inspired further dacoities.
  • Highlighted militant resistance.
Chittagong Armoury Raid 1930 Chittagong, Bengal Surya Sen
  • Raided British armouries, police stations.
  • Indian Republican Army planned attack.
  • Aimed to seize arms, disrupt rule.
  • Proclaimed “Provisional Government”.
  • Deployed troops, hunted revolutionaries.
  • Arrested Sen, executed in 1934.
  • Imposed martial law in Bengal.
  • Viceroy: Lord Irwin.
  • Suppressed by 1933, Sen executed.
  • Inspired youth, women (e.g., Pritilata).
  • Weakened revolutionary groups.
  • Symbolized militant defiance.
Massacres
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre 1919 Amritsar, Punjab General Reginald Dyer (British)
  • Fired on unarmed crowd protesting Rowlatt Act.
  • Killed 379–1,000, injured 1,200+.
  • Trapped crowd in enclosed garden.
  • Part of Rowlatt Satyagraha fallout.
  • Formed Hunter Commission to investigate.
  • Dyer relieved of command, not prosecuted.
  • Defended by British conservatives.
  • Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford.
  • Ended April 13, 1919, massacre condemned.
  • Galvanized nationalist movement.
  • Led to Non-Cooperation Movement.
  • Exposed British brutality.

    • Edited Bengalee (1879–1925).

    - Important artistic works in modern India -
    Work Time Language/Region Category/Subcategory Author Description & Key Details
    Novels
    Durgesh Nandini 1865 Bengali/Bengal Novel/Historical Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
    • First major Bengali novel, set during Mughal era.
    • Blends romance, adventure, and patriotism.
    • Inspired Bengal Renaissance and nationalist literature.
    • Popularized historical fiction in India.
    Anand Math 1882 Bengali/Bengal Novel/Patriotic Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
    • Depicts Sannyasi Rebellion (1770s), promoting nationalism.
    • Contains *Vande Mataram*, adopted as nationalist anthem.
    • Influenced Swadeshi Movement (1905–1911).
    • Banned briefly by British for seditious content.
    Debi Chaudhurani 1884 Bengali/Bengal Novel/Social Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
    • Portrays a woman’s transformation into a revolutionary leader.
    • Addresses women’s empowerment and patriotism.
    • Reflects Bengal’s socio-cultural awakening.
    • Influenced feminist themes in Indian literature.
    Chandrakanta 1888 Hindi/North India Novel/Fantasy Devaki Nandan Khatri
    • First major Hindi prose novel, a fantasy-adventure.
    • Popularized Hindi literature among masses.
    • Influenced modern Hindi storytelling.
    • Adapted into films and TV series later.
    Newspapers
    Shome Prakash 1858 Bengali/Bengal Newspaper/Reformist Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
    • Advocated social reforms (widow remarriage, education).
    • First Bengali newspaper to focus on social issues.
    • Influenced Bengal Renaissance.
    • Published weekly, widely read by intellectuals.
    Rast Goftar 1851 Gujarati/Bombay Newspaper/Reformist Dadabhai Naoroji
    • Voice of Parsi community, promoted social reforms.
    • Critiqued British policies, supported nationalism.
    • Published in Gujarati and English.
    • Precursor to Indian National Congress’s ideology.
    The Hindu 1878 English/Madras Newspaper/Nationalist G. Subramania Iyer
    • Advocated moderate nationalism, Indian rights.
    • Influenced South Indian political discourse.
    • Oldest English daily still in circulation.
    • Critiqued British policies on education, economy.
    Maratha 1881 English/Maharashtra Newspaper/Nationalist Bal Gangadhar Tilak
    • Promoted Swadeshi, criticized British policies.
    • Companion to Kesari, aimed at English readers.
    • Fueled nationalist sentiment in Maharashtra.
    • Targeted educated elite for political awakening.
    Bande Mataram 1906 English/Bengal Newspaper/Revolutionary Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh (Editor)
    • Advocated complete independence, Swadeshi.
    • Banned by British in 1908 for seditious content.
    • Inspired revolutionary youth.
    • Key voice of extremist faction in Congress.
    Indian Sociologist 1905 English/London Newspaper/Revolutionary Shyamji Krishna Varma
    • Published from London, advocated armed resistance.
    • Voice of India House, inspired revolutionaries.
    • Banned in India by British.
    • Circulated among Indian diaspora.
    The Talwar 1909 English/Paris Newspaper/Revolutionary Madam Bhikaji Cama
    • Published abroad, called for overthrow of British rule.
    • Distributed among Indian diaspora, revolutionaries.
    • Linked to Paris Indian Society.
    • Promoted anti-colonial propaganda.
    Al-Hilal 1912 Urdu/Bengal Newspaper/Nationalist Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
    • Promoted Hindu-Muslim unity, Khilafat Movement.
    • Banned by British in 1914 for anti-colonial stance.
    • Influenced Muslim political awakening.
    • Reached wide Urdu-speaking audience.
    New India 1915 English/Madras Newspaper/Nationalist Annie Besant
    • Advocated Home Rule, Indian self-governance.
    • Popularized Home Rule League’s agenda.
    • Suppressed by British during World War I.
    • Influenced South Indian nationalism.
    Commonwealth 1916 English/Madras Newspaper/Nationalist Annie Besant
    • Supported Home Rule, constitutional reforms.
    • Companion to New India, targeted elite readers.
    • Influenced South Indian nationalism.
    • Promoted dialogue on self-governance.
    Navjivan 1919 Gujarati/India Newspaper/Nationalist Mahatma Gandhi
    • Promoted non-violence, Swadeshi, and satyagraha.
    • Published from Ahmedabad, linked to Sabarmati Ashram.
    • Key platform for Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922).
    • Translated into Hindi, English for wider reach.
    Books (Non-fiction)
    Drain of Wealth 1867 English/Bombay Book/Economic Dadabhai Naoroji
    • Introduced “Drain of Wealth” theory, critiquing British exploitation.
    • Foundation for Indian economic nationalism.
    • Influenced Congress’s economic critiques.
    • Presented as evidence in British Parliament.
    Bahubivah 1873 Bengali/Bengal Book/Social Reform Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
    • Critiqued polygamy, advocated women’s rights.
    • Supported Widow Remarriage Act (1856).
    • Influenced Bengal’s social reform movement.
    • Written as a polemical treatise.
    Vital-Vidhvansak 1870 Marathi/Maharashtra Book/Social Reform Jyotiba Phule
    • Critiqued caste system, Brahmin dominance.
    • First major Marathi text on caste reform.
    • Inspired Satyashodhak Samaj’s ideology.
    • Targeted lower-caste empowerment.
    Nibandhamala 1874 Marathi/Maharashtra Book/Essays Vishnushastri Chiplunkar
    • Series of essays critiquing British rule, promoting nationalism.
    • Published in *Nibandhmala* journal (1874–1881).
    • Inspired Marathi literary renaissance.
    • Advocated cultural pride, education reform.
    Economic History of India 1901 English/Bengal Book/Economic Romesh Chunder Dutt
    • Analyzed British economic policies’ impact on India.
    • Highlighted famines, deindustrialization.
    • Key text for nationalist economic arguments.
    • Used as reference by Congress leaders.
    Desher Katha 1910 Bengali/Bengal Book/Nationalist Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar
    • Advocated Swadeshi, critiqued British exploitation.
    • Popular among Bengal revolutionaries.
    • Influenced youth during Partition of Bengal (1905).
    • Written in accessible Bengali prose.
    Hind Swaraj 1909 Gujarati/India Book/Political Mahatma Gandhi
    • Advocated Swaraj, non-violence, and self-reliance.
    • Written during voyage from London to South Africa.
    • Banned by British, inspired Civil Disobedience (1930).
    • Linked to Sabarmati Ashram’s ideology.
    Gita Rahasya 1915 Marathi/Maharashtra Book/Philosophical Bal Gangadhar Tilak
    • Interpretation of Bhagavad Gita, emphasizing action (Karma Yoga).
    • Written in Mandalay jail, inspired nationalists.
    • Linked to Swadeshi Movement’s ideology.
    • Translated into multiple languages.
    My Experiments with Truth 1927 Gujarati/India Book/Memoir Mahatma Gandhi
    • Autobiography detailing Gandhi’s life and philosophy.
    • Published in *Navjivan*, serialized 1925–1929.
    • Inspired global non-violent movements.
    • Key source for Gandhian principles.
    A Nation in Making 1925 English/Bengal Book/Memoir Surendranath Banerjee
    • Chronicles early nationalism, Congress’s formation.
    • Reflects moderate nationalist perspective.
    • Key source for UPSC history syllabus.
    • Details Indian National Association’s role.
    The Indian Struggle 1934 English/India Book/History Subhas Chandra Bose
    • Documents freedom struggle (1920–1934).
    • Critiques British rule, advocates militant nationalism.
    • Banned by British, published abroad.
    • Highlights INA’s early ideology.
    Discovery of India 1946 English/India Book/History Jawaharlal Nehru
    • Written in Ahmednagar Fort jail during Quit India.
    • Traces India’s history, culture, and nationalist aspirations.
    • Key text for understanding Indian identity.
    • Influenced post-independence vision.
    Poems/Songs
    Amar Sonar Bangla 1905 Bengali/Bengal Poem/Patriotic Rabindranath Tagore
    • Written during Bengal Partition, inspired Swadeshi.
    • Adopted as Bangladesh’s national anthem (1971).
    • Reflects Bengal’s cultural nationalism.
    • Linked to Tagore’s knighthood renunciation (1919).
    Subh-e Azadi 1947 Urdu/Punjab Poem/Reflective Faiz Ahmed Faiz
    • Reflects on Partition’s cost, incomplete freedom.
    • Published at independence, critiques communal strife.
    • Key Urdu poem of Modern India.
    • Resonates with partition’s trauma.
    Songs from Prison 1932 English/India Poem/Political Mahatma Gandhi (Translated)
    • Collection of poems written during imprisonment.
    • Reflects Gandhian philosophy, non-violence.
    • Inspired satyagrahis during Civil Disobedience.
    • Published in multiple languages.
    Plays
    Nil-Darpan 1860 Bengali/Bengal Play/Social Dinabandhu Mitra
    • Depicts exploitation of indigo farmers by British planters.
    • Sparked Indigo Revolt (1859–1860).
    • Banned by British, first major anti-colonial play.
    • Performed widely in Bengal.
    Shatranj ke Khilari 1924 Hindi/North India Play/Satirical Premchand
    • Satirizes decadence of Awadh nawabs under British influence.
    • Critiques colonialism’s cultural impact.
    • Adapted into a film by Satyajit Ray (1977).
    • Reflects social realism.
    Films
    Pundalik 1912 Marathi/Maharashtra Film/Silent Dadasaheb Torne
    • First Indian feature film, based on a saint’s life.
    • Marked the beginning of Indian cinema.
    • Screened in Bombay, limited distribution.
    • Precursor to mythological genre.
    Raja Harishchandra 1913 Marathi/Maharashtra Film/Silent Dadasaheb Phalke
    • First full-length Indian feature film, mythological theme.
    • Established Phalke as “Father of Indian Cinema.”
    • Promoted cultural nationalism via cinema.
    • Screened widely, set industry standard.
    Hatimtai 1929 Hindi/Bombay Film/Silent P.N. Charatkar
    • Adventure film based on Persian folklore.
    • Popularized stunt genre in silent era.
    • Reflected growing Indian film industry.
    • Attracted diverse audiences.
    Alam Ara 1931 Hindi/Bombay Film/Talkie Ardeshir Irani
    • First Indian talkie (sound film), a romantic drama.
    • Introduced playback singing in Indian cinema.
    • Blockbuster, marked shift to sound era.
    • Set template for Bollywood musicals.
    Jhansi ki Rani 1953 Hindi/Bombay Film/Historical Sohrab Modi
    • First Indian Technicolor film, depicts Rani Lakshmibai’s rebellion (1857).
    • Promoted nationalist pride post-independence.
    • Technological milestone in Indian cinema.
    • Revived 1857 legacy for modern audiences.
    Post-1947 Works
    My Dear Kuttichathan 1984 Malayalam/Kerala Film/Fantasy Jijo Punnoose
    • First Indian 3D film, a children’s fantasy.
    • Technological breakthrough in Indian cinema.
    • Popular in South India, dubbed in multiple languages.
    • Marked regional cinema’s innovation.
    Taal 1999 Hindi/Bombay Film/Musical Subhash Ghai
    • Musical drama, blending traditional and modern themes.
    • Known for A.R. Rahman’s iconic soundtrack.
    • Globalized Bollywood, screened at international festivals.
    • Reflected India’s cultural transition in the 1990s.

    Indian National Congress Nationalist Party A.O. Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji, G.K. Gokhale, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel
    PhaseTimeframeKey LeadersKey EventsSplits/Notes
    Moderate1885–1905Dadabhai Naoroji, G.K. Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, M.G. Ranade, Pherozeshah MehtaPetitions, annual sessions, demand for Swaraj, Indian Councils Act 1892Gokhale rejected knighthood (1910)
    Extremist1905–1920Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo GhoshSwadeshi Movement (1905), Boycott, Home Rule League (1916)Surat Split 1907 (Moderates vs. Extremists); Tilak rejected knighthood
    Gandhian1920–1947Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel, Maulana Azad, Subhas Chandra BoseNon-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930, Sabarmati start), Quit India (1942)Bose resigned 1939, formed Forward Bloc
    • Founded 1885, Bombay, by A.O. Hume to promote Indian representation.
    • Timeline: 1885 (founding), 1907 (Surat Split), 1920 (Non-Cooperation), 1930 (Dandi Salt March), 1942 (Quit India), 1947 (independence).
    • Evolved from elite platform to mass movement under Gandhi.
    • Led India to independence (1947).
    • Launched major movements: Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India.
    • Negotiated with British (Round Table Conferences, 1930–1932).
    • Influenced global non-violent struggles (e.g., Martin Luther King Jr.).
    All India Muslim League Communal Party Aga Khan III, Nawab Salimullah, Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Liaquat Ali Khan, Muhammad Iqbal
    PhaseTimeframeKey LeadersKey EventsSplits/Notes
    Early1906–1930Aga Khan III, Nawab Salimullah, Viqar-ul-MulkLoyalist stance, secured separate electorates (1909)Aligned with Congress in Lucknow Pact (1916)
    Nationalist1930–1940Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Muhammad IqbalJinnah’s return (1934), poor 1937 election performanceIqbal’s Two-Nation Theory (1930)
    Separatist1940–1947Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Liaquat Ali KhanLahore Resolution (1940), Direct Action Day (1946), Pakistan demandDominant in 1946 elections
    • Founded 1906, Dhaka, to protect Muslim political interests.
    • Timeline: 1906 (founding), 1916 (Lucknow Pact), 1940 (Lahore Resolution), 1947 (Pakistan).
    • London branch (1908–1913) advocated Muslim rights abroad.
    • Achieved Pakistan (1947) under Jinnah’s leadership.
    • Shaped Partition through Two-Nation Theory.
    • Influenced communal politics, Muslim representation.
    • Criticized for escalating communal tensions (e.g., Direct Action Day).
    Swaraj Party Nationalist Party Chittaranjan Das, Motilal Nehru, Vithalbhai Patel
    PhaseTimeframeKey LeadersKey EventsSplits/Notes
    Pro-Changer1923–1926C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, Vithalbhai PatelContested 1923 elections, disrupted councilsOpposed by no-changers (Gandhians)
    Decline1926–1930Motilal NehruWeakened after Das’s death (1925)Reintegrated into Congress
    • Founded 1923 within Congress to contest elections.
    • Aimed to obstruct legislative councils from within.
    • Supported Swaraj (self-rule) demand.
    • Won seats in 1923 elections, exposed council flaws.
    • Internal split: Pro-changers vs. no-changers.
    • Reintegrated into Congress by 1930, influenced Nehru Report (1928).
    Forward Bloc Revolutionary Party Subhas Chandra Bose, Sardul Singh Caveeshar
    PhaseTimeframeKey LeadersKey EventsSplits/Notes
    Early1939–1941Subhas Chandra BoseFormed after Bose’s Congress exit, anti-British protestsBanned by British
    INA Phase1942–1945Subhas Chandra Bose, Rash Behari BoseLinked to Indian National Army, fought in WWIIOperated from Southeast Asia
    • Founded 1939 by Bose after resigning from Congress.
    • Aimed for immediate independence via militant means.
    • Timeline: 1939 (founding), 1942 (INA formation), 1945 (INA trials).
    • INA trials (1945) galvanized nationalist sentiment.
    • Weakened after Bose’s death (1945).
    • Influenced post-independence socialist politics.
    Communist Party of India Socialist Party M.N. Roy, S.A. Dange, P.C. Joshi
    PhaseTimeframeKey LeadersKey EventsSplits/Notes
    Early1925–1942M.N. Roy, S.A. DangeOrganized labor strikes, Kanpur Bolshevik Case (1924)Banned until 1942
    Post-Legalization1942–1947P.C. Joshi, B.T. RanadiveSupported Quit India peripherally, peasant movementsInternal ideological debates
    • Founded 1925, Kanpur, to promote socialism and anti-colonialism.
    • Timeline: 1925 (founding), 1942 (legalized), 1946 (Telangana Rebellion).
    • Focused on labor and peasant struggles.
    • Strengthened labor movements (e.g., Bombay textile strikes).
    • Influenced peasant uprisings (e.g., Telangana 1946).
    • Limited electoral success pre-1947.
    Congress Socialist Party Socialist Party Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Minoo Masani
    • Founded 1934 within Congress to promote socialism.
    • Aimed to combine Gandhian nationalism with socialist ideals.
    • Timeline: 1934 (founding), 1936 (Lucknow session), 1942 (Quit India).
    • Criticized Congress’s right-wing policies.
    • Influenced Congress’s socialist resolutions (e.g., Karachi 1931).
    • Key role in Quit India Movement.
    • Formed Socialist Party (1948) post-independence.
    Hindustan Socialist Republican Association Revolutionary Party Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad, Sukhdev Thapar
    • Founded 1928, Delhi, for armed revolution against British rule.
    • Evolved from Hindustan Republican Association (1924).
    • Timeline: 1928 (founding), 1929 (Lahore Conspiracy), 1931 (Bhagat Singh’s execution).
    • Promoted socialist and anti-imperialist ideals.
    • Lahore Conspiracy Case (1929) inspired youth.
    • Bhagat Singh’s execution (1931) galvanized nationalism.
    • Suppressed by British, limited long-term impact.
    Home Rule League Nationalist Party Annie Besant, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, G.S. Khaparde
    • Founded 1916 by Besant (All India) and Tilak (Maharashtra) for self-governance.
    • Timeline: 1916 (founding), 1917 (Besant’s arrest), 1918 (merged with Congress).
    • Modeled on Irish Home Rule, used newspapers (*New India*).
    • Attracted educated middle class.
    • Popularized self-rule demand, influenced Lucknow Pact (1916).
    • Besant’s arrest (1917) sparked protests.
    • Merged with Congress post-1918, weakened after Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
    All India Liberal Federation Liberal Party Tej Bahadur Sapru, M.R. Jayakar
    • Founded 1919 to advocate constitutional reforms within British framework.
    • Timeline: 1919 (founding), 1921 (supported Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms).
    • Represented moderate elites, opposed mass movements.
    • Influenced Round Table Conferences (1930–1932).
    • Limited mass support, overshadowed by Congress.
    • Contributed to Government of India Act 1935 debates.
    Radical Democratic Party Liberal Party M.N. Roy
    • Founded 1940 by M.N. Roy after leaving communism.
    • Promoted radical humanism, opposed fascism and imperialism.
    • Timeline: 1940 (founding), 1944 (supported war effort).
    • Limited political impact due to small base.
    • Influenced intellectual debates on humanism.
    • Dissolved post-1947, Roy focused on philosophy.
    Socialist Party Socialist Party Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia
    • Founded 1948, evolved from Congress Socialist Party.
    • Advocated democratic socialism, land reforms.
    • Timeline: 1948 (founding), 1949 (opposed Congress policies).
    • Influenced socialist policies in early independent India.
    • Limited electoral success, merged into Praja Socialist Party (1952).
    All India Scheduled Castes Federation Liberal Party (with Social Justice orientation) B.R. Ambedkar
    • Founded 1942 to represent Dalit interests.
    • Demanded political rights, social equality.
    • Opposed Congress’s caste policies.
    • Influenced Poona Pact (1932), reserved seats.
    • Limited electoral success, merged into RPI (1956).
    • Strengthened Dalit political identity.
    Independent Labour Party Socialist Party B.R. Ambedkar
    • Founded 1936 to advocate for workers, Dalits.
    • Focused on labor rights, caste equality.
    • Contested 1937 elections.
    • Won seats in Bombay (1937).
    • Influenced labor and Dalit policies.
    • Merged into Scheduled Castes Federation (1942).
    Post-1947 Political Parties
    Bhartiya Jana Sangh Right-Wing Party Syama Prasad Mookerjee, Deendayal Upadhyaya
    • Founded 1951 to promote Hindu nationalism, cultural unity.
    • Opposed Congress’s secular policies.
    • Precursor to BJP, gained traction in North India.
    • Limited electoral success until 1977 (Janata coalition).
    Swatantra Party Right-Wing Party C. Rajagopalachari, Minoo Masani
    • Founded 1959 to advocate free-market policies, limited government.
    • Opposed Congress’s socialist policies.
    • Third-largest party in 1967 elections.
    • Declined post-1971, merged with Janata Party.
    Congress for Democracy Nationalist Party Jagjivan Ram, Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna
    • Founded 1977 to oppose Indira Gandhi’s Emergency policies.
    • Supported democratic restoration.
    • Merged with Janata Party, contributed to 1977 election victory.
    • Short-lived, dissolved post-1977.
