    Social Reform
    Arya Samaj Social Reform Dayananda Saraswati, Lala Lajpat Rai
    • Founded 1875, Bombay, to revive Vedic principles.
    • Opposed idol worship, caste system, child marriage.
    • Promoted women’s education, widow remarriage.
    • Established gurukuls for Vedic learning.
    • Founded DAV schools/colleges, educated thousands.
    • Shuddhi movement reconverted Muslims/Christians to Hinduism.
    • Influenced Hindu nationalism, social reforms.
    • Active in Swadeshi Movement.
    Brahmo Samaj Social Reform Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Debendranath Tagore, Keshab Chandra Sen
    • Founded 1828, Calcutta, for monotheistic Hindu reform.
    • Opposed sati, idol worship, caste system.
    • Promoted education, women’s rights.
    • Contributed to Sati abolition (1829).
    • Established Brahmo schools, influenced Bengal Renaissance.
    • Split into factions (1866, 1878), weakened impact.
    Satya Shodhak Samaj Social Reform Jyotiba Phule, Savitribai Phule
    • Founded 1873, Pune, to uplift lower castes, women.
    • Opposed Brahmin dominance, caste system.
    • Promoted education for Shudras, women.
    • Opened schools for girls, lower castes.
    • Influenced non-Brahmin movement in Maharashtra.
    • Laid groundwork for Dalit upliftment.
    Indian Reform Association Social Reform Keshab Chandra Sen
    • Founded 1870, Calcutta, to promote social reforms.
    • Focused on women’s education, widow remarriage.
    • Linked to Brahmo Samaj’s progressive wing.
    • Supported Widow Remarriage Act (1856).
    • Established schools, women’s organizations.
    • Limited impact due to Brahmo splits.
    Sarvodaya Samaj Social Reform Mahatma Gandhi, Vinoba Bhave
    • Founded 1920s, inspired by Gandhi’s upliftment philosophy.
    • Promoted village self-reliance, non-violence.
    • Active in rural development, education.
    • Influenced Bhoodan Movement (post-1947).
    • Supported Gandhian constructive programs.
    • Limited formal structure pre-1947.
    Revolutionary Groups
    Ghadar Revolutionary Group Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, Kartar Singh Sarabha
    • Founded 1913, USA, for armed revolution against British.
    • Published *Ghadar* newspaper, mobilized diaspora.
    • Planned mutiny among Indian soldiers.
    • Launched Ghadar Mutiny (1915), inspired revolutionaries.
    • Suppressed by British, leaders executed.
    • Influenced later revolutionary groups.
    Anushilan Samiti Revolutionary Group Barindra Ghosh, Aurobindo Ghosh, Prafulla Chaki
    • Founded 1902, Calcutta, for armed resistance.
    • Organized assassinations, arms collection.
    • Linked to Swadeshi Movement.
    • Alipore Bomb Case (1908) exposed activities.
    • Inspired Bengal revolutionaries, youth.
    • Suppressed by British, weakened post-1910.
    Jugantar Revolutionary Group Bagha Jatin, Surendranath Tagore
    • Founded 1906, Bengal, as Anushilan offshoot.
    • Focused on bombings, arms smuggling.
    • Published *Jugantar* newspaper.
    • Attempted German arms plot (1915).
    • Suppressed after Bagha Jatin’s death (1915).
    • Inspired revolutionary nationalism.
    Free Indian Legion Revolutionary Group Subhas Chandra Bose, A.C.N. Nambiar
    • Founded 1942, Germany, to fight British with Axis support.
    • Recruited Indian POWs, aimed to invade India.
    • Linked to INA under Bose.
    • Limited combat role, merged with INA (1943).
    • INA trials (1945) sparked nationalist upsurge.
    • Symbolized anti-colonial resistance.
    Committees
    Radcliffe Committee Committee Cyril Radcliffe
    • Formed 1947 to demarcate India-Pakistan boundary.
    • Operated under Partition Plan, tight deadline.
    • Included British and Indian members.
    • Created Radcliffe Line, defined Partition borders.
    • Criticized for rushed, arbitrary divisions.
    • Contributed to Partition violence, displacement.
    Butler Committee Committee Sir Harcourt Butler
    • Formed 1927 to examine princely states’ relations with British.
    • Aimed to clarify paramountcy, state autonomy.
    • Recommended maintaining princely state autonomy.
    • Influenced Government of India Act 1935.
    • Limited impact on nationalist movement.
    Khilafat Committee Committee Maulana Mohammad Ali, Shaukat Ali, Maulana Azad
    • Founded 1919 to protect Ottoman Caliphate.
    • Aligned with Congress for Hindu-Muslim unity.
    • Launched Khilafat Movement (1919–1924).
    • Strengthened Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).
    • Collapsed post-1924 (Caliphate abolition).
    • Promoted communal unity temporarily.
    Labor Organizations
    Hind Mazdoor Sabha Labor Organization Jayaprakash Narayan, R.S. Ruikar
    • Founded 1948, linked to socialist movement.
    • Aimed to protect workers’ rights, promote unionization.
    • Active in industrial centers (Bombay, Kanpur).
    • Strengthened labor unions post-independence.
    • Influenced labor laws in 1950s.
    • Competed with communist unions.
    Kisan Sabha Labor Organization Sahajanand Saraswati, N.G. Ranga
    • Founded 1936, Lucknow, to address peasant grievances.
    • Demanded land reforms, debt relief.
    • Linked to Congress, communists.
    • Mobilized peasants in Bihar, UP (1930s).
    • Influenced Congress’s agrarian policies.
    • Weakened by internal ideological splits.
    U.P. Kisan Sabha Labor Organization Jawaharlal Nehru, Purushottam Das Tandon
    • Founded 1918, UP, to support peasant rights.
    • Focused on tenancy reforms, anti-zamindar campaigns.
    • Aligned with Congress’s agrarian wing.
    • Organized peasant protests (1920s–1930s).
    • Contributed to UP Tenancy Act 1939.
    • Merged into broader Kisan Sabha (1936).
    Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association Labor Organization Mahatma Gandhi, Anasuya Sarabhai
    • Founded 1918, Ahmedabad, to represent textile workers.
    • Promoted non-violent labor negotiations.
    • First major Indian trade union.
    • Won wage increases, better conditions (1918 strike).
    • Model for Gandhian labor movements.
    • Influenced national labor policies.
    Religious Orders
    Tabernacle of New Dispensation Religious Order Keshab Chandra Sen
    • Founded 1880, Calcutta, as Brahmo Samaj offshoot.
    • Promoted universal religion, social reforms.
    • Emphasized devotional practices.
    • Influenced Bengal’s religious reform.
    • Limited following due to Sen’s death (1884).
    • Merged back into Brahmo Samaj.
    Calcutta Unitarian Committee Religious Order Raja Ram Mohan Roy, William Adam
    • Founded 1823, Calcutta, for Unitarian Christian-Hindu dialogue.
    • Promoted monotheism, social reforms.
    • Precursor to Brahmo Samaj.
    • Influenced Brahmo Samaj’s formation (1828).
    • Limited impact due to small membership.
    • Supported anti-sati campaign.
    Jesuit Order Religious Order Francis Xavier (early), local missionaries
    • Active in India since 16th century, expanded in colonial era.
    • Focused on missionary education, conversions.
    • Established schools in Goa, Madras.
    • Founded colleges (e.g., St. Xavier’s, Bombay).
    • Influenced Western education in India.
    • Criticized for aggressive proselytization.
    Governance Bodies
    Constituent Assembly Governance Body Jawaharlal Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar, Rajendra Prasad
    • Formed 1946 to draft India’s Constitution.
    • Elected by provincial assemblies, included diverse leaders.
    • Operated 1946–1950.
    • Adopted Constitution of India (1950).
    • Ensured democratic framework, fundamental rights.
    • Ambedkar’s role as drafting committee chair critical.
    Political Advocacy
    Poona Sarvajanik Sabha Political Advocacy M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi
    • Founded 1870, Pune, to represent public interests.
    • Critiqued British policies, demanded reforms.
    • Precursor to Indian National Congress.
    • Influenced early nationalism, Congress formation.
    • Published *Journal of Poona Sarvajanik Sabha*.
    • Declined post-1890s due to Congress’s rise.

    • Founded 1916 by Besant (All India) and Tilak (Maharashtra).

    • Held December 1916 (Table 1).

    • Launched 1917, Bihar, against indigo planter exploitation.

    • Used non-violent resistance, investigations.
    • Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 eased peasant burdens.
    • Established Gandhi as national leader.
    • Inspired Kheda, other satyagrahas.
    Kheda Satyagraha 1918 Mahatma Gandhi, Sardar Patel
    • Launched 1918, Gujarat, against high taxes during famine.
    • Non-violent protest, tax refusal.
    • Patel’s first major campaign.

    • Strengthened Gandhi’s leadership, Patel’s role.
    • Boosted Congress’s rural base.
    Chelmsford’s War Conference 1918 Lord Chelmsford, Bal Gangadhar Tilak
    • Held April 1918 (Table 1).
    • Sought Indian WWII support.
    • Led to Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
    • Limited nationalist backing.
    Rowlatt Act 1919 Mahatma Gandhi, Muhammad Ali Jinnah
    • Passed March 1919, allowed detention without trial.
    • Aimed to curb revolutionary activities.
    • Sparked nationwide protests.
    • Led to Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919).
    • Gandhi launched anti-Rowlatt campaign.
    • Strengthened nationalist resolve.
    Jallianwala Bagh Massacre 1919 General Dyer, Mahatma Gandhi, Rabindranath Tagore
    • April 13, 1919, Amritsar, British fired on unarmed crowd.
    • Protest against Rowlatt Act, Baishakhi gathering.
    • Over 400 killed, thousands injured.
    • National outrage, Tagore renounced knighthood (1919).
    • Hunter Committee (1919) criticized Dyer.
    • Boosted Non-Cooperation Movement.
    Hunter Inquiry Committee 1919 Lord Hunter, Mahatma Gandhi
    • Formed 1919 to investigate Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
    • Included British, Indian members.
    • Gandhi testified, criticized British response.
    • Condemned Dyer, but no major punishment.
    • Exposed British brutality, fueled nationalism.
    • Limited justice for victims.
    Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms 1919 Edwin Montagu, Lord Chelmsford
    • Enacted via Government of India Act 1919.
    • Introduced dyarchy in provinces, limited self-rule.
    • Response to nationalist demands, WWI support.
    • Rejected by Congress as inadequate.
    • Led to Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).
    • Expanded Indian participation in councils.
    Khilafat Movement 1919–24 Maulana Mohammad Ali, Shaukat Ali, Mahatma Gandhi
    • Launched 1919 to protect Ottoman Caliphate.
    • Congress supported for Hindu-Muslim unity.
    • Included non-cooperation, protests.
    • Strengthened Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).
    • Collapsed after Caliphate abolition (1924).
    • Temporary communal unity, later tensions.

    • Announced August 1940 to gain WWII support.

    Cripps Mission 1942 Sir Stafford Cripps, Jawaharlal Nehru, Maulana Azad
    • Sent March 1942 to secure WWII support.

    Quit India Movement 1942 Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Aruna Asaf Ali
    AspectDetailsKey FiguresImpact

    • Delivered August 8, 1942, Bombay, launched Quit India.

    • Led to widespread protests, repression.

    • Formed 1942 during Quit India in Ballia, Satara, Midnapore.

    • Formed 1942, Southeast Asia, from Indian POWs.

    Free Indian Legion 1942 Subhas Chandra Bose, A.C.N. Nambiar
    • Formed 1942, Germany, from Indian POWs.

    • Contributed to INA’s broader impact.
    • Inspired anti-colonial sentiment.

    • Proposed 1944 to resolve Congress-League deadlock.
    • Suggested plebiscite in Muslim-majority areas.
    • Rejected by Jinnah, Gandhi.
    • Failed to bridge communal divide.
    • Influenced later partition talks.
    • Highlighted Congress’s negotiation efforts.
    Wavell Plan 1945 Lord Wavell, Jawaharlal Nehru
    • Proposed June 1945, interim government with Indian leaders.
    • Discussed at Shimla Conference.
    • Failed due to League’s veto demand.
    • Led to 1946 elections, Cabinet Mission.
    • Exposed communal tensions.
    • Showed British intent for gradual exit.
    Shimla Conference 1945 Lord Wavell, Muhammad Ali Jinnah
    • Held June–July 1945 (Table 1).
    • Discussed Wavell Plan.
    • Failed due to communal deadlock.
    • Led to Cabinet Mission.
    INA Trials 1945 Subhas Chandra Bose, Shah Nawaz Khan
    • Held 1945, Red Fort, tried INA officers for treason.
    • Defended by Congress, Nehru as lawyer.
    • Sparked public protests, naval mutiny.
    • Galvanized anti-British sentiment.
    • Contributed to Royal Indian Navy Mutiny (1946).
    • Hastened British exit plans.

    • February 1946, Bombay, naval ratings revolted.
    • Protested poor conditions, INA trials.
    • Spread to Karachi, Calcutta.
    • Suppressed, but shook British confidence.
    • Congress mediated surrender, Patel’s role.
    • Accelerated independence talks.

    • Sent March 1946 to plan Indian independence.
    • Proposed federal structure, constituent assembly.
    • Rejected by Congress, League over grouping.
    • Formed Constituent Assembly (1946).
    • Direct Action Day (1946) escalated communal violence.
    • Led to interim government, partition talks.
    Constituent Assembly 1946–50 Jawaharlal Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar
    • Formed December 1946 (Table 1).
    • Drafted India’s Constitution.
    • Adopted Constitution (1950).
    • Established sovereign India.

    AspectDetailsKey FiguresImpact
    PlanMountbatten Plan, June 1947, proposed partitionMountbattenCreated two nations

    • August 1947, India and Pakistan gained independence.

    - Pre-interim, interim, and dominion government -
    Government Time Period Key People and Responsibilities Purpose Policies/Issues
    Viceroy’s Executive Council 1935–August 1946
    • Lord Linlithgow: Viceroy, presided over council
    • Sir Firoz Khan Noon: Defence (Indian member)
    • Sir Ramaswamy Mudaliar: Commerce
    • B.R. Ambedkar: Labour (joined 1942)
    • To advise the Viceroy under the Government of India Act 1935.
    • To include Indian leaders in limited governance roles.
    • To maintain British control during WWII and nationalist demands.
    • Policies: Implemented provincial autonomy (1937 elections); supported WWII efforts (Indian troops, resources).
    • Issues: Congress resigned ministries (1939, WWII protest); limited Indian authority; communal tensions escalated (Muslim League’s Pakistan demand, 1940).
    • Outcome: Paved way for Cabinet Mission Plan (1946).
    Interim Government September 2, 1946 – August 15, 1947
    NameResponsibility
    Jawaharlal NehruVice-President, External Affairs, Commonwealth Relations
    Vallabhbhai PatelHome Affairs, Information and Broadcasting
    Rajendra PrasadFood and Agriculture
    Maulana Abul Kalam AzadEducation
    John MathaiFinance
    Jagjivan RamLabour
    Rajkumari Amrit KaurHealth
    Baldev SinghDefence
    Liaquat Ali KhanFinance (Muslim League, joined October 1946)
    Abdur Rab NishtarPosts and Air (Muslim League)
    I.I. ChundrigarCommerce (Muslim League)
    • To govern India during transition to independence (Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946).
    • To involve Indian leaders (Congress, Muslim League) in administration.
    • To prepare for Constituent Assembly and address communal harmony.
    • Policies:
      • Launched Constituent Assembly (December 1946, Nehru’s Objectives Resolution).
      • Promoted food security (Prasad’s rationing) and labour welfare (Ram’s policies).
      • Asserted India’s foreign policy (Nehru’s non-alignment groundwork).
    • Issues:
      • Muslim League’s boycott (September 1946), joined later, causing friction (e.g., Liaquat’s budget strained Congress).
      • Communal riots (Direct Action Day, August 1946; Noakhali, 1947).
      • Failure to prevent partition (Mountbatten Plan, June 1947).
    Dominion Government August 15, 1947 – January 26, 1950
    • Jawaharlal Nehru: Prime Minister, External Affairs
    • Vallabhbhai Patel: Deputy Prime Minister, Home, States
    • Rajendra Prasad: President of Constituent Assembly (later first President)
    • B.R. Ambedkar: Law, Chairman of Drafting Committee
    • To govern independent India as a dominion under the Indian Independence Act 1947.
    • To finalize the Constitution via the Constituent Assembly.
    • To manage partition aftermath and integrate princely states.
    • Policies: Integrated 565 princely states (Patel’s diplomacy); adopted Constitution (November 26, 1949, effective January 26, 1950); initiated refugee rehabilitation.
    • Issues: Communal violence (1947–48, millions displaced); Gandhi’s assassination (January 1948); Kashmir conflict with Pakistan (1947–48).
    • Outcome: Established Republic of India (1950).
    - All educational institutes of modern India -
    Name Time Location Established by Purpose Outcome
    Calcutta Madrasa 1780 Kolkata, West Bengal Warren Hastings To promote Islamic studies, including Arabic, Persian, and Mohammedan law, and train Muslim youth for administrative roles in British courts Produced competent officers for British administration; introduced English education via the Anglo-Persian Department in 1854, evolving into a key Muslim educational institution
    Sanskrit College 1791 Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh Jonathan Duncan To study Hindu law, philosophy, Sanskrit texts, Vedas, Puranas, Ayurveda, and other traditional disciplines Preserved and promoted Sanskrit learning; became a center for traditional Indian scholarship, influencing cultural and religious studies
    Fort William College 1800 Kolkata, West Bengal Lord Wellesley To train British civil servants in Indian languages (e.g., Persian, Bengali, Hindi) and customs for effective colonial administration Fostered translation of texts into English; trained administrators but closed in 1854, with its library contributing to the National Library
    Hindu College 1817 Kolkata, West Bengal Raja Ram Mohan Roy, David Hare, Sir Edward Hyde East, and others To impart modern Western education, including English, to upper-class Hindus for government service Pivotal in the Bengal Renaissance; evolved into Presidency College (1855), a leading secular institution with notable alumni
    Serampore College 1818 Serampore, West Bengal William Carey, Joshua Marshman, William Ward To provide education in arts, sciences, and Christian theology, open to all castes Became India’s first modern university (1827); affiliated with the University of Calcutta (1857), continues as a key educational institute
    Sanskrit College 1824 Kolkata, West Bengal James Prinsep, Thomas Babington Macaulay, and others To promote Sanskrit literature, linguistics, and traditional Indian learning Evolved into Sanskrit College and University, a hub for liberal arts and Indological research with a vast manuscript collection
    Elphinstone College 1834 Mumbai, Maharashtra Mountstuart Elphinstone and local leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji To provide Western education in arts, sciences, and literature to Indian youth Produced luminaries like Bal Gangadhar Tilak and B.R. Ambedkar; remains a prestigious affiliate of the University of Mumbai
    Calcutta Medical College 1835 Kolkata, West Bengal Lord William Bentinck To train Indians in Western medicine and surgery for colonial medical services Asia’s oldest medical school; trained generations of doctors, shaping modern healthcare in India
    Bethune School 1849 Kolkata, West Bengal John Elliot Drinkwater Bethune To promote female education, offering secular instruction to Indian girls Pioneered women’s education; became Bethune College (1879), a leading women’s institution
    University of Calcutta 1857 Kolkata, West Bengal Court of Directors of the East India Company To provide multidisciplinary higher education modeled on the University of London One of South Asia’s first modern universities; produced scholars and leaders, shaping intellectual and nationalist movements
    University of Mumbai 1857 Mumbai, Maharashtra Court of Directors of the East India Company To offer higher education in arts, sciences, law, and engineering Became a major educational hub with over 700 affiliated colleges; fostered research and professional education
    University of Madras 1857 Chennai, Tamil Nadu Court of Directors of the East India Company To provide Western-style higher education in multiple disciplines Influenced South India’s intellectual landscape; remains a leading university with diverse academic programs
    Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College 1875 Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh Sir Syed Ahmad Khan To provide modern education to Muslims, combining Western sciences and Islamic values Evolved into Aligarh Muslim University (1920); became a center for Muslim intellectual and political activity
    Banaras Hindu University 1916 Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh Madan Mohan Malaviya, Annie Besant, and others To promote Hindu culture alongside modern sciences, arts, and technology Asia’s largest residential university; produced leaders like Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, advancing education and nationalism
    University of Mysore 1916 Mysore, Karnataka Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV To provide comprehensive education in commerce, management, and sciences First university in Karnataka; gained NAAC five-star status, known for theoretical and practical education
    - Art and culture in modern India -
    Category Details
    Painting
    • Company School
      • Time: 18th–19th century
      • Location: Kolkata, Delhi, Patna
      • Purpose: Document Indian life for British patrons
      • Features: Watercolors, realistic depictions of flora, fauna, monuments, hybrid Indo-European style
      • Key Figures/Patronage: East India Company, artists like Sewak Ram
      • Notable Detail: Known as “Patna Qalam,” influenced by Mughal miniatures
    • Bengal School
      • Time: Early 20th century (1900s–1930s)
      • Location: Kolkata, Shantiniketan
      • Purpose: Revive Indian art, counter Western academic style, promote nationalism
      • Features: Wash technique, mythological themes, inspired by Ajanta and Mughal art
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Abanindranath Tagore, Rabindranath Tagore, E.B. Havell
      • Notable Detail: Tagore’s “Bharat Mata” (1905) became a nationalist icon
    • Progressive Artists’ Group
      • Time: 1947–1950s
      • Location: Mumbai
      • Purpose: Blend Indian themes with global modernism, post-independence identity
      • Features: Abstract, expressionist styles, vibrant colors, social themes
      • Key Figures/Patronage: F.N. Souza, M.F. Husain, S.H. Raza, Government of India
      • Notable Detail: Souza’s controversial nudes challenged social norms
    • Contemporary Art
      • Time: 1980s–present
      • Location: Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru
      • Purpose: Address globalization, identity, social issues
      • Features: Mixed media, installations, digital art, feminist and Dalit perspectives
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Subodh Gupta, Bharti Kher, India Art Fair
      • Notable Detail: Gupta’s “Very Hungry God” (2006) sold for $1.4M at Sotheby’s
    Architecture
    • Victoria Memorial
      • Time: 1906–1921
      • Location: Kolkata, West Bengal
      • Purpose: Commemorate Queen Victoria, showcase British imperial grandeur
      • Features: Indo-Saracenic style, white Makrana marble, dome inspired by Taj Mahal
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Lord Curzon, architect William Emerson
      • Notable Detail: Houses museum with 28,000 colonial artifacts
    • Gateway of India
      • Time: 1911–1924
      • Location: Mumbai, Maharashtra
      • Purpose: Mark King George V’s visit, later independence symbol
      • Features: Indo-Saracenic arch, basalt stone, Gujarati and Islamic motifs
      • Key Figures/Patronage: British Government, architect George Wittet
      • Notable Detail: Last British troops left India through it in 1948
    • Chandigarh Capitol Complex
      • Time: 1951–1965
      • Location: Chandigarh, Punjab
      • Purpose: Symbolize modern India’s aspirations, house state government
      • Features: Modernist concrete, geometric forms, Palace of Assembly, Open Hand monument
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Le Corbusier, Jawaharlal Nehru
      • Notable Detail: UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016)
    • Akshardham Temple
      • Time: 2005
      • Location: Delhi
      • Purpose: Promote Hindu spirituality, cultural tourism
      • Features: Pink sandstone, 141-ft central monument, 20,000 carved figures
      • Key Figures/Patronage: BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha
      • Notable Detail: World’s largest Hindu temple complex at inauguration
    Literature
    • Bengali Renaissance
      • Time: 19th–early 20th century
      • Location: Kolkata, West Bengal
      • Purpose: Social reform, nationalism through vernacular literature
      • Features: Novels, poetry, essays; themes of identity, modernity
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Rabindranath Tagore (Gitanjali, 1913 Nobel), Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (Anandamath)
      • Notable Detail: “Vande Mataram” from Anandamath became nationalist anthem
    • Hindi Literature
      • Time: Early 20th century–present
      • Location: Uttar Pradesh, Delhi
      • Purpose: Promote Hindi as national language, social reform
      • Features: Chhayavad poetry, realist novels, Premchand’s social critique
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Munshi Premchand (Godan), Harivansh Rai Bachchan
      • Notable Detail: Premchand’s “Sevasadan” (1918) addressed women’s issues
    • Indian English Literature
      • Time: 19th century–present
      • Location: Pan-India, diaspora
      • Purpose: Globalize Indian narratives, post-colonial identity
      • Features: Novels, poetry; themes of partition, diaspora, hybridity
      • Key Figures/Patronage: R.K. Narayan (Malgudi Days), Salman Rushdie (Midnight’s Children)
      • Notable Detail: Rushdie’s Booker Prize (1981) boosted Indian English fiction
    Music
    • Hindustani Classical Revival
      • Time: 19th–20th century
      • Location: North India (Kolkata, Varanasi)
      • Purpose: Preserve classical music amid colonial decline
      • Features: Gharana system (e.g., Gwalior, Kirana), khayal, thumri
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar, All India Radio
      • Notable Detail: Paluskar’s Gandharva Mahavidyalaya (1901) formalized training
    • Film Music
      • Time: 1930s–present
      • Location: Mumbai, Chennai
      • Purpose: Entertainment, cultural integration
      • Features: Blend of classical, folk, Western; catchy melodies, playback singing
      • Key Figures/Patronage: R.D. Burman, Lata Mangeshkar, Bollywood studios

    • Indian Fusion Music
      • Time: 1960s–present

      • Features: Sitar with jazz, rock; electronic fusion
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Ravi Shankar, A.R. Rahman

    Dance
    • Bharatanatyam Revival

      • Features: Natya Shastra-based, mudras, abhinaya, revived devadasi tradition
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Rukmini Devi Arundale, Kalakshetra Foundation
      • Notable Detail: Kalakshetra (1936) globalized Bharatanatyam
    • Kathak Revival
      • Time: 20th century
      • Location: Uttar Pradesh, Delhi
      • Purpose: Revive courtly dance, promote national heritage
      • Features: Intricate footwork, spins, Lucknow and Jaipur gharanas
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Birju Maharaj, Sangeet Natak Akademi
      • Notable Detail: Maharaj’s Bollywood choreography (Devdas, 2002)
    • Contemporary Dance
      • Time: 1980s–present
      • Location: Mumbai, Delhi
      • Purpose: Express modern themes, global fusion
      • Features: Blend of classical, Western ballet, experimental choreography
      • Key Figures/Patronage: Astad Deboo, Uday Shankar
      • Notable Detail: Deboo’s fusion performances at Olympics (2010)
    Theatre and Cinema
    • Parsi Theatre
      • Time: 1850s–1930s
      • Location: Mumbai, Kolkata

    • Bollywood
      • Time: 1930s–present

      • Notable Detail: India produces 1,000+ films annually, global diaspora reach
    • Parallel Cinema

    Crafts and Textiles
    • Khadi Movement

    • Channapatna Toys
      • Time: 18th century–present
      • Location: Channapatna, Karnataka

    - Later Mughals and Eighteenth Century India - Overview of Historical Themes - Decline of the Mughal Empire (First Half of 18th Century) - Theme 1 - Decline of Mughal Empire (First Half of 18th Cen) - Rise of Autonomous States (Middle Decades of 18th Century) - Theme 2 - Rise of Autonomous States (Middle Decades of 18th Cen) (Successor, New, Independent Kingdoms) - Rise of British Supremacy (Second Half of 18th Century) - Theme 3 - Rise of British Supremacy (Second half of 18th Cen) - Mughal Emperors and Their Reigns - Bahadur Shah I (1707 - 1712) - - He took over the reins afer Aurangzeb, but the real control lay in the hands of prime Minister, Zulfiqar Khan. - Policies: - Adopted a “Pacific policy” towards other powers. His reign saw the recognition of Marwar and Mewarʼs autonomy. - Bahadur Shah allowed the Maratha Prince Shahu, held as Mughal captive since 1689, to go back to Marathaʼs and also conceded to Marathaʼs demand of Sardesmukhi in the Deccan. - Challenges: - Sikhs under Leadership of Banda Bahadur revolted against the Mughal Authority, Bahadur Shah defeated Banda Bahadur at Lohgarh. - Jahandar Shah (1712 -1713) - - Jahandar Shah won the war of Succession, with the support of noble kingmaker Zulfiqar Khan (Irani Party), First Puppet Mughal Ruler. - Policies: - Abolished Jaziya and had a subtle pacifying approach towards other regions and religions. Under him, Marathas were further granted Sardesmukhi rights over Deccan. (Collection by Mughals) - Under him, Evil practice of Revenue Farming or Ijarah was introduced. - Downfall: - Killed by Farukhsiyar with the help of Sayyid Brothers. - Farrukh Siyar (1713 - 1719) - - FS came to power with the help of Sayyid Brothers. - Policies: - Adopted policy of Religious Tolerance - Abolished Jaziya. - Issued Farman of 1717. - Events: - During his reign, Mughals executed Banda Bahadur. - Downfall: - Killed by the conspiracy of Sayyid Brothers and Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath (It was the first time in Mughal History that an Emperor was killed by his nobles) - Muhammad Shah (1719 - 1748) - - Sayyid's now placed Muhammad Shah on the throne, but Muhammad Shah colluded ( secretly cooperating or conspiring) with Nizam ul Mulk and killed SayyidBrothers. - Character: - Muhammad was not the Man of Moment to save the Mughal Empire - He was weak Minded and Frivolous and came to be known as 'Rangeela'. - Developments: - During his tenure - - Powerful nobles began to carve Semi Independent States. (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh) - Marathas began their northern expansion. - Invasions: - 1739 - Nadir Shah & Ahmed Shah Abdali (one of Nadir Shah's top generals) (7) invaded India and defeated Mughals in various Battles. - 1739 - Battle of Karnal - Nadir Shah defeated Mughals and imprisoned Muhammad Shah and annexed areas west of Indus into Persian Empire. - During this time Nadir Shah became the Mughal Emperor for 57 Days. - During this battle only, the Kohinoor and Peacock throne was looted from Mughals. - Nadir Shah gained the strategically important Mughal territories to the west of Indus including Kabul. - Ahmad Shah (1748 - 1754) - - He was an incompetent ruler who lef the state affairs in the hands of Udham Bai (Queen Mother) - Challenges: - During his reign, Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded India twice. Ahmad Shah surrendered Punjab and Multan to Persian invaders to appease him. - Power Shift: - During Ahmad Shah reign, Imad-ul-Mulk became the new wazir and kingmaker - Succession: - Afer his death till 1757, Muhammad Shah was succeeded by several weak and inefficient rulers. - Alamgir II (1754 - 1759) - - Came to the throne with the help of Imad-ul-Mulk. - Key Events: - It was during his reign that the Battle of Plassey (1757) happened. - Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded and plundered India in 1757 & 1759. - In 1757, Abdali captured Delhi and before his return Abdali had recognised Alamgir II as the Mughal Emperor and Rohilla chief, Najib-ud-Daula as Mir Bakshi of Empire, who was to act as personal 'Supreme Agent' of Abdali. - In 1758, Najib-ud-Daula was expelled from Delhi by Maratha Chief, Raghunath Rao, who also captured Punjab (Ceded to Persians by Ahmed Shah) - Downfall: - In Nov 1759, Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk got the emperor murdered and raised Shah Jahan III on throne (who again didn't amount to much) - Shah Alam II (1760 - 1806) - - Maratha power by 1760 had swept Northern India, and thus Shah Alam II was installed as rightful heir by Marathas. - Major Battles: - His reign saw the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) & Battle of Buxar (1764). - Third Battle of Panipat (1761) - In 1758, Najib-ud-Daula (Installed as Mir Bakshi by Adbali) was expelled from Delhi by Maratha Chief, Raghunath Rao, who also captured Punjab (Ceded to Persians by Ahmed Shah) and thus in order to take revenge, Abdali invaded India again in 1761 and defeated Marathas in the Third Battle of Panipat. - Legacy: - He is the first Mughal Emperor who became an East India Company Pensioner. - “Sultant-e-Shah Alam, Az Dili ta Palam” - It was used sarcastically to describe the weak rule of Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II (ruled 1759-1806), whose actual control was so diminished that his authority barely extended beyond Delhi to Palam (a small area near modern-day Delhi Airport). - Akbar Shah II (1806 - 37) - - Policies: - Akbar Shah II gave the Title of ʻRajaʼ to Ram Mohan Roy and sent him to England to seek a raise in his pension. - Decline: - In 1835, EIC stopped calling itself a subject of the Mughal Emperor. - Also, discontinued issuing coins in his name by deleting Persian lines on Companyʻs coins to this effect. - Bahadur Shah II (1837 - 57) - - Last Mughal Ruler of India. - Key Event: - During his tenure - Revolt of 1857 occurred. - Fate: - Afer the Revolt of 1857, He was captured and deported to Rangoon (Burma, now Myanmar) where he died in November 1862. - And with him died - ʻThe Mughal Empireʼ - Causes of Decline of Mughal Empire - Aurangzeb's misguided policies - His reimposition of Jizya in 1679 alienated Rajputs, Marathas, and Sikhs; prolonged Deccan campaigns from 1681-1707 drained treasury and military resources. - Weak successors - Post-Aurangzeb rulers like Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar Shah, and Muhammad Shah lacked the military prowess or administrative skill to maintain centralized control. - Wars of succession & Role of kingmakers - Frequent succession conflicts, such as Jahandar Shah vs. Farrukh Siyar, empowered nobles like Zulfiqar Khan and Sayyid Brothers to manipulate emperors, weakening imperial authority. - Nature of mughal state - A centralized feudal system dependent on loyal governors crumbled as provincial loyalty eroded after Aurangzeb, leading to fragmentation. - Degeneration of Mughal nobility - Factionalism between Irani and Turani nobles, coupled with corruption—e.g., revenue farming under Jahandar Shah—undermined governance and military cohesion. - Jagirdari Crisis - Over-allocation of jagirs—land grants—by the early 18th century reduced imperial revenue, as nobles hoarded income, crippling the state financially. - Rise of Regional powers - Marathas, Sikhs, and successor states like Hyderabad exploited Mughal weakness, asserting autonomy and challenging imperial dominance by the 1730s. - Invasions of Irani & Durrani Kingdoms - Nadir Shah's 1739 sack of Delhi and Ahmad Shah Abdali's seven invasions—e.g., 1748, 1757—looted wealth and annexed territories like Punjab, exposing Mughal vulnerability. - Advent of European Powers - East India Company's victories, like Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764, shifted power to the British, reducing Mughals to pensioners by Shah Alam II's reign. - Disintegration of Mughal Empire & Aftermath - - Successor States (Hyderabad, Carnatic, Bengal, Awadh) - New States (Sikh, Marathas) - Independent States (Mysore, Kerala, Rohilkhand) - Rise of Regional States - - Successor States - Hyderabad - Hyderabad founded in 1724 by Qlich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) - He fought in the Battle of Shaker-Kheda against Mubariz Khan - Viceroy of Deccan at that time. - Carnatic - In the 18th century, the Mughal sub of Carnatic came under the authority of the Governor of Deccan (Nizam of Hyderabad). - Following the lines of the Governor of Deccan, they also declared Independence. - Accordingly, the Nawab Saadatullah of Carnatic, appointed his nephew Dost Ali as his successor, without the prior approval of his superior, the Nizam. - However, in 1740, Marathas invaded Carnatic, killed Nawab Dost Ali and took his son-in-law Chanda Sahib as prisoner to Satara. - Thereafer the affairs of Carnatic deteriorated and this proved an opportunity to European counterparts to interfere in the affairs of Carnatic which eventually led to Carnatic Wars. - Bengal - In Bengal, Murshid Quli Khan started the process of autonomy in about 1717. - He was appointed as Diwan of Bengal along with the position of Subahdar of Bengal given later on. (An Exception). - Murshid Quli Khan is also known for his new revenue system introduced in Bengal known as Malzamani System. - The Dynastic Rule of Quli Khan was challenged by Alivardi Khan (Battle of Gheria) who assumed power through a coup and killed Sarfaraz Khan. - Thus under Alivardi's rule the areas of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa were essentially established as a sovereign state in Eastern India. - In 1765, Alivardi Khan died and nominated his grandson Siraj ud Daula as his successor. - Awadh - Saadat Khan (popularly known as Burhan-ul-Mulk) became the Subahdar of Awadh in 1722, aiming to establish Awadh as an independent power center and decline of the Mughal Empire - provided a perfect opportunity for this. - Successors faced numerous rebellions and challenges while at the same time enlarging their empire. - Safdar Jung and later on Shuja ud Daula, further solidified Awadhʼs autonomous political framework by 1764. - New States - Marathas - - Chhatrapati Shivaji established the Maratha Kingdom in the areas of western Deccan near about the 17th century. - Internal conflicts among Maratha chiefs led to the establishment of a new Maratha Governance system under Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa (Prime Minister to King Shahu). - First Peshwa - Balaji Vishwanath made the post Hereditary making his son Baji Rao next Peshwa. - Under the Baji Rao Maratha confederacy, emerged supreme represented Gaekwads at Baroda, Bhosle at Nagpur, Holkar at Indore, Scandia at Gwalior and Peshwa at Poona. - He also captured Bassein and Salsette ports from the Portuguese. - Marathas fought the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) against Abdali as a protectorate of the Mughal Empire under Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, famously known as Nana Saheb. - Sikhs - Sikh confederacy emerged in response to intense Mughal suppression in the later half of 18th century. - Sikhs initially organized themselves under 12 Misls (Groups) each under a local chief. - This confederation transitioned into the Sikh empire following the accession of Misldar Ranjit Singh Sukerchakiya (Originally a Governor under the Afghan King) as the sovereign Maharaja of Punjab, marking the beginning of a new Era of Sikh domination in north India. - Independent Kingdoms - Mysore - Mysore historically was not under the Mughal Empire; Mysore was originally a viceroyalty of the Vijayanagar Empire. - Mysore was transformed from Viceroyalty to an independent state under Wodeyar Dynasty. - Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan overthrew the Wodeyar rulers in the late 18th century. - Kerala - Martanda Varma established an independent state of Kerala with Travancore as his capital. - He extended the boundaries of his state from Kanyakumari to Cochin. - Jats - Churaman and Badan Singh succeeded in setting up the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in the 18th century, - But it was under Suraj Mal that Jat power reached its zenith. - Rohilkhand - Ali Muhammad Khan took advantage of the collapse of authority in North India following Nadir Shah's invasion to set up a petty kingdom, Rohilkhand - Other Important Battles - Battle of Palkhed - 1728 - Marathas vs Nizam - Fought on February 28, 1728, near Palkhed in present-day Maharashtra; Peshwa Baji Rao I used guerrilla tactics to encircle and defeat Nizam-ul-Mulk's larger army, forcing the Nizam to recognize Maratha rights to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan, marking an early Maratha victory in their northern expansion. - Battle of Kharda - 1795 - Marathas vs Nizam - Fought on March 11, 1795, near Kharda in Maharashtra; the Maratha Confederacy under Peshwa Madhavrao II and generals like Daulat Rao Scindia decisively defeated Nizam Ali Khan of Hyderabad, extracting a large indemnity and territorial concessions, showcasing Maratha dominance over the Nizam in the late 18th century. - Advent of Europeans in India - Overview of European Arrival - - Introduction - In the 15th century, the Ottoman Empire seized control of the sea route to India through the Mediterranean , making it difficult for Europeans to reach India by their traditional route. - This prompted European countries to compete with one other from the 15th century onwards to discover new maritime routes to India. - This quest for new routes was fuelled by a strong desire to do trade with India, which was regarded as the land abundant with superior goods. - By the 17th century, all European nations had established commercial empires in India. - Their operations were primarily focused on coastal port cities in India and did not infringe upon the sovereignty of indigenous polities. - They utilised existing trade networks to exchange goods for bullion, shifing the balance of foreign trade in Indiaʼs favour and feeling economic growth. - However, conflicts emerged among these European powers as they sought to secure trade monopolies and territorial control. - By the 1750ʼs British East India Company emerged as a dominant force in India, surpassing all other European trading companies. - Prelude to European Arrival in India - - Key Events Leading to Exploration - Fall of Constantinople in 1453 - Age of Discovery - direct sea route to South East Asia (Image) - Treaty of Tordesillas between Spain and , 1494 - Fun Fact - In the year 1519, a Spanish Fleet under the command of Ferdinand Magellan set out to find a westward sea route to Asia, Ship returning to Spain three years later. Making it first circumnavigation of the world in Human History. - Major European Powers in India - - Overview - Portuguese (1498) - Arrived first, establishing a maritime empire focused on spice trade and coastal control, led by Vasco da Gama. - Dutch (1602) - Focused on Southeast Asia but traded in India for cloth and spices, competing with the Portuguese and English. - English (1608) - Formed the East India Company, eventually dominating India through trade and territorial conquests. - Danes (1616) - Established minor trading posts, with limited commercial success but notable missionary impact. - French (1664) - Last to arrive, set up factories and competed with the British, leading to the Carnatic Wars. - Portuguese (1498) - The Beginning of Portuguese Exploration - - Portuguese king Henry (1393-1460) encouraged maritime navigation by opening training and research institutes for the Purpose, Thus Portuguese became the first one to have navigated the entire African coastline. - Bartholomew Dias (Bartolomeu Dias) in 1488 became the first known European to sail around the southern tip of Africa, reaching the Indian Ocean from the Atlantic. - He originally named the cape "Cape of Storms" (Cabo das Tormentas) due to the rough seas. - However, King John II of Portugal later renamed it "Cape of Good Hope" (Cabo da Boa Esperança) as it symbolized the promise of a new sea route to India. - Early Portuguese Ventures - - In 1497, Vasco da Gama under the patronage of King Emmanuel reached Calicut on May 17,1498 which was ruled by a king named Zamorin (Local Hindu ruler) (Samuhtri Mana Veda) - He came over as a trader and the cargo he bought from India was sold for 60 times the cost of his voyage. (He returned to India two more times) - He successfully established a sea route from Europe to India that would permit trade with the far East, without the use of costly and unsafe silk road caravan routes, of the Middle East and central Asia. - Pedro Alvarez Cabral (1500), he came over with the intention of striking a treaty with the local ruler of Calicut and setting up the Portuguese factory. - However, a conflict ensued with the Arab merchants because of which plan was dropped. (Some sources mention the first factory of Portuguese to be in Calicut (1500)) - Eastern Spices were very important for European traders as without refrigeration, food spoiled easily, and spices were important for masking the flavour of rancid or spoiled meat. - In 1503, the 1st Portuguese factory was set up at Cochin (Kochi) - In 1505, the 2nd Portuguese factory was set up at Cannanore (Kannur) - Their factories were called Feitorias and it also served as bases for a naval fleet called Armadas. - Formation of Portuguese State of India - Formation of Portuguese State of India ( Estado da India, 1503 -1504) - The Portuguese State of India was meant to be a governing body of the various Portuguese fortresses and colonies overseas and it was required to function under a viceroy. - In effect, the formation of this body indicated that the Portuguese would no longer be content with the mere spice trade but would set out to establish a Christian Portuguese state in the East and launch a holy war against Islam there. - Another important post - Vendor da Fazenda, responsible for revenues and the cargoes and dispatch of fleets. - Key Portuguese Viceroys - Francisco De Almeida (1505-1509) became the 1st Portuguese Viceroy in India. (3 Year Term) - He initiated the Blue Water Policy which aimed at Portuguese Mastery over the Sea. - Blue water policy involved - Strong Navy: - Maintaining powerful naval fleets (armadas) to patrol the Indian Ocean. - Strategic Fortresses: - Building fortified bases at key coastal locations (like Kilwa, Kannur, Anjadiva, Cochin) to control entry points, choke points, and support naval operations, rather than deep inland expansion. - Cartaz System: - Implementing a system where non-Portuguese ships were required to purchase a license or pass (cartaz) from the Portuguese to trade in the Indian Ocean. Ships found without a cartaz could be confiscated or sunk. This enforced Portuguese control and generated revenue. - Naval Warfare: - Actively engaging and destroying rival naval powers (like the fleets of Egypt, Gujarat, and the Zamorin of Calicut) to eliminate competition, culminating in the decisive Battle of Diu (1509). - He is credited with construction of Fort Anjediva on Anjediva Island lying at the Border of Muslim Bijapur and Hindu Vijayanagara states. - Additional Point - The combined forces of Egyptian and Gujarat navies defeated Portuguese armies off the coast of Diu. Next year he avenged his defeat by crushing both the armies combined. - Alfonso de Albuquerque was the greatest Viceroy of Portuguese in India, - He expanded the trading centres which till his reign were confined to Calicut and Cochin. (Headquarters at Cochin) - He conquered Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510 (Adil Shah) (Helped by Timmaya (a privateer or admiral, possibly under the Vijayanagara Empire or operating independently from Honavar) in lieu of supply of Horses (instead of, in place of, or as a substitute for)), (First bit of Indian territories to be under Europeans since the time of Alexander the Great) - Similarly other areas such as Malaysia, Daman & Diu were also brought under the Portuguese. - In Bengal, Hooghly and Balasore became the Portuguese trading centres. - He was an efficient administrator and brought natives into the administration of these areas and also encouraged the Propagation of Christianity and inter marriages. - He abolished Sati in the regions under his rule. - He introduced new plants such as Tobacco and Cashew nuts and also new varieties of Coconut. - Nino de Cunha - Next Portuguese Viceroy, he transferred the Government head office from Cochin to Goa, thus making Goa the official Capital of Portuguese in India. - He secured Bassein (Vasai) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat by helping him in battle against Humayun (1534). - Few Years later he killed Bahadur Shah of Gujarat by deceit by inviting him to a Portuguese Ship (1537) - He set up settlements in Bengal with their headquarters at Hooghly. - Decline of Portuguese Power - The Viceroys afer him were not that efficient and thus the result was that Portuguese began to decline in India. - In 1661, The Portuguese were at war with the Spain and needed support from England, which led to marriage of Princess Catherine elf Portugal to Charles II of England, who imposed a dowry that included the insular and less inhabited areas of Southern Bombay while the Portuguese managed to retain all the mainland territory north of Bandra up to Thana and Bassein - Beginning of strong English presence in India as well. - In 1739, the Marathas, under Chimaji Appa, captured Salsette and Bassein (Vasai), dealing a major blow to Portuguese power in western India. - The Battle of Bassein (1739) marked the beginning of the Portuguese territorial decline in India. - The Portuguese finally lef India in the mid 17th century AD, but three of their settlements - Goa,, Daman and Diu remained in their hands till 1961. (First one to come to India and the last one to Leave) (Operation Vijay 1961) - Causes of Failure of Portuguese in India - Lack of Good Leadership - While the early Portuguese efforts were spearheaded by capable and often ruthless leaders like Vasco da Gama, Francisco de Almeida, and especially Afonso de Albuquerque (who established key territorial bases like Goa, Malacca, and Hormuz), the quality of leadership that followed often proved inadequate for the challenges faced. - Many subsequent Viceroys and Governors lacked the strategic vision, administrative competence, and military acumen of their predecessors. - Corrupt Administration - Neglected by the home Government, The salaries of the officials were low and thus they indulged in corruption and malpractice. - In 1580, Portugal was merged with Spain (This union lasted for 60 years) which neglected the Portuguese interests in India and moreover they discovered Brazil which diverted their attention from India. - Treaty of Tordesillas between Spain and Portugal, 1494 (Image) - It divided the non-European world between Spain and Portugal along a specific meridian. Portugal was granted Africa, Asia, and the eastern part of South America (which included Brazil), while Spain received the lands to the west (most of the Americas). - - Portuguese society was dominated by the aristocracy and merchants did not enjoy the social influence necessary to mould state policy according to their interests, making it difficult for Portugal to maintain its maritime empire. - Religious Policy and their forceful conversion of natives into Christianity - Rise of Dutch and English Maritime Power. - Impact of Portuguese Coming to India - Spread of Christianity to Malabar and the Konkan Coast. - Missionaries like Saint Francis Xaviers, Father Monserrate played a crucial role in propagating the Christianity faith in India. In 1540, all temples of Goa were destroyed. - Western Education was imparted in the native Language as they opened up schools and colleges. - Also, - They brought the Printing Press to India - Bible came to be printed in Kannada and Malayalam Language. - Brought Some crops with them for production such as Tobacco, Some fruits and vegetables. - Potato, Lady Finger, Sweet Potato, tobacco, corn, lady finger, Pineapple, Groundnuts, Cashew, Almond etc. - Portuguese contributed to the Mughal use of field guns (Matchlocks), and the artillery of the stirrup. - - Cartaz System - The Portuguese East India Company introduced Sea Pass in the Indian Ocean Region in the early 16th century. - In the 15th century, both the Arab and Persians were dominant in the Indian Ocean region, However by the 16th century due to their strong naval Power Portuguese superseded the Muslim dominance and thus introduced the carat system as a mark of their sovereignty and dominance. - The carat pass issued by the Portuguese entitled the holder freedom of movement in the Indian Ocean. - First time it was issued in 1502. As a result, Indian and Perso-Arab merchants suffered and eventually, the maritime trade declined. - The Dutch (Netherlands/Holland) - Introduction to Dutch Presence - - Afer the Portuguese came the Dutch, they were innovative people in business and in shipping techniques. - By 1600 they had established an elaborate system of Eastern Trade from the Persian Gulf to Japan and traded mainly in redistribution of goods to Northern Europe. - In 1596, Cornelius de Houtman was the first Dutch traveler to reach India. - Their main Interest was in the Indonesian Archipelago and the Spice Islands and not India. - However they discovered that Indian Trade was necessary to carry out trade with South-West Asia, as there was a good demand for Indian cloth in the Indonesia region. - In return, Indians demanded pepper and spices. - Hence, the FIRST credit of making ʻIndian Clothʼ as an item of export goes to the Dutch. - Dutch Factories - In 1605, the first factory was established at Masulipatnam (AP), which was under the Sultan of Golconda - Second factory at Pettopoli (Nizampatnam) - In 1610, they signed a treaty with the king of Chandragiri and established their headquarters at Pulicat. - Here they minted their gold coins called pagoda. - Soon they established various trading depots and factories all over India. - In 1690, their headquarters were transferred from Pulicat to Nagapattinam. - The heads of Dutch factories were called factors who were classified as traders and the Dutch model of Trade was based on the Cartel (refers to an agreement or association between competing firms or entities to control aspects of a market) or Cooperative System. - Anglo-Dutch Rivalry - Battle of Bedra - In 1623, the Amboyna massacre took place in Indonesia where the Dutch killed 10 Englishmen and 9 Japanese. - Afer this event, the Dutch restricted themselves to the Malay Archipelago and the English to India. - In 1759, The Dutch were defeated by the English in the decisive Battle of Bedara/ Hooghly (Bengal)/Chinsurah, thus ending the Dutch power in India. - The English (1608) - Establishment of the English East India Company - In 1599, a company to trade with the East was formed under the auspices of the group of merchants known as Merchant Adventurers, the Company popularly came to be known as East India Company. - In 1600, EIC was granted a royal charter by Queen Elizabeth giving it the exclusive privilege of trading east of the Cape of Good Hope for a period of 15 years. - Initially, their main area of interest was Spice Islands in Indonesia, however due to the overwhelming presence of Dutch, they shifed their preference towards India and thus in 1608, Surat in Gujarat was established as the trade transit point and the company ships were docked there. - The Company now planned to open up a factory in Surat and sent Captain Hawkins for the same. - He was the first Englishmen to set foot on Indian soil. - He could speak Turkish and came in a ship called ʻHectorʼ. - On arrival, he went to Jahangir's court in Agra. - In 1609, the English were given the royal Farman to set up factories on the west Coast. - However, Hawkins had to leave India at that time due to Portuguese intrigues. - Early English Factories - In 1612, The English, under the command of Captain Thomas Best, defeated the Portuguese at Swally near Surat. - Impressed by this triumph, Emperor Jahangir granted the English a Royal Farman in 1613 allowing them to open their first permanent factory at Surat in 1613 and trade in Cambar, Ahmedabad and Goa. - Imp - First temporary factory at Masulipatnam in 1611. - In 1615, Sir Thomas Roe arrived in India, sent by King James I as an ambassador to the court of Jahangir. - He was successful in obtaining a royal Farman according to which English were allowed to set up their factories in the whole of India. - In 1616, English opened their first factory in the south at Masulipatnam. (First one on in South East Coast) - English Factories in the South - 1. In 1632, Sultan of Golconda issued a Golden Farman in favour of the English, permitting them to trade freely from the ports of Golconda on annual payment gf 500 pagodas. - 2. In 1639, Francis Day was able to obtain Madras on lease from the Raja of Chandragiri and shifed the centre of their activity to Madras. - Raja allowed the Company to fortify Madras. - Thus the English set up a small factory and built a small fort around it called Fort St. George. - 3. In 1690, The British bought the Fort Devanpatnam, near Madras and renamed it to Fort David. - English Factories in Deccan - In 1622, King Charles II of England received Bombay as dowry on marrying a Portuguese Princess. - In 1668, the Crown transferred it to the Company on an annual rent of ten pounds. - Bombay quickly replaced Surat as the Company's main depot on the West Coast. - English Factories in Bengal - On the SOUTH-EASTERN coast, the first English factory was set up in Orissa in 1633 - In 1651, at Hugli, the first English factory was set up in Bengal upon receiving permission from Sultan Shuja. - In 1658, all establishments of the Company in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and Coromandel Coast were brought under the control of Fort St. George. - In 1667, Company was given a farman for trade in Bengal by the Emperor Aurangzeb. - In 1690, Job Charnock established a factory at Sutanati which was fortified in 1697 and called Fort Williams. - In 1698, the Bengal factories were placed under Fort Williams. - The Farman of 1691 granted by Aurangzeb exempted the company from payment of custom duties in Bengal in return for an annual payment . - Later In 1717, Company secured from Mughal Emperor Farukh Siyar a Farman confirming the privileges granted EARLIER and extending them to Gujarat and Deccan. (Mission led by John Surman) - Farman of 1717 - The "Magna Carta of the Company" - Main Provisions: - In Bengal: - Taxes on the Company's import and export were waived for an annual payment of ₹3,000. - The Company was permitted to issue dastaks (trade passes) for the transportation of its goods. - The Company was allowed to rent more land around Calcutta. - In Hyderabad: - The Company retained its existing privileges of duty-free trade. - The Company had to pay the prevailing rent for Madras, but no additional trade duties were imposed. - In Surat: - For an annual payment of ₹10,000, the East India Company was exempted from all trade duties. - Other Provisions: - The coins minted by the Company in Bombay were to have legal currency throughout the Mughal Empire. - The original company faced opposition to its monopoly, which led to the establishment of a rival company and the fusion (1708) of the two as the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies. - The United Company was organized into a court of 24 directors who worked through committees. - Danes (1616) - Danish Presence in India - The Danish East India Company was established in 1616 and they set up trading outposts in 1620 at Tranquebar near Tanjore (Tamil Nadu). (Nayak king of Thanjavur) - In 1755, they founded a colony called Frederick Nagore near Serampore in Bengal. - Occupied twice by English, they failed as a commercial venture. - In 1771, the Danish Company went bankrupt and Serampore was transferred to the Danish crown. - Serampore became a safe haven for missionaries in India and earned immense fame for the cultural and educational activities of the missionaries. - In 1845, Serampore was ceded to English, thus ending the Danish presence in India. - Two Danish Missionaries, the first protestant missionaries, arrived on 9 June 1706. - The Danish settled in Andaman and Nicobar in 1755, but due to the threat of malaria they abandoned it in 1848. - Danish Presence in India, which also included the Nicobar Islands, played a notable role in missionary activities. - In 1801, the Danish were defeated at Tranquebar by the British army. - In 1845, Denmark sold all its Indian colonies to Britain, ending its presence in India and transferring these areas to British control. - French (1664) - - Introduction to French Presence - The French were the last colonial power to set up their foot in India. - In 1664, Colbert formed the Company des Indes Orientales. - King Louis IV granted the French Company licence to trade with India and the East Indies. - French Factories - In 1668, they set up their first factory at Surat with Francis Caron as the Director General. - In 1669, they set up a factory at Masulipatnam. - In 1672, Caron was succeeded by Francois Martin who received a village as a grant from the King of Bijapur Sher Khan Lodhi and founded Pondicherry, which later became their capital. - In 1693, The Dutch snatched Pondicherry but it was restored to the French under the Treaty of Ryswick. - In this way, French established its firm base in India. - Afer that, they further consolidated their position by adding several bases including Mahe, Karaikal, Balasore and Kasimbazar. - The real trouble started when the French won control of Tanjore which the British considered vital for their trade security and the Anglo-French rivalry. - Rise of British Supremacy: Carnatic Wars - The Anglo-French Rivalry - Overview of British Ascendancy - Introduction - The mid-18th century saw the gradual transformation of the English East India Company from a trading company into a political power. - During the period 1600 to 1744, the slowly expanded its trade network in India, simultaneously easing out the rivals though a strategy combining diplomacy and war. - Though the rise of British supremacy in India is usually traced to 1757 with the British victory in the Battle of Plassey, the ground for the victory was laid in South India where the British might was successfully tested out against the French Company. - Anglo-French Struggle for Supremacy - The Carnatic Wars - - Reasons for Political Power Acquisition - Why did these foreign powers start gaining Political Power ? - When the decline of Mughal Authority (Nadir Shah Invasion of 1740) and the weak regional powers (Marathas - Nizam of Hyderabad) proved incapable of safeguarding the interests of European companies in India, they saw the necessity to empower themselves militarily. - Further, they were commercial entities, seeking to maximize their profit margins, which necessitated the elimination of competition and establishment of monopoly. - Not that they only wanted to monopolize their trade and sell dear, but they also wanted to acquire power, necessitating the acquisition of some political control over the country they traded with. - Emergence of Rivalry in South India - Why this rivalry emerged in the South India - In this context, the emergence of hostilities between the English and the French was but natural. - South India emerged as the arena for Anglo-French rivalry as it had become the main centre for French activities with Pondicherry as capital. - The French had also begun to wield influence in the neighbouring states of Hyderabad and Mysore. - Besides, there was not much scope in western India because of powerful Marathas, while Eastern India was under the direct control of Alivardi Khan, therefore it was only in Southern India that conditions became favourable, especially after the death of Nizam-ul-Mulk of Hyderabad in 1748. - First Carnatic War (1740-1748) - Background of Hostility - Austrian War of Succession - - The immediate context for conflict between two European rivals in India was provided by the War of Austrian Succession in Europe which broke out in Europe in 1740 between Austria and Prussia. - In this war, Britain and France joined opposite camps. - Perhaps conscious of their relatively weaker position, the French tried hard to prevent the extension of war to India and Dupleix (The French General) advised his English counterpart to maintain neutrality. - Dupleix - Introduced the innovative concept of Subsidiary Alliance in India - But the English did not agree, instead deliberately adopting an aggressive stand and seized some French ships off the south-eastern coast of India to provoke France. - The French had no fleet in India, hence Dupelix messaged La Bourdonnais (The French Governor of Mauritius) for reinforcements . - He immediately siphoned 3000 men towards the Coromandel Coast. - As soon as the help arrived, French attacked the English and captured the British possessions in Fort St. George, Madras and nearby areas, and Robert Clive was taken as prisoner of War, and thus the First Carnatic War had begun. - Battle of St. Thomas (River Adyar) - Anwarrudin, the Nawab of Carnatic, disapproved of the hostilities in his kingdom, thus when the English appealed to him for protection, Nawab asked the French to quit Madras, but the French were in no mood to retreat and neglected the advice. - The Nawab now sent a large army to fight the French. - A large Indian Army of 10,000 men met a small French army of 230 European and 700 Indians soldiers on the bank of River Adyar near St. Thomas in 1746. - But to everyone's surprise, a handful of properly trained soldiers of the French army routed Anwaruddin's vast army. - This highlighted the superiority of the European army and exposed the weakness of the military of the Indian rulers. - End of the War - Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle - Thereafter in 18th century political chaos, there was no dearth of Indian princes who would invite Dupleix's assistance to turn the scales in their favour. - In this way, it was Duplex who first showed the way of intervening in disputes of the Indian rulers and thereby acquiring political control - a technique which was later perfected by the English company. - Even as the French continued the siege, the War of Austrian Succession came to an end by the Treaty of Aix la Chapelle on the basis of mutual restitution of conquests. - This ended the first round of Anglo French rivalry in India too. - Madras was restored to the English and the French got Louisburg in North America, and thus the first war ended in a draw. - Second Carnatic War (1749-1755) - Background - Succession Disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad - Dynastic feuds in South India proved the content for the second round of Anglo-French conflict in the South. - The succession disputes at both Carnatic and Hyderabad provided the French Governor General Dupelix an opportunity to intervene in Indian Politics. - In 1740, The Marathas had invaded the Carnatic and killed Nawab Dost Ali (Ruler of Carnatic) and took his son-in-law Chanda Sahib as prisoner to Satara. - In 1743, The Nizam of Hyderabad (Nizam ul Mulk) felt prompted to come to the Carnatic and appoint Anwarrudin Khan as the Nawab of Carnatic. - But in 1748, the Chanda Sahib was freed by the Marathas and the same year, Nizam-ul-Mulk died. - His son Nasir Jung succeeded him but his grandson, Muzaffar Jung laid claim to the throne. - Muzaffar Jung now allied with Chanda sahib to gain their respective seats in Hyderabad and the Carnatic. - Intervention by Dupleix - He was able to intervene in the wars of succession that started after the death of Nizam ul Mulk. - He pledged support to Muzaffar Jung and Chanda Sahib, thus a tripartite struggle was developed. - In August 1749, the three allies ambushed and killed Anwaruddin at the Battle of Ambur, near Vellore. - His son Muhammad Ali fled to Trichinopoly and Chanda Sahib became the Nawab of Carnatic and thus began the second phase of the Anglo-French War (2nd Carnatic War). - After this the allies marched to Deccan, The French army surprised and killed Nasir Jung and installed Muzaffar Jung as the Nizam of Hyderabad. - He rewarded Dupleix by appointing his honorary Governor of all the Mughal Dominions south of the River Krishna and other territories were ceded to the French. - In return, Dupleix placed at the disposal of Muzaffar Jung the service of his best officer named Bussy. - Soon afterwards, Muzzafar Jung was killed in an accidental skirmish (a minor, unplanned, or preliminary fight between small groups of troops). - However, Bussy maintained French influence in the Deccan by quickly placing his nominee Salabat Jung on the throne. - In this way, Bussy went on to control Deccan's political fortune for 7 years. - Thus the French power in the South was now at its heights from where it was going to fall badly. - Emergence of Robert Clive - Meanwhile, Muhammad Ali had taken refuge in the fortress of Trichinopoly and the repeated attempts of Chanda Sahib and the French to capture the fortress had failed. - The British, realising that the situation implied a serious threat to their position in Southern India, now decided to put their entire strength behind Muhammad Ali. - Robert Clive saves the day for the British, He suggested that French pressure on Muhammad Ali could be released by attacking Arcot, the capital of Carnatic. - Thus, attack upon Arcot was to be used as a diversionary tactic and thus Chanda Sahib would have to divert an effective part of his army for the protection of Arcot. - Siege of Arcot - Clive stormed Arcot with a small force of only 210 men and captured it, Thus Chanda Sahib alarmed by the attack on his capital, sent the best troops from Trichinopoly which comprised 4000 men to recapture Arcot. - Clive successfully sustained the famous siege for 53 days. - In the meantime, Clive received help in the form of reinforcements from Madras and some Indian allies (Mysore, Tanjore and Marathas). - Clive then came out of the besieged town, attacked and defeated Chanda Sahib (Beheaded), Muhammad Ali then became the undisputed Nawab of Carnatic. - The fate of French Governor Dupleix was sealed after the defeat of Arcot, The Directors of the French Company did not appreciate his political ambitions and disproved of the expenses they involved and recalled him. - On 1 August 1754, Godeheu succeeded Dupleix as French Governor General in India. - Treaty of Pondicherry - Godeheu signed a peace treaty, The Treaty of Pondicherry with the English in 1755. - As per this treaty, both the companies agreed not to interfere in the quarrels of the Indian princes. - After this treaty, French continued to maintain their hold over Hyderabad for some time, but they had lost much of their prestige and their predominant position in the Deccan had been definitely undermined. - On the other hand, English influence had been established in Carnatic, with their candidate Mohammad Ali installed as the Nawab of Carnatic. - Third Carnatic War (1757-1763) - Background - Seven Years War - - Like the first Carnatic War, This Third war was also the echo of the Hostilities happening in Europe Between the British and the French. - The Seven Years War broke out in Europe and both the forces joined the opposite camps and this ended the short peace between the European companies in India as well. - Arrival of Count De Lally (April 1758) - This time the French Government made a determined effort to oust the English from India, For this purpose, The French sent an impressive French army headed by Count De Lally, who reached India after a long voyage of 12 Months in April 1758. - Lally started his work vigorously and attacked Fort St. David and captured it and other small English possessions in this region. - But the French victory was only short-lived as problems of varying nature began to surface on the horizon. - Lally's attack on Madras ended in failure as he could not get naval support in time. - The French Company also faced shortage of ammunition and lack of funds to pay the troops. - Upon that, Lally was rude and overbearing in his conduct with the subordinates I.e the Company's servants of Pondicherry. - He held a very low opinion of them and looked down upon them as dishonest rogues to be set right with threats and punishments. - In such circumstances, both Lally and his soldiers distrusted each other and the French troops felt badly demoralised. - At this critical juncture, rash and headstrong Lally committed another great blunder of fighting personal battles with the British. - Having assessed the situation, The English sent an army from Bengal to the Northern Circars. - They occupied Rajahmundry and Masulipatnam and also concluded a favourable treaty with Nizam Salabat Jung. - French Influence in Deccan was thus irrevocably lost. - - Battle of Wandiwash (1760) - The Final Blow to French Rule in India - The Battle of Wandiwash took place on 22 January 1760 in present-day Tamil Nadu. - It was a decisive confrontation between the British (led by General Eyre Coote) and the French (led by Count de Lally). - The British completely defeated the French, capturing Bussy, one of Lally's key commanders. - After their defeat, the French retreated to Pondicherry, their main stronghold in India. - Lally sought help from Nawab Hyder Ali of Mysore, but due to miscommunication, Hyder's forces returned without fighting. - The British laid siege to Pondicherry, and after months of struggle, the French surrendered on 16 January 1761. - With this, French power in India collapsed. The British soon captured Jinje and Mahe, ensuring that the French had no remaining territories in India. - Peace of Paris (1763) - The Third Carnatic War ended officially in 1763 with the conclusion of the Peace of Paris, at the end of Seven Years' War. - As per the treaty, Pondicherry and some other French settlements were no doubt returned to France, but these were never to be fortified again and could only function as mere trading centres. - The worst fate awaited Lally, He was detained as a prisoner of war for two years, after which he was allowed to return to his home country, where far from receiving any favourable treatment, he was first imprisoned and then executed. - Thus the Third Carnatic War brought down the curtain to the Anglo-French rivalry in India and cleared the way for the establishment of the British Empire. - Reasons for Defeat of the French Against the English - Continental Ambitions of France - France in the 18th century remained preoccupied with its continental ambitions, which considerably strained its resources. - The French Monarchs of the time were fighting for the 'natural frontiers' of their country, which meant acquisition of territory towards the Rhine and towards Italy. - Such an expansionist policy of France kept it perpetually trapped in the wars of Europe and diverted its energies away from colonial acquisition. - In the end, the French gained almost nothing on the continent and even lost their colonial possessions. - On the other hand, England did not covet an inch of European territory but followed its single minded objective of colonial expansion, an objective in which it achieved considerable success. - Difference in the Organisation of the Two Companies - The French East India Company was largely funded by the monarch, with guaranteed dividends for shareholders. - As a result, the company's directors were appointed by the king and had little personal interest in its success. - When facing financial difficulties, the French government provided subsidies to keep it running. - This made the company financially weak and unable to support Dupleix's costly wars. - On the other hand, the British East India Company was an independent commercial corporation. - It was managed by a court of directors who had a strong interest in the company's growth. - The company maintained good financial health and was even considered a major source of revenue for the British government. - Different Systems of Government - The French Government was autocratic and suffered from corruption and inefficiency. - The English Government was run by an enlightened oligarchy, under which it was making immense progress towards a constitutional set up. - Other Reasons - Seats of Power - The French centered their power in Pondicherry, a single coastal enclave vulnerable to siege, while the English diversified their strongholds across Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta, giving them strategic resilience and broader influence over Indian rulers. - Naval Strength - British naval superiority, exemplified by control of the seas during the Seven Years' War, allowed them to disrupt French supply lines and reinforce their own positions, whereas the French navy, often delayed or under-resourced, failed to support Lally effectively, as seen at Madras and Wandiwash. - Lack of Enthusiasm and Enterprise - French efforts in India lacked consistent enthusiasm from the home government and company directors, who prioritized European wars over colonial ventures, contrasting with the English East India Company's proactive and profit-driven leadership, which eagerly backed military campaigns like Clive's at Arcot. - Personal Incompetence of Commanders and Generals - French commanders like Lally, despite initial vigor, displayed arrogance and poor coordination—e.g., alienating subordinates and failing to secure Hyder Ali's aid—while English leaders like Clive and Eyre Coote demonstrated adaptability, strategic foresight, and effective alliances with Indian powers. - Rise of British Supremacy (2): Conquest of Bengal (1757-1765) - Overview of British Conquest - Introduction - The Beginning of British conquest in India may be traced back to the Battle of Plassey in 1757, in which the English forces defeated the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daulah. - In fact, the history of British conquest in Bengal is the history of gradual transfer of power from Nawabs to British during the short period of eight years, from 1757 to 1764, the main cause of conflict being the commercial rivalry between the British and the Bengal Nawabs. - Why All Eyes on Bengal? - High agricultural production particularly rice. - Great Water Transport system for moving goods. - By mid 1700ʼs, Bengal was top producer of silk and cotton textiles in India. - Bengal was also a big supplier of saltpeters, needed for making gunpowder in Europe. - Therefore in the initial years of settlement, British, Dutch and French all had settlements in Bengal - - British in Calcutta - Dutch in Chinsurah - French in Chandernagore - Background to British Dominance in Bengal - Early European Presence - Since the 17th century, Bengal had emerged as a happy hunting ground of the Dutch, the English and the French company who were attracted to Bengal mainly owing to its rich resources. - In 1651, at Hugli The first English factory was set up upon receiving permissions from Sultan Shuja, the subahdar of Bengal. - Then he also granted the English East Indian Company the privilege of free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in return for lump sum payment of 350 pounds at a time when Companyʼs exports from Bengal were worth more than 50,000 pounds a year. (This was because Sultan Shuja was pleased by the service of British Doctor who successfully cured a royal lady of a disease). - Thereafer, English factories were set up at Kasimbazar, Patna etc. - In 1698, they obtained the zamindari of the villages of Sutanati, Kalikata and Gobindpura from Subahdar (Azim us Shan) on payment of Rs 1200. - In 1700, the Bengal factories were placed under Fort William. - Soon the villages grew into a city known as Calcutta. - Rise of Independent Nawabs - In 1717, Emperor Farrukhsiyar appointed Murshid Quli Khan, the Diwan of Bengal and also at the same time Subahdar of Bengal. - Taking advantage of his position, Murshid Quli Khan now declared himself as the Nawab of Bengal and became the first independent Nawab of Bengal.
