(F.S Farman of 1717) - In 1740, Alivardi Khan, the Deputy Governor of Bihar, deposed and killed Nawab Sarfaraz khan (Grandson of Murshid Quli). - Alivardi Khan rightly did not allow fortification of French and English factories at Chandernagore and Calcutta. - In 1755, Alivardi Khan dies nominating his grandson Siraj-ud-Daulah as his successor. - Siraj-ud-Daulah (April 1756 - June 1757) - Succession Challenges - Two other contenders for the throne, Shaukat Jung (Faujdar) and Ghaseti Begum (Alivardi's Daughter) challenged Siraj's succession. - This resulted in intense court factionalism and support was offering to different warring groups by a dominant group in the Nawabʼs court comprising Jagat Seth, Amir Chand, Mir Jaffar, zamindars and others who were also opposed to Siraj. - This seriously destabilised the administration of Bengal and the advantage was taken by English East India Company. - Main Reasons for Conflict with the English Company - Farman of 1717 - This Farman became a perpetual source of conflict between the Bengal Nawabs and the English Company. - It meant loss of revenue to the Bengal Government and second, the Company's servants misused Dastaks to evade taxes on their private trade. - Shelter to Krishna Das - The English Company had given shelter to Krishna Das, a traitor , who fled with immense treasures against the Nawabʼs will. - Support to Ghaseti Begum - The Company had also offended the Nawab by giving support to the claims of Ghaseti Begum (Daughter of Alivardi Khan) - Immediate Cause - The breaking point cam when the English Company, anticipating another round of Anglo-French struggle, began to strengthen the fortification of Fort William and mounted guns on its walls. - Siraj pleased repeatedly with the English to desist from further fortification, but to no avail. - Seeing his own authority flouted in his own dominion, Siraj-ud-Daulah decided to launch an offensive. - Capture of Fort William & Black Hole Tragedy - On 15 June 1756, Siraj-ud-Daulah surrounded Fort William. - The siege lasted for five days. - During this, some of the 146 persons escaped through the back door down the Hooghly River, took refuge and waited for held from Madras. - When the fort fell on 20 June, The Nawab renamed Calcutta as Alinagar, placed it under the charge of Manik Chand, and himself returned to Murshidabad. - Subsequently, these 146 persons were captured and and put in a small room of the fort popularly known as Black Hole, in conditions of excessive heat and crowding owing to summer solstice. - It is believed out of 146 persons, only 26 survived the next morning, this is known as Black Hole tragedy. - This incident was held up as an example of British heroism and Nawabʼs callousness. - Siraj-ud-Daulah was portrayed a cruel monster and held directly responsible for the deaths. - Aftermath of Black Hole Tragedy - Meanwhile, help came from Madras in the form of strong naval force under the command of Robert Clive. - Manik Chand, the Nawabʼs officer in charge of Fort William, was bribed and he surrendered afer a brief pretence (A reason or excuse that is not true) of resistance. - Consequently, In February 1757, The Nawabs had to make peace with the English and sign the humiliating Treaty of Alinagar. - As per the Treaty, the Nawabs had to restore to the English their - - Former privilege of trade - Grant permission to fortify Calcutta. - Pay compensation amount for the losses suffered by the English. - British Still Not Satisfied - In this way, Clive had regained Calcutta and even forced the Nawab to concede to all English demands. - Still, the English were not satisfied, They had decided to replace the Nawabs with Mir Jafar. - With this in mind, they placed an impossible set of demands before the Nawab, thus making a war inevitable. - Clive organised a web of intrigue with the leaders in the Nawabʼs court. - Mir Jafar - Mir Bakshi (Commander in chief of Nawabʼs Army) - Manik Chand - Officer in charge of Calcutta. - Jagat Seth (Rich Bankers of Bengal) - These disaffected nobles of Sirajʼs court joined hands with the English to oust Siraj and install their protege, leading to Plassey conspiracy of 1757. - The Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) - Battle Details - On 23 June 1757, both armies met at Plassey, 30 km south of Murshidabad. - The English force comprised of 950 European infantry and 2100 Indian sepoys, while that of the Nawab comprised of 50,000 men commanded by the treacherous (Deceptive or betraying trust) Mir Jafar. - Only a small group of Nawabʼs soldiers fought bravely, they were led by Mir Madan and Mohan Lal. - Afer Mir Madan was killed, Mir Zafar played upon the fears of Nawab and advised him to retire from the battlefield, leaving the command in the hands of his generals. - The trick was well played, once the Nawab retired with 2000 men, a large part of Nawabʼs army led by Mir Jafar and Rai Durlabh merely looked upon, as Clive routed the rest of Nawabʼs forces. - As a result, the Nawab had to flee but was captured and put to death by an assassin, Muhammad Ali Beg. - ʻPlassey was a transaction in which the rich bankers of Bengal and Mir Jafar sold out the Nawab to the Englishʼ - Aftermath of Battle of Plassey - Mir Jafar was proclaimed as the Nawab of Bengal (he was promised the Nawabship by Clive even before the Battle of Plassey) - Robert Clive was confirmed as the Governor of Bengal (Cliveʼs first Governorship : 1757 - 1760) along with that English got - - The Company was granted undisputed right to free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Orrisa. - It was also understood that British officials would no longer need to pay any taxes on their private trade. - The Company received the zamindari of 24 Parganas near Calcutta. - Mir Jafar paid out a sum of Rs 50 Lakh as gif to bribe to the Companyʼs officials, besides a large amount as personal present to Clive and compensation for Companyʼs losses. - All French settlements in Bengal were surrendered to the English. - Significance of Battle of Plassey - The battle was hardly significant from the military point of view as the English army showed no military superiority. - It was a mere skirmish, resulting in 65 casualties on the English side and 500 on the Nawabʼs side. - More than the might of the English, it was treachery of the Nawabʼs confidants that decided the fate of the battle of Plassey - The British emerged as kingmakers in Bengal - British now appointed their man, Mir Zafar, as the new Nawab. - Zafar was completely dependent on the English for maintenance of his position in Bengal. - Hence, an English force of 6000 troops was stationed in Bengal for Nawabʼs protection with the natural consequence that all real power passed into Companyʼs hand and Mr. Watts, the British Resident at Murshidabad, began to wield considerable influence. - Transformation in the position of the English Company - The victory in Plassey brought about a great transformation in the position of the English Company in Bengal. - Until now the English Company was just one of the European companies trading in Bengal. - Afer Plassey, the Company emerged supreme and established its monopoly over Bengal trade by marginalising the French and the Dutch companies. - The English also emerged as powerful contenders in Bengal politics. - Vast Resources of Bengal placed at British disposal - - The first instalments of wealth paid to the company immediately afer Plassey was paid in silver coins, carried in more than 100 boats. - Bengal was then the most prosperous province in India - its manufactures were in huge demand not only in India but also in world outside. - Victory in Bengal played a decisive role in Anglo-French struggle. - In fact, with the revenues of Bengal, the English were able to meet the cost of conquest of rest of the country. - Thus, the ʻPlassey Revolutionʼ as it is called, proved to be a battle with far-reaching consequences. - The victory in Plassey marked the beginning of British conquest of Bengal and later of India. - It helped the company and it servants to amass unimaginable wealth at the cost of the people of Bengal. - ʻThere never was a battle in which the consequences were so vast, so immediate and so permanentʼ - ʻThe Battle of Plassey was followed by “A night of eternal gloom for India”ʼ - Mir Jafar (June 1757 - October 1760) - Challenges Faced by Mir Jafar - Immediately afer his succession, Mir Jafar began to face some serious problems - Some Zamindars refused to accept Mir Jafar as their ruler. - Mir Jafar also suspected the loyalty of some of his soldiers, who had not been receiving their regularly their regular salary, and that of his officials like Rai Durlabh. - Deposition of Mir Jaffar - Mir Jafarʼs growing dependence on the Company for military support was used by the Company to demand more finances and other privileges from the Nawab, Thus He failed to meet the heavy demand of money promised. - Mir Jafar, who had played the role of ʻCliveʼs jackalʼ, soon began to repent the deal he had struck and to shed off the British yoke, Jafar began intriguing with the Dutch against the British. - Clive however thwarted this design by defeating the Dutch in the decisive Battle of Bedra. - But by now the English Company had grown considerably suspicious of the Nawab and had begun to look for a suitable replacement. - Major Events Between Battle of Plassey and Buxar - Third Anglo Carnatic War - Battle of Wandiwash - Fought in January 1760, the British under Eyre Coote defeated the French at Wandiwash, ending French ambitions in South India and securing British dominance in the Carnatic region. - Third Battle of Panipat - Marathas (Mughals) vs Ahmed Shah Abdali - Fought on January 14, 1761, Ahmad Shah Abdali's victory over the Marathas weakened their power in North India, indirectly benefiting British expansion by reducing a major rival. - Mir Qasim Comes to the Throne (October 1760 - 1763) - Succession and Initial Relations - Meanwhile, Mir Jafarʼs son, Miran, died and once again conflict over succession followed. - The conflict was between Miranʼs son and Mir Qasim, the son-in-law of Mir Zafar. - Mir Qasim secretly promised the necessary funds if the the English Company agreed to support his claim to the Nawabship. - Mir Zafar was ultimately forced to abdicate in favour of his son-in-law, Mir Qasim. - In this way, Mir Jafar sowed as he had repeat, got betrayal in return for betrayal. - Mir Qasim rewarded his benefactors by granting the Company the Zamindari of Burdwan, Mindapore and Chittagong. - He also promised to give the Company half of the share in chunam trade of Sylhet. - The first few months of Mir Qasimʼs reign went very well, but soon the relationship with the British embittered due to several reasons, But Mir Qasim belied English hopes. - He was able and efficient ruler and wanted to free himself from foreign control. - Changes Introduced by Mir Qasim - He moved the capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr in Bihar, away from the influence of the Company at Calcutta and court intrigues at Murshidabad. - Completely overhauled the bureaucracy by Men of his choice and sought to improve the finances of the state. - Sought to modernise his army along European line and preparations were made for the manufacture of guns at Monghyr - Conflict Between Mir Qasim and Company - The misuse of Companyʼs dastaks for private trade was perpetual cause of tension between the English Company and the Nawabs. - The Companyʼs servants were not paying any duty on their goods, whereas the local merchants had to pay duty with the following consequences - - The Nawab lost tax revenue - The local merchants faced unequal competition - Further, the Companyʼs servants even sold the dastaks to Indian merchants for a commission. - Frustration Increases Between Mir Qasim and Company - The Companyʼs servants were not even constant with duty free trade and used coercive methods to get things at cheaper rate. - They ignored the officials of the Nawab and forcibly took away the good and commodities of the peasants and merchants for a fourth part of their value. - They also used violence and oppression to force the peasants into buying goods at prices many times higher their value. - An Attempt at Settlement - In such conditions, though Mir Qasim did not seek independence from the British, he did seek to limit the fast expanding encroachments of the English on his jurisdiction, which were driving him to desperation. - Afer he appealed to British, A compromise was made that the Nawab would give the English traders a share in the inland trade provided they paid 9% duty. - It was also agreed that the Nawab alone would be competent to grant dastaks and his authority would be ultimate in the resolution of disputed regarding trade. - Unfortunately, the agreement was disproved by the Calcutta Council, as most of the Council members themselves participated in Inland trade and they rather favoured the deposition of Mir Qasim, which would provide them with yet another opportunity for receiving bribes. - A Masterstroke or Blunder by Mir Qasim - Out of desperation, Mir Qasim abolished all inland duties to bring the Indian merchants on the same footing as the English, provoking hostilities by an attack on Patna town. - In this way, war between the Nawab and the English broke out in 1763 and the Nawab was defeated in a series of battles that year. - Subsequently, he fled to Awadh and formed an alliance with Shuja-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Awadh) and Shah Alam II (fugitive Mughal Emperor) in a final bid to overthrow the English, which will ultimately lead to the Battle of Buxar (1764). - Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) - Battle Details - The three allies closed with the Companyʼs army at the battlefield of Buxar. - Allies forces stood at nearly 40,000 to 60,000 whereas the English forces stood at nearly 7,000 commanded by Major Munro. - It was a close contested battle with heavy casualties on both sides and ended in the victory of the superior military power, the British. - This was one of the most decisive battles in Indian History. - It firmly established the British as masters of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. - Awadh was placed at their mercy. - Consequences of Battle of Buxar - Buxar sealed the fate of Bengal Nawabs and transferred it into the hands of the English Company. - Mir Jafar was Brought back to the throne of Bengal, this time on much harsher terms. - Hand over the districts of Midnapore, Burdawan and Chittagong to the English - Permitted them duty free trade in Bengal (with exception of 2% duty on salt). - He and his successors had to pay Rs 5 Lakh per month to the English Company, allow Companyʼs intervention in matters of appointments and reduce military establishments. - Mir Jafar died shortly thereafer and his minor son, Nizam-ud-Daulh was appointed as Nawab. - Clive was appointed as Governor and Commander-in-Chief of Bengal (Clive second Governorship). - Primarily he took up the tasks of defining relations with the defeated powers and showed considerable practical wisdom in his settlements. - Settlement with Nawab of Awadh - Clive went to Awadh, met Shuja-ud-Daula at Allahabad and concluded with him the first Treaty of Allahabad. - As per the treaty, - Nawab of Awadh was to pay a war indemnity of Rs 50 Lakh to company. - Nawab was made to surrender Allahabad and Kora to emperor Shah Alam. - The Nawab was made to enter an offensive and defensive treaty with the Company. - In this way, Nawab of Awadh became dependent on the Company. - Settlement with Mughal Emperor, Shah Alam II - Clive concluded with the Second Treaty of Allahabad with the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, as per the treaty - - The Emperor was taken into Companyʼs protection and given the districts of Kora and Allahabad ceded by Awadh (The Emperor resided in the fort of Allahabad for 6 years as a virtual prisoner of the English). - In return, the Emperor issued a Farman dated 12 August 1765 granted to the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in return for the Company making an annual payment of Rs 26 Lakhs to him and providing for the expenses of the Nizamat of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa which was fixed at Rs 53 Lakhs. - In this way, the Farman legalised the Companyʼs gain in Bengal, it established a Dual system in Bengal in theory and converted the Emperor into useful ʻrubber stamp of the companyʼ - Afer the death of Mir Zafar, Nizam-ud-Daulah was allowed to succeed his father on the following conditions - - The Nawab would surrender Defense and Foreign Affairs (both were Nizamat functions) into the hands of the Company and civil administration into the hands of a Naib-Subahdar nominated by the Company. - Going by this strategy, Company gained Diwani from the Emperor and Niamat functions form the Nawab of Bengal. - In this way, the infamous dual system was ʻdualʼ only in theory, while in practice the Company acquired all real power in Bengal. - The Nawab lost all independent military or financial power and become a mere figurehead. - Dual System of Administration in Bengal (Dyarchy or Double Governance System) - Structure and Functioning - Dual System meant the system of Governance where the Company exercised Diwani (right to collect revenue) functions while the Nawab of Bengal exercised the Nizamat functions (defence, Law and order and administration of justice). - However, Nizam-ud-Daulah was allowed to succeed as Nawab of Bengal only on the condition that he surrendered the Nizamat functions. - Hence in reality, Dual System was just a sham as it was company that exercised all political power and merely used the Nawab and his administrate as an instrument for its purposes. - Thus, in practice, dual system referred to the system of Government whereby the Company acquired all real power while the ʻresponsibilityʼ for administration rested on the shoulders of the Nawab. - A fatal divorce of power form responsibility was inherent in this dual system. - Impacts of the Dual System - The advantage of this system was that British had power without responsibility. - This had adverse consequences for the people of Bengal, as neither the company nor the Nawab cared for their welfare. - In the words of Clive himself - ʻSuch a state of confusion, bribery, corruption and extortion was never seen or head of in any country but Bengalʼ - Thus began the Drain of Wealth from Bengal. - The Company stopped sending money from England to buy Indian goods. - These goods were now purchased form the revenue of Bengal and sold abroad. - This Drain of Wealth greatly improvised Bengal and was a major factor responsible for the terrible Bengal famine of 1770. - Though the famine was caused by failure of rains, the devastating effects were accentuated by policies of British. - Due to the Dual System of Government, The English Company acquired a real power without any responsibility while the position of Nawab was virtually reduced to a cipher. - Other Adverse impacts include - - Disruption of trade and Commerce - Company merchants exercised strict monopoly and would undersell the Indian merchants in Bengal, pushing many of them in destitution and beggary. - It ruined Indigenous Industry and skill - Company used its political power to compel the cotton weavers of Bengal to buy raw material from and sell woven cloths to the Company exclusively at arbitrary prices. - The Company also encouraged the industries selectively. - Significance of Battle of Buxar - Afer this battle, the English emerged as the supreme power. - Now the Nawab of Bengal was their puppet, the Nawab of Awadh a pliant ally and the Mughal Emperor their pensioner. - Lands from Bengal upto Allahabad lay at their feet and the roads to Delhi were open. - While the Plassey made them, a powerful factor in Bengal politics, Buxar made them a powerful factor in the politics of north India. - Battle of Plassey decided the fate of Bengal while Battle of Buxar decided the Fate of India. - In fact, the British now emerged as strong contenders for the Indian Empire. - Rise of British Supremacy (3): Anglo Mysore Wars - Kingdom of Mysore - - Political History of Mysore - Mysore was located south of Hyderabad at the junction of eastern and western Ghats. - Originally a viceroyalty under the Vijayanagar Empire in the 16th century. - With the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire, they declared themselves as Independent and were only a nominal part of the Mughal Empire. - In the early 18th century, Wadiyar/Wodeyar King Chikka Krishnaraja ruled Mysore. - Two of his ministers, Nanjaraja (Prime Minister) and Devaraja (Commander in Chief) seized power and reduced the king to a mere puppet. - The mid 18th century saw the emergence of Mysore as the second most significant power in south India, afer Hyderabad. - The foundation of Mysore power were laid by Hyder Ali, which was later consolidated by his able son, Tipu Sultan - Hyder Ali - - Rise to Power - He began his career as a petty officer in the Mysore Army. - Though Uneducated, he was a man of great energy and intellect. - He gradually rose in the Mysore Army to be a brilliant commander. - In 1761, Hyder overthrew Nanjaraja and established authority over Mysore. - He established his control over rebellious poligars (Zamindars) and conquered Bindur, Malabar etc. - Military and Expansionist Ambitions - He was an expansionist at heart and naturally clashed with other regional powers - Maratha, Nizam and the English. - Faced Maratha raids in 1764, 1766, and again in 1771 as the Marathas recovered fast under Peshwa Madhav Rao. - He also inflicted a heavy defeat on the English near Madras in 1769. - His most remarkable achievement was his vision to modernise his army along the European lines and this way he had the best standing army among the regional powers of India. - He inducted French Experts and established a modern Arsenal at Dindigul. - Formed the first Indian controlled corps of sepoys armed with firelocks, bayonets, and backed by artillery served by Europeans - Hyder died during the course of the second Anglo Mysore War (1782) and was succeeded by his son, Tipu Sultan. - Tipu Sultan - - Assertion of Autonomy - Afer assuming the throne, he strongly asserted his autonomy. - In 1787, he assumed the title of Padshah, issued coins in his own name with any reference to the Mughal Emperor. - He even issued a new Calendar. - He also sought a Sanad (Royal order) from the Ottoman Khalif to legitimize his rule. - Being a realist, he recognised Mughal authority when it suited him and defied it when it did not. - Administration and Welfare - For the General Public - he took great care for the welfare and happiness of his people. - More than any other 18th century Indian ruler, Tipu thoroughly recognised the threat that the English posed to South India and thus raised an efficient military force, employed French officers to train his troops and even raised a French corps, Made efforts to build modern Navy in 1796. - Economically - He was very sound and understood the importance of modern trade and Industry. - Hence promoted both Inland and Foreign Trade but imposed tight government regulations and control over it. - Set up a number of Factories in Mysore Territory such as those of sugar, silk fabrics etc. - Sent Emissaries to France, Turkey, Iran, Myanmar etc. - Tried to set up trading companies on the European Lines - which did not fructify, - Pioneered iron cased rocket technology, - Worked for modernisation of Agriculture and introduced sericulture in Mysore. - Under his Administration, He acted like a despotic one - Himself being the civil. Political and military authority of the State. - There was no office of Wazir in his office but there were separate departments each under a different officer such as Military department, Finance department etc. - Personal Interests and Legacy - He was an avid learner and had a library with books on different subjects. - Tipu showed keen interest in the French Revolution and is believed to have planted the ʻTree of Libertyʼ at Seringapatam, became a member of the Jacobian Club and allowed himself to be addressed as Citizen Tipu. - His famous Line - “Better to live a day as a lion than a lifetime as a Sheep”. - He ruled Mysore till his death at the hands of the British in 1799 - where he died defending his capital during the course of Fourth Anglo Mysore War. - British Expansion in South India - Threats to British Interests - Hyder and Tipuʼs dominance over the rich trade of Malabar Coast was seen as the threat to the English Companyʼs Trade in pepper and cardamom. - In 1785, Tipu declared an embargo (an official ban or restriction on trade, commerce, or communication with a particular country or entity) on export of pepper and cardamom through the ports within his kingdom. - In 1788, he clearly forbade dealings with English traders. - Thus Mysore was also seen as a threat to English control over Madras. - Moreover, The French Alliance with Mysore was seen as a threat to English dominance. - The British home government was in need of finances for growing expenditure in Napoleonic wars, and so it encouraged an aggressive expansionist policy of the Companyʼs merchants. - Anglo Mysore Wars (1767 - 1799) - - Overview - The rise of Mysore under Hyder Ali was viewed as a threat by the neighbouring states - the Marathas - The Nawabs of Carnatic and The Nizam of Hyderabad. - The Marathas and the Nizam formed an alliance against Mysore and also co-operated with the English Company to curb Mysore. - But the Nizam was equally apprehensive of the Marathas and therefore cooperated with the English company against the Marathas also. - First Anglo Mysore War (1767 - 1769) - Hyder Aliʼs friendship with French alongside the Mysore border dispute with Nawab of Carnatic is considered as one of the main reasons for this war. - The immediate context of war was provided by the rivalry over control of Northern Circars. - This part was under the Nizam of Hyderabad and The English Company was seeking an overland connection between its territories in Madras and Bengal, and the Northern Circars was a series of coastal territories that lay in between. - The Nizam of Hyderabad initially rejected the British demand, however later signed a treaty with the Company in view of his poor financial condition. - As per this treaty, the Company got the Northern Circars and in return promised to give military support to the Nizam in his endeavours against Hyder Ali. - At the same time, Nizam had formed an alliance with the Marathas as both felt threatened by the expansionist attitude of Hyder Ali. - Hyder himself was annoyed with the English as they had set up a fortified outpost at Vellore. - In this way, The Marathas, The Nizam and the English entered into a tripartite treaty against Hyder Ali and attacked Mysore in 1766. - Hyder successfully persuaded the Nizam and the Marathas to join hands with him against the English. - He then launched an offensive attack against the Company and reached upto the gates of Madras, He forced the Madras Council to sign peace on his terms in 1769, known as the Treaty of Madras. - As per the treaty, both the powers agreed to help each other in case of an attack by a third party. - Second Anglo Mysore War (1780 - 1784) - The British had no intention of abiding by the Madras treaty. - When the Marathas invaded Hyderʼs territory in 1771, the English Company did not come to his help. - So this feeling of being betrayed laid the foundation of the Second Mysore War, On the other hand the French proved more helpful to Hyder with his military demands. - Further, The American War of Independence had broken out in 1775 and the French help to American colonists made Governor General Warren Hastings extremely anxious of Hyderʼs reaction with the French. - Under these circumstances, The Company attempted to capture Mahe (A French settlement on the Malabar Coast within Hyderʼs Jurisdiction), which was a direct challenge to Hyder Ali. - The English had also offended Hyder Ali when an English force trespassed on Hyderʼs territory in order to take over Guntur in Northern Circars. - The English capture of Mahe provided the immediate context for the second Mysore War, The English won over the Marathas and the Nizam (Bribery). - In July 1781, The English Army under Sir Eyre Coote defeated Hyder Ali at Porto-Novo. - Skirmishes continued for the time being. - But later Hyder Ali died of cancer in December 1782 during the course of the second Mysore War. - Tipu, son and successor continued the war. - However in 1783, The American War of Independence ended, and the French sailed back to Europe leaving Tipu to fight his own battles. - The Madras Government also desired peace due to lack of resources and uncertainty of the Maratha attitude. - Tipu also needed time to strengthen his own administration. - Thus the war ended with the Treaty of Mangalore (March 1784) signed on the basis of mutual restitution of each otherʼs territories. - This was the last British treaty with an Indian ruler on an equal footing. - Third Anglo Mysore War (1790 - 1792) - - The above treaty was only a temporary respite before a final showdown. - Lord Cornwallis had become the Governor General in 1786 and through his diplomacy he brought the Marathas and The Nizam to the English side. - Convinced of the inevitability of the war, Tipu also sought help from the Turks and the French by sending embassies to Constantinople and France during 1784-1787. - However, Tipuʼs attack on Travancore became the immediate cause of the Third-Mysore War as the English were already itching for a war and decided to side with the ruler of Travancore. - The War started in 1790, supported by the Marathas and the Nizamʼs troops, Cornwallis himself headed a large army and approached Seringapatanam. - Tipu suffered a serious setback and showed initiative for peace. - Thus, the Treaty of Srirangapatnam was signed in 1792 under which - - Tipu had to surrender half of his territory to the Company and his allies. - While the Company acquired Baramahal, Dindigul and Malabar - The Marathas gained territory on the Tungabhadra side. - Nizam acquired territories form the Krishna to beyond the Pennar. - Tipu also had to pay war indemnity with Rs. 3 crore, but as he was unable to pay this sum indemnity, his two sons were kept as prisoners with Cornwallis. - Afer Cornwallis, Sir John Shore became the Governor General but he adopted the Policy of non-intervention towards Mysore. - For this reason, John Shore is known as the Father of policy of non-intervention. - Fourth Anglo Mysore War (1799) - Lord Wellesly sailed for India in 1797, this was a period when English were struggling against the French all over the world. - Napoleon Bonaparte had captured Egypt and Syria and he now turned towards India. - In 1801, he made an alliance with Czar Paul of Russia and drew up a serious plan to invade India via Herat and Kandahar. - The English realised that the consequences of a defeat at the hands of Napoleon would mean an end to its commerce that had brought immense financial and political gains. - In Napoleonʼs plan, Tipu Sultan of Mysore saw the right opportunity to oust the English from India. - He entered into negotiations with the French and started making elaborate preparations for war with the Company. - He planted a ʻFlag of Libertyʼ at Srirangapatna, styled himself ʻCitizen Tipuʼ. - He employed the French Commandant Monsieur Raymond and raised a corps of 14000 men with his help. - Wellesly alarmed by this, Tried to convert as many as Indian states into the subsidiary allies of the Company, either by persuasion or by force. - War began in February 1799 and was over by May, The English Company won a decisive victory at the Battle of Serinagapatnam. - Tipu was killed while defending the city before French help could reach him. - He died a heroes death defending the capital. - The Company, The Nizam and The Marathas annexed much of the remaining Mysorean territory. - The remaining core around Mysore and Serinagapatnam, was restored to the minor Indian prince, two year old Krishnaraj belonging to the Wadiyar Dynasty, whose forefathers had been the actual rulers before Hyder Ali became the defacto ruler. - A special Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance was imposed on the Wadiyar King and Mysore virtually became a dependance of the British. - Tipuʼs family was imprisoned in Vellore and his two sons pensioned. - Afer the success , Wellesley arrogantly pronounced “Now the Kingdom of the East is under our feet” - Rise of British Supremacy (4) - Anglo Maratha Wars (1777 - 1818) - Overview - From the ashes of the Mughal Empire had emerged the Marathas and the English East India Company. - Both had emerged victorious in their own spheres - The Marathas among other Indian states, The English among other European contenders in India. - But now, Towards the last quarter of the 18th century, the two came face to face and indulged in direct clash and conflict. - The 1st, 2nd and 3rd Anglo Maratha Wars were fought between the army of the English East India Company, which afer the 1757 was de facto ruler of Bengal, and the Maratha Empire, in the Deccan. - Maratha Empire comprised of five major chiefs - The Peshwas of Poona - Bhonsle of Nagpur - Scindia at Gwalior - Holkar at Indore - Gaekwad at Baroda. - Peshwa was the nominal head of this Maratha confederacy and there existed bitter mutual rivalry among all of them, Particularly Scindia and Holkar. - Their strength had already been weakened by their defeat in the Third battle of Panipat (1761), in which the Marathas were defeated by the Ahmed Shah Abdali. - The wars started in 1777 and ended with British victory in 1818. - This lef the British in control, directly or indirectly via treaties of Princely states, of a vast proportion of India, making India the jewel in the crown of the British Empire. - First Anglo-Maratha War (1775 - 1782) - Background - It was a result of the excessive ambition of the English, accentuated by the internal strife of the Marathas. - The Bombay Government under the British had its longing eyes upon the Maratha territories, particularly the ports of Salsette and Bassein and hoped to gain political influence at the Poona Court. - The dispute over succession to the Peshwaship afer the death of fourth Peshwa Madhav Rao gave the English the much needed opportunity to intervene in the Maratha affairs. - Story - Afer Madhav Rao's death in 1772, his brother Narayan Rao succeeded him as the fifh Peshwa. - However, Narayan Raoʼs uncle Raghunath Rao got him assassinated and named himself as the next Peshwa, although he was not a legal heir. - Narayan Raoʼs widow Gangabai then gave birth to a son afer her Husbands death (Swaii) and he was legally the next Peshwa. - Then happened the Barbhai conspiracy under Nana Phadnavis which removed Raghunath Rao from the seat. - Treaty of Surat - Thus out of frustration, Raghunath Rao went over to the British and tried to capture power with their help. - This was the immediate background of the Anglo-Maratha War. - The war began with the Treaty of Surat and ended with the Treaty of Salbai. - In Raghunath Rao, the Bombay government saw a plaint tool and hoped to set up in Maharashtra the type of Dual Government as Clive had done in Bengal. - This treaty was signed between Raghunath Rao and the British Government at Bombay on 7 March 1775. - As per the treaty it was decided that the British would help Raghunath Rao in becoming the Peshwa by sending 2500 soldiers. - In return, Raghoba would cede territories of Salsette and Bassein and revenues from Surat and Bharauch to the British. - Treaty of Surat and Battle of Adas - In accordance with the Treaty of Surat, A British Army reached Surat led by Colonel Keating. - On 18 May 1775, at Adas (Battle of Adas) there took place a terrible battle between the English and the Maratha Armies. - In this battle, though the Marathas were defeated, however they retained control over Poona. - The Reversal with Treaty of Purandar - When a copy of Treaty of Surat reached the superior British Government in Bengal, it condemned the treaty as unjust and unauthorised. - Further, Warren Hastings sent Colonel Upton to Poona Darbar and signed the Treaty of Purandar. - Thus the Treaty of Purandar was signed between the British Government at Calcutta and Poona Court and it stated the following. - The Treaty of Surat was annulled. - The British lef the side of Raghunath and it was decided that Raghunath will be given a monthly pension of Rs 25,000 by Peshwa Government and he will reside in Gujarat. - Plot Twist - Treaty of Purandar Not Implemented - However, The Treaty of Purandar was not implemented due to a sudden turn of events. - The American War of Independence had erupted. - In 1775 and 1778, France joined on the American side against England. - At the same time, A French adventurer, Chevailer de St. Lubin, reached Poona. - This greatly alarmed Warren Hastings, who immediately scrapped the Treaty of Purandar, sent a large force to reinforce Bombay Government and sanctioned operations against the Marathas. - Movie Begins - First Anglo-Maratha War - Thus the Bombay Government resumed the war and sent an army towards Poona under Colonel Egerton (Later replaced by Colonel Cockburn). - The English and Maratha forces met on the outskirts of Poona. - The Maratha Army was led by the brilliant General Mahadji Schinde. - He lured the English Army into valleys of the Western Ghats near Talegaon (Battle of Talegaon) and trapped them from all side. - The Marathas also used the ʻScorched Earth Policyʼ, burning farmlands and poisoning wells. - Treaty of Wadgaon - The English were forced to retreat to villages named Wadgaon. - Finally by mid January 1779, The English surrendered and the Bombay Government was forced to sign a humiliating treaty with Poona Darbar called as Treaty of Wadgaon. - A per this treaty, it was decided that Bombay Government would return all territory conquered by it afer 1773 and the Scindias would get a part of revenue from Bharuch. - Humiliation Too Much for Hastings - Hastings refused to accept this humiliating treaty of Wadgaon. - He quickly sent an army from Bengal which soon captured Ahmedabad and Vasai. - But the British Army got defeated by Marathas in poona. - But meanwhile Gwalior was captured by British and eventually Scndia was seated in the Battle of Sipri. - Finally the Treaty of Salbai was signed between the British and the Poona Government. - Treaty of Salbai - This treaty between the British and The Poona Government was signed with the mediation by the Mahdji Scindia. - The treaty was signed on the basis of mutual restitution of each otherʼs territories or ʻstatus quo ante bellumʼ. - The main provision of this territory were - - Madhav Narayan Rao will be accepted as Peshwa. - British will give up the cause of Raghunath Rao and he be given an yearly pension of Rs 3.5 Lakhs. - The Company gave up Bassein and other territories captured since the Treaty of Purandar , but retained Salsette and The Elephanta Island. - Scinida got back the entire territory on the west of Yamuna. - Treaty of Salbai - First War Ends in Draw - In this way, the British attempt to gain supremacy in the Marahta state proved premature. - The First Anglo Maratha war was drawn. - Both sides had a taste of each otherʼs strength which ensured mutual respect and peace for the next 20 years. - It also gave British the required time to concentrate on other fronts especially Mysore. - Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803 - 1805) - Prelude to War - Lord Wellesly came to India in 1798 and aggressively followed his policy his subsidiary alliance. - The Marathas earlier refused all offers to accept subsidiary alliance, however their internal differences ultimately drove them into Wellesleyʼs trap. - Story - - Due to internal ongoing politics among the Marathasm Peshwa Baji Rao II murdered the brother of Jaswant Rao Holkar. - It led to Holkar forces defeating Sindhia and the Peshwa and installing an adopted brother on the throne of Pune. - The Peshwa of Poona sought assistance from Wellesley, resulting in Wellesley singing a treaty on December 31, 1802 known as the Treaty of Bassein. - This treaty, essentially a subsidiary alliance with the Peshwa, would ultimately mark the downfall of the Maratha Empire.l) - Imp Point - Subsidiary Alliance - Hyderabad (1798), Mysore (1799), Tanjore (1799), Awadh (1801), Peshwa (1802), Scindia (1803), Gaekwad (1803) - Treaty of Bassein (Subsidiary Alliance, 31 December 1802) - This treaty of ʻperpetual and general allianceʼ was signed between Peshwa Bajirao II and the English Company. - It was a treaty of the Subsidiary Alliance. - The main provisions of this treaty were - - Peshwa accepted the Companyʼs protection and had to pay a large annual subsidy. - Peshwa accepted that an English army and Resident will be stationed at Poona and no European enemy of the English will be kept in the Maratha Army. - Peshwa accepted that his foreign relations with other states will go under under British control. - Also - - To surrender the city of Surat - To give up all claims of Chauth on the Nizamʼs dominion - In this way, The Peshwa lost his independent authority and eventually the other Maratha chiefs were reduced to a similar position of subordination to the Company. - Company received a native infantry regiment permanently stationed at Poona. - City of Surat was surrounded by the British along with other territories. - Peshwa gave up all the claims on Chauth on the Nizamʼs dominion.\ - Peshwa also agreed not to sign any future negotiations with any other power without the consent of East India Company. - This treaty, sometimes described as granting the English - “Key to India” - According to Sir Thomas Munro, as a result of the Second Anglo Maratha War, the British became the “complete masters of India and nothing can shake our power, if we take proper measure to confirm it” - This affected the patriotic feeling of other Maratha chiefs and provoked the Second Anglo - Maratha War that began the breakup of Maratha confederacy. - Daulat Rau Sindhia and Raghuji Bhonsle immediately formed an alliance against the English. - They tried to include Yashwant Rao Holkar but could not success. - Gaekwad remained neutral. - In this way, even in times of national danger, the Maratha chiefs did not unite. - Course of the War - The English decided to attack all Maratha Regions. - The War was fought in 2 main centres - in Deccan under Arthur Wellesley and in north India under General Lake. - The Maratha Forces due to disunity had to face bitter losses on both sides. - It is noteworthy that now the control of Delhi passed from the Marathas into British hands and once again the blind Mughal ruler, Shah Alam II, became a pensioner of the Company (He had first became a pensioner of the Company afer his defeat in the Battle of Buxar in 1764). - In this way, Scindia and Bhonsle faced total defeat within five months and had to sign two separate treaties with the English Company. - Alarmed by the defeat of Bhonsle and Scinida, This Time Holkars made an attempt to form a coalition of Indian rulers to fight against the British, but all his attempts proved to be unsuccessful, thus the Marathas were defeated, reduced to British vassalage and isolated from one another. - Defeat of Bhonsle led to - Treaty of Deogaon - Defeat of Scindia led to - Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon - Defeat of Holkar - Led to Treaty of Rajpurghat - Third Anglo Maratha War (1817 - 1819) - Background - The third and final phase of the Anglo-Maratha war started with the arrival of British Governor Lord Hastings. - He tried to establish the supremacy of English East India Company in India and resumed the threads of aggressive policy abandoned in 1805 with the recall of Wellesley. - The breathing space that the Marathas had got since 1805 was not utilised by consolidating their power but wasted in mutual conflicts. - Hastingsʼ main objective now was to destroy the independence of the three Maratha rulers - The Bhonsle, The Scindia and the Holkar. - Course of the War - Peshwa Baji Rao II who had earlier signed the Treaty of Bassein with time, began to feel strangulated and began to show signs of Independence. - Also the Treaty of Bassein, described as a Treaty with the Cipher, wounded the feelings of other Maratha Leaders, and they saw this treaty as absolute surrender of Independence. - Immediate Cause - Lord Hastingsʼ actions against the Pindaris were seen as a transgression of the sovereignty of the Marathas, there served to once again unite the Maratha confederacy. - A repentant Bajirao II made a last bid in 1817 by rallying together the Maratha Chiefs against the English in the course of the Third Anglo Maratha War. - But Marathas were now too weak to win against British - Different Battles were fought at different end by the British and the various powers of Marathas, however they all were defeated and forced to sign isolated treaties all together (Peshwa was defeated at Khirki, Bhonsle at Sitabuldi and Holkar at Mahidpur) - June 1817 - Treaty of Poona with Peshwa - November 1817 - Treaty of Gwalior with Scinida - January 1818 - Treat of Mandsaur with Holkar - Aftermath of Anglo Maratha War - In this way, The entire Maratha force was routed by superior military power of EIC. - Peshwa was forced to breakup the Maratha confederacy - Hastings decided to get rid of both - Peshwa and the Peshwaship. - Hence the Peshwa was dethroned, pensioned off and ordered to spend last days of his life in Bithoor near Kanpur. - His kingdom was brought under British Control and the enlarged Presidency of Bomday was brought into existence. - To satisfy the Maratha pride, a small kingdom of Satara was carved out of Peshwaʼs kingdom and given to Partap Singh, a direct descendant of Shivaji. - Thus by 1818, The entire Indian subcontinent except Sindh and Punjab had been brought under British Control, directly or indirectly. - Why Marathas Lost? - Inept Leadership - Maratha leaders like Baji Rao II lacked the strategic vision and unity of earlier figures like Shivaji, often prioritizing personal gain over collective resistance, weakening their response to British aggression. - Defective Nature of Maratha State - The Maratha Confederacy's decentralized structure, with autonomous chiefs like Scindia and Holkar, fostered rivalry rather than cooperation, undermining a unified front against the British. - Loose Political Setup - The lack of a strong central authority after the Third Battle of Panipat left the Marathas politically fragmented, making it easier for the British to exploit divisions through diplomacy and treaties. - Inferior Military System - Despite early adoption of European tactics, the Marathas failed to modernize consistently, relying on outdated cavalry against the British's disciplined infantry and artillery. - Unstable Economic Policy - Frequent internal conflicts and reliance on plunder rather than a stable revenue system drained Maratha resources, leaving them financially unable to sustain prolonged wars against the well-funded EIC. - Superior English Diplomacy and Espionage - The British, under leaders like Wellesley and Hastings, masterfully used treaties like Bassein and espionage to turn Maratha factions against each other, securing allies like the Nizam and isolating opponents. - Progressive English Outlook - The British leveraged industrial advancements and organizational efficiency, contrasting with the Marathas' traditional feudal approach, giving them an edge in logistics, communication, and sustained warfare. - War Years Summary - - Rise of British Supremacy (5) - Annexation of Punjab, Sindh and Awadh - Conquest of Sindh (1843) - Background - In the 18th century, Sindh was ruled by Kallora chiefs, in 1758, an English Factory was built at Thatta, owing to a royal order given by the chief. - This advantage was taken by the English up to 1775 when a not-too-friendly ruler, Sarfaraz Khan, made the English close their factory. - In 1780's, Sindh was captured by Talpuras, a Baloch Tribe, led by Mir Fateh Ali Khan. - After his death, it came to be shared by his 4 brothers, Known as 'Char Yar' who called themselves the Amirs of Sind. - Context of Anglo-French Rivalry - After 1807, The Anglo French rivalry shifted to North West. - After the French defeat in naval conflict, Napoleon planned to invade India via land route. - Alarmed by this, various diplomatic missions were sent to the frontier states and likewise Selton mission was sent to Sindh by Lord Minto, with the help of these diplomatic missions, friendly treaties were concluded with the respective governments to counter French Challenge. - Thus, in 1809, The Treaty of Eternal Friendship was signed with the Amirs, who promised not to allow the French to settle in Sindh. - In 1820, the treaty was renewed further to exclude Americans also from Sindh. - But soon the commercial and navigational value of the Indus began to attract the attention of the Company's authorities, therefore a new treaty was signed in 1832 between the Sindh and the English (Lord Bentick) according to which - - Amirs allowed a free passage to English travellers and merchants thorough Sindh and also allowed the use of Indus for commercial pursuits. - No English merchant would settle down in Sindh, and passports would be needed for travellers. - During the Great Game, Sindh was seen from a larger perspective of defence for Indian from the Russian threat. - Therefore, Sindh was a necessary prelude to annexation of Afghanistan. - Thus Sindh was conquered to counter Russia. - Soon Ranjit Singh captured Rojhan, a town on the Sindh frontier giving the Company a chance to offer protection to the Amirs. - The Amirs had neither desired nor asked for foreign help, yet they were forced to sign a Subsidiary Treaty in 1839 and accept a British Resident at Hyderabad. - Therefore the Amirs had virtually passed under British protection. - Context of Afghan War - During the Afghan War, Amirs found themselves saddled with the responsibility of helping the British forces, Parts of their territory were taken up for this and also they had to donate large amounts of money in order to maintain the troops which in reality they did not want. - In 1842, when Ellenborough succeeded Auckland, he was eager to find a pretext for the annexation of Sindh and in doing so, regain the English prestige which had suffered during the first Afghan War. - In September 1842, Chalres Napier was appointed as British Resident in Sindh. - He charged the Amirs for hostility and disaffection towards the British Government and therefore Sindh was annexed. - After all this he said - 'We have no right to seize Sindh, but we shall do so and a very advantageous, useful, humane, piece of rascality it will be'. - Sindh was finally annexed in 1843 after a brief campaign (Battle of Miani and Dabo) led by Sir Charles Napier. - Napier called the Sindh war as 'The tail of the Afghan Storm'. - Napier meant that the war in Sindh was a continuation or aftereffect of Britain's involvement in Afghanistan. - In 1847, Sindh was made part of British India's Bombay Presidency. - Please note - British annexation of Sindh in the 19th century was also intricately linked to the control of opium trade. - Side note - There were three Anglo-Afghan Wars - 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842) Cause: British feared Russian influence in Afghanistan and wanted to install a pro-British ruler. Key Event: British installed Shah Shuja as ruler, but faced strong resistance. Outcome: British forces suffered a disastrous retreat from Kabul in 1842, with almost the entire army being massacred. Result: British defeat and withdrawal from Afghanistan. - 2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878-1880) Cause: British again feared Russian influence in Kabul after Sher Ali welcomed a Russian envoy but rejected a British envoy. Key Event: British invaded Afghanistan and captured Kabul. Outcome: Treaty of Gandamak (1879), making Afghanistan a British protectorate in foreign affairs. Result: British victory, but internal instability continued. - 3rd Anglo-Afghan War (1919) Cause: After World War I, Afghanistan sought to reclaim its independence from British control. Key Event: Afghan forces under Amanullah Khan attacked British India. Outcome: Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919), granting Afghanistan full independence in foreign affairs. Result: Afghan victory—Afghanistan regained control over its foreign policy. - Conquest of Punjab (Anglo Sikh Wars) - Background - Punjab under Ranjit Singh - In 1799, Ranjit Singh was recognised as the Governor of Lahore by Zaman Shah, the ruler of Afghanistan. - In 1801, He proclaimed himself as the Maharaja of Punjab and by 1805, Ranjit Singh had acquired Jammu and Amritsar, making him the ruler of Punjab. - Due to the Russian French Threat, Metcalfe was sent to Punjab to conclude a favourable treaty with Ranjit Singh which was done on the condition that English would remain neutral in case of Sikh Afghan War and would consider Ranjit Singh the sovereign of the entire Punjab. - However the negotiations failed, but with time he agreed to sign the Treaty of Amritsar (April 25,1809) with the Company. - Sutlej as the boundary line for his dominions. - In 1838, Ranjit Singh was coerced into singing the Tripartiate Treaty with the English and Shah Shuja in oder to invade Afghanistan and install Shah Shuja as the ruler. - However, Ranjit Singh declined to allow British Troops. - Punjab after Ranjit Singh - Maharaja Ranjit Singh died in June 1839, His death was followed by political instability. (Sukerchakia Misl) - He left behind a military state which was guarded by 40,000 soldiers and the strength of this army increased three fold within 5 years of his death which proved to be a great burden on the shrinking resources of the state. - When the soldiers could not be paid properly, they went out of control and interfered in politics. - Alongside, death of his successors one after the another proved to be another big issue which deteriorated the affairs of the state, and the incompetent heirs were unable to check the forces of disorder. - In 1843, Dalip Singh, a minor son of Maharaja, was proclaimed king under the guardianship of Rani Jindan. - English had long been casting their eyes over the waters and the rich fertile lands of Punjab and waited for the right opportunity to interfere and moreover only the Punjab was the only dominion left in the entire India subcontinent which was outside their domination. - In 1843, Major Broadfoot was appointed as Company's political agent in Punjab. - He stressed on the disorder in Punjab and recounted every tale of corrupt behaviour at the court. - In 1844, Lord Ellenborough was succeeded by Lord Hardinge as Governor-General, he undertook various rigorous measures to strengthen the Company's military position. - The Company took a hypocritical stand and contended that the preparation were only defensive in nature and calculated to meet a possible attack from the Sikhs so that they could shift the responsibility of war on the shoulders of the Sikhs. - Rani Jindan dreaded the absolute power of the Khalsa army and found her only hope of security in urging it on to challenge British supremacy. - In 1845, Lal Singh, a lover of Rani Jindan, had won over the army on his side and became the wazir and made Teja Singh the new commander of the Sikh forces. - To the Sikhs, The British moves appeared more as an act of aggression rather than defence. - Therefore the Sikh troops led by Lal Singh, crossed the Satluj and took offensive actin against the English troops commanded by Sir Hugh Gough. - On 13 December, Hardinge, waiting for the opportunity, made his declaration of war. - First Anglo Sikh War (1845-46) - Five successive battles were fought between the British and the Sikh Army. - These were the battles of Mudki, Ferozshah, Baddowal and Aliwal and Sabroan - The fifth and the most decisive battle - Battle of Sobraon was fought on 10 February. - Due to treachery by Lal Singh and Teja Singh, ,who gave critical information to the British, the battle resulted in defeat of Sikhs, after which the British occupied Lahore and forced the Sikhs to sign the Treaty of Lahore which meant - - Maharaja gave up all these territories south of River Satluj. - To pay Rs. 1 crore war indemnity, and upon its failure in order to compensate British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh for Rs 75 Lakhs. - Minor Dalip Singh was accepted as king with Queen Jindan as guardian and Lal Singh was Wazir. - Sir Henry Lawrence became the British Resident at Lahore. - Sikhs disliked Kashmir begin sold to Gulab Singh and once again revolted under the leadership of Lal Singh, the revolt was suppressed by the British and once again Treaty of Bharioval was signed which included - - Rani Jindan's guardianship was cancelled and she was pensioned off. - A Council of 8 Sikh Chiefs under the Chairmanship of British Resident was appointed for governance work. - It was decided that a permanent British Army will be placed at Lahore until Dalip Singh became a major. - Second Anglo Sikh War (1848 - 1849) - After the Treaty of Bhairowal, The British Resident became the virtual ruler of Punjab with unlimited civil and military powers. - When Rani Jindan showed her resentment towards such usurpation of powers, her jewellery was seized and she was sent to Sheikhpura. - Her pension was also arbitrarily reduced. - The New Governor General Dalhousie soon got his opportunity for annexation when 2 British officers, Vans Angew and Lt. Anderson were murdered and other Sikh chiefs joined hands together in order to refer against the British. - Thus Dalhousie declared war and three battles were fought - Battle of Ramnagar - Indecisive - Battle of Chillianwala - Indecisive - Battle of Gujarat - Sikh Army was defeated due to treachery by its officials - Battle of Guns. - Conquest of Punjab - After the collapse of the Sikh army, Dalhousie advocated for annexation, stating, - “There never can be now any guarantee for the tranquility of India until we shall have effected the entire subjugation of the Sikh People and destroyed its power as an Independent Nation.” - On 29 March 1849, Punjab was formally annexed (forcible or legal incorporation of one territory into another) by the British. - Maharaja Dalip Singh was pensioned off and sent to England. - The Kohinoor Diamond was taken from Dalip Singh and surrendered to the British Crown. - For administration, Punjab was initially governed by a three-member board. - In 1853, the board was abolished, and Punjab was placed under a Chief Commissioner. - John Lawrence became the first Chief Commissioner of Punjab. - Annexation of Awadh - Early Confrontation - The state of Awadh came into direct confrontation with the British during the Battle of Buxar in 1764 when Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh) joined the opposing forces. - Awadh then lay at the mercy of the British, but Clive decided not to annex it. - At that time, Awadh was restored to the Nawab after signing the Treaty of Allahabad (1765). - The Treaty of 1801 (Subsidiary Alliance) - When Governor-General Lord Wellesley came to India, he forced the new Nawab, Saadat Ali Khan, to sign a new treaty in the year 1801. - As per this treaty, the Nawab had to cede half of his territory. - He was also required to act as per the advice of the Council of British officers. - This treaty of 1801 laid the foundation for the annexation of Awadh, as British interference in its administration led to rampant corruption and misgovernance, with the blame placed entirely on Saadat Ali Khan. - Final Annexation - By the mid-19th century, British opinion strongly favored the annexation of Awadh. - The British imperialists believed that only Britain had the capacity for good governance. - However, Dalhousie's primary interest lay in Awadh's economic potential as a market for Manchester goods. - Accordingly, in 1848, when Lord Dalhousie became Governor-General, he skillfully planned the annexation of Awadh. - He appointed Colonel Sleeman as Resident in Lucknow, who actively sought evidence of misgovernance in Awadh. - Finally, in 1856, Awadh was annexed by Lord Dalhousie on the pretext of maladministration, based on Outram's report (who succeeded Sleeman). - The Nawab, Wajid Ali Shah, was placed under house arrest in Calcutta. - This incident particularly angered the sepoys of the British Army, as many of them were from Awadh. - The new land revenue system introduced after the annexation further intensified the people's discontent, leading to nearly three-fourths of the adult population of Awadh, including landholders, peasants, and sepoys, participating in the Revolt of 1857. - British Expansion Beyond Borders - Anglo Nepal War - - Overview - The British wanted protection from the Chinese in the North, therefore they looked at Nepal as a stable buffer state between India and Tibet or China. - However, the Gorkhas also wanted to expand their territories in the south (As they were unable to do it in the Chinese territory of the North), so in May 1814, they attacked three police stations at Butwal, then under the EICʼs authority. - Governor General Hasting took it as a challenge to Companyʼs authority and decided to launch an offensive campaign against them. - This led to the Nepal War in October 1814, finally the Nepalis were defeated and forced to sign the Treaty of Sugauli (March 1816). - Nepal accepted a British Resident. - it means Nepal agreed to allow a British official (Resident) to be stationed in its capital, Kathmandu, to act as a diplomatic representative of the British East India Company. - Nepal ceded (to give up control of land, rights, or power, usually through a treaty, war, or agreement) the territories of Garhwal, Kumaon and abandoned claims to Terai region. - Nepal also withdrew from Sikkim - The British gained the districts of Garhwal and Kumaon and a resident was placed at Kathmandu and even they allowed no diplomatic mission, other than that of Britain into Nepal , but in return they treated the Nepalese ruler as sovereign. - British Expansion beyond Borders - Burma - - - First Anglo Burmese War (1824 - 1826) - Immediate Cause - In 1823-24, The Burmese Military, in its pursuit for rebels, entered and occupied Assam and Manipur and prepared to attack Chittagong. - These territories were, however, claimed by the English in India. - The British Indian Army attacked Burma in retaliation, which came to be known as the First Anglo Burmese War. - Course and Outcome - In 1824, The British Indian army attacked Burma. - The Burmese forces led by Maha Bandula were easily defeated and the King was forced to sign a peace treaty, Treaty of Yandabo. - As per the Treaty, The English regained control over Assam, Manipur and occupied Arakan and Tenasserim region, Thus the King lost most of his coast. - The King was forced to accept a British resident at his capital and pay war indemnity - Second Anglo Burmese War (1852) - Background - In 1839, an English resident claimed that the Burmese Officials did not treat him well and lef. - Meanwhile, Burma emerged as a major supplier of timber and other costly items like tin, pepper and ivory. - The delta of Irrawaddy river also emerged as a major supplier of rice to Bengal and to the growing settlements in south-east Asia. - These developments tempted the British to look for an opportunity to annex Burma. - Immediate Context - Two British captains were heavily fined by Burmese Government on certain charges brought against them. - Following the incident, the British merchants sent a petition to then Governor General Lord Dalhousie, providing the desired opportunity. - Thus in 1852, Dalhousie decided to attack Burma on the pretext of restoring the dignity of the English. - Finally the Burmese were defeated, territories annexed gaining the entire coast of Bay of Bengal and the Burmese King was forced to shif his capital to Mandalay. - Third Anglo Burmese War (1885) - It took place in 1885 when the English attacked Burma on the pretext that the King was intriguing with the French in Vietnam to weaken English control over Asia. - The war ended in English victory and annexation of Upper Burma, thus Burma was turned into a province of British India (1937 onwards, Burma was governed as a separate colony) - British Expansion beyond Borders - Afghanistan - - Afghanistan - The Russian Threat - The 19th century was a period of diplomatic competition between the British and Russian empires for spheres of influence in Asia known as ʻthe Great Gameʼ to the British and the ʻTournament of Shadowsʼ to the Russians. - Thus, any Russian advance in Central Asia was always assumed in London to be directed towards the conquest of India. - In 1832, British had expanded its franchise which was condemned by Emperor Nicolas I of Russia. - This set the stage for ʻcold war between autocratic Russia and democratic Britainʼ. - In 1837, British fearing the instability of Afghanistan, The Sindh and the increasing power of the Sikh Kingdom in the northwest, raised the spectre of a possible Russian invasion of British India through Afghanistan, the only entrance to India from Central Asia. - Afghanistan - British Reaction to Russian Threat - Forward Policy - One reaction was to secure commanding influence in Afghanistan, either by Annexation or by creating it as a buffer stage. (View held by conservatives) - Policy of Masterly Inactivity (Also known as ʻStationary Schoolʼ) - Another reaction was to reach a diplomatic understanding with Russia and follow as policy of non-intervention as far as Afghanistan was concerned. (View held by Liberals). - First Anglo Afghan War (1838 - 1842) - British Reaction to Russian Threat - In 1830s, The British became over anxious to protect Afghanistan leading the the First Anglo Afghan War which proved to be a great disaster for the British. - A direct consequence of this was the annexation of Sindh (1843) and Punjab (1849) and made the British Indiaʼs frontier directly co-terminus with that of Afghanistan. - The concern for imperial defence and search for a scientific border in the north-west brought the English in contact with the Afghans. - Afghanistan was considered as a buffer state against the Napoleonic France and Czarist Russia. - It was felt that Afghanistan should be under the control of a friendly prince. - Initially, the Relations with Dost Mohammad (Amir of Afghanistan) was good but with time he began showing signs of friendship with Russia. - The concern for imperial defence and search for a scientific border in the north-west brought the English in contact with the Afghans. - Afghanistan was considered as a buffer state against the Napoleonic France and Czarist Russia. - It was felt that Afghanistan should be under the control of a friendly prince. - Initially, the Relations with Dost Mohammad (Amir of Afghanistan) was good but with time he began showing signs of friendship with Russia. - In September 1837, British sent a commercial mission to Afghanistan (Burnes Mission), but in reality it was to judge the political situation there. - During the rounds of negotiation which could not lead to any fruitful result, Dost Mohammad received the Russian ambassador and with much warmth. - Afer the failure of this Burns Mission, Governor General Auckland decided to follow a ʻForward Policyʼ, he planned to depose Dost Muhammad and entrust the country in the hands of some Friendly prince. - Course of the War - Tripartite Treaty - Between English, Shah Shuja (Ex-ruler of Afghanistan) and Ranjit Singh - combined forces of the three parties, known as ʻArmy of the Indusʼ launched an attack on Kabul. - The combined forces won but there were glitches in this plan as Shah Shuja (New Amir of Afghanistan) was unacceptable to the people of Afghanistan and his position could be maintained only with the help of British Army. - Thus a small garrison was placed at Kabul under the command of General Elphinstone, but the English continued to face retaliation. - Thereafer, numerous battles were fought and in the end - disastrous retreat began from Kabul in 1842. - Elphinstone along with his garrison were annihilated in the snow covered passes and Shah Shuja was murdered. - Aucklandʼs grandiose plan had exploded like ballon and he was soon replaced by Lord Ellenborough, He ordered the retreat of forces and securing the release of prisoners and subsequently Dost Mohammad was re-established his authority in Kabul. - Second Anglo Afghan War (1878 - 1880) - The Second Afghan war (1878 -1880) occurred at the time of Governor-General Lytton and ended with the Treaty of Gandamak. - As per this treaty, the Amir Yakub Khan Agreed to station a permanent British Resident at Kabul and conduct his foreign policy on advise of the Government of India. - Thus, Afghanistan was created as a buffer state between the British Indian and Russian Empire. - Reasons for Expansion beyond Indian Frontiers - Shifting Financial Base of the East India Company (From Trade to Land Revenue) - As trade profits declined due to European competition and monopolies eroded, the EIC increasingly relied on land revenue from conquered territories to sustain its operations and fund further expansion. - Need for New Markets and Supplies - The Industrial Revolution in Britain demanded raw materials like cotton, timber, and opium, and new markets for manufactured goods, driving the EIC to secure regions like Burma and Awadh. - Need to Safeguard Indian Empire - The perceived threats from Russia, France, and local powers like the Gorkhas necessitated buffer states—Nepal, Afghanistan, Burma—to protect British India's frontiers and trade routes. - Tibet & History with British - Treaty of Lhasa (1904) - with Tibet - Tibet would respect the frontier to Sikkim - Tibet would not grant any concessions to any foreign power, but would give some control over the foreign affairs of Tibet. - Thus reducing Tibet to the status of a protectorate of the British. - Afer the Chinese Revolution of 1911, the British accepted Chinaʼs suzerainty over eastern Tibet, and the western zone was declared autonomous. - It was decided to draw a boundary line between Tibet and British India known as the Manmohan Line - Other Important Points - Duran Line - British India and Afghanistan - Established in 1893 by Sir Mortimer Durand, this line demarcated the border between British India and Afghanistan, aimed at securing a scientific frontier against Russian influence, though it remains contested to this day. - Treaty of Punakha (1910) - recognising the Bhutanese ruler as sovereign in all matters expect foreign relations, which were placed under British control. - Revolt of 1857 - Political Causes - Discontent among Ruling Chiefs and Royal Families - Broken pledges and oaths resulted in loss of political prestige for some. - Policies such as 'Subsidiary Alliance' and 'Doctrine of Lapse' caused alarm and suspicion in the minds of others. - Doctrine of lapse - The Doctrine of Lapse was formally introduced in 1848 by Lord Dalhousie, who was the Governor-General of India from 1848 to 1856. - However, the policy had been informally applied even before Dalhousie's tenure, but he aggressively implemented it to annex several princely states that had no direct male heirs. - Key Features of the Doctrine of Lapse: - Applied mainly to Hindu states where adoption was a customary way to continue dynastic rule. - Justified under the pretext of ensuring "good governance" but primarily used for British expansion. - Several states were annexed under this policy, including: - Satara (1848) - Sambalpur (1850) - Jhansi (1853) - Nagpur (1854) - Subsidiary alliance - The Subsidiary Alliance was a diplomatic and military strategy introduced by Lord Wellesley in 1798 to expand British influence in India. - Key Features of the Subsidiary Alliance: - British troops in Indian states: - The Indian ruler had to accept a British contingent within their territory for protection. - Ban on foreign alliances: - The ruler could not form alliances with any other foreign power or Indian state without British approval. - No employment of Europeans: - The state was prohibited from employing any European officials without British consent. - British Resident: - A British Resident (official representative) was stationed in the state to oversee administration. - Financial burden: - The Indian ruler had to pay for the maintenance of British troops. If they failed, part of their territory would be annexed. - States that Accepted the Alliance: - Hyderabad (1798) : First state to sign. - Mysore (1799) : After Tipu Sultan's defeat. - Awadh (1801) : Forced to cede half of its territory. - Peshwa (1802) : Signed under pressure after defeat by Holkars. - Collapse of Rulers (Erstwhile Aristocracy) - Adversely affected sections of Indian society dependent on cultural and religious pursuits for sustenance (Basic Necessities for Survival). - Alien Rule of the British - Practice of 'Absentee Sovereignty' embittered (feeling resentful, angry, or full of bitterness due to past experiences, unfair treatment, or disappointments) Indians against the British. - Absentee Sovereignty refers to a situation where a ruler or sovereign exercises control over a territory without being physically present there. - The governance is typically conducted through appointed officials or local representatives. - Example in British India: - The British exercised absentee sovereignty over India, meaning the British Crown ruled India while the actual governance was carried out by the East India Company (till 1858) and later by British officials under the British Raj (1858-1947). - The decisions affecting India were made in London, while Indians had little to no direct representation in their own governance. - Anti-British feelings particularly strong in regions like Burma, Assam, Coorg, Sind, and Punjab, unjustly annexed to the British Empire. - Abolition of Regal Titles - Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah II had grown old and weak. - Lord Dalhousie recognized succession of Mughal Prince Faqir-Ud-Din but imposed strict conditions, opposing an imperium in imperio (a Latin phrase meaning "a state within a state."). - In 1856, Faqir-Ud-Din died, and Lord Canning declared the next prince in succession would renounce (To formally give up, reject, or abandon something) the regal (Relating to a king or queen; majestic, royal, or dignified) title and ancestral Mughal palaces. - British abolished regal titles of Nawabs of Carnatic and Tanjore. - Economic Causes - Exploitative Land Revenue Settlements Introduced by British - Huge drain of wealth, destruction of industry, and increasing land revenue (Permanent, Ryotwari, and Mahalwari settlements) were common in the latter half of the eighteenth century. - Summary Settlement of Awadh - Proceeded to remove taluqdars wherever possible. - Pre-British times: Taluqdars held 67% of villages in Awadh; post-Summary Settlement, reduced to 38%. - Southern Awadh taluqdars hardest hit, some losing over half their villages. - British land revenue officers aimed to settle land with actual owners, reducing peasant exploitation while increasing state revenue. - East India Company used political power to fund British trade and commerce at the cost of Indians. - New Plantation System (1833) - Resulted in incalculable misery for Indian peasants. - Permitted Englishmen to acquire land plantations in India. - Hardest hit: Peasants on indigo plantations in Bengal and Bihar (Teen Kathiya System). - Zamindars (traditional landed aristocracy) often lost land rights, leading to loss of status in villages. - Dispossessed taluqdars seized opportunities during the sepoy revolt, especially in Awadh. - Destruction of Indian Trade, Handicraft, and Industry - High tariffs in Britain against Indian goods damaged Indian trade and manufacture. - Encouraged import of British goods to India. - Ruin of millions of artisans and craftsmen not accompanied by new industrial growth. - Annexation of Indian states cut off major sources of patronage. - Moneylenders and Traders as New Landlords - Peasants, compelled by new revenue settlements, resorted to loans from moneylenders/traders at usurious rates. - Moneylenders often evicted peasants for nonpayment of debts. - Ruination of Indian industry increased pressure on agriculture and land. - Social Causes - Arrogant Attitude of the British and Racial Discrimination - Racial overtones and superiority complex characterized British behavior. - Indiscrimination and assaults on Indians by Englishmen became common. - British Interference in Religion and Culture - Activities of Christian missionaries raised alarm among Hindus and Muslims (Charter Act of 1813). - Missionary-established educational institutions inculcated Western education and culture, replacing oriental learning. - The Charter Act of 1813 was a significant legislation passed by the British Parliament that renewed the East India Company's charter but also introduced major changes in the governance of India. - Key Provisions of the Charter Act of 1813 - End of Trade Monopoly (Except for Tea & China Trade) - The Act abolished the East India Company's monopoly over Indian trade, except for tea and trade with China. - This allowed private British merchants to trade freely with India. - Company's Political Authority Continued - Though the trade monopoly ended, the Company's political and administrative control over British India was renewed for another 20 years. - Permission for Christian Missionaries - For the first time, Christian missionaries were officially allowed to enter India for propagation of Christianity and establishing educational institutions. - Financial Provision for Education - A sum of ₹1 lakh was allocated annually for the promotion of education in India. - This laid the foundation for British-sponsored education policies. - Regulation of Indian Trade & Commercial Policies - The British Crown asserted sovereignty over British India, making it clear that the Company ruled in trust for the British Government. - Restrictions were placed on the activities of Indian merchants and artisans in certain trades. - Power of Governors Extended - The Governor-General and Governors of Presidencies were given more legislative powers to regulate and administer their territories. - Significance of the Charter Act of 1813 - It marked the beginning of free trade in India under British rule. - Led to increased missionary activities, influencing Indian society and culture. - Laid the groundwork for British intervention in Indian education. - Strengthened British control over the Indian subcontinent. - Legislations - Prohibition of female infanticide, sati, and slavery. - Widow marriage legislation. - Religious Disabilities Act (1850) modified Hindu customs (e.g., a change of religion did not debar (To exclude or prevent someone from doing something) inheritance from a heathen (A person who does not belong to a widely practiced religion) father). - Military Causes - Low Salary and Poor Prospects of Promotion - Conditions of service in the Company's Army conflicted with sepoys' religious beliefs and prejudices. - Vellore Mutiny (a rebellion or open resistance against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors against their commanding officers) (1806) was a precursor to 1857, reflecting such tensions. - Indian sepoys unhappy with emoluments (salary, wages, or other benefits received as compensation for holding an office or employment) compared to British counterparts. - No foreign service allowance (batta) when serving in Sindh or Punjab. -
