Racial discrimination in promotion and privileges; sepoys felt subordinate. - Sepoys as 'peasants in uniform,' consciousness tied to rural population. - Post Office Act (1854) withdrew sepoys' free postage privilege. - Rumours - Reports of bone dust in flour rations close to 1857. - The most infamous rumor was that the new Enfield rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat. - A rumor spread that the British planned to gradually replace Indian sepoys with European soldiers, leading to fear of mass unemployment among sepoys. - Religious reasons - Crossing seas meant loss of caste for religious Hindus. - General Service Enlistment Act (1856) required Bengal Army recruits to serve anywhere needed, decreed (officially ordered or declared by an authority) by Lord Canning's Government. - Restrictions on wearing caste/sectarian marks and rumors of chaplains' (Religious officials or priests, usually Christian) proselytizing (act of trying to convert someone to a different religion or belief) who were maintained at Company expense was seen as interference in religious affairs. - Invincibility of British Rule Shattered - British losses in Afghan Wars (1838-1842), Punjab Wars (1845-1849), and Crimea War (1854-1856) emboldened (given courage or confidence to act boldly or assertively) sepoys. - Sepoys awaited a trigger (greased cartridge event) to express anger. - Long history of revolts: Bengal (1764), Vellore (1806), Barrackpore (1825), Afghan Wars (1838-1842). - Events Leading to the Revolt - 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur - The regiment refused to use the newly introduced Enfield rifles, as the cartridges were rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat, which hurt religious sentiments. - The soldiers mutinied in February 1857, but the British quickly suppressed it. - As punishment, the regiment was disbanded in March 1857. - 34th Native Infantry - On March 29, 1857, Mangal Pandey, a soldier of the 34th Native Infantry at Barrackpore, attacked a British officer in protest against the use of greased cartridges. - He was captured, tried, and executed on April 6, 1857. - The entire regiment was disbanded in May 1857 for failing to stop Pandey's actions. - 7th Awadh Regiment - On May 3, 1857, soldiers of the 7th Awadh Regiment refused to obey their British officers, showing signs of rebellion. - The British took strict action, and the regiment was dissolved. - 3rd Native Cavalry - April 24, 1857: Ninety soldiers of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut refused to use the greased cartridges, considering it a violation of their religious beliefs. - May 9, 1857: Eighty-five of these soldiers were court-martialed, dismissed from service, sentenced to 10 years of imprisonment, and publicly shackled as punishment. - May 10, 1857: The remaining soldiers revolted against the British. - They freed their imprisoned comrades. - Killed several British officers and unfurled the banner of rebellion. - Marched to Delhi, marking the beginning of the larger uprising of 1857. - The Great Revolt - Began at Meerut (58 km from Delhi) on May 10, 1857; spread to Punjab (north), Narmada (south), Bihar (east), Rajputana (west). - Delhi - Local infantry joined, killed European officers (e.g., Simon Fraser), seized city. - Bahadur Shah Zafar proclaimed emperor; traditional symbol of India's unity. - Indian chiefs proclaimed loyalty to Mughal emperor. - May 12: Rebelling sepoys overcame Lt. Willoughby, seized Delhi—a blow to British prestige. - Bahadur Shah urged chiefs/rulers to form a confederacy against British. - Spread of Revolt - Bengal Army rose; Awadh, Rohilkhand, Doab, Bundelkhand, central India, Bihar, East Punjab shook off British authority. - Civil population rebelled, especially in north-western provinces and Awadh. - Widespread participation: Peasantry, artisans, shopkeepers, laborers, zamindars, mendicants, priests, civil servants gave it popular character. - Peasants/petty zamindars attacked moneylenders/zamindars, destroyed debt records, targeted British law courts, revenue offices, police stations. - Limited spread: North of Narmada largely undisturbed. - Notable Hindu-Muslim unity during revolt. - Storm Centres and Leaders of the Revolt - - Delhi: - Bahadur Shah II was declared the symbolic leader of the revolt, though he had little real power. - The actual command was held by General Bakht Khan, who led troops from Bareilly. - Kanpur: - Nana Saheb, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, led the rebellion in Kanpur. - He expelled the British, declared himself Peshwa, and recognized Bahadur Shah II as the emperor. - Tantya Tope played a key role in the military operations. - Lucknow: - Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt on June 4, 1857. - She gained massive local support, especially from those loyal to the deposed Nawab of Awadh. - Jhansi: - The British had rejected the claim of Damodar Rao, the adopted son of Rani Lakshmibai and Gangadhar Rao, under the Doctrine of Lapse. - Rani Lakshmibai took up arms against the British, emerging as one of the most prominent leaders of the revolt. - Bareilly: - Khan Bahadur Khan led the rebellion against the British in this region. - Bihar: - Kunwar Singh, a zamindar from Jagdishpur, joined the sepoys in Arrah. - He had a deep resentment against the British, as he had lost his estates due to their policies. - Faizabad: - Maulvi Ahmadullah played a key role in the rebellion in Awadh. - He led a strong resistance against the British and was acknowledged as a leader in May 1857. - Singhbhum (Chotanagpur region): - Gonoo, a tribal cultivator, led the Kol tribals in their uprising. - Chaurasee Des: - Shah Mal mobilized local cultivators and acted as an independent ruler. - He established a justice system and an intelligence network. - He was eventually killed in July 1857. - Suppression of Revolt - Fall of Delhi (September 20, 1857) - British forces led by General John Nicholson captured Delhi after intense fighting. - Bahadur Shah II taken prisoner; his sons publicly executed by William Hodson. - Mughal rule effectively ended; Bahadur Shah exiled to Rangoon, died in 1862. - Kanpur Campaign - Nana Saheb expelled the British and declared himself Peshwa. - British forces under Havelock and later Colin Campbell recaptured Kanpur. - Nana Saheb fled to Nepal (1859); fate uncertain. - Tantya Tope continued guerrilla warfare, captured April 1859, executed. - Fall of Jhansi and Death of Rani Lakshmibai (June 1858) - Jhansi besieged by Sir Hugh Rose; Rani Lakshmibai escaped to Kalpi. - Joined Tantya Tope, fought at Gwalior; died in battle. - Suppression in Bihar and Awadh - Kunwar Singh led the rebellion in Bihar; wounded in battle, died April 1858. - Begum Hazrat Mahal led resistance in Awadh; fled to Nepal after defeat. - Maulvi Ahmadullah fought in Faizabad; killed in battle (1858). - Other Centers of Revolt - Bareilly: Khan Bahadur Khan led resistance; captured and executed. - Chotanagpur: Gonoo led Kol tribal revolt; British suppressed rebellion. - Chaurasee Des: Shah Mal led peasant resistance; killed in July 1857. - Final Defeat and Reestablishment of British Rule - By 1859, major leaders dead or in exile; British fully reestablished control. - Harsh retribution: mass executions, village destruction, and land confiscations. - Key British Officers - Delhi and Lucknow: Sir Colin Campbell. - Jhansi and Gwalior: Sir Hugh Rose. - Banaras: Colonel James Neill. - Reasons for Failure - Limited Territorial Spread - No all-India veneer; eastern, southern, western India largely unaffected. - Certain classes/groups (e.g., Scindia of Gwalior) worked against revolt. - Opposition by Big Zamindars - Acted as "breakwaters to storm"; Awadh tehsildars backed off with land restitution promises. - Moneylenders/merchants saw interests protected under British. - Support by Educated Indians - Viewed revolt as backward-looking, hoped British would modernize India. - Most Indian rulers refused to join, often aided British. - European Modern War Machinery - Indian soldiers poorly equipped (swords, spears, few guns) vs. British with Enfield rifles. - Electric telegraph kept British commanders informed. - Poor Organization - No coordination or central leadership. - Leaders (Nana Saheb, Tantya Tope, Kunwar Singh, Laxmibai) outmatched by British generals. - Rebels lacked clear understanding of colonial rule, forward-looking program, ideology, or societal alternative. - Diverse elements with differing grievances and political concepts. - Consequences - End of Company Rule and Beginning of Crown Rule - The British Crown assumed direct control over India; the East India Company was abolished. - Announced by Lord Canning at the Allahabad Durbar through the Queen's Proclamation on November 1, 1858. - Proclamation assured non-interference in religious practices, equal treatment under British law, and protection of princely states. - Administrative Changes - A new position, Secretary of State for India, created to oversee governance. - Viceroy replaced the Governor-General as the highest authority in India. - The British Indian Army reorganized to reduce reliance on Indian soldiers, increasing European troop ratio. - Sepoy recruitment favored non-rebellious communities like Sikhs, Gurkhas, and Pathans. - Strengthening of British Control - Policy of divide and rule intensified; communal divisions were subtly encouraged. - Indian princely states, previously under threat from the Doctrine of Lapse, were assured their sovereignty under British suzerainty (a situation where a powerful state (suzerain) controls the foreign affairs and overall authority of a weaker state while allowing it internal autonomy). - Land and property of rebels were confiscated (forcibly taken away, usually by a government or authority, without compensation), weakening Indian elites and zamindars. - Social and Economic Impact - British policies became more conservative, avoiding social reforms that could trigger unrest. - Heavy economic exploitation continued, draining India's wealth. - Large-scale displacement due to land confiscations and repressive revenue policies led to worsening conditions for peasants. - Impact on Indian Nationalism - The brutal suppression and racial policies of the British fueled resentment (feeling of anger, bitterness, or deep dissatisfaction, often due to perceived injustice, unfair treatment, or oppression). - The Revolt, despite its failure, inspired later nationalist movements, laying the groundwork for the Indian freedom struggle. - Awareness grew among Indians about the need for unity against British rule. - Military Reforms - British increased European troop strength in India. - Artillery was kept exclusively under British control. - Indian regiments were divided to prevent large-scale mutinies in the future. - Psychological Impact - The British viewed Indians with increased suspicion and treated them as an inferior race. - The revolt instilled both fear and realization among Indians, leading to the emergence of organized political movements in later decades. - Post 1857 Scenario - Aftermath of Revolt of 1857 - The Act for Better Government of India, 1858 - Passed August 2, 1858, before revolt fully suppressed. - Exposed Company's administrative limitations. - Provisions - India governed by Crown via Secretary of State and 15-member council (advisory). - Initiative/final decision with Secretary of State; dual system of Pitt's India Act ended. - Governor-General became Viceroy (increased prestige, not authority). - Formal assumption of power by Crown; end of Company administration. - Queen's Proclamation, 1858 - Announced by Lord Canning at Allahabad durbar, November 1, 1858. - Governor-General titled 'Viceroy'. - Provisions - End of annexations/expansion; respect for native princes' dignity/rights. - Indian states to recognize British Crown's paramountcy. - Freedom of religion without British interference. - Equal/impartial protection under law, equal opportunities in government services, respect for old Indian rights/customs in law-making. - Changes in the Army - Thorough reorganization; “division and counterpoise” policy. - Reduced Indian soldiers, increased European soldiers. - Recruits from 'martial' (related to war, the military, or soldiers) races (Punjab, Nepal, NW frontier) loyal during revolt. - Army separated from civilians. - Indian artillery units (except mountain batteries) defunct (something that is no longer in existence, operation, or function); higher posts reserved for Europeans. - Military Policy Changes - European soldier ratio: Bengal (1:2), Bombay/Madras (1:3 or 2:5). - Big positions/artillery reserved for Europeans. - Awadh, Bihar, Central India soldiers deemed non-martial; Punjabis, Gorkhas, Pathans (loyalists) recruited heavily (half of army by 1875). - Changes in Approach - Reformist zeal faded; conservatives in Britain viewed Indians as beyond reform, ending reform era. - Empire became more autocratic, denying educated Indians' power-sharing aspirations. - Divide-and-rule policy intensified, using one class/community against another. - Systematic economic exploitation began without fear. - Government structure remodeled on 'master race' notion, widening ruler-ruled gulf. - Other Changes - Policy towards Upper Class (Princes and Landlords) - Annexation policy abandoned. - Princes/landlords rewarded and befriended. - Britain as paramount power; Queen Victoria titled 'Empress of India' (1876). - Hostility (unfriendly, aggressive, or opposed to something) towards Higher Education - British became hostile, curtailed (reduced, limited, or cut short) education post-Indian National Congress (1885). - Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 - Annual competitive exam in London for equality/transparency. - Rules framed to keep civil services a British preserve. - Change in Attitude towards Educated Indians - Indian Councils Act of 1861 - Sir Bartle Frere's 1860 Minute pushed for Indian representation in Legislative Council due to ruler-ruled miscommunication. - Marked start of active Indian representation. - Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 (repeated for emphasis) - Exam in London; rules preserved British dominance. - The Azamgarh Proclamation of 1857 - Authored mostly by Firoz Shah (grandson of Bahadur Shah II). - Highlights - Detailed complaints of social groups against unfair colonial authority. - Proclaimed Mughals' capacity to establish suzerainty over India. - Advised rulers/chieftains to accept Delhi throne, defend people. - Claimed both Hindus and Muslims ruined under English tyranny. - Assured brighter future post-English defeat; urged acceptance of Badshahi Government. - British Portrayal of the Revolt - The Clemency of Canning - Governor-General Canning's leniency to win sepoy loyalty mocked in British press. - The British magazine Punch published a cartoon/illustration showing Canning as father figure over bloodied sepoy, titled 'The Clemency of Canning'. - The phrase "Clemency of Canning" became a symbol of British hypocrisy—where brutal repression was expected, and any attempt at mercy was ridiculed. - Ironically, while he was mocked in Britain, in India, his policies were still seen as oppressive, as he upheld British control while trying to pacify the population. - Political Associations before 1885 & Formation of Indian National Congress - Political Associations before the Indian National Congress - Early Nineteenth Century Associations - Dominated by wealthy and aristocratic elements. - Local or regional in character. - Demands through long petitions to British Parliament: - Administrative reforms. - Association of Indians with the administration. - Spread of education. - Second Half of Nineteenth Century Associations - Increasingly dominated by educated middle class (lawyers, journalists, doctors, teachers, etc.). - Wider perspective and larger agenda. - Political Associations in Bengal - Raja Ram Mohan Roy - Morning Star of Reform Movement; first great leader of modern India. - Pioneer of political movement in India. - Well-read, influenced by Western ideas; first to focus Englishmen's attention on Indian grievances (complaints, injustices, or issues that cause dissatisfaction and resentment). - Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha (1836) - Formed by associates of Raja Rammohan Roy. - Aim: Discuss government policy, seek redressal through petitions and memorandums. - Landholders Society/Zamindari Association (1838) - Founded by Dwarka Nath Tagore, RadhaKanta Deb, and others. - Purpose: Safeguard interests of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. - Credited with launching organized political activity in India using constitutional methods for grievance redressal. - Marked beginning of organized political activity and constitutional agitation. - Bengal British India Society (1843) - Objectives: - Collection and dissemination of information on the actual condition of British India's people. - Employ peaceful, lawful means to secure welfare, extend just rights, and advance interests of all classes. - British Indian Association (1851) - Merger of Landholders' Society and Bengal British India Society. - Suggestions to British Parliament for Company Charter: - Establishment of a separate, popular legislature. - Separation of executive from judicial functions. - Reduction in salaries of higher officers. - Abolition of salt duty, abkari, and stamp duties. - Charter Act of 1853 partially met demands by adding 6 legislative members to Governor General's Council. - Continued functioning post-Indian National Congress formation. - Branches established in Bombay (Bombay Association) and Madras (Madras Native Association) in 1852. - Political Associations in Bombay - Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) - Founded in 1867 by Mahadeo Govind Ranade and others. - Objective: Serve as a bridge between government and people. - Platform for voicing political concerns: - Demanded Indian representation in Parliament. - Protested Vernacular Press Act. - Involved in settling agrarian disputes. - Considered a precursor to Indian National Congress (also formed in Maharashtra). - Bombay Presidency Association (1885) - Started by Badruddin Tyabji, Pherozshah Mehta, and K.T. Telang. - Championed Indian interests. - Hosted first Indian National Congress meeting in Bombay, end of 1885. - Political Associations in Madras - Madras Native Association (1852) - Branch of British Indian Association of Calcutta, founded by Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty. - Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) - Founded by M. Viraraghavachari, B. Subramanya Aiyar, and P. Anandacharlu. - Purpose: Coordinate activities of local associations. - Political Associations in England - East India Association (1866) - Organized by Dadabhai Naoroji in London. - Purpose: Discuss Indian issues, influence English public men to promote Indian welfare. - Later established branches in prominent Indian cities. - Other National Associations - India League (1875) - Started by Sisir Kumar Ghosh. - Objective: Stimulate nationalism and encourage political education. - Ghosh: Noted journalist, founder of Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengali newspaper). - Indian Association (1876) - Most important pre-Congress organization. - Also known as Indian National Association of Calcutta. - Founded by Surendra Nath Banerjee and younger Bengal nationalists. - Aims: - Create strong public opinion on political questions. - Unify Indians in a common political program. - Demands: - Simultaneous civil service exams in England and India. - Indianization of higher administrative posts. - Campaigned against repressive Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act. - Arms Act (1878) - This act disarmed Indians by prohibiting them from possessing firearms without a license. - The law excluded Europeans and Anglo-Indians, which was seen as a racial discrimination tactic. - The British justified it as a measure to prevent uprisings after the 1857 Revolt. - It was heavily criticized by nationalists like Surendranath Banerjee, who saw it as an insult to Indians and a way to weaken their ability to resist British rule. - Vernacular Press Act (1878) - This act curbed the freedom of Indian-language newspapers, preventing them from criticizing British policies. - Any newspaper publishing “seditious” material could be shut down without trial. - The law mainly targeted Indian-owned vernacular newspapers, while English newspapers run by the British were exempt. - Indian editors and journalists protested strongly, with newspapers like Amrita Bazar Patrika switching from Bengali to English overnight to evade the law. - Sponsored all-India conference in Calcutta, December 28-30, 1883: - Attended by over 100 delegates from across India. - Annual subscription: Rs 5; showed signs of a broad-based nationalist movement. - Became leading representative of Bengal's educated community and major force in Indian politics. - Indian Civil Service Agitation: - Response to Lytton reducing ICS exam age from 21 to 19 in 1876. - Organized pan-India agitation. - Formation of Indian National Congress - The word "Congress" means an assembly or gathering of people to discuss issues and make collective decisions. - It was commonly used for deliberative bodies and political organizations in various parts of the world, including the United States Congress and the Congress of Vienna (1815). - Factors Promoting the Growth of Nationalism in India - Political Unity - Most regions united politically/administratively under British rule for the first time. - Introduced uniform system of law and government. - Development of Communication and Transport - Railways, telegraphs, postal services, roads, and canals facilitated communication. - Enabled organization of national movement on an all-India basis. - English Language and Western Education - English-educated Indians led the national movement, developed nationalism. - Western education spread liberty, equality, freedom, and nationalism concepts. - The Role of the Press - English and vernacular press aroused national consciousness. - Social and Religious Movements of the Nineteenth Century - Leaders of Brahmo Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission, Arya Samaj, Theosophical Society fostered pride in the motherland. - Economic Exploitation by the British - Systematic ruin of Indian trade and native industries. - Racial Discrimination - Post-1857 Revolt bitterness and suspicion; Indians faced insults, humiliation, contemptuous treatment. - Administration of Lytton - Delhi Durbar during famine. - Vernacular Press Act curbed press liberty. - Arms Act prevented Indians from keeping arms. - Measures created widespread discontent. - The Ilbert Bill Controversy - Presented under Lord Ripon to remove racial inequality between Indian and European judges. - Opposed by British residents; bill modified. - Rise of Middle-Class Intelligentsia - Understood contradictions between Indian and colonial interests. - Impact of Contemporary Movements in the World - Influenced Indian nationalism. - Indian National Conference - Two sessions in 1883 and 1885 with representatives from major Indian towns. - Main architects: Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose (Indian Association). - Role of Nationalist Art and Literature - Neel Darpan (1860s, Dinbandhu Mitra): Bengali play reflecting indigo farmers' plight. - Anand Math (Bankim Chandra Chatterjee): Contains 'Vande Mataram'. - Bhartendu Harishchandra (father of modern Hindi): Urged Swadeshi in plays and poems. - Role of Political Associations prior to INC - Set stage for national body. - A.O. Hume's Contribution - Retired English civil servant; mobilized intellectuals. - Organized first Indian National Congress session at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, December 1885. - Governor-General: Lord Dufferin. - Hume: General Secretary of Congress (1885-1906). - Hume and Lord Ripon viewed educated middle class as legitimate, with aspirations to be met. - Initial Plans and Changes - Originally named 'Indian National Union'. - First session planned for Poona; shifted to Bombay due to cholera outbreak. - Phases of Congress - First Phase (1885-1905): Moderate Phase; vision and activities dim and vague. - Second Phase (1905-1918): Extremist Phase; Swaraj (Self-Government) as political goal. - Third Phase (1919-1947): Mass Mobilization under Mahatma Gandhi; Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence) as goal. - 1st Congress Session - Attended by 72 delegates; presided by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (barrister, first Indian to contest British House of Commons election, lost). - Bonnerjee's Speech: - Declared Congress's faith in British sense of justice. - Positioned Congress as loyal well-wisher of government. - Demanded greater Indian representation in government and higher posts. - Delegates: 39 lawyers out of 72. - Proceedings conducted in strict parliamentary fashion; 9 resolutions adopted. - Bipan Chandra's Observation: - 'If Hume wanted to use the Congress as a safety valve, the early Congress leaders hoped to use him as a “lightening conductor”'. - Safety Valve Theory (British Perspective) - Proposed by British officials, particularly William Wedderburn and others. - They believed that A.O. Hume (a retired British civil servant) helped create the INC to provide a controlled platform for expressing Indian grievances. - The British feared that growing discontent among Indians, if left unchecked, could lead to another revolt like 1857. - By allowing Indians to vent their frustrations in a moderate, loyalist manner, the British hoped to prevent a more radical rebellion. - Lightning Conductor Theory (Indian Leaders' Perspective) - Early nationalist leaders, including Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendranath Banerjee, and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, saw the INC as a means to channel Indian aspirations toward self-governance. - Instead of being passive participants in a British-controlled political setup, they aimed to use the Congress as a "lightning conductor" to safely direct growing nationalist energy into constitutional agitation and political awareness. - They hoped that Hume's involvement would provide protection from harsh British repression, as direct confrontation could lead to a crackdown. - Controversies on Origin: - Safety Valve Theory (Official Conspiracy Theory). - Annual Meetings: - Congress met every December in different parts of India post-1885. - Women's Participation: - 1890: Kadambini Ganguly (first woman graduate of Calcutta University) addressed session, symbolizing commitment to women's status in national life. - Consolidation of British Empire in India - Evolution of the East India Company (EIC) - Transition from Trading to Political Power - Initially established as a trading enterprise. - Gradually expanded control over India through conquests. - Evolved into a formidable political force. - Shift from Commercial to Territorial Entity - Transformed from primarily commercial to predominantly territorial in nature. - Issues with Company Administration - Misuse of Power - Widespread abuse of authority by company officials. - Led to growing concerns in Britain about governance in Indian territories. - Financial Crisis - Continuous wars and administrative mismanagement caused severe financial distress. - Revenue Maximisation - British Government sought to maximize revenue from EIC territories. - British Parliament's Intervention - Concerns about Company's administration pressured Parliament. - Introduced constitutional laws to regulate and control Company operations. - Let's Understand Company Structure - Important Learning from the Past - - Dual Government of Bengal - - Failed dual government in Bengal, coupled with abuse of power and corruption, prompted British Parliament to regulate EIC activities. - Abolished by Warren Hastings in 1772. - Additional Fact - Bengal Famine of 1770 (Chhiattorer Monnontor) - Estimated 10 million deaths. - Causes of the Famine - Natural Causes - Failure of Monsoons (1768-1769): - The famine was triggered by a severe drought in 1769, leading to crop failure. - Scarcity of water affected agriculture, reducing rice and grain production drastically. - Floods and Pestilence (1770): - After the drought, Bengal experienced floods, destroying whatever little crops were left. - Epidemics spread due to malnutrition and contaminated water. - British Economic Policies - Excessive Taxation by the East India Company: - The Company did not lower land taxes despite widespread starvation. - The revenue demand was fixed at 10% even during the famine, forcing farmers to sell what little food they had. - Destruction of Local Economy: - The British forced farmers to grow cash crops (indigo, opium, and jute) instead of food grains. - This reduced food availability and made the population vulnerable to starvation. - Profiteering by British Officials: - The East India Company and British merchants hoarded grain and sold it at high prices instead of distributing it to the starving population. - Exports Continued During the Famine: - While millions starved, the Company continued exporting rice and wheat to England and other British territories. - Consequences of the Famine - Massive Population Decline - Nearly 10 million deaths, reducing Bengal's population by one-third. - Entire villages were wiped out, and the region became severely underpopulated. - Collapse of Agriculture and Economy - With fewer farmers left, agricultural production fell drastically for years. - The famine weakened Bengal's economy, allowing the British to tighten their control over the region. - Social and Political Impact - Forced Migration: Survivors fled to neighboring regions, leaving Bengal devastated. - Rise of Banditry: Many famine victims turned to crime, leading to lawlessness. - Stronger British Rule: With the local economy and ruling class weakened, British dominance increased. - Regulating Act of 1773 - Background - Company had acquired political power and revenue-yielding territories, becoming an empire. - British Parliament realized Company could no longer remain outside state control. - Subjected Company to constitutional laws and Acts. - Regulating Act of 1773 (Factors Leading to the Act) - Dual Government of Bengal - Led to rampant corruption and a fatal divorce of power from law and order. - Abuses of private trade peaked (e.g., Clive returned to England at 34 with wealth yielding £40,000/year). - Wealth attracted British Parliament's interest, suggesting Crown takeover. - 1767 intervention demanded £400,000 annually from Bengal's plunder. - Jealousy in Britain - Company officials dubbed 'Nabobs' (corrupt Nawab analogy), symbolizing exploitation. - Military Setbacks - Defeat against Hyder Ali of Mysore in 1769. - Financial Crisis in EIC - Continuous wars and expansion pushed Company to bankruptcy by 1770. - Committee formed; Lord North presented bill on May 18, 1773, becoming Regulating Act. - Loan - Separate Act granted Company £1,40,000 at 4% interest. - Regulating Act of 1773 (Main Provisions) - Main Aim - Regulate Company activities in India and England. - Control by British Government - Allowed Company to retain territories but regulated its activities. - Restructuring of Company - - Direct Parliamentary control over Court of Directors (CoD) for the first time. - Raised qualifications for Court of Proprietors (CoP) and Court of Directors CoD (no re-election, no private trade). - CoD required to report all civil, military, and revenue matters of Bengal to British Government. - Provided liberal salaries, prohibited private trade, bribes, and money lending. - In India - Established empowered central authority to address lack of supreme authority. - New Bengal Presidency to check corruption. - Governor of Bengal designated 'Governor General of Bengal' with 4-member Executive Council. - Decisions by majority, binding on GG (Governor-General); GG had ordinary and casting vote, no veto. - Warren Hastings: First Governor General. - Established Supreme Court of Justice at Calcutta. - Composed of Chief Justice (Sir Elijah Impey) and three puisne judges. - Regulating Act of 1773 (Limitations) - Intentionally vague in provisions. - Neither gave state definite control over Company nor Company definite control over servants. - Broke down under its own defects when implemented. - Amending Act (Act of Settlement 1781) - Objective - Resolve conflicts over Supreme Court jurisdiction left vague in 1773 Act. - Key Provisions - Jurisdiction Exemptions - Governor-General (GG) and Council, plus Company servants, exempted from Supreme Court jurisdiction for official actions. - Exclusion from Revenue Matters - Supreme Court excluded from revenue matters or collection issues. - Calcutta Jurisdiction - Supreme Court authority over all Calcutta residents. - Hindus and Muslims tried under respective personal laws. - Regulatory Authority - GG and Council empowered to establish rules for Provincial Courts and Councils. - First effort to delineate (describe, outline, or portray something in detail) executive and judiciary functions in India. - Pitt's India Act of 1784 - Background - Introduced by William Pitt to address Regulating Act weaknesses. - Aimed to bring Company administration under British Parliament's supreme control. - Fox-North Coalition's similar bill defeated, causing ministry resignation (first British ministry wrecked on Indian issue). - Pitt's India Act of 1784 (Main Provisions) - Increased Control of British Government - Areas controlled by Company officially termed “British Possessions in India.” - Governance Structure - Court of Directors managed commercial affairs. - Board of Control (6 commissioners) appointed for political affairs. - Introduced Double Government: Company ruled, Board controlled. - Civil and military government subordinated to British Government until 1858. - Anti-Corruption Measures - Mandated EIC officials to declare assets; introduced stringent corruption penalties (framework lasted until 1858). - Changes with Respect to Company's Governance in India - Governor General and Council - Council reduced to 3 members (including Commander-in-Chief). - Madras and Bombay presidencies subordinated to Bengal; Calcutta became capital. - GG and Council subordinated to British Government; war declaration required Directors' sanction. - Non-Intervention Principle - Introduced to end further wars and conquests in Indian princely states. - Significance - Increased British Control - Board of Control shifted power from EIC to British Government. - Ambiguity in Governance - Confusion in power division between Board of Control and Court of Directors. - Allegation of Favouritism and Anti-Corruption Measures - Addressed through asset declarations and penalties. - Act of 1786 - Background - Pitt introduced bill to convince Cornwallis to accept Governor-Generalship. - Cornwallis sought combined GG and Commander-in-Chief powers. - Provisions - Merged offices of GG and Commander-in-Chief in one person. - Empowered GG to override Council majority on war and peace matters. - Charter Act of 1793 - Background - Concerns about: - Power concentration in GG's hands. - Need to regulate Company's financial and commercial activities. - Codify laws for fairness and transparency in governance. - Provisions - Extension of Company's Charter - Extended trade monopoly and political control for 20 years. - Increased Power of Governor General - GG could bypass Council decisions. - Revenue Collection and Economic Reforms - Company empowered to issue trade licenses to individuals and employees. - Separated revenue collection and legal duties, ending Maal Adalats (revenue courts). - Codification of Laws - Laid foundation for governance by written laws (started in Bengal). - Laws to be printed and translated into Indian languages for public familiarity with rights. - Charter Act of 1813 - Background - Britain's Industrial Revolution sought markets and raw materials. - Public and parliamentary opposition to EIC trade monopoly demanded free trade and laissez-faire policies. - Company's expanded territories made dual commercial-political role nearly impossible. - Napoleonic Wars shifted British trade focus to India. - Christian missionaries pushed for access against Company restrictions. - Charter Act of 1813 (Main Provisions) - Retention of Territories and Revenue - Renewed Company's Charter for 20 years; allowed territory possession and revenue collection. - Declared Crown sovereignty over Company territories. - Ending Company's Monopoly - Trade monopoly broken, except for tea, opium, and China trade. - Expanded Jurisdiction of Indian Courts - Granted greater jurisdiction over British and European subjects. - Christian Missionaries Allowed - Permitted missionaries to settle in India under license (facilitated Bishop appointment in Calcutta). - Funding for Education - Allocated Rs. 1 Lakh yearly for literature and sciences among Indian subjects. - Civil Services Reforms - Proposed open competition for civil service; Indians eligible but opposed and unimplemented. - Charter Act of 1813 (Assessment of the Act) - Economic Liberalisation - Encouraged competition and growth by allowing Indian and European trade. - Social and Religious Changes - Facilitated Christianity spread and social reforms. - Educational Advancement - Funded Indian education, recognizing its importance. - Charter Act of 1833 - Background - Also known as Saint Helena Act (transferred Saint Helena island to Crown). - EIC trade monopoly seen as harmful to British administration and Indians. - Industrial Revolution drove demand for export markets. - Whigs (Liberals) in power (1830); Macaulay and James Mill influenced Act. - Charter Act of 1833 (Main Provisions) - Legal British Colony - India made a British colony; Government of India (GOI) established over all British territories. - Removed restrictions on Europeans/British acquiring property in India. - Office of GG - Executive Powers - GG of Bengal became GG of India (William Bentinck, first GG); Council called Indian Council. - Controlled civil, military, and revenue matters. - Financial centralization under GG's Council. - For the first time, Government officially termed Government of India. - Office of GG - Legislative Powers - GG in Council gained exclusive legislative powers: - Repeal (to officially revoke, cancel, or annul a law, rule, or decision), alter (to change or modify something), or amend (to make changes or improvements to a law, document, or policy, often to correct errors or make it more suitable) laws for all persons in British India territory. - Deprived Bombay/Madras Governors of legislative powers (restored in 1861). - From now on, the rules made by company are called 'Acts' (earlier called regulations). - Act provided for appointment of 4th Council member (no voting rights). - His addition to the council was to help in making laws, thus his work was fully legislative. Macauly was the first one to be appointed. - Court of Directors could veto GG's laws. - GG's decision prevailed in Council disputes. - Abolition of Commercial Privileges - Ended Company's trade privileges; ordered to wind up commercial business. - Role shifted from that of purely commercial body to purely administrative. - Charter extended 20 years for non-trade functions (e.g., raising armies, ruling territories). - Minister for Indian Affairs - Replaced President of Board of Control. - Formation of Law Commission - Appointed in 1834 under Lord Macaulay to codify laws. - Resulted in Indian Penal Code and Civil/Criminal Procedure Codes. - Civil Service Reform - First Act to allow Indian natives in administration. - Court of Directors to nominate via competitive exams; 'fitness' as eligibility criterion. - No discrimination based on religion, birth, descent, or color. - System not effectively implemented soon after. - Slavery Abolition - GG directed to work towards abolition (achieved via Indian Slavery Act of 1843). - New Presidency - Proposed Agra and Fort William presidency from Bengal division (never implemented). - Charter Act of 1833 (Significance) - Culmination of centralization process begun with Regulating Act. - Paved way for British India unification and strong central government. - Transfer of powers from Madras/Bombay to GG restrained government's ability to resolve public matters. - - Charter Act of 1853 - Background, Significant Challenges - High costs and delays from Board of Control and Court of Directors raised EIC efficiency concerns. - Politically informed Indians (e.g., Bombay Association, Madras Native Association) demanded decentralization and greater governance participation. - Charter Act of 1853 (Main Provisions) - Indian Territories - Held 'in trust for the Crown' until Parliament directed otherwise. - Company ceased as commercial agency, remained political agent for Crown. - Legislative Provisions - Separated GG Council's legislative and executive functions. - Added 6 legislative councillors, forming Indian Legislative Council (ICS): - Chief Justice and puisne judge of Calcutta Supreme Court. - Four representatives (Bengal, Madras, Bombay, NW Provinces; civil servants with 10+ years). - Powers of Legislative Councillors: - Ask questions, discuss Executive Council policy, highlight government lapses. - Bills referred to Select Committees; business conducted publicly. - GG assent required for laws; GG could veto bills. - Executive Provisions - Law member became full member of GG Executive Council (strength back to 4). - Directors and Their Powers - Reduced from 24 to 18 (6 Crown-appointed). - Divested of patronage; appointments opened to competitive exams (Macaulay Committee). - Empowered to: - Constitute new Presidency. - Alter state boundaries. - Incorporate newly acquired states. - Created Lt. Governorship of Punjab (1859) due to administrative difficulties. - Governor of Bengal - Separate post created. - Open Competition System - Established for civil servant selection; opened covenant civil service to Indians. - Assessment of the Act - Marked beginning of Parliamentary system in India: - Verbal discussions in legislative capacity (previously written). - Bills passed through stages, referred to select committees. - Legislative business conducted publicly; proceedings officially published. - Indian National Movement (1885 - 1905) - Early Nationalism - Events Leading to Formation of INC - By 1885, need for a pan-Indian political organization evident, recognized by nationalists since 1870s through various initiatives: - Laws Causing Discontent - Vernacular Press Act (1878) and Arms Act (1878) met with widespread opposition. - Ilbert Bill Controversy - The bill aimed to allow Indian judges and magistrates to try British and European offenders in criminal cases. - However, this faced massive backlash from the British community in India, leading to racial tensions and ultimately, a compromise that diluted the bill's original intent. - British women were at the forefront, spreading fear that "uneducated Indian judges" could misuse power against British women. - European businesses, clubs, and officials opposed the idea of being tried by "native" judges. - The British government diluted the bill to pacify the European community. - The final version (passed in 1884) allowed Indian judges to try Europeans, but only if a jury consisting of at least half Europeans was present. - Early Political Groupings - Indian National Association established by Surendranath Banerjee in Kolkata. - Theosophical Society Meeting (1884) - Annual meet in Madras; delegates from across India recognized need for a mediator to unite regional leaders. - Chose A.O. Hume as mediator due to his wide acceptance and liberal views. - Formation of Indian National Union (May 1885) - Hume secured Viceroy's approval to create “Indian National Union.” - Affiliated with government; platform to voice Indian public opinion. - Led to inception (beginning or starting point of something) of Indian National Congress (INC). - The Indian National Congress - First Session - Held at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, December 25-31, 1885. - Governor-General: Lord Dufferin. - Hume: General Secretary (1885-1906). - Originally named 'Indian National Union'; planned for Poona but shifted to Bombay due to cholera outbreak. - Views of Hume and Lord Ripon - Educated middle class in India was permanent; its legitimate aspirations should be met, grievances addressed. - Controversies Surrounding Inception of Indian National Congress - Safety Valve Theory - A safety valve is a device in a steam engine that releases excess pressure to prevent an explosion. - Proposed by Lala Lajpat Rai and nationalist historians. - Suggests British, fearing another 1857-like revolt, allowed educated Indians to express grievances in a controlled manner. - A.O. Hume, a retired British officer, played a key role in founding INC, raising suspicions of British influence. - Hume as a ‘Lightning Conductor' - A lightning conductor (or lightning rod) is a device used to safely direct lightning to the ground, preventing damage to buildings. - Early leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji saw Hume as a shield against British repression. - Believed Hume's role gave INC legitimacy and prevented direct British crackdowns. - Role of Elite Indians and Limited Representation - Initially dominated by Western-educated elites, lawyers, and professionals. - Limited participation from peasants, workers, and the masses. - Criticized for being a bourgeois organization with little mass appeal in its early years. - Hindu-Muslim Representation - British attempted to portray INC as Hindu-dominated. - However, early INC had Muslim leaders like Badruddin Tyabji and R.M. Sayani. - Divide-and-rule policy later led to the creation of the Muslim League in 1906. - First Session Details - Attended by 72 delegates; presided by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee. - Bonnerjee: Barrister, first Indian to contest British House of Commons election (lost). - 9 Resolutions Passed (General Idea, No Need to Memorize): - Abolish Indian Council of Secretary of State for India. - Expand and reform Imperial and Local Legislative Councils (Indian Councils Act of 1861). - Establish Legislative Councils for Punjab, etc. - Implement simultaneous Public Service Exams in England and India; raise candidate minimum age. - Early Composition of INC - Educated middle class had largest representation. - Legal profession most heavily represented. - Brahmins prominent among castes. - Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras presidencies led participation. - Masses and landed class largely absent. - Early Nationalists (1885 - 1905) - The Moderates - Moderate Phase (1885-1905) - Known as period of Tea-Party Politics or Political Mendicancy. - Grew from 72 delegates (Bombay, 1885) to 434 (Calcutta, 1886). - Delegates elected from local bodies nationwide; decided to meet annually in different regions. - Called Moderates for trusting British justice, protesting within legal bounds. - Method of Work of the Moderates - Peaceful, constitutional agitations within law. - Relied on prayers, petitions, meetings, speeches, resolutions (via press and Congress sessions). - Sent deputations (official groups of representatives sent to present demands, grievances, or requests to an authority) to Britain: - Dadabhai Naoroji became British MP, worked for Indian interests. - 1889: British Committee of INC established. - 1890: Weekly journal 'India' started to educate British public on Indian issues. - 1892: Planned INC session in London postponed due to British objections, never resumed. - Indian Councils Act of 1892 - The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was a significant constitutional reform introduced by the British government to address growing political demands in India. - While it fell short of Congress's expectations, it was the first step toward legislative representation for Indians. Key Provisions of the Act: - Expansion of Legislative Councils - Increased the number of members in the Imperial Legislative Council and Provincial Legislative Councils. - However, the majority of the members were still British officials, ensuring continued government control. - Indirect Representation of Indians - Some non-official seats were reserved for Indians. - These Indians were nominated rather than elected. - The British government carefully controlled nominations, ensuring only loyal Indians were selected. - Budget Discussions Introduced - For the first time, council members were allowed to discuss the budget. - However, they could not vote on it or influence financial decisions. - Right to Ask Questions - Members could now ask questions to the government on administrative matters. - However, supplementary questions (follow-ups) were not permitted, limiting accountability. - Achievements via Indian Councils Act of 1892: - The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was one of the first major political victories for early Congress leaders. This led them to further put their other demands. - Demands - Political Demands - Congress leaders saw the 1892 Act as inadequate and continued pushing for more substantial political reforms. - Formation of Provincial Councils - Provincial Councils were legislative bodies established at the provincial level in British India to assist in governance and administration. - They were introduced as part of constitutional reforms to decentralize power and involve Indians in governance, albeit in a limited manner. - Congress wanted independent legislative councils for major provinces. - This would decentralize governance and allow Indians to influence regional policies. - Abolition of the Indian Council - The Indian Council in London advised the Secretary of State for India. - Congress demanded its abolition, as it was an unrepresentative body dominated by British officials, with no Indian voice in policymaking. - Increased Indian Opportunities in Civil Services - Congress demanded simultaneous ICS (Indian Civil Service) exams in London and India. - At the time, the ICS exam was conducted only in London, which restricted Indian participation due to financial and logistical barriers. - End of Aggressive Foreign Policy Against Indian Neighbors - The British followed an imperialistic foreign policy in Afghanistan, Burma, and Tibet. - Congress leaders argued that India was being forced to bear the financial and military burden of unnecessary wars for British expansion. - They demanded a peaceful and non-aggressive foreign policy to avoid excessive taxation and exploitation of Indian resources. - Economic Demands - End economic drain. - Enquire into economic and industrial conditions. - Reduce land revenue. - Abolish salt tax. - Encourage modern industry via direct government aid. - Agriculture-Related Demands - Develop agricultural banks to curb moneylender atrocities. - Extend irrigation facilities to prevent famines. - Introduce permanent settlement nationwide. - Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal fixed revenue permanently, benefiting zamindars but providing stability to peasants. - So, they requested its implementation nationwide. - Military Demands - Repeal Arms Act. - Appoint Indians to commissioned army ranks. - Reduce military expenditure. - Social Demands - Increase welfare expenditure. - Secure civil rights: freedom of speech, thought, association, press. - Improve plantation laborers' conditions. - British Reaction to Congress - Initially flexible; post-1887, attitude stiffened. - Branded nationalists as 'Disloyal Babus,' 'Seditious Brahmins,' 'Violent Villains.' - Lord Dufferin: Congress represented a 'Microscopic Minority.' - Encouraged pro-British elements (e.g., Sir Sayed Ahmed Khan, Raja Shiv Prasad of Banaras). - Formed Aligarh Movement and United India Patriotic Association to counter Congress. - Advanced 'Divide and Rule' policy to widen Hindu-Muslim divide. - 1890s: Government employees forbidden from attending Congress meetings. - Achievements of the Moderates - Political Achievements - Indian Councils Act of 1892. - ICS Examination in India (1893): House of Commons resolution for simultaneous exams. - Demand for Swaraj: - 1905 Benaras Session: First demand for self-rule within British Empire (GK Gokhale). - 1906 Calcutta Session: Explicit demand by Dadabhai Naoroji. - Birth of democratic ideas. - Trained Indians in political work; laid foundation for Extremists. - Economic Achievements - Economic Critique of British Rule: - Dadabhai Naoroji, RC Dutt, DE Wacha advanced 'Drain of Wealth' theory. - Naoroji's 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India': Per capita income Rs 20 (1867-68). - RC Dutt's 'Economic History in India' detailed exploitation. - Welby Commission (1895): Enquired into Indian expenditure. - Constitutional Agitation Within Law - Believed British wanted justice but were unaware of real conditions. - Two-pronged methodology: - Create public opinion, arouse consciousness, unite people on political questions. - Persuade British Government and public for reforms. - Used 'prayer and petition'; resorted to constitutional agitation if unsuccessful. - A petition is a formal written request submitted to an authority, typically signed by multiple people, to express grievances, seek redressal, or demand action on a specific issue. - Extremists - Rise of the Extremists (Phase of Militant Nationalism or Radical Politics) - Note: 'Militant' and 'Terrorists' had different meanings then; described extremist approaches vs. Moderates. Revolutionaries were a militant extremist faction. - Growth of Militant Nationalism - Radical trend emerged in 1890s; took shape by 1905 (Bengal Partition). - Recognition of the True Nature of British Rule - Economic Miseries (1890s): - Severe famines killed 90 lakh (1896-1900). - Bubonic plague hit Deccan; large-scale riots followed. - Government curtailed rights: - Tilak's imprisonment (sedition), Official Secrets Act, Indian Universities Act. - Official Secrets Act, 1923 - The Official Secrets Act (OSA), 1923 is a law enacted by the British government in India to prevent the disclosure of classified information related to state security. - It was primarily aimed at controlling espionage, unauthorized communication of secret information, and protecting government interests. - Key Features - Protection of Classified Information - Prohibits sharing of government documents or sensitive state information. - Espionage and National Security - Any attempt to collect, record, or publish official information can be considered a criminal offense. - Severe Penalties - Violations can lead to imprisonment up to 14 years, fines, or both. - Applies to Both Government & Citizens - Not just officials but any individual leaking sensitive information can be prosecuted. - Restrictions on Journalists & Whistleblowers - Used to control media disclosures, sometimes criticized for suppressing transparency. - Indian Universities Act, 1904 - The Indian Universities Act, 1904, was introduced by Lord Curzon as part of his educational reforms to increase British control over Indian higher education institutions. - Key Features - Increased Government Control - Viceroy gained greater authority over university governance, administration, and finances. - Changes in University Senates - Size of the governing body was reduced, giving more power to nominated British officials. - Strict Affiliation Rules - New colleges had to meet stricter standards before being recognized by universities. - More Funding, but Less Autonomy - Universities received increased government grants, but their independence was curtailed. - Restrictions on Nationalist Activities - Universities and colleges were discouraged from supporting nationalist movements. - Growth of Confidence and Self-Respect - Faith in self-effort grew; Tilak, Aurobindo, Bipin Chandra Pal urged reliance on Indian character and capacities. - Belief that masses could make sacrifices to win freedom. - International Influences - Defeat of European powers: - Italians by Ethiopians (1896). - The Battle of Adwa (1896) marked Ethiopia's victory over Italy, proving that a non-European nation could resist colonial rule. - This challenged the myth of European superiority and inspired anti-colonial struggles worldwide. - British reverses in Boer Wars (1899-1902). - The Boer Wars (South African Wars) saw the British Empire struggling against Afrikaner (Dutch-descended) settlers in South Africa. - Japan's victory over Russia (1905). - Japan's victory in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) was the first time an Asian power defeated a major European nation. - Inspiration from nationalist movements in Ireland, Russia, Egypt, Turkey, Persia, China. - Growth of Education - Spread of education increased awareness. - Unemployment/underemployment among educated highlighted poverty and underdevelopment. - Reaction to Increasing Westernisation - Intellectuals (Swami Vivekananda, Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, Dayananda Saraswati) inspired nationalists. - Countered Western superiority myth with India's rich past; Dayananda's 'India for Indians.' - Dissatisfaction with Achievements of Moderates - Young Congress members dissatisfied with Moderates' 15-20-year record. - Criticized 'Three P's' (prayer, petition, protest) as 'political mendicancy.' - Indian Councils Act of 1892 disappointing. - Repressive Measures: - 1897: Natu brothers deported without trial (linked to 'Poona Vaibhav' editorials). - 1897: Tilak and editors imprisoned for anti-government rhetoric. - 1898: 'Feeling of disaffection' made an offence. - 1899: Reduced Indian members in Calcutta Corporation. - 1904: Indian Official Secrets Act restricted press freedom. - Tilak's Views: - Called Congress 'a Congress of flatterers,' sessions 'holiday recreation.' - Founded New English School (1880, later Fergusson College). - Opposed armed struggle; advocated Swaraj via self-help, determination, sacrifice. - Slogan: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.' - First Congress leader with multiple imprisonments for outspokenness. - Reactionary Policies of Curzon - Curzon's seven-year rule (missions, commissions, omissions) provoked reaction. - Refused to recognize India as a nation. - Measures: Official Secrets Act, Indian Universities Act, Calcutta Corporation Act, Bengal Partition. - The Calcutta Corporation Act of 1899 was a legislation introduced by the British government to reduce Indian control over municipal governance in Calcutta (now Kolkata). - It was part of British efforts to curb the rising influence of educated Indians in local administration. - Key Provisions of the Act - Reduced Indian Representation - The act reduced the number of elected Indian members in the Calcutta Municipal Corporation and increased the number of nominated (British) officials. - Increased British Control - The majority of the corporation was placed under British officials, ensuring government dominance over municipal decisions. - Reversal of 1888 Reforms - Earlier, the Calcutta Municipal Act of 1888 had given Indians greater representation, but this new act undid those reforms, limiting self-governance. - Lord Curzon's Policy - The act was part of Lord Curzon's repressive policies, aimed at restricting Indian political aspirations. - Existence of a Militant School of Thought - Early 20th-century nationalist thinkers advocated militancy: - Bengal: Raj Narain Bose, Ashwini Kumar Datta, Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal. - Maharashtra: Vishnu Shastri Chiplunkar, Bal Gangadhar Tilak. - Punjab: Lala Lajpat Rai. - Tilak as leading representative. - Tenets (a principle, belief, or doctrine that is held to be true): - Hatred for foreign rule. - Swaraj as national goal. - Direct political action. - Belief in masses' capacity to challenge authority. - Readiness for personal sacrifices. - Emergence of a Trained Leadership - New leadership channeled masses' political struggle potential. - Energy released during Swadeshi agitation against Bengal Partition. - Believed Swaraj required direct action, self-reliance, sacrifice, strong will. - Faith in masses; aimed to make Congress and national movement mass-based. - Inspired by India's past but focused on building the future. - Mode of Action - The Extremists' Ideology - Inspired by Swami Vivekananda, Dayananda Saraswati, Bankim Chandra Chatterjee. - Programmes: - Boycott and Swadeshi. - National Education: - National Scheme of Education for students boycotting government institutions. - Bengal Council of National Education set up by Gurudas Banerjee. - Non-Cooperation or Passive Resistance. - Co-operative Organizations. - Work of Extremists - Tilak's Actions: - 1891: Opposed Age of Consent Bill (raised age from 10 to 12); argued against British interference in private life. - The Age of Consent Bill of 1891 was a legislative measure introduced by the British government to raise the age of consent for girls in India from 10 to 12 years. - The bill was intended to curb child marriages and reduce instances of marital rape, but it sparked strong opposition from conservative sections of Indian society, including many nationalists. - Organized Ganpati and Shivaji Festivals. - Published newspapers: Mahratta (English), Kesari (Marathi). - 1895: Ousted Gokhale and Ranade from Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, giving Extremists control. - Gokhale formed Deccan Sabha, completing Moderate-Extremist split in Maharashtra. - Aurobindo's Contributions: - 1893-94: 'New Lamps for the Old' articles in Indu Prakash; criticized Congress as out of touch with 'proletariat,' 'dying of consumption.' - Extremist Groups: - Maharashtra: Led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak. - Bengal: Led by Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh. - Punjab: Led by Lala Lajpat Rai (Lal-Bal-Pal trio). - The Lal-Bal-Pal trio refers to three prominent leaders of the Indian nationalist movement during the late 19th and early 20th centuries: - Lala Lajpat Rai ("Lal") - Punjab - Bal Gangadhar Tilak ("Bal") - Maharashtra - Bipin Chandra Pal ("Pal") - Bengal - Difference Between Moderates and Extremists - Understanding of Swaraj - Moderates: Demanded gradual self-governance within the British Empire. - Extremists: Demanded complete independence (Swaraj) as a birthright. - Attitude towards British Benevolence - Moderates: Believed in British justice and fair play; sought reforms through loyalty and dialogue. - Extremists: Considered British rule exploitative and oppressive; saw British promises as deceptive. - Methodology: 3 P's (Moderates) vs. 3 S's (Extremists) - Moderates (3 P's - Prayer, Petition, Protest) - Used constitutional means: appeals, petitions, and peaceful protests. - Relied on debates and resolutions in councils and British Parliament. - Example: Opposition to Vernacular Press Act (1878) through petitions. - Extremists (3 S's - Self-Reliance, Swaraj, Swadeshi) - Advocated self-sufficiency in governance, economy, and education. - Used mass mobilization, boycotts, and direct action. - Example: Partition of Bengal (1905) → Swadeshi Movement & Boycott of British goods. - View on Public Mobilization - Moderates: Relied on the educated elite and legal discussions. - Extremists: Mobilized the masses, including peasants and youth, for nationalistic fervor. - Response to British Repression - Moderates: Avoided confrontation; believed in dialogue and resolutions. - Extremists: Advocated active resistance and saw repression as a reason for intensified struggle. - Key Leaders - Moderates: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee. - Extremists: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai. - Some Important Moderates - Surendranath Banerjee - Known as the Indian Burke. - Opposed Bengal Partition. - Founded Indian Association (1876) for political reforms. - Convened Indian National Conference (1883), merged with INC in 1886. - G. Subramanya Aiyar - Preached nationalism via Madras Mahajana Sabha. - Founded The Hindu and Swadesamitran. - Dadabhai Naoroji - Grand Old Man of India; India's unofficial ambassador in England. - First Indian British MP. - Wrote 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India,' detailing Drain Theory: - Wealth drained via salaries, savings, pensions, British troop payments, company profits. - Dayananda Saraswati - First to call for Swaraj (1876: 'India for Indians'); some call him 'Grandfather of Indian Nation.' - Bankim Chandra Chatterjee (1838-1894) - Wrote 'Vande Mataram' in Anandmath (1882, Sanyasi Rebellion backdrop) to counter British influence. - First sung by Rabindranath Tagore at 1896 Congress Session. - First 2 verses adopted as National Song in October 1937 by Congress. - Lord Curzon - Curzonian Attack - Governor-General and Viceroy of India (1899-1905) - Believed to know more about India and its problems than any prior Viceroy. - Arrived amid 1896-97 famine and plague; aimed to reform every department. - Method: Appoint expert commissions, then enact legislation. - Reforms and Policies - Police Reforms - 1902 Police Commission under Sir Andrew Frazer. - Found police corrupt, oppressive, lacking public trust. - Recommendations: Increase salaries, establish training schools, provincial police service, Central Department of Criminal Intelligence. - Education Reforms - 1902 Universities Commission to address discipline and declining standards. - Curzon viewed universities as factories of political revolutionaries. - Indian Universities Act of 1904: Increased control over universities, strict affiliation rules for private colleges. - Army Reforms - Led by Lord Kitchener, Commander-in-Chief. - Indian Army split into Northern and Southern Commands. - Battalions subjected to rigorous “Kitchener Test.” - Foreign Policy - Mission to Tibet (Colonel Younghusband) to counter Russian influence. - Mission to Persian Gulf (Sir Henry McMahon). - Other Works - Famine Commission under Sir Anthony MacDonnell. - Irrigation Commission under Sir Colin Scott Moncrieff. - Co-Operative Credit Societies Act, 1904: Cheap loans for cultivators. - Ancient Monuments Act, 1904: Protected historical monuments. - Partition of Bengal announced (1905). - PUSA Agricultural Institute established (1903). - Indian National Movement (1905 - 1917) - Extremist Phase & Swadeshi Movement - Key Events - Partition of Bengal - Swadeshi Movement - Surat Split - National movement vs national struggle - The term movement implies a more structured, ideological, and mass-based approach to achieving independence. - It often includes political, social, economic, and cultural dimensions. - National struggle is a more intense, direct, and often confrontational effort against oppression or foreign rule - The term struggle implies sporadic, unorganized, or passive resistance, often without a clear long-term strategy. - Partition of Bengal - - Background - British claimed Bengal (78 million people, a quarter of British India's population) was too large for efficient administration. - Originally included Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Assam. - 1874: Assam separated as Chief Commissioner's Province. - Decision publicized in December 1903. - Plan: Divide into two provinces: - Bengal (Western Bengal, Bihar, Orissa). - Eastern Bengal and Assam. - Motives: - Linguistic division to reduce Bengalis to a minority in Bengal. - Religious division: Western half Hindu-majority, Eastern half Muslim-majority. - Note: Nationalists supported separating linguistically divergent Orissa and Bihar for administrative efficiency. - Implementation - Scheme began with Curzon's Minute on Terrestrial Redistribution, June 1, 1903. - July 20, 1905: Curzon ordered division: - Eastern Bengal and Assam: 31 million. - Rest of Bengal: 54 million (18 million Bengalis, 36 million Biharis/Oriyas). - Anti-Partition Campaign - Leadership: Surendranath Banerjee, K.K. Mitra, Prithwishchandra Ray. - Methods: Petitions, public meetings, memoranda, propaganda via newspapers (Hitabadi, Sanjibani, Bengalee). - Objective: Pressure government through educated public opinion in India and England to prevent partition. - July 1905: Government ignored opposition, announced partition. - August 7, 1905: Boycott Resolution passed at Calcutta Town Hall meeting; launched Swadeshi Movement targeting Manchester cloth and Liverpool salt. - October 16, 1905: Partition effective; observed as mourning day in Bengal. - Vande Mataram became movement's anthem. - Rabindranath Tagore composed 'Amar Sonar Bangla' (later Bangladesh's anthem, 1971). - Tagore called for Raksha Bandhan (Rakhi) as unity symbol. - Ramendra Sunder Trivedi urged Aradhana (unlit hearths) as mourning sign. - Leaders Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose addressed large gatherings. - Movement spread beyond Bengal: - Poona/Bombay: Tilak. - Punjab: Lala Lajpat Rai, Ajit Singh. - Delhi: Syed Haider Raza. - Madras: Chidambaram Pillai. - INC 1905 Session (Gokhale's presidency): - Condemned partition and Curzon's reactionary policies. - Supported anti-partition and Swadeshi Movement. - Militant Nationalists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh): - Wanted movement to extend nationwide, evolve into mass struggle for Swaraj. - Moderates: Limited scope to Bengal, opposed broader escalation. - Swadeshi Movement - INC Calcutta Session (1906, Dadabhai Naoroji's presidency) - Declared goal: 'Self-government or Swaraj like the UK or colonies.' - Four resolutions: Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education. - Moderate-Extremist Dispute - Deadlock at Surat Session (1907, Rash Behari Ghosh): Congress split. - Extremist Expression - Periodicals: - New India (Bipin Chandra Pal). - Vande Mataram (Aurobindo Ghosh). - Sandhya (Brahmabandhav Upadhyaya). - Yugantar (Bhupendranath Dutt). - New Forms of Struggle - Boycott of Foreign Goods - Public burning of foreign cloth, boycotts of foreign salt/sugar. - Priests refused to solemnize marriages with foreign goods; washermen refused to wash foreign clothes. - First suggested by Krishna Kumar Mitra in Sanjibani. - Public Meetings and Processions - Key methods for mass mobilization and popular expression. - Corps of Volunteers (Samitis) - Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (Ashwini Kumar Dutta, Barisal) highly effective. - Imaginative Use of Festivals and Melas - Spread political messages via traditional events. - Tilak's Ganapati and Shivaji festivals in western India and Bengal. - Bengal's folk theatre used for propaganda. - Emphasis on Self-Reliance (Atma Shakti) - Swadeshi Enterprises: - Textile mills, soap/match factories, tanneries, banks, insurance companies, shops. - Reasserted national dignity, honor, confidence; regenerated villages economically/socially. - Acharya P.C. Ray founded Bengal Chemicals Factory. - Programme of National Education - Bengal National College (inspired by Tagore's Shantiniketan) with Aurobindo Ghosh as principal. - National schools/colleges emerged nationwide. - National Council of Education (August 15, 1906): Organized literary, scientific, technical education on national lines, using vernaculars. - Bengal Institute of Technology for technical education; funds raised to send students to Japan. - Charly's Circular: Bengal Chief Secretary threatened student activists with disciplinary action. - Workers - October 1905: Printer's Union formed after strikes in government presses; first real labor union. - Peasants - Minimal peasant mobilization; participation negligible. - 1906: Southern Andhra/Tamil Nadu held Vandemataram Movement gatherings supporting Bengal. - Muslims - Failed to gain Muslim support; a key weakness. - 1906: All India Muslim League formed under Nawab Salimullah of Dacca with government patronage to advance Muslim interests. - Eastern Bengal saw communal riots at movement's peak. - The Surat Split - Benaras Session (December 1905, Gokhale's presidency) - Moderate-Extremist differences emerged. - Extremists: Extend Boycott/Swadeshi beyond Bengal, include all associations (government service, courts, councils) for a nationwide mass movement. - Moderates: Limit movement to Bengal, opposed boycotting councils; favored constitutional methods. - Calcutta Session (December 1906) - Moderate enthusiasm waned due to Extremist/revolutionary popularity. - Dadabhai Naoroji elected president; Swaraj defined as self-government like UK/colonies. - Extremists called for widespread passive resistance, boycotts of schools, colleges, councils, courts, municipalities. - Moderates' Shift - Encouraged by rumored council reforms, toned down Calcutta programme. - Misjudged reforms as rewards rather than a tactic to isolate Extremists. - Surat Session (1907) - Extremists: Wanted session in Nagpur with Tilak or Lajpat Rai as president, reaffirming Swadeshi, boycott, education resolutions. - Moderates: Chose Surat to exclude Tilak; elected Rashbehari Ghosh, sought to drop resolutions. - Government Strategy - Three-pronged approach: Repression, Conciliation, Suppression. - Stage 1: Mild repression of Extremists to intimidate Moderates. - Stage 2: Placate Moderates with concessions, hint at further reforms if Extremists distanced, isolating Extremists. - Post-Swadeshi - Stage 3: With Moderates aligned, government suppressed Extremists fully, then ignored Moderates. - 1907-1911 Laws to Check Anti-Government Activity: - Seditious Meetings Act, 1907: - Prohibited public gatherings deemed seditious. - Required prior approval for political meetings. - Aimed at curbing nationalist protests and anti-British speeches. - Indian Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act, 1908: - Targeted newspapers publishing content inciting violence or rebellion. - Allowed confiscation of printing presses and penalization of publishers. - Suppressed nationalist journalism and free speech. - Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1908: - Declared certain organizations as unlawful for anti-government activities. - Empowered the government to detain individuals without trial. - Used against extremist nationalist groups and revolutionary societies. - Indian Press Act, 1910: - Imposed heavy security deposits on newspapers critical of the government. - Allowed seizure of newspapers publishing seditious material. - Further tightened control over the press after earlier laws proved ineffective. - Extremist Leaders' Fate: - Tilak: Jailed in Mandalay (Burma) for 6 years. - Aurobindo and B.C. Pal: Retired from active politics. - Lajpat Rai: Left for abroad. - First World War and Nationalist Response in India - Home Rule League Movement - Overview of the Home Rule League Movement - The Home Rule Movement emerged as India's response to the First World War, reflecting a growing demand for self-governance. - It was inspired by the Irish Home Rule Leagues and marked the rise of a more aggressive approach to Indian politics. - First World War (1914-1918) - When the First World War began, the Moderates chose to support British war efforts, seeing it as both a duty and a strategic move to negotiate concessions later. - The Extremists disagreed with this approach, but Bal Gangadhar Tilak took a unique stance. He pledged loyalty to the British Crown and encouraged Indians to assist Britain during its time of need, hoping this support would yield political gains. - Opinion of Industrialists - Wealthy Indian industrialists viewed the war as a chance to profit. The conflict disrupted British industrial production, creating shortages that increased demand for goods from Indian industries. - This economic boost fueled the growth of Indian industries, and industrialists wanted to maintain this momentum after the war. They were eager to organize and back nationalist movements to protect their interests. - Reasons for the Home Rule League Movement (HRLM - Why?) - Some nationalists believed that only popular pressure could force the British government to grant political concessions. - The Moderates grew disillusioned with the limited reforms of the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909), which failed to meet their expectations. - Ordinary people were suffering from wartime hardships, including high taxes and rising prices, making them ready to join aggressive protests. - The war exposed the hypocrisy of imperialist powers. As major nations fought each other and spread propaganda, the myth of white superiority weakened, inspiring Indians to challenge British rule. - Tilak, released from prison in June 1914, was prepared to lead. He reassured the government of his loyalty and signaled to the Moderates that he sought administrative reform, not revolution, similar to the Irish Home Rule model. - Annie Besant, an Irish theosophist living in India since 1896 and president of the Theosophical Society, decided to expand her work by launching a movement for Home Rule, modeled on the Irish example. She later became INC president in 1917. - Background on Theosophical Society: Founded in 1875 by H.P. Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott in New York, it established its first headquarters in Adyar, near Madras, in 1882. - Objectives of the Movement (What?) - The Home Rule League campaign aimed to educate the common person about home rule, presenting it as self-government within the British Empire. - Methods of the Movement (How?) - The movement sought to achieve its goals through widespread political education and engagement. - This included holding public meetings, setting up libraries and reading rooms with books on national politics, organizing conferences, conducting classes for students on political issues, and spreading propaganda through newspapers, pamphlets, posters, illustrated postcards, plays, and religious songs. - It also involved collecting funds, organizing social work, and participating in local government activities. - Composition of the Leagues - Both Tilak and Besant understood that success required the support of the Moderate-dominated Indian National Congress (INC) and full cooperation from the Extremists. - After failing to bridge the Moderate-Extremist divide at the 1914 INC session, Tilak and Besant chose to launch their own political initiatives. - By early 1915, Annie Besant began campaigning for post-war self-government, inspired by white colonies like Canada and Australia. She used her newspapers, *New India* and *Commonweal*, and organized public meetings and conferences. - At the 1915 INC session, Tilak and Besant's efforts gained traction. The Congress agreed to admit Extremists, committed to educative propaganda, and revived local-level Congress committees. - Tilak's League - Established in April 1916 during the Bombay Provincial Conference in Belgaum, with G.S. Khaparde as a founding member. - Operated in Maharashtra (excluding Bombay city), Karnataka, Central Provinces, and Berar, with six branches. - Demands included Swarajya (self-rule), formation of linguistic states, and education in vernacular languages. - Tilak famously declared, “Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it,” during this agitation. - In his speeches, Tilak avoided religious appeals, opposed untouchability, and urged Brahmins to tolerate non-Brahmins. He stated, “If God were to tolerate untouchability, I would not recognize him as God at all.” - The British government issued Tilak a show-cause notice, but the High Court cleared him, giving the Home Rule Movement legal legitimacy. By 1917, Tilak's league had 14,000 registered members. - Besant's League - Launched in September 1916 in Madras, covering the rest of India, including Bombay city. - Had 200 branches, loosely organized compared to Tilak's League. George Arundale served as organizing secretary, and Sir S. Subramaniam Aiyer (Grand Old Man of South India) was honorary president. - Earlier in 1916, impatient followers like Jamnadas Dwarkadas, Shankerlal Banker, and Indulala Yagnik set up Home Rule groups, started the Bombay newspaper *Young India*, and created an All India Propaganda Fund for pamphlets. - Key figures like Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, Bhulabhai Desai, Chittaranjan Das, Madan Mohan Malaviya, Mohammad Ali Jinnah, Tej Bahadur Sapru, and Lala Lajpat Rai later joined, some leading local branches.
