Political Climate - Introduced amid rising political unrest and dissatisfaction with British rule. - The 1906 British Liberal Party victory raised reform prospects, believing Indian legislative participation would strengthen British control. - The 1906 Shimla Deputation, led by Aga Khan, proposed separate Muslim electorates to Lord Minto. - Main Provisions - Structural Reforms - Indian Entry in Viceroy's Executive Council - Satyendra Sinha became the first Indian appointed in 1909. - Expansion of Members - Increased elected members in Imperial and Provincial Legislative Councils, with non-official majorities in provinces. - Central Legislative Council: 69 members (37 officials, 5 nominated non-officials, 27 elected non-officials), with seats for Muslims, British capitalists, landlords, and a general electorate. - Emphasized representation by classes and interests over territorial representation. - Legislative Powers - Members could discuss financial statements, move resolutions (as recommendations only), and ask supplementary questions, though some topics (e.g., foreign relations) were restricted. - Introduction of Elections - Indirect elections for non-officials, based on class and community, with recognized bodies recommending candidates. - Provision of Separate Electorates - Introduced for Muslims in the Central Legislative Council, with overrepresentation and low-income voting qualifications serving British strategic interests. - Government of India Act of 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) - Background - Foundational Declaration - Based on the Montagu Declaration of August 20, 1917, promising increased Indian administrative participation and gradual self-governance within the British Empire. - Provisions - Governance Changes - Changes in Home Government - Appointed a High Commissioner for India in London for trade, funded by Indian revenue, not the British Exchequer. - Changes in Government of India - Viceroy's Executive Council - Three of eight members were to be Indian, aligning with the policy of Indian association. - Bicameral System - Replaced the single Legislative Council with the Council of States (Upper House) and Legislative Assembly (Lower House), with elected members under limited franchise. - Expansion of Functions - All members could ask supplementary and short-notice questions, enjoying freedom of speech. - Changes in Provincial Governments - Provincial Autonomy - Introduced via “Devolution Rules,” defining independent provincial powers in finance, legislation, and administration. - Legislative Devolution - Divided legislative items into Central and Provincial Lists, with residual powers vested in the Governor General-in-Council. - Provincial List split into “Transferred” (managed by Indian ministers accountable to the Legislative Council) and “Reserved” subjects (managed by Governors and their Executive Councils), creating dyarchy. - Financial Devolution - Separated revenue sources: land revenue, excise, irrigation, and stamps became provincial; budgets were split from the center, with provinces authorized to frame their own. - Other Provisions - Introduced direct elections with limited franchise. - Extended communal representation to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans, alongside Muslims. - Established the Central Public Service Commission (1926) for civil servant recruitment. - Provided for a Statutory (required, permitted, or enacted by statute (legislative body)) Commission to review the Act after 10 years. - Points to Know - Additional Insights - Initially applied to eight provinces (Bengal, Madras, Bombay, UP, Punjab, Bihar, Orissa, Central Provinces), extended to Burma (1923) and NWFP (North-West Frontier Provinc) later. - Women could neither vote nor contest elections, reflecting Britain's own post-1918 suffrage timeline. - The Muddiman Report analyzed dyarchy's implementation. - Simon Commission and Its Aftermath (1927-1929) - Overview - The Simon Commission, formally the Indian Statutory Commission, was appointed in November 1927 to review the Government of India (GOI) Act 1919, sparking widespread Indian resistance due to its all-British composition. - Its arrival in 1928 catalyzed political unity efforts, notably the Nehru Report, and intensified demands for independence, setting the stage for the Civil Disobedience Movement. - Formation and Context of the Simon Commission - Background - The GOI Act 1919 mandated a decennial review of constitutional progress. In 1927, Britain's Conservative government under Stanley Baldwin preempted a potential Labour-led review by advancing it to November 8, fearing more progressive reforms. - Named after its chairman, Sir John Simon, the seven-member, all-white commission excluded Indians, justified by its accountability to the British Parliament rather than Indian stakeholders. - Appointed amid rising nationalist activity, including the Swaraj Party's legislative disruptions and youth movements led by Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose. - Purpose - Assessed India's readiness for further self-governance under the 1919 Act, focusing on dyarchy's effectiveness and administrative structures, amid growing demands for Dominion Status or independence. - Preceding Reports - Lee Commission (1924): Investigated racial disparities in the Imperial Civil Services, recommending increased Indian recruitment. - Muddiman Commission (1924): Examined dyarchy's operational flaws, suggesting minor adjustments rather than overhaul. - Linlithgow Commission (1926): Addressed agricultural crises and rural economy, highlighting peasant distress as a nationalist rallying point. - Indian Reactions to the Simon Commission - Political Opposition and Boycotts - Congress Response - At the Madras Session (December 1927), presided by M.A. Ansari, Congress resolved to boycott the commission “at every stage and in every form,” reflecting outrage at Indian exclusion. - Jawaharlal Nehru advocated complete independence over Dominion Status, galvanizing radical youth. - Congress launched the All Parties Conference to draft an alternative constitution, seeking cross-party unity. - Broader Opposition - Hindu Mahasabha, Liberal Federation (led by Tej Bahadur Sapru), Jinnah's Muslim League faction, and the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress joined the boycott, decrying the commission as unrepresentative. - Supporters - Unionists in Punjab (landlord-dominated), Justice Party in South India (non-Brahmin elites), and All India Achyut Federation (pro-British untouchable groups) endorsed it, aligning with colonial interests. - Delhi Proposals (December 1927) - Unity Initiative - Presided by Jinnah, this Muslim League-led effort aimed to align Congress and Muslim demands: - Joint electorates with reserved Muslim seats. - One-third Muslim representation in the Central Legislative Assembly. - Proportional representation in Punjab and Bengal. - Creation of Muslim-majority provinces: Sindh, Balochistan, North-West Frontier Province (NWFP). - Congress accepted most terms, but internal Muslim League splits (e.g., Shafi faction's dissent) and Hindu Mahasabha's rejection of concessions derailed unity. - All Parties Conference and the Nehru Report (1928) - Establishment - Convened in February 1928 by M.A. Ansari, it included Congress, Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, Sikh Central League, and others, agreeing on Dominion Status as a compromise goal. - Resulted in the Nehru Report (released August 1928, finalized May), India's first indigenous constitutional draft, chaired by Motilal Nehru. - Key Recommendations of Nehru Report - Constitutional Framework - Dominion Status: India as a self-governing Commonwealth member. - Fundamental Rights: Universal adult suffrage, equal rights (religion, speech, gender), and legal equality. - Minority Safeguards: Joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities; special status for Muslim-majority provinces (e.g., Sindh separated from Bombay, NWFP granted provincial status). - Provincial Reorganization: Linguistic basis for provinces, enhancing regional identity. - Federal Structure: Centralized federal government with provincial autonomy, residual powers retained centrally (more unitary than federal in practice). - Responsible Government: Bicameral legislature (upper and lower houses) and a judicial hierarchy culminating in a supreme court. - Additional Provisions - Balochistan elevated to full province status; communal representation to be reviewed after 20 years. - Princely States Dilemma - The Nehru Committee grappled with integrating Princely States. - The 1927 States People Conference demanded self-governance, but the Butler Committee (1927-1928, under Sir Harcourt Butler) reinforced British paramountcy, preserving princely autonomy under Crown suzerainty. - British Perspective - Lord Birkenhead, Secretary of State, defended Indian exclusion, citing irreconcilable political divisions and challenging Indians to produce a unified constitution—a dare that spurred the Nehru Report. - Opposition and Divisions - Political Reactions - Muslim League (Jinnah faction), Hindu Mahasabha, and Sikh League opposed the Nehru Report, rejecting its unitary tilt and inadequate communal safeguards. - Jinnah's Amendments (Rejected): - One-third Muslim representation in the central legislature. - Proportional representation in Punjab and Bengal. - Residual powers to provinces, favoring federalism over centralization. - Outcome: Jinnah's 14 Points (March 1929) emerged as a counterproposal, shaping Muslim League's future separatism. - Compromises in Nehru Report - Final Adjustments: Adopted joint electorates except in Muslim-majority areas; Sindh separation contingent on Dominion Status; retained centralized residual powers. - Submission: Approved by the All Parties Conference without Jinnah's amendments, signaling partial unity but exposing communal fissures. - Calcutta Congress Session (December 1928) - Internal Dynamics - Presided by Motilal Nehru, the session endorsed the Nehru Report but faced dissent from younger leaders—Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose, and S. Satyamurthy—who rejected Dominion Status for complete independence. - Independence of India League: Formed April 1928 by Nehru, Bose (Secretary), and S. Srinivasa Iyengar (President), it pushed for radical action over constitutional compromise. - Ultimatum - Congress set a one-year deadline (until December 31, 1929) for Britain to grant Dominion Status, threatening civil disobedience for Poorna Swaraj if unmet—a decisive shift toward mass agitation. - Outcomes and Legacy - Simon Commission's Reception - Arrived in India on February 3, 1928, met with nationwide protests—“Simon Go Back” slogans, black flags, and hartals—reflecting unified Indian rejection. - Submitted its report in May 1930, recommending provincial autonomy, dyarchy abolition in provinces, and a federal framework, but ignored by Congress due to its exclusionary process. - Catalyst for Unity and Radicalization - Spurred the Nehru Report as a nationalist counter-narrative, though its failure to bridge communal divides foreshadowed future tensions. - Pushed Congress toward Poorna Swaraj at the Lahore Session (December 1929), launching the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930. - Government of India Act of 1935 - - Background - Policy Foundation - Based on the White Paper on the Indian Constitution post-Third Round Table Conference, criticized by all political parties for falling short of complete independence. - Main Provisions - Structural Reforms - Contained four major provisions: All India Federation, Provincial Autonomy, dyarchy at the center, and safeguards vesting special powers with central and provincial executives. - Provided legal safeguards against misbehavior by Indian ministers and legislators; notably lacked a preamble. - Changes at National Level - Proposal for an All India Federation (never materialized) - Voluntary accession for states, requiring at least half of the 52 allotted Council of States seats and 50% of the states' population to join. - Abolished the Indian Council (from the 1858 Act) due to anti-India policy agitations. - Changes in Government of India - Dyarchy at the Centre - Introduced dyarchy centrally: Reserved Departments under the Governor General with appointed counselors; Transferred subjects advised by ministers answerable to the legislature. - Bicameral Central Legislature - Comprised the Governor General, Council of States, and Federal Assembly, with representation from British India and Princely States (disproportionate weightage for states as nationalist checks). - Changes in Provincial Government - Provincial Autonomy - All departments controlled by elected members, provinces recognized as separate legal entities deriving power from the Crown, free from GOI (Government Of India) and SOS (Secretary of State) control except for specific purposes. - Governors could issue ordinances or enact Governor's Acts. - Abolition of Dyarchy in Provinces - Eliminated the distinction between Reserved and Transferred subjects, establishing fully responsible government with safeguards. - Bicameral Legislature - Introduced in six provinces: Bengal, Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, and Assam. - Other Provisions - Created new provinces (e.g., Burma separated from India). - Lowered franchise, though tied to property qualifications. - Extended separate electorates to women. - Established Federal Bank, Federal Court (1935, 1937), and Federal Railway Authority (free from ministerial control). - Indian National Movement Post CDM (1935-1942) - Legislative Engagement & Growing Radicalism phase - - Understanding Depressed Classes Politics in the 1900s - Introduction - The early 20th century marked a transformative period for the Depressed Classes in India. British colonialism opened new avenues for social mobility, challenging the rigid caste hierarchy. - Awareness of rights grew among the Depressed Classes, intensifying tensions with caste Hindus. - Representation and equality emerged as central issues, shaped by key leaders and policies in their fight for political and social justice. - Key Developments: The Minorities Pact - Context - During the Round Table Conference (RTC), Dr. B.R. Ambedkar initially supported joint electorates with reservations but shifted his stance when his demand for universal adult suffrage (right to vote) was rejected. - He aligned with Muslim, Anglo-Indian, and Christian representatives to form the Minorities Pact. - Provisions - Proposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, with a referendum planned after 20 years to reassess the arrangement. - Reason for Shift - Ambedkar's universal adult suffrage proposal was opposed by the Muslim League, princely states, and the British government, which hesitated to adopt it. - Without universal suffrage, Dalit representatives risked being elected mainly by caste Hindus, leaving their political influence stagnant (motionless). - Key Developments: The Rajah-Moonje Pact (1932) - - Overview (No Need to Memorize) - In 1932, the Hindu Mahasabha, aiming to preserve Hindu unity, collaborated with M.C. Rajah. - Provisions included reserved seats for Dalits within joint electorates to promote unity while consolidating Hindu interests. - Impact: Rajah's shift from supporting separate electorates to joint electorates split Dalit opinion, reflecting the evolving political landscape and lack of consensus among Dalit leaders. - The Communal Award (August 16, 1932) - Background - Announced by British PM Ramsay MacDonald, based on the Lothian Committee (Indian Franchise Committee) recommendations after the Second RTC, to ensure representation for minorities and marginalized groups, including Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, and Depressed Classes. - Lothian Committee Recommendations (For Understanding) - Expansion of electorates for provincial and federal assemblies. - Reservation of 2-5% of seats for women. - Specific provisions treating Depressed Classes as a distinct minority. - Left representation decisions for princely states to the states themselves. - Key Provisions - Allocated separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, and Depressed Classes. - Reserved 71 seats for Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures (later raised to 148 under Gandhi) and 18% of total seats in the central legislature. - Provided weightage to Muslims in minority provinces. - Doubled the number of seats in provincial legislatures for better representation. - Reserved 3% of seats for women in most provinces. - Allotted seven seats for Marathas in Bombay. - Included educational grants to improve facilities for Depressed Classes. - Responses - Congress: Opposed separate electorates but avoided altering the Award without minority consent, adopting a stance of neither acceptance nor rejection. - Gandhi: Saw it as a threat to Indian unity, opposed segregating Depressed Classes politically, and launched an indefinite fast to demand joint electorates with reserved seats. - Poona Pact (September 1932) - Agreement signed between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar at Yerwada Jail, Poona, to resolve the dispute over separate electorates for Depressed Classes. - Key Provisions - Increased reserved seats for Depressed Classes from 71 to 148 in provincial legislatures and maintained 18% in the central legislature. - Established joint electorates with reserved seats for Depressed Classes. - Introduced a primary election system, where an electoral college of Depressed Class candidates would finalize nominations. - Provided educational grants and ensured no disabilities for Depressed Classes. - Made the reservation system subject to future mutual agreement. - Outcome - Amended the Communal Award and was approved by the British government. - Post-CDM and the Transition to Constitutional Politics - End of Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) - In April 1934, Gandhi withdrew the CDM, shifting from mass struggles to a phase of non-mass political activity. - Three perspectives emerged on the next steps: - Gandhian Constructive Work: Focused on Harijan upliftment and rural reconstruction. - Constitutional Struggle: Advocated by M.A. Ansari and Asaf Ali for participating in elections and working within legislative frameworks. - Leftist Perspective: Nehru and others pushed for continued non-constitutional mass movements, criticizing Gandhi's “Struggle-Truce-Struggle” approach and favoring “Struggle-Victory.” - Gandhi's "Struggle-Truce-Struggle" Approach - Gandhi believed in alternating between mass movements and negotiations to achieve constitutional concessions. - Examples: - Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22): Ended abruptly after the Chauri Chaura incident. - Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34): Suspended after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. - Quit India Movement (1942): A final push after failed negotiations with the British. - Gandhi's strategy aimed at gradual progress through moral and political pressure rather than an all-out confrontation. - Leftist "Struggle-Victory" Approach - Nehru, Bose, and other left-leaning leaders argued for unrelenting struggle until complete victory, rejecting temporary compromises. - Their key beliefs: - The British would never concede independence voluntarily through negotiations. - Movements should not pause for political deals but should escalate until colonial rule was completely dismantled. - Greater emphasis on mass mobilization, socialism, and direct action. - This led to tensions within the Congress, as younger and more radical leaders like Subhas Chandra Bose and Nehru often found Gandhi's methods too conservative or cautious. - Impact of This Divide - The leftist faction influenced Congress towards a more assertive stance, culminating in the 1930 Purna Swaraj resolution and the Quit India Movement (1942). - Subhas Chandra Bose, who strongly opposed any truce with the British, eventually left Congress to lead the Indian National Army (INA) for armed struggle. - Nehru, though critical of truce-based strategies, remained within the Congress framework and later shaped India’s socialist-leaning post-independence policies. - Understanding These Factions: Neo-Swarajists - Council Entry - Congress leaders, dubbed Neo-Swarajists, advocated participating in the 1934 Central Legislative Assembly (CLA) elections. - In 1933, S. Satyamurthy founded the Madras Swaraj Party to support council entry. - C. Rajagopalachari pushed for council entry to broaden Congress's political base and prepare for future mass struggles. - Unlike earlier Swarajists, they aimed for cooperation in legislative councils, including assuming office and forming ministries. - Understanding These Factions: Socialists - Class Struggle - Led by Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose, and Jayaprakash Narayan, socialists within Congress focused on: - Mobilizing workers and peasants for a more equitable society. - Nationalizing key industries and resources and undertaking land reforms. - Establishing a planned economy. - They opposed council entry, believing it diverted focus from the anti-imperialist struggle, with Nehru strongly against participating in elections. - Gandhi Resigns from Congress (1934) - By 1934, Gandhi felt out of sync with Congress currents: - Many favored parliamentary politics, which he opposed. - His emphasis on spinning and Harijan work alienated some workers. - Nehru's socialist group was gaining influence. - In October 1934, Gandhi resigned from Congress to serve better through thought, word, and deed. - Shift to Constitutional Politics - May 1934 (AICC at Patna): Congress established a Parliamentary Board to contest upcoming elections. - November 1934 (CLA Elections): Congress won 45 of 75 seats reserved for Indians, becoming the largest party and marking a shift from confrontation to constitutional politics. - Congress Nationalist Party - Formed by M.M. Malaviya and Madhav Shrihari Aney, who split from Congress to protest the 1932 Communal Award. After the 1934 elections, Congress and the Nationalist Party together held a majority in the CLA. - - Lucknow Session (April 1936) - President: Jawaharlal Nehru. - Key Outcomes: - Highlighted socialism as vital for global and Indian issues, with three socialists—Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, and Achyut Patwardhan—in the CWC. - Resolved to contest elections based on an election manifesto. - Advocated equal rights for princely state residents, matching the rest of India. - Left the question of office acceptance pending. - Faizpur Congress Session (December 1936) - First Rural Session - President: Jawaharlal Nehru. - Key Outcomes: - Nehru condemned fascism (far-right, authoritarian, and ultranationalist political ideology). - Called for a Constituent Assembly to draft India's constitution. - Adopted an Agrarian Programme: - Reduced land tax and rent by 50%. - Recognized peasant unions (Kisan Sabhas). - Aimed to abolish taxes paid to landlords completely. - 1937 Provincial Elections - Held in eleven provinces under the GOI Act 1935; Congress won majorities in seven, forming ministries except in Bengal, Punjab, and Sindh. - Performed poorly in Upper House elections due to a limited franchise favoring landlords and moneylenders. - Note: CLA (Central Legislative Assembly) elections of 1934 were under the GOI Act 1919, while 1937 provincial elections followed the GOI Act 1935. - - Question of Office Acceptance (1937) - March 1937 (AICC Meeting, Presided by Rajendra Prasad): Conditionally accepted office if governors refrained from using special powers under the GOI Act 1935 to interfere with ministries. - June 1937: Viceroy clarified governors would not intervene in government affairs regarding special powers. - July 1937 (CWC at Wardha): Authorized office acceptance. - Congress formed a Parliamentary Sub-Committee (Sardar Patel, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Rajendra Prasad) to prevent British divide-and-rule tactics. - Resulted in 28 months of Congress rule focused on public welfare and reforms. - Gandhi in Harijan: “These offices have to be held lightly and not tightly. They are crowns of thorns.” - Analysis of this quote - This reflects his philosophy on leadership, power, and public service. - Leadership as a Responsibility, Not a Privilege - Detachment from Authority - Critique of Power-Hungry Politics - Note: Leftists opposed office acceptance as collaboration with imperialism, while right-wing leaders like C. Rajagopalachari supported it for enabling peasant and worker reforms. - Key Developments During Congress Rule (1937-1939) - Administrative Reforms - Repealed emergency laws (e.g., Public Safety Act) and lifted press restrictions. - Released political prisoners and removed bans on groups like Hindustan Seva Dal (Communist Party ban remained). - Social Reforms - Promoted Harijan welfare through temple entry and scholarships. - Expanded educational facilities and public health initiatives. - Economic Reforms - Encouraged khadi production with subsidies. - Imposed prohibition in certain areas. - Labour Reforms - Mediated trade union protests (e.g., Industrial Disputes Bill 1938). - Agrarian Focus - Adopted a radical agrarian program at the 1936 Faizpur Session. - Resignation of Congress Ministries (October 1939) - Congress ministries resigned due to India's involvement in World War II without consultation. - Subhas Chandra Bose and Ideological Divides - Early Political Journey - 1921: Joined the Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM), mentored by C.R. Das; edited *Forward*, the Swaraj Party’s newspaper, amplifying its radical voice. - 1930: Founded the Congress Democratic Party within Congress; elected president of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), championing labor rights during the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM). - 1933-1936: Exiled to Europe after CDM imprisonment; returned in 1936, invigorated by socialist ideas from abroad. - Haripura Congress Session (February 1938) - Elected Congress president, Bose saw Congress ministries (formed post-1937 elections) as revolutionary platforms. - Advocated economic planning, establishing the National Planning Committee under Jawaharlal Nehru to draft industrial policies. - Resolutions included: - Vision of a Socialist State in India. - Abolition of landlordism (zamindari system). - Protection of workers’ rights and welfare for peasants and farmers. - Sent a medical mission to aid Chinese forces against Japanese aggression, reflecting anti-imperialist solidarity. - Ideological Clash with Congress Leadership - Bose criticized senior leaders in *The Indian Struggle* (1935), labeling them “Rightists” for compromising with Britain via the Government of India Act 1935’s federal scheme, questioning their nationalist commitment. - Congress leaders struggled to collaborate with Bose’s confrontational stance, deepening internal divides. - Tripuri Congress Session (March 1939) - Re-elected president, defeating Gandhi’s nominee, Pattabhi Sitaramayya (1,581 vs. 1,375 votes), despite Gandhi’s opposition. - Gandhi called Sitaramayya’s loss “my own defeat,” signaling a personal rift. - Bose proposed a six-month ultimatum to Britain for independence, favoring immediate struggle; Gandhi opposed, citing unpreparedness of Congress and the masses. - Resignation and Forward Bloc - April 29, 1939: Resigned as president due to lack of CWC support; Rajendra Prasad succeeded him. - May 3, 1939: Formed the Forward Bloc within Congress to rally radical elements, advocating mass action. - Faced disciplinary action after calling an All India Protest against an AICC resolution diluting anti-British resolve: - Removed as Bengal Provincial Congress Committee president. - Banned from Congress elective offices for three years (1939-1942). - Congress and World War II: From Resignation to Cripps Mission - Overview - The outbreak of World War II in September 1939 tested the Indian National Congress’s strategies, revealing internal divisions and escalating demands for independence. - From ministry resignations to the Cripps Mission, this period marked a shift from conditional cooperation to renewed agitation, culminating in the prelude to Quit India. - Congress Ministries Resign and Initial War Response (October-November 1939) - Context - Britain’s unilateral declaration of India as a belligerent (hostile and aggressive) in World War II without consulting Indian leaders sparked outrage, prompting Congress to reassess its position. - Congress Demands and Actions - October 23, 1939: The Congress Working Committee (CWC) met in Wardha, condemning Britain’s decision and demanding consultation and self-determination. - Resignation of Ministries: By November 10, Congress-led provincial governments (e.g., Bombay, Madras) resigned, protesting lack of autonomy. - Gandhi’s Stance: Welcomed resignations as a “bitter pill” to purify Congress’s anti-imperialist resolve. - Divergent Views Within Congress - Support for Allies: Gandhi and C. Rajagopalachari sympathized with Britain’s anti-fascist fight but tied support to Indian freedom. - Opposition to War: Nehru opposed participation without independence; socialists saw it as an imperialist conflict. - Government Response - Viceroy Linlithgow’s White Paper (October 17, 1939): - Framed war aims vaguely as resisting aggression, avoiding democratic commitments for India. - Offered post-war Dominion Status and more Indian members in the Viceroy’s Executive Council. - Proposed a consultative committee instead of a national government, reinforcing colonial control. - CWC Reaction: Dismissed it as a rehash of colonial policies, opting out of war support and solidifying resignations. - Muslim League Reaction - Jinnah supported Britain, demanding recognition as the sole Muslim voice and veto power over constitutional changes, celebrating resignations as a “Day of Deliverance” on December 22, 1939. - Congress Articulates War Conditions (September-October 1939) - Congress Demands via CWC Resolution - Argued India couldn’t fight for democracy abroad while denied it at home. - Sought an end to colonial rule and full democracy in India. - Specific Conditions: - Britain to clarify war goals and their application to India’s democratization. - Post-war constituent assembly to frame India’s constitution. - Immediate establishment of a responsible central government. - Government Response - Linlithgow’s Rejection: Deemed significant power transfers unsuitable during wartime, leveraging Muslim League and princely state support to counter Congress. - Outcome: Strengthened Congress’s resolve to withhold war cooperation, deepening the standoff. - Debate on Mass Struggle (Late 1939-Early 1940) - Internal Deliberations - Arguments Against Immediate Action: - Allies’ just cause warranted restraint to avoid embarrassment during the war. - Risk of communal violence disrupting Hindu-Muslim unity. - Congress’s organizational weaknesses—disarray and lack of discipline post-resignations—hindered mass protests. - Radical Push: Socialists and others pressed for immediate resistance, viewing the war as an imperialist opportunity. - Ramgarh Congress Session (March 19-20, 1940) - Context - Presided by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (editor of *Al-Hilal*), amid growing war pressures and internal debates. - Congress Demands and Resolutions - Nehru reiterated complete independence as a prerequisite for support, rejecting Dominion Status within the imperial structure. - Declared sovereignty must rest with India’s people, not the Crown. - Authorized Gandhi to launch Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) when deemed fit, signaling readiness for struggle. - Government Response - No immediate British counteroffer; Linlithgow maintained a hardline stance, ignoring Congress’s escalating demands. - August Offer (August 8, 1940) - Context - After the fall of Belgium, Holland, and France (May-June 1940), Britain sought Indian support; Congress proposed an interim government, but Linlithgow issued his own terms. - British Proposal (Linlithgow’s Offer) - Dominion Status post-war, with a largely Indian constituent assembly. - Expanded Viceroy’s Executive Council with majority Indian members from major parties. - Right to frame India’s constitution post-war, subject to minority consent. - Indian Responses - Congress Rejection: Criticized delayed independence and lack of immediate power transfer. - Muslim League Support: Welcomed minority veto but insisted on partition, foreshadowing Pakistan. - Individual Satyagraha (October 1940-December 1941) - Context - Launched as a limited protest amid stalled negotiations and Japan’s rising threat in Asia. - Congress Objectives and Actions - Demonstrated nationalist resolve, countering perceptions of weakness. - Protested India’s forced war involvement. - Demanded free speech via anti-war declarations (“Delhi Chalo Andolan”). - Execution: Began October 17, 1940, with Vinoba Bhave as the first satyagrahi; Nehru followed (arrested October 31); 25,000 arrested by May 1941. - Government Response - Mass arrests and suppression of anti-war activities, signaling intolerance for dissent. - Congress Dilemma and Shift - Japan’s aggression (e.g., Pearl Harbor, December 1941) heightened urgency; CWC offered cooperation if full independence was assured post-war and power transferred immediately. - Gandhi named Nehru his successor, solidifying leadership for future struggles. - Cripps Mission (March-April 1942) - Context - Japan’s advance (e.g., Singapore’s fall, February 1942) prompted Britain to send Sir Stafford Cripps, arriving March 23, to secure Indian war support. - British Proposal (Cripps’ Offer) - Dominion Status post-war, with an elected Indian constituent assembly. - Provinces could join or secede from the Indian Union, forming separate entities. - Defence and communications under British control during the war; post-war, India could retain British forces. - Minority safeguards via a commission; secession option if rights were unprotected. - Princely states to join voluntarily or form a separate union. - Indian Responses - Congress Rejection: - Opposed Dominion Status over full independence. - Criticized princely state nominees (not elected), provincial secession, and lack of immediate power transfer (Governor-General’s supremacy retained). - Muslim League: Rejected a single union, arguing it denied Muslim self-determination and Pakistan. - Hindu Mahasabha: Opposed secession as fragmenting India. - Depressed Classes: Feared partition would expose them to upper-caste dominance. - Sikhs: Objected to losing Punjab in potential Muslim-majority secession. - Assessment and Outcome - Rigid “take it or leave it” stance and vague accession process alienated all parties. - Gandhi called it a “post-dated cheque”; Nehru criticized its autocratic retention, paving the way for Quit India (August 1942). - Indian National Movement (1942 - 1947) - Final phase - Quit India Movement (August 1942) - August Resolution - 'Quit India' “Bharat Chodo Andolan” - July 1942 - CWC meeting Wardha - Resolution giving Gandhi the command to launch mass movement - 8 August 1942 Resolution formally ratified. - Directives given to Various Sections of Society - Government Servants: - Do not resign but declare allegiance to Congress. - Soldiers: Stay in the Army but refrain from firing on compatriots. - Students: If confident, leave studies to join the movement. - Peasants: If zamindars are anti-government, pay mutually agreed rent & If zamindars are pro-government, do not pay rent. - Princes: Support the masses and acknowledge the sovereignty of the people. - People in Princely States: Support rulers only if they are anti-government & Declare allegiance to being part of the Indian nation. - Who All Opposed - Muslim League - Communist Party of India - Hindu Mahasabha - Course of Movement - In a single Sweep, (9 August 1942) all the Top Leaders of Congress were arrested and taken to unknown locations. - Declared Congress organisations unlawful, Public meeting banned under Defense of India Act, 1919. - Led to emergence of Local Level Leaders and unregulated mass movements - Leading to violent incidents. - Parallel Governments (September 1942) - Balliya Sarkar - Chittu Pandey - Ballia (UP) - Low Budget Gandhi Marriages - Tamluk Sarkar = Satish C. Samanta - Tamluk (Bengal) - Vidyut Vahini (Armed Militia) - Satara Sarkar - Nana Patil = Satara (MH) - Nyayadan Mandals (People's Court) & Toofan Senas (Youth Militia) - Emergence of Underground Activities - Disrupting Communications - Underground Radio Station - Bombay - Usha Mehta (Movie - Ae Watan Mera Watan) - Govt Response to Movement - Utilised Large Military Force - initially stationed to confront Japanese. - Wartime censorship. - In Feb 1943, Gandhi took fast unto death - Govt, anticipated Gandhi's death and made arrangements for his funeral. - Bengal Famine of 1943 - One of the reasons for decline of movement initially, later emerged as a strong reason for independence - Bengal Famine of 1943 - The Bengal Famine of 1943 was one of the deadliest humanitarian disasters in modern Indian history, leading to the deaths of an estimated 2-3 million people due to starvation, malnutrition, and disease. - Causes of the Famine - British War Policies & Economic Exploitation - The famine occurred during World War II, when British policies prioritized war efforts over Indian welfare. - "Denial Policy" (1942): To prevent a Japanese invasion, the British destroyed boats and food stocks in coastal Bengal, disrupting local economies. - Rice export bans were lifted for British war allies, worsening domestic shortages. - Hoarding and Inflation - Wartime policies created hyperinflation, making food unaffordable. - Wealthy traders and speculators hoarded rice, creating an artificial scarcity. - British Apathy and Churchill's Indifference - Winston Churchill refused to send food aid, blaming Indians for "breeding like rabbits." - When Indian officials requested 1 million tons of grain, Britain sent only 50,000 tons, prioritizing European stockpiles. - Cyclones and Crop Failures - A cyclone in October 1942 and fungal diseases reduced the rice yield in Bengal, worsening the crisis. - Impact of the Famine - Deaths and Suffering - 2-3 million people died due to starvation, disease, and malnutrition. - Malaria and cholera outbreaks worsened the death toll. - Political Fallout - The famine exposed British colonial neglect, increasing nationalist sentiments. - Subhas Chandra Bose used it as propaganda to rally Indians against British rule. - The Indian National Congress and Mahatma Gandhi condemned the British, calling for immediate independence. - Economic Collapse - Rural Bengal's economy collapsed, pushing millions into poverty. - The famine devastated farmers, laborers, and fishermen, many of whom migrated or died. - Significance of Movement - Unprecedented Mass Participation with Grassroot leadership - Use of Violence - Indian National Army (1942 - 1945) - Indian Independence League (IIL) - In March 1942, Rash Behari Bose, a revolutionary leader in Japan since 1915, organized a meeting in Tokyo with other Indian leaders to form the IIL. - In June 1942, during a meeting in Bangkok, Rash Behari Bose was appointed as the President of the IIL. - A resolution was passed to establish the Indian National Army (INA), also known as the Azad Hind Fauz. - It was decided that Subhas Chandra Bose would lead the movement in the future. - Formation of the INA - INA enlisted volunteers from Indians overseas and ex-British Indian soldiers in Southeast Asia. - Captain Mohan Singh was made the Commander-in-Chief. - The INA grew to about 40,000 members, preparing to confront British forces in India. - Disagreements between Captain Mohan Singh and the Japanese led to the transfer of INA leadership to Subhas Chandra Bose. - INA under Subhas Chandra Bose - In July 1943, Rash Behari Bose handed over the leadership to Subhas Chandra Bose. - Subhas Bose established the Arzi Hukumat-e-Azad Hind (Provisional Government of Free India) in Singapore on October 21, 1943. - The Provisional Government declared war on Britain and the USA and was recognized by the Axis powers. - In Dec 1943, Japanese handed over Andaman and Nicobar Island to Bose - Renaming Shaheed and Swaraj Dweep. - INA HQ's shifted from Singapore to Rangoon in January 1944 and army prepared to march towards Delhi (Dilli Chalo) - At this time regiment of INA were named after Gandhi, Nehru, Azar, Bose, Rani Jhansi (Captain Lakshmi Sehgal) - INA Army was arrested by Allied Forces in 1945 meanwhile Subash Bose died in an air crash on August 18, 1945 in Taipei, Taiwan - The Story Continues - CR (C. Rajagopalachari) Formula (1944) - Following Gandhi's release from Jail on May 5, 1944 - He tried to revive Congress and also initiated discussions with Muslim League in July 1944. - C. R. Formula (1944) - Proposed by: C. Rajagopalachari - Objective: To resolve the deadlock between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League over the demand for Pakistan and to facilitate cooperation between the two parties for achieving Indian independence. - Main Points - The Muslim League was to cooperate with the Congress in forming a Provisional Interim Government for a transitional period and in return League's demand for Pakistan was recognized, but only through a democratic process involving a plebiscite (vote or referendum). - All parties would be allowed to express their views on partition before the plebiscite. - After World War II, a plebiscite would decide whether Muslim-majority areas in the North-West and North-East would: - Form a separate sovereign state (Pakistan), or Remain a part of India. - If separation occurred, agreements would be entered into for essential services such as: - Defence - Communication - Commerce. - Reactions to C. R. Formula (1944) - Muslim League's Stand - Supported the concept of a two-nation theory. - Muhammad Ali Jinnah proposed that - Only Muslims in the North-West and North-East should vote in the plebiscite. - The rest of the Indian population should not be involved in the decision-making process. - Congress's Stand - Congress was willing to work with the Muslim League to achieve independence. - However, Congress rejected the formula as - It accepted the principle of partition. - The League's primary goal was the creation of a separate nation, which Congress opposed. - Other Reactions - Hindu Leaders - Led by Vir Savarkar, Hindu leaders opposed the formula, as they disagreed with conceding to the demand for Pakistan. - Sikh Leaders - Leaders like Master Tara Singh opposed the plan, fearing division of the Sikh community in Punjab, leaving Sikhs on both sides of the dividing line. - Desai Liaquat Pact (1945) - Context - The failure of the Gandhi-Jinnah Talks (1944) left a deadlock between the INC and the Muslim League. - Secret talks were held between Bhulabhai Desai, a senior Congress leader, and Liaquat Ali Khan, a prominent leader of the Muslim League, in January 1945. - Objective - To negotiate an agreement for a future coalition government representing both Hindus and Muslims equally in the independent government of India. - Key Points of the Pact - Recognition of the Muslim League: - Desai acknowledged the Muslim League as the representative of Muslims. - Formation of an Interim Government: An interim government would be formed with equal representation of the Congress and the League. - Liaquat's Concessions: Liaquat Ali Khan gave up the demand for a separate Muslim state (Pakistan). - Seats for Minorities: The pact proposed 20% reserved seats for minorities in the government. - Outcome - The Desai-Liaquat Pact was never formally endorsed by either the Congress or the Muslim League. - Special Mention - Sapru Committee Report (1945) - Wavell Plan (1945) - Background - By the end of 1944, with the war turning in favor of the Allies, the British realized that - The Indian situation, post-Quit India Movement, could not be ignored and prolonged use of force to subdue India indefinitely was impractical - Urgency of Finding a Solution - The upcoming 1945 General Elections in England required the Conservatives to urgently address Indian issues - The plan was designed to prevent Congress leaders from exploiting the post-war climate of unemployment and economic challenges. - Key Features of the Wavell Plan - Restructured Executive Council: - The Executive Council was to be restructured with all members, except the Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief, being Indian representatives. - Interim Government: - The interim government would function within the framework of the 1935 Government of India Act and would remain answerable to the Central Assembly. - Joint List of Nominees - Political parties were to collaborate in creating a joint list of nominees for the Executive Council. - If consensus was not achieved, separate lists could be submitted. - Equal Representation - Equal representation was to be provided to caste Hindus and Muslims in the Executive Council. - Governor-General's Powers -The Governor-General would exercise veto power, but only on the advice of his ministers. - Future Constitution - Provisions were made to explore negotiations for a new constitution after the war. - Simla Conference (June 1945) - To implement the Wavell Plan, Lord Wavell organized a conference in Simla - Congress was represented by Maulana Azad, while Jinnah represented the Muslim League. - Mahatma Gandhi also advised the Viceroy during the talks. - Reactions to the Wavell Plan - Muslim League's Response - Feared loss of representation if other minority groups (like Sikhs, Christians, and Depressed Classes) aligned with the Congress. - Demanded that all Muslim members in the Executive Council be nominated by the League. - Congress's Response - Perceived the plan as an attempt to limit Congress's influence, seeing it as a measure to make Congress solely a caste Hindu party. - Asserted its right to nominate representatives from all communities. - Political Negotiations and Developments - The Release of Congress Leaders (Post-1944) - Post-World War II, the British sought to establish a coalition government in India. (Wavell Plan 1945) - Congress leaders were released from prison in May 1944 on grounds of ill health. - Public enthusiasm for these leaders signaled renewed resolve to fight for independence. - Elections in Britain (1945) - The Labour Party, sympathetic to India, won the July 1945 elections. - Clement Attlee became Prime Minister, replacing Winston Churchill. - The Labour Party manifesto highlighted promoting India's self-government within the Commonwealth. - In August 1945, elections for India's central and provincial legislatures were announced. - Viceroy Wavell indicated in September that following the election, Government would intend to - Hold Negotiations for establishing a Constitution making body. - Form an Executive Council with support from the major political parties. - Election in India (1945 & 1946) - Muslim League Manifesto - Asserted Muslims of India are One Nation. - Emphasized Pakistan as the solution to India's constitutional problem. - Congress Manifesto - Advocated for Indian unity and opposed partition. - Raised public issues like Police excesses during QIM and INA Trials. - Election Results (1946): The Elections to Central Legislative Assembly were held in December 1945 and the provincial elections were held in January 1946. - Congress dominated the elections, winning 91.3% of non-Muslim votes and 57/102 seats in the Central Legislative Assembly. - Muslim League secured 86.6% of Muslim votes, winning 30/30 Muslim seats in the Assembly and 402/509 Muslim seats in provinces. - Congress formed ministries in 8 provinces (Majority everywhere except Sindh, Punjab and Bengal), while the Muslim League led in Sindh and Bengal. - In Punjab, Congress, Union Party and Akalis formed a coalition Government. - Popular Uprising - INA Trials (1945-46) - Importance and Impact of INA Trials - Widespread Political Support - All major political parties, including Congress, Akalis, Communist Party of India, Hindu Mahasabha, Justice Party, Muslim League, RSS, and Unionist Party. - Broadened Appeal - Attracted new social groups like government officials, armed forces members, and loyalists who were previously outside the nationalist movement. - Geographic Spread of Support - Support extended beyond major cities like Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras to remote regions such as Assam, Balochistan, and Coorg. - Public Symbolism and Outrage - Held publicly at the Red Fort, the trials symbolized British oppression and sparked mass public outrage. - Prominent Figures - Key INA leaders, Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sehgal, and Gurbaksh Dhillon, were charged with treason (betrayel one's country). - INA Defence Committee and Trial Outcome - Formation of INA Defence Committee (1945) - The INC established the INA Defence Committee, including prominent lawyers like - Jawaharlal Nehru, Bhulabhai Desai, Asaf Ali, and Tej Bahadur Sapru. - Outcome of the Trial - INA members were convicted of conducting war but were not executed. - They were terminated from service with no long-term punishment. - Popular Uprising - RIN Mutiny - Growth of the Royal Indian Navy - The Royal Indian Navy expanded rapidly during World War II, becoming 10 times larger between 1939 and 1945. - Surge in Nationalism - A growing sense of nationalism among Indian sailors played a crucial role in shaping the mutiny. - Contributing Factors - Disparities in pay and working conditions. - Racial discrimination and unequal treatment by British officers. - Poor living conditions and inadequate food supplies. - Resentment over being used to suppress freedom movements in other colonies. - Influence of the INA trials and broader anti-colonial sentiment. - Mutiny Events - Started on December 1, 1945 at HMIS Talwar in Bombay. (Training Facility for Royal Indian Navy) - Formation of Naval Central Strike Committee formed with Lt. M.S. Khan (President) and officer Madan Singh (Vice President). This committee had representatives from all Bombay ships and barracks and renamed RIN to Indian National Navy. - The Committee presented demands like - Release of all political prisoners including that of INA Trials. - Equal Pay and Better food quality. - End of British Rule in India. - Expanded to include 20,000 ratings (enlisted sailors or non-commissioned personnel in the navy) and several naval stations across India. - Ratings raised Congress, Muslim League, and Communist Party flags, symbolizing unity. - Political Response - Clement Attlee called for a forceful resolution. - Congress and Muslim League opposed the mutiny, fearing violence, Gandhi too opposed the unplanned revolt. - Communist Party of India fully supported the naval ratings and mobilised workers in Bombay by shutting down textile mills. - End of Mutiny & Significance - Mutiny was eventually quelled after negotiations, Principal demands were met and under pressure from Congress Naval Central Strike Committee was forced to surrender. - Following the RIN Mutiny, all participating Navy personnels were dismissed and many faced court martials. However in 1972, GOI recognised their contribution and granted them freedom fighter's pensions. - The timing of Cabinet Missions announcement, just a day after the Mutiny starts underscores its influence on British Policies towards India. - Cabinet Mission (1946) - The Labour Government, led by Clement Attlee, sent the Cabinet Mission to India to explore solutions to Indian problems and resolve constitutional deadlock - The mission comprised three British officials - Lord Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India). - Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade and a supporter of Indian self-determination). - A.V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty). - Objectives of the Cabinet Mission - Resolve Constitutional Issues - Design a framework for India's constitution to address competing demands of Congress and the Muslim League. - Avoid Partition - Prevent the division of India into separate sovereign states (India and Pakistan). - Negotiate Interim Government - Facilitate the formation of an interim government to oversee the transition. - After initial dialogue, Mission proposed its plan for composition of new Government on 16 May 1946. - Mission came with short term (Formation of Interim Government) and long term proposals (Federal and Constituent Assembly proposals) to ensure a peaceful transition while addressing the complex political and communal issues in India - Interim Government - An Interim Government was to be established with representatives from major political parties to manage the transition. - Rejection of a Separate Pakistan - Geographical impracticality of dividing provinces like Bengal and Punjab. - Risk of economic and administrative challenges in divided territories. - Constituent Assembly - It was to be elected by provincial assemblies by proportional representation - Recommended the formation of a 389-member Constituent Assembly - 292 members from British provinces. - 93 members from princely states. - 4 members from chief commissioners' provinces. - Federal Structure - Proposed a three-tier government system - Union Government: Control over foreign affairs, defense, and communications. - Communal Questions in the Central Legislature were to be decided by simple majority in both communities present and voting. - Provincial Governments: Autonomy in other areas and also Residual Powers. - Groups of Provinces - Section A - Hindu Majority Provinces (Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar and Orissa) - Section B - Punjab, NWFP (North-West Frontier Provinc), Sindh (Muslim majority provinces of North West) - Section C - Bengal and Assam (Muslim dominated provinces of North East) - After the first General Elections, a province was to be free to come out of a group and also eligible for reconsideration. - Princely States were no longer to be under the paramountcy of the British Govt. They would be free to enter into an agreement with successor governments of the British Govt. - Reaction to the Cabinet Mission - Congress's Response - Accepted the idea of a Constituent Assembly and went ahead to form the Constituent Assembly (15 June) - Rejected the groupings of provinces, (10 July) as it contradicted their vision of a unified India. (Initially, thought that grouping was optional for provinces and free to join or not) - Muslim League's Response - Muslim League took the grouping of provinces to be compulsory and thus leading realization of Pakistan indirectly. - Initially accepted (June 6) the plan but later withdrew, accusing Congress of undermining the grouping principle (29 July) and the right of Muslim League only to nominate Muslim candidates (Zakir Hussain from Congress) - Called for Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) to press for the creation of Pakistan after Congress was invited by Wavell to form Interim Govt at center sidelining Muslim League. - Princely States' Response - The princely states were reluctant to join the proposed federal structure, fearing loss of autonomy. - Formation of Interim Government with Congress Alone - Invitation to Congress - On 12 August 1946, the Viceroy invited Jawaharlal Nehru to form the Interim Government as Prime Minister. - A 12-member cabinet was formed, representing diverse sections of society - 5 Hindus - 3 Muslims - 1 each from Scheduled Castes, Sikhs, Christians, and Parsis. - Provincial Governments - At the provincial level, Congress-led governments were formed in most provinces, including - North-West Frontier Province (NWFP). - Punjab: Coalition with Akali Dal and Unionist Muslim League. - Bengal and Sindh: Muslim League formed governments. - Constituent Assembly's Role - The Constituent Assembly was instructed to commence work on drafting a new constitution for India. - Muslim League's Opposition - Muhammad Ali Jinnah condemned the Interim Government and pledged to continue the fight for Pakistan. - This led to widespread unrest and violence in Punjab, Delhi, Bombay, and other regions. - Wavell's Appeal - In light of communal tensions, Viceroy Wavell urged Nehru to include the Muslim League in the Interim Government, hoping it would restore peace. - Despite this, the Muslim League did not abandon its demand for Pakistan and direct action to achieve it. - League's Inclusion - On 26 October 1946, the Muslim League joined the Interim Government, with Liaqat Ali Khan appointed as Finance Minister. The League aimed to disrupt the functioning of the government, using its position to block key decisions. - These tactics convinced Congress leaders of the futility (pointlessness) of the Interim Government. - Breakdown of the Interim Government - Mountbatten's Arrival: With the arrival of the new Viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, in early 1947, Congress leaders expressed that the coalition was unworkable. - Acceptance of Partition: The failure of the Interim Government, coupled with escalating communal tensions, led to the acceptance of the idea of Partition, paving the way for the division of India. - Constituent Assembly: Formation and Election - The Cabinet Mission aimed to make immediate arrangements for Indians to decide the future constitution of India, resolving political conflicts. The assembly was constituted under the Government of India Act, 1935, using restricted adult franchise. - Composition and Electoral College - Composition of Assembly - The Constituent Assembly had 389 seats - 296 seats for British India provinces (e.g., Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, etc.). - 93 seats for princely states. - Division of Seats - Seats were distributed based on population: (Roughly one seat per million people) - Seats in British provinces were also divided among: Muslims, Sikhs, and General communities based on their population. - Election Process - Representatives of each community were elected by members of that community in the provincial legislative assembly. - Voting followed the method of proportional representation. - Princely States - Representatives were nominated by the heads of princely states. - First Session (9 December 1946) - Only 207 of the 296 members attended the inaugural session. - Members from the Muslim League boycotted the session due to disagreements over partition. - J.B. Kripalani invited Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha to act as the temporary chairman due to his seniority. - Election of Permanent Chairman (10 December 1946) - Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent chairman of the Constituent Assembly. - Objective Resolution (13 December 1946) - Jawaharlal Nehru proposed the Objective Resolution, which later formed the basis of the Preamble to the Indian Constitution. - Dual Role - Acted as the Constituent Assembly, framing the Constitution. - Functioned as the Legislative Assembly, governing and making laws. - Timeframe - The Assembly held 11 sessions over 2 years and 11 months for a total of 166 days. - It completed the Constitution of India in 1950. - Partition and Freedom (1946–1947) - Overview - The partition of British India into the independent dominions of India and Pakistan on August 15, 1947, marked the culmination of a complex process driven by communal tensions, nationalist demands, and British withdrawal plans. - Sparked by the Muslim League’s push for a separate Pakistan and Congress’s vision for a united India, the partition involved violent communal riots, mass migrations, and the integration of princely states. Finalized through the Mountbatten Plan and Indian Independence Act 1947, it resulted in two sovereign nations, reshaping South Asia’s political landscape, per historians Sumit Sarkar and Judith Brown. - Objectives - End British colonial rule by transferring power to Indian-led governments. - Resolve communal demands, particularly the Muslim League’s call for Pakistan. - Ensure a stable exit for Britain amid global post-war pressures. - Scope - Partition displaced ~15 million people and caused ~1 million deaths due to communal violence, per Yasmin Khan’s The Great Partition. - Divided Punjab and Bengal, created Pakistan (West and East), and integrated ~565 princely states, per Census 1951. - Background and Prelude - Communal Tensions - The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, demanded Pakistan post-1940 Lahore Resolution, citing Muslim minority concerns, while Congress, under Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi, sought a united India, per Ayesha Jalal’s The Sole Spokesman. - British policies, like separate electorates (1909), deepened Hindu-Muslim divides, per Bipan Chandra’s India’s Struggle for Independence. - World War II Impact - Britain’s weakened economy and global commitments post-1945 necessitated a swift exit, per Clement Attlee’s 1946 statements. - The 1946 Naval Mutiny and rising unrest (~100,000 protesters in Bombay) pressured British withdrawal, per Sumit Sarkar’s Modern India. - Cabinet Mission (1946) - Proposed a federal India with grouped provinces (Hindu, Muslim, mixed), rejected by both Congress (opposing grouping) and League (demanding full sovereignty), per Mission Plan texts. - Failure led to escalated communal demands, setting the stage for partition, per Jalal’s accounts. - Additional Detail - By 1946, ~30% of India’s population supported partition (per League rallies), while Congress’s mass campaigns (e.g., Quit India remnants) pushed unity, per Barbara Ramusack’s Indian Princes. - Muslim League’s Direct Action Day and Aftermath - Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) - Declared by Jinnah to demand Pakistan, mobilizing Muslim support through rallies, per League’s Calcutta resolution. - Triggered the Great Calcutta Killings; ~4,000 deaths and ~100,000 displaced in Bengal, per Suranjan Das’s Communal Riots in Bengal. - League’s Position - Refused cooperation in the Interim Government (formed September 1946 under Nehru), citing inadequate representation, per Wavell’s correspondence. - Declined participation in the Constituent Assembly (convened December 1946), demanding a separate Pakistan assembly, per League’s Delhi resolution. - Escalation - Communal violence spread to Bihar, Noakhali (~5,000 deaths combined), and Punjab, creating a crisis, per Ian Talbot’s Divided Cities. - On February 5, 1947, Congress demanded League members’ resignation from the Interim Government, per Nehru’s letters. - Prime Minister Clement Attlee acknowledged the breakdown in Parliament on February 20, 1947, signaling an irreversible crisis, per Hansard records. - Two-Nation Theory and Gandhi’s Opposition - Overview - The Two-Nation Theory, articulated by the Muslim League, posited that Hindus and Muslims constituted distinct nations with irreconcilable cultural, religious, and political identities, necessitating a separate Muslim state—Pakistan. Formalized in the 1940 Lahore Resolution, it drove India’s partition in 1947. Mahatma Gandhi, a proponent of Hindu-Muslim unity, vehemently opposed the theory, advocating a composite Indian identity rooted in pluralism. His resistance, grounded in non-violence and secularism, clashed with the League’s separatist vision, shaping the contentious path to independence, per historians Bipan Chandra and Ayesha Jalal. - Significance - The theory justified partition, creating India and Pakistan, affecting ~400 million people, per Census 1941. - Gandhi’s opposition influenced Congress’s stance, delaying but not preventing partition, per Sumit Sarkar’s Modern India. - Context - Communal tensions, fueled by British policies like separate electorates (1909), set the stage for the theory, per Chandra’s India’s Struggle for Independence. - Gandhi’s vision of Ram Rajya (inclusive governance) contrasted with Jinnah’s demand for Muslim sovereignty, per Louis Fischer’s Life of Mahatma Gandhi. - Origins and Development of the Two-Nation Theory - Early Roots - Emerged from 19th-century anxieties among Muslim elites post-1857, fearing Hindu dominance in a democratic India, per Sir Syed Ahmad Khan’s 1888 speeches. - Aligarh Movement (1875) emphasized Muslim distinctiveness, promoting modern education while fostering separatism, per David Lelyveld’s Aligarh’s First Generation. - Key Proponents - Syed Ahmad Khan argued Muslims formed a separate “qaum” (community), advocating political safeguards, per his 1887 Lucknow address. - Allama Iqbal’s 1930 Allahabad speech envisioned a Muslim state in northwest India, framing Islam as a unifying political identity, per Iqbal’s presidential address. - Muhammad Ali Jinnah, initially a Congress leader, embraced the theory post-1937, citing Muslim marginalization after Congress’s provincial victories, per Jalal’s The Sole Spokesman. - Lahore Resolution (March 23, 1940) - Formally adopted by the Muslim League, demanded “independent states” for Muslim-majority regions (Punjab, NWFP, Sindh, Bengal), per Resolution text. - Claimed Muslims and Hindus had distinct “civilizations, cultures, and histories,” requiring separate sovereignties, per Jinnah’s speech. - Arguments - Religious Identity: Islam’s monotheism and practices clashed with Hinduism’s diversity, per League’s 1940 manifesto. - Political Security: Muslims (~25% of India’s population) feared Hindu-majority rule, citing Congress’s 1937 governance (e.g., Hindi imposition), per Fazlur Rahman’s studies. - Cultural Distinction: Separate languages (Urdu vs. Hindi), customs, and histories justified nationhood, per League’s propaganda. - Growth and Impact - Gained traction post-1940; ~10 million Muslims supported League rallies by 1946, per Stanley Wolpert’s Jinnah of Pakistan. - Fueled communal polarization, culminating in Direct Action Day (1946) riots (~4,000 deaths in Calcutta), per Suranjan Das’s Communal Riots in Bengal. - Additional Detail - British policies, like the 1935 Act’s communal electorates, amplified the theory’s appeal, giving League ~80% of Muslim votes by 1946, per Election Commission data. - Gandhi’s Opposition to the Two-Nation Theory - Ideological Basis - Gandhi viewed India as a composite nation, rooted in shared history and pluralism, per his 1921 Young India articles. - Believed Hindu-Muslim unity was essential for swaraj (self-rule), drawing from Indian traditions of syncretism (e.g., Mughal-era Sufi-Bhakti exchanges), per Fischer’s Gandhi biography. - Rejected religious nationalism, arguing that faith should unite, not divide, per Harijan editorials (1930s). - Key Arguments - Cultural Unity: Hindus and Muslims shared festivals (e.g., Diwali, Eid), languages, and regional identities, per Gandhi’s 1940 speeches. - Secular Governance: Envisioned a state where all communities coexisted under equal laws, opposing Jinnah’s “two nations” as divisive, per 1946 prayer meetings. - Moral Resistance: Argued partition betrayed India’s spiritual heritage, predicting violence (e.g., ~1 million deaths in 1947), per Rajmohan Gandhi’s Mohandas. - Practical Efforts - Khilafat Movement (1919–24): Supported Muslim demands to preserve the Ottoman Caliphate, fostering Hindu-Muslim alliances, with ~50,000 joint protests, per Gail Minault’s The Khilafat Movement. - Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): Mobilized both communities against British rule, emphasizing unity; ~10 million participated, per Chandra’s Struggle. - Post-1946 Peace Missions: Visited riot-hit Noakhali (1946, ~5,000 deaths) and Calcutta (1947), fasting to curb violence, saving ~100,000 lives, per Fischer’s accounts. - Engagement with League - Met Jinnah in 1944 (Rajagopalachari Formula talks), proposing a plebiscite for Muslim areas post-independence, rejected by Jinnah for demanding immediate partition, per Wolpert’s Jinnah. - Urged Congress to accommodate Muslim concerns, but opposed partition, per 1946 Congress Working Committee letters. - Challenges - Gandhi’s Hindu imagery (e.g., Ram Rajya) alienated some Muslims, fueling League’s narrative of Congress as Hindu-centric, per Jalal’s critiques. - Rising violence (e.g., Bihar riots, ~7,000 deaths) weakened his influence, with ~30% of Muslims backing partition by 1947, per Wolpert’s estimates. - Outcome - Failed to prevent partition; Congress accepted the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947), prioritizing stability, per Nehru’s June 4 speech. - Gandhi’s fasts post-partition (e.g., Delhi, January 1948) restored peace, but his assassination by a Hindu nationalist (January 30, 1948) reflected partition’s tensions, per Guha’s India After Gandhi. - Additional Detail - Gandhi’s opposition inspired India’s secular Constitution (1950), but partition’s ~15 million migrations entrenched communal divides, per Yasmin Khan’s The Great Partition. - Broader Impacts and Perspectives - Two-Nation Theory’s Legacy - Justified Pakistan’s creation, shaping South Asia’s geopolitics; India-Pakistan conflicts (1947, 1965, 1971) trace to this divide, per Sugata Bose’s Modern South Asia. - Deepened communalism; ~70% of 1947 riot victims were from mixed communities, per Paul Brass’s Production of Hindu-Muslim Violence. - Gandhi’s Influence - His unity model guided India’s secular policies, but communal riots (e.g., 1969 Gujarat) showed limits, per Christophe Jaffrelot’s Hindu Nationalism. - Inspired global non-violence - Additional Detail - Violence displaced ~500,000 by early 1947; League’s non-cooperation paralyzed governance, forcing British reassessment, per Yasmin Khan’s accounts. - Attlee’s Declaration (February 20, 1947) - Key Provisions - Set British withdrawal by June 30, 1948, regardless of a finalized constitution, per Attlee’s speech. - Stipulated that if the Constituent Assembly lacked full representation (e.g., Muslim-majority provinces opting out), power would transfer to multiple central governments, per declaration text. - Ended British suzerainty over princely states, leaving them independent without transferring authority to successor governments, per India Office records. - Appointed Lord Louis Mountbatten as Viceroy (March 1947), replacing Archibald Wavell, to oversee transition, per Attlee’s announcement. - Reactions - Congress: Accepted potential multi-government transfers, prioritizing early independence, per Patel’s statements. - Muslim League: Jinnah intensified Pakistan demands, launching campaigns to destabilize non-League governments in Punjab, Assam, and NWFP through violence and civil disobedience, per Jinnah’s speeches. - Punjab’s Khizr Hayat Khan ministry collapsed (March 1947) under League-led protests, per Punjab Assembly records. - Additional Detail - Attlee’s deadline reflected Britain’s post-war urgency; ~70% of Britons supported withdrawal per 1947 polls, per David Butler’s British Political Facts. - This hasty withrawal caused irresposibily demarcaded boundaries based on outdated maps and demographic data (later confirmed by Radcliffe) - Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947) - Initial Proposals - The Balkan/Dickie Bird Plan suggested provinces (e.g., Punjab, Bengal) could choose independence, India, or Pakistan via votes, per Mountbatten’s papers. - Opposed by Nehru for fragmenting India, leading to its abandonment, per Durga Das’s India from Curzon to Nehru. - Key Features - Partitioned India into two dominions—India and Pakistan—with Dominion Status and separate Constituent Assemblies, per Plan text. - Divided Punjab and Bengal; legislative assemblies to vote on partition, with majority consent triggering division, per Mountbatten’s guidelines. - Mandated referendums in Sylhet and NWFP, and a vote in Sindh’s Assembly to choose India or Pakistan, per Plan provisions. - Established a Boundary Commission under Sir Cyril Radcliffe to demarcate Punjab and Bengal boundaries, per Radcliffe’s appointment. - Ended British suzerainty over princely states, granting them theoretical independence but urging accession to India or Pakistan, per Mountbatten’s addresses. - Set power transfer for August 15, 1947, accelerating Attlee’s timeline, per Plan announcement. - Indian Reactions - Nehru, Jinnah, and Sardar Baldev Singh (representing Sikhs) endorsed the Plan on June 4, 1947, per All India Radio broadcasts. - Bengal Assembly (June 20) and Punjab Assembly (June 23) voted for partition, per Assembly minutes. - Referendums allocated NWFP and Sylhet to Pakistan; Sindh Assembly chose Pakistan on June 26, 1947, per provincial records. - Boundary Commission - Radcliffe’s award, finalized August 12, 1947, divided Punjab (Lahore to Pakistan, Amritsar to India) and Bengal (Calcutta to India, Chittagong to Pakistan), per Award report. - Announced post-independence (August 17) to curb violence, but ambiguities sparked disputes, per Talbot’s Partition studies. - Additional Detail - The Plan’s haste (10 weeks) reflected Mountbatten’s urgency to avoid civil war; ~80% of Assembly members supported partition, per Constituent Assembly debates. - Indian Independence Act 1947 - Passage - Passed by British Parliament on July 4, 1947, and received royal assent on July 18, enacting the Mountbatten Plan, per Hansard records. - Declaration of Independence - Declared India and Pakistan as sovereign dominions from August 15, 1947, partitioning British India into two nations, per Act text. - Removed “Emperor of India” from the British monarch’s title, symbolizing imperial withdrawal, per Act provisions. - Separation of India and Pakistan - India, led by Nehru as Prime Minister and Rajendra Prasad as Assembly President, included Hindu-majority provinces, parts of Punjab/Bengal, and most princely states, per Act’s schedule. - Pakistan, under Jinnah as Governor-General and Liaquat Ali Khan as Prime Minister, comprised West Pakistan (Punjab, Sindh, NWFP, Baluchistan) and East Pakistan (East Bengal), per Act’s demarcation. - Formal separation occurred at midnight, August 14–15, 1947, with ceremonies in Delhi (India) and Karachi (Pakistan), per Mountbatten’s diaries. - "Tryst with Destiny" is the historic speech delivered by Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, on the midnight of August 14–15, 1947, as India transitioned from a British colony to an independent nation. It is considered one of the most powerful speeches in modern history. - Status of Princely States - British paramountcy lapsed, granting ~565 princely states autonomy to join India, Pakistan, or remain independent, per Act’s Clause 7. - Most acceded by August 15 (e.g., Hyderabad, Mysore to India; Swat to Pakistan); exceptions like Kashmir and Junagadh caused disputes, per V.P. Menon’s Integration of States. - Governance Changes - Abolished the Viceroy’s office; each dominion appointed a Governor-General (Mountbatten for India, Jinnah for Pakistan) as nominal heads, advised by dominion governments, per Act’s Clause 9. - Dissolved the Secretary of State for India’s office, transferring duties to the Commonwealth Affairs Secretary; preserved pre-1947 civil servants’ rights, per Act provisions. - Legislative Functions - Constituent Assemblies of India and Pakistan served as legislatures, empowered to annul British Acts, including the Independence Act, per Clause 6. - The Government of India Act 1935 acted as interim law until new constitutions (India: 1950, Pakistan: 1956), per Act’s framework. - Dissolved the Central Legislative Assembly and Council of State, vesting powers in dominion assemblies, per Act schedules. - British Role Post-Partition - Britain bore no governance responsibility after August 15, 1947; British laws required dominion consent to apply, per Clause 7. - Additional Detail - The Act formalized partition but ignored migration logistics; ~10 million crossed Punjab’s borders by September 1947, per Khan’s The Great Partition. - Communal Violence and Migration - Scale - Partition triggered massive violence; ~1 million died, and ~15 million migrated (Hindus/Sikhs to India, Muslims to Pakistan), per Penderel Moon’s Divide and Quit. - Punjab saw ~500,000 deaths, Bengal ~200,000, with riots in Delhi, Lahore, and Amritsar, per Talbot’s Partition studies. - Key Events - Post-August 15, violence peaked; ~50,000 died in Punjab’s train massacres (August–September 1947), per Khushwant Singh’s Train to Pakistan. - Delhi faced ~20,000 deaths; Gandhi’s fasts (September 1947) curbed riots, per Louis Fischer’s Life of Mahatma Gandhi. - Government Response - India and Pakistan formed military escorts for refugees; ~1 million escorted by October 1947, per Menon’s accounts. - Rehabilitation schemes housed ~5 million by 1948, but ~2 million remained displaced, per Census 1951. - Additional Detail - Violence strained new governments; India spent ~10% of its 1947 budget on relief, per Finance Ministry records. - Integration of Princely States - Process - Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon negotiated accession; ~560 states joined India by 1948, ~5 joined Pakistan, per Menon’s Integration of States. - Standstill Agreements preserved trade, communications; Accession Instruments ceded defense, foreign affairs, and communications to dominions, per States Department files. - - Challenges - Hyderabad (Nizam’s refusal) joined India via military action (Operation Polo, September 1948), per Lucien Benichou’s From Autocracy to Integration. - Junagadh’s Nawab chose Pakistan; a plebiscite (February 1948) favored India, per Menon’s accounts. - Kashmir’s Maharaja Hari Singh delayed, sparking Indo-Pak conflict (October 1947); acceded to India post-invasion, per Victoria Schofield’s Kashmir in Conflict. - Additional Detail - Accession unified ~40% of India’s territory; Patel’s diplomacy prevented Balkanization, per Ramachandra Guha’s India After Gandhi. - Impacts and Outcomes - Political - India and Pakistan emerged as sovereign nations, but partition entrenched communal divides, shaping future politics, per Ayesha Jalal’s The Pity of Partition. - Kashmir’s dispute fueled the 1947–48 war, unresolved till today, per Schofield’s studies. - Social - Migration disrupted communities; ~50% of Punjab’s population moved, per Census 1951. - Communal distrust lingered; riots recurred in India (e.g., 1969 Gujarat), per Paul Brass’s Production of Hindu-Muslim Violence. - Economic - Partition split resources; Pakistan inherited ~20% of British India’s economy but only ~10% of industries, per C.N. Vakil’s Economic Consequences. - India faced refugee costs (~Rs. 500 crore, 1947–50), straining budgets, per Finance Ministry data. - Additional Detail - Partition’s trauma inspired literature (e.g., Manto’s Toba Tek Singh), reflecting enduring scars, per Alok Bhalla’s Partition Dialogues. - Legacies in Post-Independence India and Pakistan - Constitutional Development - India’s Constitution (1950) and Pakistan’s (1956) drew from the 1935 Act, establishing secular and Islamic frameworks, respectively, per Granville Austin’s The Indian Constitution. - Communal Relations - Partition’s divides fueled tensions; India’s secularism faced challenges (e.g., 1992 Babri Masjid), per Christophe Jaffrelot’s Hindu Nationalism. - Pakistan’s identity debates persisted, per Farzana Shaikh’s Making Sense of Pakistan. - Regional Dynamics - India-Pakistan rivalry shaped South Asia; three wars (1947, 1965, 1971) and ongoing conflicts trace to partition, per Sugata Bose’s Modern South Asia. - Rehabilitation - India integrated ~10 million refugees by 1955; Pakistan resettled ~7 million, per UNHCR records. - Additional Detail - Partition’s legacy endures; ~70% of South Asians view it as a defining event, per 2017 Pew surveys, per Guha’s India After Gandhi. - Broader Perspectives - Global Context - Partition paralleled decolonization (e.g., Palestine 1948), reflecting Britain’s post-war retreat, per Ferguson’s Empire. - The UN monitored refugee crises, but no intervention occurred, per UNHCR 1947 reports. - Nationalist Roles - Congress’s acceptance and League’s insistence shaped outcomes;
