Gandhi’s unity pleas failed, per Fischer’s Gandhi biography. - Women activists (e.g., Mridula Sarabhai) aided refugees, per Aparna Basu’s Women in India’s Freedom Struggle. - Socio-Cultural Impact - Partition disrupted syncretic traditions; Punjab’s Sufi shrines lost cross-community worship, per Anna Bigelow’s Sharing the Sacred. - Films (e.g., Garm Hava) and novels captured trauma, per Bhalla’s Partition literature studies. - Economic Linkages - Division skewed development; India retained ~80% of industries, Pakistan struggled, per Vakil’s economic studies. - Refugee labor boosted India’s urban growth (e.g., Delhi’s 1947–60 boom), per Census 1961. - Additional Detail - Historians debate responsibility: Jalal blames British haste, Chandra cites communal politics, reflecting complex legacies, per The Pity of Partition. - More info related to partition in post-independence notes - British Governance and Administration in India (1757-1947) - Overview - The British administrative system, evolving from the East India Company’s trade-centric operations post-1757 Battle of Plassey to a sophisticated governance framework under Crown rule after 1857, aimed to entrench British supremacy, extract resources, and reshape India’s socio-political landscape. Built on judicial, civil, military, and police pillars, it integrated central, provincial, and local governance to balance control with limited Indian participation, ensuring stability and imperial profit. This system, while efficient, marginalized Indians, fueled nationalist resistance, and left enduring legacies, per historians like Bipan Chandra and Judith Brown. - Objectives - Execute British policies to consolidate territorial and economic dominance. - Secure revenue and maintain law and order to sustain colonial rule. - Transform India into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods, aligning with imperial interests. - Scope - Established authority over 60% of India’s territory by 1856 through conquest and diplomacy. - Governed ~400 million people by 1947, managing diversity via centralized control and selective co-option of elites. - Historical Context and Expansion - Pre-Colonial Governance - Mughal and regional systems relied on decentralized authority, with zamindars, jagirdars, and panchayats managing local affairs, per Satish Chandra. Courts used customary or Sharia law, varying by community. - Village panchayats resolved disputes, allocated resources (e.g., irrigation), and maintained social order, fostering autonomy, per Tapan Raychaudhuri. - British Expansion Strategies - Direct Conquest - Military victories annexed key regions: Bengal (1757 Plassey), Mysore (1799), Maratha territories (1818), Sindh (1843), Punjab (1849). Leaders like Robert Clive and Arthur Wellesley secured territorial dominance, per John Keay’s India: A History. - Ring Fence Policy - Warren Hastings (1772-1785) created buffer zones around British territories, neutralizing threats (e.g., Marathas, French) via treaties with neighbors, per Percival Spear. - Subsidiary Alliance - Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) bound rulers (e.g., Hyderabad, Awadh) to British protection. They paid for Company troops, accepted Residents, and ceded foreign policy, losing sovereignty, per Barbara Metcalf. - Doctrine of Lapse - Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856) annexed states like Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), and Nagpur (1854) if rulers lacked male heirs or were deemed unfit, sparking resentment that fueled the 1857 Revolt, per R.C. Majumdar. - Additional Detail - Exploiting Indian disunity (e.g., Mughal decline, Maratha rivalries), the British controlled ~1 million square miles by 1857, leveraging diplomacy and force, per Philip Mason’s The Men Who Ruled India. - Central Governance - Structure and Evolution - East India Company (1757-1857) - Governed via a London-based Court of Directors and a Calcutta-based Governor-General, established by the Regulating Act 1773. The Board of Control (Pitt’s India Act 1784) oversaw policies, balancing trade and governance. - Key Acts - Regulating Act 1773: - Created Governor-General post (Warren Hastings first), Supreme Court in Calcutta. - Pitt’s India Act 1784: - Strengthened Crown oversight, curbed Company autonomy. - Charter Act 1833: - Ended Company’s trade monopoly, centralized legislation under Governor-General. - Charter Act 1853: - Expanded Governor-General’s Council, introduced civil service exams. - Crown Rule (1858-1947) - Government of India Act 1858 transferred authority to the Crown, with a Secretary of State for India (London) and Viceroy (India) replacing the Governor-General. - Legislative Framework - Indian Councils Act 1861: - Added Indian nominees to Viceroy’s Council (e.g., Satyendra Nath Tagore), advisory only. - Indian Councils Act 1892: - Allowed limited elections for legislative councils, elite-based. - Government of India Act 1919: - Introduced dyarchy in provinces, expanded Indian roles. - Government of India Act 1935: - Proposed federation, granted provincial autonomy, expanded legislatures, though princely states stalled federation. - Additional Detail - Viceroys like Lord Curzon (1899-1905) centralized power (e.g., Bengal Partition 1905), while Lord Ripon (1880-1884) pushed liberal reforms, per Sumit Sarkar’s Modern India. - Key Governors and Viceroys - Warren Hastings (1772-1785): - Laid judicial, revenue foundations; faced impeachment for corruption. - Lord Cornwallis (1786-1793): - Reformed judiciary, civil services; introduced Permanent Settlement. - Lord Wellesley (1798-1805): - Expanded via Subsidiary Alliance; founded Fort William College. - Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856): - Annexed states, built railways, telegraph. - Lord Ripon (1880-1884): - Promoted local governance, repealed Vernacular Press Act. - Lord Curzon (1899-1905): - Partitioned Bengal, centralized control. - Lord Irwin (1926-1931): - Negotiated Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) amid unrest. - Lord Linlithgow (1936-1943): - Oversaw 1935 Act, World War II policies. - Lord Mountbatten (1947): - Managed independence, partition. - Additional Detail - Viceroys balanced imperial directives with Indian demands; Curzon’s partition sparked Swadeshi, while Ripon’s reforms inspired Congress’s founding (1885), per Barbara Ramusack. - Voting Rights - Limited Franchise - Pre-1909: - No elections; councils appointed by British. - Morley-Minto Reforms (1909): - Introduced separate electorates (e.g., Muslims), with ~100,000 voters (0.03% of population), restricted to propertied men. - Government of India Act 1919: - Expanded electorate to ~1 million (0.3%), still elite-based (landowners, professionals). - Government of India Act 1935: - Increased voters to ~35 million (10%), including some women, but property and literacy barriers excluded 90%. - Additional Detail - Voting rights co-opted elites while marginalizing masses, fueling demands for universal suffrage, achieved in 1950, per Granville Austin’s The Indian Constitution. - Provincial Governance - Structure - Provinces (e.g., Bengal, Bombay, Madras) were led by Governors or Lieutenant-Governors under the Viceroy, with Executive and Legislative Councils. Indian representation grew post-1861, though British retained veto power. - Post-1919 dyarchy assigned “transferred” subjects (e.g., education, health) to Indian ministers, “reserved” subjects (e.g., finance, police) to British officials. - Key Reforms - Morley-Minto Reforms (1909): Expanded councils (e.g., 27 non-officials in Imperial Council), introduced communal electorates. - Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919): Implemented dyarchy, with elected Indian ministers, though Governors could override via “certification.” - Government of India Act 1935: Granted full autonomy, with elected ministries (e.g., Congress governments 1937-39), but Governors held emergency powers. - Advantages - Trained Indian leaders (e.g., C.R. Das in Bengal) in governance, per Judith Brown. - Improved provincial services (e.g., Bombay’s schools doubled, 1920-1930). - Drawbacks - British control over key sectors limited Indian influence; dyarchy confused accountability. - Communal electorates deepened Hindu-Muslim divides, per Ayesha Jalal’s The Sole Spokesman. - Additional Detail - Provincial autonomy under 1935 Act empowered Congress, but resignations in 1939 (over World War II) exposed British overreach, per Sumit Sarkar. - Local Self-Governance - Pre-Colonial Legacy - Village panchayats managed disputes, irrigation, and festivals, while urban guilds oversaw trade, per Irfan Habib. Autonomy varied by region, strongest in South India. - British Reforms - Ripon’s Resolution (1882) - Lord Ripon established municipal boards (e.g., Calcutta, Madras) and rural District/Taluka Boards to manage sanitation, roads, schools. Funded by local taxes (e.g., octroi), with limited elections (~1% voted, propertied men). - Post-1919 Expansion - Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms devolved local governance, creating Zilla Parishads (district councils) and Mandal Panchayats (village clusters) in provinces like Bombay, UP. - Functions: Oversaw primary education, health, water, but relied on provincial grants, limiting autonomy. - Government of India Act 1935 - Mandated elected councils; Zilla Parishads coordinated ~10-20 Mandal Panchayats per district. Electorate grew to ~5% (property-based), excluding women and lower castes broadly. - Structures - Municipalities (Urban Local Bodies) - Structure: Municipal Committees and Corporations - Introduced: Significantly developed after Lord Ripon’s Resolution on Local Self-Government (1882). - Functions: - Sanitation, roads, water supply, lighting, markets - Limited taxation and spending powers - Composition: - Partially elected, mostly nominated members - British officials (like District Magistrates) held veto and supervisory powers - Example: Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras Municipal Corporations - District Boards (Zilla Parishads) - Role: Managed rural district-level development - Functions: - Primary education, district roads, hospitals, and budget allocations - Control: - Headed by the District Collector or British officials - Elected Indian members had little power - Taluka or Tehsil Boards - Level: Sub-district administrative units - Functions: - Coordinated between village and district boards - Handled local roads, minor irrigation, schools - Village Panchayats (Rural Local Bodies) - Revived in some provinces as advisory bodies - Functionality: - Dispute resolution, basic sanitation, and village-level issues - Challenges: - Often dominated by zamindars, landlords, and moneylenders - Lacked financial independence and legal powers - Cantonment Boards - Setup: In military or garrison towns - Controlled by: British military authorities - Purpose: Civic administration of areas occupied by British troops - Port Trusts - Cities: Bombay, Calcutta, Madras - Function: Managed ports, docks, and shipping trade - Controlled by: British officials and commercial elites - Advantages - Fostered Indian participation; leaders like Gokhale emerged via municipal boards. - Improved urban infrastructure (e.g., Bombay’s waterworks, 1890s). - Inspired post-1947 Panchayati Raj, per Ambedkar’s 1948 vision. - Drawbacks - Restricted franchise (95% excluded) reinforced elitism, per David Washbrook. - British oversight (Collectors, Governors) curtailed independence. - Rural neglect; <10% villages had schools by 1900, per Famine Commission. - Additional Detail - Local bodies served as safety valves, co-opting elites to defuse nationalism, but their inefficacy fueled Congress’s rural campaigns, per Gandhi’s 1920s programs. - Judicial System - Pre-Colonial Context - Hindu disputes followed customary law, resolved by panchayats or zamindars. Muslim cases used Sharia via Qazis, per Satish Chandra. Systems varied, lacking uniformity. - British Reforms - Warren Hastings (1772-1785) - Goals: Resolve disputes (tenants, officials), codify laws (e.g., A Code of Gentoo Laws, 1776). - Structure - Mofussil Diwani Adalat: Civil cases (property, contracts) in districts. - Faujdari Adalat: Criminal cases (theft, assault) under Qazis/Muftis. - Sadar Diwani/Nizamat Adalats: Appellate courts in Calcutta. - Regulating Act 1773: Created Supreme Court (Calcutta) for Europeans, clashing with Company courts. - Lord Cornwallis (1786-1793) - Plan of 1787: - Collectors handled Maal Adalats (revenue) and Diwani Adalats (civil). - Plan of 1790: - Shifted criminal justice to Company officers; Faujdari Courts became Circuit Courts. - Plan of 1793: - Separated revenue and judiciary; District Judges ran Diwani Adalats, Collectors focused on taxes. - Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835) - Abolished sati (1829), streamlined courts, promoted Indian judges (Munsifs). - Indian High Courts Act 1861 - Established High Courts (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras), merging Supreme and Sadar courts, blending British and Indian law. - Advantages - Standardized procedures, reducing arbitrary rulings, per Philip Woodruff. - Trained Indian legal professionals (~1,000 Munsifs by 1900). - Drawbacks - Ignored customary law, alienating communities (e.g., Hindu inheritance cases). - Costly, slow; Bengal litigation rose 300% (1800-1850), per Ranajit Guha. - Favored British interests, shielding Company officials, per Eric Stokes. - Additional Detail - Judicial biases (e.g., lenient trials for Europeans) fueled unrest, with 1857 sepoys citing unfair courts, per Rudrangshu Mukherjee. - Civil Services - Overview - The Indian Civil Service (ICS) managed revenue, law, and governance, evolving from traders to a “steel frame” bureaucracy, per David Gilmour’s The Ruling Caste. - Evolution - Formative Stage (1675-1765) - Covenanted Civil Service handled trade posts under contracts, separating from military roles. - Administrative Growth (1765-1853) - Regulating Act 1773: - Banned private trade, bribery. - Pitt’s India Act 1784: - Set recruitment rules; Cornwallis split Covenanted (European) and Uncovenanted (Indian) services. - Charter Act 1793: - Filled posts internally. - Wellesley (1800): - Founded Fort William College, replaced by Haileybury (1806-1857). - Charter Act 1833: - Proposed open exams (delayed). - Charter Act 1853: - Introduced competition via Macaulay Committee; exams began 1855 (London). - Imperial Era (1858-1947) - Indian Civil Service Act 1861: - Allowed 7-year residents to qualify. - Statutory Civil Service (1879): - Reserved 20% posts for elite Indians. - Aitchison Commission (1886): - Proposed Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate services. - Islington Commission (1912): -Reserved 25% posts for Indians. - Government of India Act 1919: - Created All India, Central, Provincial services; exams in India from 1922. - Government of India Act 1935: - Retained ICS, Police, Medical Services as All India; others provincialized. - Advantages - Professionalized governance; ~1,000 ICS officers managed 300 million by 1900, per Woodruff. - Standardized revenue collection, per John Strachey. - Drawbacks - Indian underrepresentation: 5% ICS officers Indian by 1910, per Aitchison data. - London exams cost Indians £500-£1,000, favoring British, per Gokhale’s critiques. - Loyalty to Crown alienated nationalists, per 1918 Congress demands. - Additional Detail - The ICS’s efficiency masked exclusion, sparking Indianization calls; Satyendra Nath Tagore’s 1864 entry was a rare milestone, per Bernard Cohn. - Military System - Overview - The British Indian Army, vital for conquest and control, comprised Company troops (pre-1858) and Queen’s army (post-1858), blending Indian sepoys with British officers, per Douglas Peers. - Structure - Presidency Armies (pre-1895): - Bengal, Bombay, Madras armies, ~250,000 troops by 1857 (80% Indian), led by British. - Indian Army (1895): - Unified under a Commander-in-Chief, split into Punjab, Bengal, Madras, Bombay commands. - Kitchener Reforms (1902): - Reorganized into North/South commands; divisions had two Indian, one British battalion. Kitchener Test ensured readiness. - Composition - Company Troops: - Local recruits (e.g., Awadh sepoys), paid Rs. 7/month, under-equipped, per Kaushik Roy. - Queen’s Army: - British regiments (e.g., Royal Fusiliers) and Indian units, ~150,000 by 1900, better armed post-1857. - Strategies - Rival Spirits: - Pitted Sikhs, Pathans, Gurkhas against each other to curb unity, per Lord Roberts (1880s). - Apolitical Soldiers: - Barred sepoys from politics (e.g., no newspapers), per Tan Tai Yong. - Martial Races: - Post-1857, favored “loyal” groups (Punjabis, Gurkhas) over Bengal Brahmins, per Lionel Caplan. - Related Committees - Peel Commission (1859): - Reorganized post-1857 army, increased British troops. - Eden Commission (1879): - Improved sepoy conditions (e.g., pensions). - Rawlinson Committee (1923): - Modernized equipment. - Skeen Committee (1925): - Proposed Indian officer training (Sandhurst model). - Advantages - Secured empire; defeated Marathas, Sikhs, and external threats (e.g., Afghanistan 1878). - Employed ~2 million Indians in World Wars, per Srinath Raghavan. - Drawbacks - Sepoy grievances (low pay, cultural insensitivity) sparked 1857 Revolt. - Indian officer exclusion (only 500 by 1939) fueled nationalism, per Chandar Sundaram. - Additional Detail - The army’s loyalty strategies failed in 1946 Naval Mutiny, reflecting nationalist penetration, per Sumit Sarkar. - Police System - Pre-Colonial Context - Mughal faujdars (rural) and kotwals (urban) maintained order, supported by zamindars and thanedars, per Radhika Singha. - British Reforms - Warren Hastings (1774-1775) - Restored faujdars to curb dacoity, violence; set up faujdar thanas (major stations) and minor posts. - Lord Cornwallis (1791) - Relieved zamindars of policing; created thanas under darogas (Indian officers), led by District Superintendents of Police (SPs). - Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835) - Abolished SP role; Collectors/Magistrates led police, with Commissioners as divisional SPs, reducing efficiency. - Indian Police Act 1861 - Created state-level forces, defined recruitment, training, and powers for order, crime prevention, and law enforcement, per 1860 Police Commission. - Indian Police Commission (1902) - Andrew Fraser’s reforms established provincial CIDs, a Central Intelligence Bureau, and split services into Imperial (British) and Provincial (Indian) branches. - Objectives - Maintain order, suppress rebellions, control crimes (e.g., dacoity, theft). - Advantages - Reduced dacoity; Bengal thanas cut robberies by 50% (1860-1900), per David Arnold. - CID improved intelligence, thwarting early nationalist plots, per John Beames. - Drawbacks - No All-India Police Service; regional disparities persisted, per 1902 Commission. - Brutality (e.g., torture in thanas) alienated Indians, per Radhika Singha. - Indian exclusion from senior ranks fueled resentment, per Gokhale’s 1900s speeches. - Additional Detail - Police loyalty to British, evident in 1919 Jallianwala Bagh, deepened distrust, inspiring Congress’s non-cooperation, per Shahid Amin. - Liberalization and Political Reforms - Context - British reforms, driven by nationalist pressure and liberal ideals, gradually expanded Indian participation, though control remained paramount, per Anil Seal’s The Emergence of Indian Nationalism. - Key Milestones - Indian Councils Act 1892 - Allowed limited elections; ~10,000 elite voters chose council members, per Ramachandra Guha. - Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) - Expanded councils, introduced separate electorates; ~100,000 voters, per John Morley’s diaries. - Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) - Established dyarchy, enlarged electorate to 1 million; Indian ministers gained limited powers, per E.S. Montagu. - Government of India Act 1935 - Granted provincial autonomy, expanded voters to 35 million (10%), included women, per Lionel Carter. - Advantages - Trained Indian leaders (e.g., Nehru, Patel) in governance, per Judith Brown. - Paved way for 1950 Constitution’s democracy, per Granville Austin. - Drawbacks - Restricted franchise excluded 90%, per Sumit Sarkar. - Communal electorates sowed division, per Ayesha Jalal. - British vetoes undermined reforms, per Gandhi’s 1930s critiques. - Additional Detail - Reforms, while progressive, aimed to delay self-rule; Congress’s 1928 Nehru Report demanded full dominion status, reflecting frustration, per B.R. Nanda. - Advantages of British Governance - Administrative Efficiency - ICS streamlined revenue, governance; Collectors managed ~1 million people each, per John Strachey. - Infrastructure - Railways (54,000 km by 1947), telegraph, ports aided connectivity, per Ian Derbyshire. - Legal Framework - High Courts standardized justice, trained ~5,000 Indian lawyers by 1900, per David Washbrook. - Political Training - Local boards, councils nurtured leaders (e.g., Gokhale, Bose), per Anil Seal. - Additional Detail - English education, via 1835 Minute, created a class (e.g., Tagore, Ranade) that drove reform, per Thomas Macaulay’s vision. - Drawbacks of British Governance - Indian Exclusion - ICS had 5% Indian officers (1910); police, army senior ranks were British, per Aitchison Commission. - Economic Exploitation - Revenue systems impoverished peasants; ~80% lived below subsistence by 1900, per Dadabhai Naoroji. - Cultural Alienation - Ignored customary law, suppressed vernacular press (1878 Act), per Ranajit Guha. - Communal Tensions - Separate electorates deepened divides, culminating in 1947 partition, per Ayesha Jalal. - Repression - Police brutality, army deployments (e.g., Jallianwala 1919) fueled unrest, per Shahid Amin. - Additional Detail - Governance prioritized British interests; famines (30 million deaths, 1770-1943) reflected neglect, per Amartya Sen’s Poverty and Famines. - Legacies in Independent India - Administrative Framework - ICS evolved into IAS (1947), retaining district governance (Collectors), per Granville Austin. - Zilla Parishads, Panchayati Raj (1959 Balwant Rai Mehta Committee) built on Ripon’s model, per Rajni Kothari. - Political Structures - 1935 Act’s federalism inspired India’s Constitution; provincial autonomy shaped state governments, per B.R. Ambedkar. - Judicial System - High Courts became Supreme Court’s foundation (1950), per George Gadbois. - Military and Police - Indian Army retained unified structure; police reforms (1977 Prakash Singh) addressed colonial brutality, per K.S. Subramanian. - Challenges - Communal electorates’ legacy fueled partition, Hindu-Muslim tensions, per Sugata Bose. - Elitist governance delayed universal suffrage, tackled in 1950, per Ornit Shani. - Rural neglect (e.g., <20% villages electrified, 1947) required decades of redress, per Planning Commission. - Additional Detail - Colonial legacies—efficiency vs. exclusion—shaped India’s mixed democracy; Nehru’s 1950s policies countered underdevelopment, per Ramachandra Guha’s India After Gandhi. - Broader Perspectives - Global Context - India’s governance mirrored British colonies (e.g., Nigeria), but its scale (~400 million governed) was unique, per Niall Ferguson’s Empire. - ICS inspired bureaucracies globally (e.g., Malaya), per Anthony Kirk-Greene. - Nationalist Resistance - Governance flaws drove Congress (1885), Swadeshi (1905), Quit India (1942), per Sumit Sarkar. - Gandhi’s satyagraha targeted judicial, police repression, per Dennis Dalton. - Socio-Cultural Impact - English education created a reformist elite, but marginalized vernacular traditions, per Gauri Viswanathan. - Army’s martial races policy entrenched ethnic stereotypes, per Mridu Rai. - Economic Linkages - Governance enabled resource extraction; railways served revenue, not welfare, per Dadabhai Naoroji’s drain theory. - Local boards’ tax focus foreshadowed India’s fiscal federalism, per Arvind Panagariya. - Additional Detail - Historians debate legacies: Amiya Bagchi sees deliberate underdevelopment, while Ferguson credits infrastructure, reflecting polarized views, per India: A History. - Economic Impact of British Rule in India (1757-1947) - Overview - British rule, starting with the East India Company’s control after the 1757 Battle of Plassey and transitioning to Crown governance post-1857, transformed India’s economy from a self-reliant, globally significant system to a colonial dependency. Policies like land revenue systems, commercialization of agriculture, and deindustrialization prioritized British profits, causing agrarian distress, industrial decline, and mass poverty. The Drain of Wealth theory, nationalist critiques, and economic legacies shaped India’s post-independence struggles, leaving challenges like underdevelopment, inequality, and infrastructural imbalances. - Pre-Colonial Economic Framework - Village Economy - Demographics - In the mid-18th century, ~90% of India’s population resided in villages, forming the economic core. - Occupations - Agriculture was primary, with landowners and tenants growing crops for self-consumption. Artisans (weavers, blacksmiths), village officials (headmen, accountants), and menial laborers (sweepers, washermen) sustained communities. - Structure - Villages, called “Little Republics” by Sir Charles Metcalfe, were self-sufficient, producing food, cloth, and tools. Traditional customs regulated rent, wages, and prices, ensuring local stability. - Additional Detail - The Jajmani system governed inter-caste exchanges, with farmers providing grain for artisanal services, fostering social and economic cohesion, as noted by historian Irfan Habib. Villages often maintained granaries for famine relief, a practice disrupted under British rule. - Urban Economy - Demographics - Urban centers housed ~10% of the population, serving diverse functions. - Types of Centers - Religious Hubs: Gaya, Banaras, Mathura, and Puri attracted pilgrims, supporting temples, scholars, and markets. - Administrative Capitals: Delhi, Agra, Lucknow, Hyderabad hosted Mughal and regional courts, driving bureaucratic and craft economies. - Commercial Ports: Surat, Cambay, Calicut, Masulipatnam linked inland markets to global trade routes. - Additional Detail - Cities like Murshidabad (Bengal’s banking hub with Jagat Seths) and Ahmedabad (textile center) thrived, financing Mughal armies and exporting goods to Europe and Asia, per Fernand Braudel’s accounts. - Agriculture - Characteristics - Subsistence farming dominated, with surplus crops bartered or shared with artisans. Monsoon dependency constrained growth, supplemented by wells and tanks. - Crops - Food Crops: Rice, wheat, bajra, jowar, barley, minor cereals like ragi sustained local diets. - Commercial Crops: Jute, raw cotton, groundnut, indigo, sugarcane fueled regional trade. - Land Tenure - Land was held communally or by hereditary owners (e.g., Mirasidars in South India). Village headmen allocated plots, balancing community needs. - Additional Detail - Mughal-era irrigation, like Shah Jahan’s Punjab canals, boosted yields, contributing to India’s 24% global GDP share in 1700, per Angus Maddison’s estimates. - Industries - Handicraft Industries - Contribution - Accounted for ~6% of 18th-century GDP, per Tirthankar Roy. - Systems - Jajmani/Balutedar: Artisans crafted for villages, paid in kind. - Urban Production: High-quality goods (silks, metalwork) for elites and exports. - Dadni System: Merchants advanced cash for bulk artisanal orders. - Karkhanas: Royal workshops in Delhi, Agra made luxury items (jewelry, carpets). - Centers - Textiles: Dhaka’s muslins, Banaras’s brocades, Ahmedabad’s calicoes, Coromandel’s chintzes were globally prized. - Additional Detail: Dhaka muslin, with 200-thread counts, fetched £100 per bolt in 1750s London, symbolizing India’s craft supremacy. - Shipbuilding - Centers: Bombay, Surat, Tuticorin, Chittagong built durable teak ships. - Leadership: Wadia Group (Bombay) supplied Mughal and British navies, outlasting European oak vessels. - Additional Detail: Indian ships, costing 20% less than European ones, carried 30% of Indian Ocean trade in the 1750s, per naval records. - Metallurgy and Others - Products: Wootz steel (South India), used in Damascus swords; jute ropes, paper, oils, perfumes, Kashmir shawls. - Additional Detail: Golconda’s diamond trade and Mysore’s iron forges exported to Persia, cementing India’s metallurgical fame. - Trade - Nature - Robust domestic (Grand Trunk Road) and global trade (Silk Road, Indian Ocean) connected India to Asia, Europe, Africa. - Exports - Cotton textiles, raw silk, indigo, opium, rice, wheat, sugar, pepper, spices (saffron, cloves), precious stones, medicinal drugs. - Imports - Pearls, wool, dried fruits, rosewater (Persia); coffee, gold (Arabia); tea, sugar (China); metals, paper (Europe). - Ports - Surat, Cambay, Calicut, Masulipatnam, Hooghly. - Trade Balance - A favorable surplus absorbed bullion, earning India the “sink of precious metals” title, per Braudel. - Communities - Hindu, Jain, Bohra merchants (Gujarat); Khatris, Lohanis (Punjab); Marwari Banias (Rajasthan); Chettiars (South India). - Additional Detail - Hundis (bills of exchange) and Sarrafs (bankers) enabled trade from Kabul to Canton, with Surat’s brokers financing Mughal campaigns. - Economic Terms - Aurang - Permanent market/warehouse for goods storage and trade, vital in Mughal and early British eras. - Banian - Indian brokers aiding European traders in finance and commerce, key in ports. - Mirasidar - Hereditary landowner in South India, holding permanent rights under Ryotwari. - Hundi - Financial instrument for credit and transfers, akin to cheques. - Jotedar - Wealthy Bengal landholders, rivaling zamindars in revenue control. - Additional Detail - Hundis, backed by trust networks, rivaled European banking, with some honored across Asia by the 1700s. - British Economic Policies - Land Revenue Systems - Context - In 1765, the Company gained Diwani (revenue rights) for Bengal, Bihar, Orissa via the Treaty of Allahabad. Robert Clive relied on Nawab’s corrupt officials, who overtaxed peasants, siphoning profits. Warren Hastings’ reforms (e.g., 1772 five-year settlements) failed to curb inefficiencies, necessitating new systems. - Permanent Settlement (1793) - Introduction - Initiated by Lord Cornwallis as a decennial trial (1790), made permanent in 1793. Known as Zamindari System, covered 19% of British India (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, parts of UP). - Features - Hereditary Rights: Zamindars could sell or transfer land, formalizing landlord status. - Revenue Split: Paid 10/11th of rent to Company, kept 1/11th. - Sunset Law: Non-payment by deadlines triggered estate auctions. - Tenant Contracts: Zamindars issued pattas specifying land and rent. - Drawbacks - Zamindars: High taxes (89% of rent) caused defaults; ~50% of Bengal estates auctioned by 1800, per B.B. Chaudhuri. - Peasants: Faced evictions, seizures, beatings; borrowed at 50-100% interest, trapping them in debt. - Agriculture: Absentee landlordism (zamindars in Calcutta) neglected irrigation, stagnating yields. - Additional Detail - Jotedars, sub-leasing land, exploited ryots more than zamindars, amassing wealth, per Sugata Bose’s studies. - Ryotwari System (1820) - Introduction - Piloted by Alexander Reed (1792, Baramahal); formalized by Thomas Munro (1820). Covered 51% of British India (Madras, Bombay, Assam, Coorg). - Features - Direct Collection: Taxes levied on ryots, bypassing intermediaries. - Ownership: Ryots gained rights to own, occupy, transfer land. - Flexible Taxes: Rates tied to soil output, adjustable. - Barren Land: Government leased uncultivated plots, sharing revenue. - Revisions: Taxes revisited every 20-30 years. - Drawbacks - Over-Assessment: Taxes at 50-60% of produce ignored droughts, bankrupting ryots. - Coercion: Officials used flogging, confiscation to enforce payments. - Debt Traps: ~40% of Madras ryots lost land by 1850, per Dharma Kumar. - Additional Detail - Munro’s vision of ryots as “yeoman farmers” failed as inflated surveys mirrored Zamindari oppression. - Mahalwari System (1822) - Introduction - Devised by Holt Mackenzie (1819), implemented by R.M. Bird (1822), revised by William Bentinck (1833). Covered 30% of British India (North-West Provinces, Punjab, Central India). - Features - Village Units: Mahals (village clusters) assessed collectively; headmen collected taxes. - State Share: 50% of net produce, raised to 66% by 1840s; revised every 30 years. - Net Produce: Taxes deducted expenses and wages. - Drawbacks - Faulty Surveys: Inflated assessments drove debt; ~20% of UP land sold by 1870s. - High Rates: Taxes hit 70% of output, impoverishing peasants. - Leadership Loss: British-appointed headmen eroded traditional authority. - Additional Detail - Outdated Mughal records (e.g., Ain-i-Akbari) misjudged yields, fueling unrest like the 1857 Revolt. - - Additional Impact - Revenue systems generated ~50% of British India’s budget by 1900, per Maddison, but over-taxation caused landlessness; ~30% of rural households were tenants by 1901 census. - Commercialization of Agriculture - Definition - Shift to cash crops for export, driven by British industrial and trade demands. - Key Crops - Silk, opium, indigo, pepper, sugarcane, tea, cotton, jute. - Causes - British factories needed cotton (Lancashire), indigo (textiles); opium funded China trade (£2 million/year, 1820s). - Revenue pressures forced ryots to grow cash crops to pay taxes. - Railways (post-1853) linked farms to ports, boosting exports. - Positive Outcomes - Export Surge: Cotton bales rose from 50,000 (1800) to 1 million (1860). - Specialization: Bengal (jute), Assam (tea), Deccan (cotton). - Monetization: Cash crops integrated rural areas into markets. - Negative Outcomes - Price Volatility: 1860s cotton crash post-Civil War ruined farmers. - Bonded Labor: Indigo ryots worked unpaid, sparking 1859 Bengal revolt. - Moneylender Grip: Loans at 20-100% interest led to foreclosures. - Food Shortages: Cash crops displaced grains, worsening famines (e.g., 1943 Bengal, 2-3 million deaths). - Additional Detail - Tea plantations (Assam, 1830s) employed ~1 million indentured workers by 1900, under brutal conditions, per Lucassen’s labor studies. - Deindustrialization - Definition - Collapse of India’s manufacturing due to policies favoring British imports and raw material exports. - Causes - Import Flood: 1813 Charter Act removed trade barriers; British cotton imports soared, taxed at 2% vs. Indian exports at 10-30%. - Patronage Loss: Mughal courts’ decline slashed demand for crafts (e.g., Dhaka muslins). - No Modernization: Britain blocked Indian factories, keeping crafts manual. - Railways: Enabled British goods’ rural reach and raw material extraction. - Mechanisms - Textiles: Pre-1780s, weavers sold freely; post-1780s, gomasthas’ Khatbandi system forced sales to Company at low rates. - Shipbuilding: Post-1820s, British policies favored English yards; Wadia’s Bombay docks declined. - Outcomes - Ruralization: Artisans joined agriculture; farming population grew from 70 million (1881) to 100 million (1931), industrial workers fell from 21 million to 13 million, per census data. - Trade Shift: Cotton cloth exports dropped from 81% (1750) to 3.7% (1850); raw cotton, opium dominated, per R.C. Dutt’s Economic History. - Social Distress: Unemployed artisans fueled 1857 Revolt, reflecting economic grievances. - Additional Detail - India’s textile exports, once rivaling China’s silk, collapsed as Manchester’s mills produced 50 times faster, per Eric Hobsbawm. - Phases of Economic Exploitation (R.P. Dutt’s Framework) - Mercantile Phase (1757-1813) - Aims - Trade Monopoly: Company controlled textiles, spices. - Bullion Solution: Indian goods offset Britain’s silver shortage for Asian trade. - Features - Plundered Bengal’s treasury (~£18 million by 1770, per Edmund Burke). - Forced artisans into low-price contracts, undermining markets. - Additional Detail - The 1770 Bengal famine (10 million deaths) stemmed from tax hikes, exposing mercantile greed. - Industrial Phase (1813-1860) - Aims - Raw Materials: Cotton, indigo, opium for British factories. - Market Creation: Sell British goods in India. - Features - 1813 Charter Act enforced one-way free trade, crippling textiles. - India’s GDP share fell from 24% (1700) to 12% (1870), per Maddison. - Additional Detail - The 1857 Revolt reflected artisans’ and peasants’ anger over industrial displacement. - Financial Phase (1860-1947) - Aims - Capital Investment: British firms profited from railways, plantations. - Debt Servicing: India’s revenues funded British loans, costs. - Features - Railways (£150 million by 1900) served colonial extraction. - Home Charges (£20 million/year by 1900) covered British salaries, pensions, debt. - Additional Detail - India’s debt, £200 million by 1914, tied revenues to London, limiting local investment. - Drain of Wealth Theory - Definition - Concept that Britain extracted India’s wealth through trade imbalances, taxes, and administrative costs, impoverishing India while enriching the metropole. - Origins - Articulated by Dadabhai Naoroji in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1871), expanded by R.C. Dutt and M.G. Ranade. - Mechanisms - Home Charges: India paid £20-30 million annually (1900s) for British salaries, pensions, military costs, and debt interest, per Naoroji’s calculations. - Trade Imbalance: Exported raw materials (cotton, opium) at low prices; imported British goods at high costs, draining ~5% of India’s GDP yearly. - Revenue Extraction: High taxes (e.g., 50-70% of produce) left no surplus for reinvestment. - Investment Bias: British capital (£1 billion by 1914) built railways, ports for extraction, not local development. - Estimates - Naoroji estimated £200-300 million drained annually by 1900, equivalent to 30-40% of India’s revenues, per his speeches in London. - William Digby (1901) pegged total drain at £6 billion from 1757-1900, dwarfing India’s economy. - Impact - Stifled industrialization, deepened poverty, and funded Britain’s global dominance, including its Industrial Revolution, per Eric Hobsbawm. - Additional Detail - The drain, termed “tribute” by Marx in 1853, was unique to India among colonies, as no reciprocal benefits (e.g., infrastructure) matched the outflow. - Nationalist Views on British Economic Policies - Dadabhai Naoroji - Argued Britain’s “moral drain” impoverished India, contrasting its 1700 prosperity with 1900 destitution. Advocated self-rule to retain wealth, per Poverty and Un-British Rule. - R.C. Dutt - Criticized revenue systems for ruining agriculture, estimating Bengal’s land tax at 60% of output vs. Mughal-era 20%, in Economic History of India (1901). - M.G. Ranade - Lamented deindustrialization’s “ruralization,” urging protective tariffs and state-led factories, per Essays on Indian Economics (1898). - Madan Mohan Malaviya - Blamed British imports for artisans’ unemployment, noting weavers’ wages fell 80% by 1880s, per 1905 Congress speeches. - Gopal Krishna Gokhale - Highlighted famines as policy failures, estimating 15 million deaths (1876-1900) due to revenue pressures, per 1906 budget critiques. - Bal Gangadhar Tilak - Linked economic exploitation to cultural decay, advocating Swadeshi to revive industries, per Kesari editorials (1900s). - Additional Detail - Nationalists’ critiques fueled Congress’s economic resolutions (e.g., 1885 demand for tax reform), shaping Swadeshi (1905) and Non-Cooperation (1920) movements. - Poverty Under British Rule - Scale - By 1900, ~80% of Indians lived below subsistence, per Naoroji’s estimates, with per capita income at £2/year vs. Britain’s £30. - National income stagnated at ~£500 million (1870-1947), while population grew from 250 to 400 million, per Sivasubramonian’s data. - Causes - Revenue Burdens: Taxes consumed 50-70% of peasant income, leaving no savings. - Deindustrialization: Artisans’ unemployment swelled rural labor, halving wages (e.g., weavers earned 2 annas/day by 1880s). - Famines: 30 million died in major famines (1770-1943), worsened by cash crop shifts and British inaction, per Amartya Sen. - Trade Drain: Wealth outflow reduced capital for local growth, locking India in agrarian poverty. - Regional Patterns - Bengal: Jotedar dominance and indigo coercion impoverished ryots; 1943 famine killed 2-3 million. - Deccan: Ryotwari taxes and 1876-78 famine (5 million deaths) deepened landlessness. - Punjab: Canal colonies benefited elites, but small farmers faced debt, per Imran Ali’s studies. - Social Impact - Malnutrition rose; life expectancy fell to 23 years by 1921 (vs. 40 in 1700). - Caste and gender gaps widened, with landless laborers (often Dalits) and women hit hardest. - Additional Detail - The 1901 Famine Commission admitted 25% of India’s population was “chronically hungry,” yet relief (e.g., workhouses) offered starvation wages (1 lb grain/day). - Economic and Social Consequences - Land Fragmentation - Cause: Deindustrialization pushed artisans into farming, subdividing plots. Average holdings shrank to ~2 acres in Bengal by 1900, per Famine Commission. - Impact: Lower yields, tenancy disputes, rural poverty; ~30% of farmers were landless by 1931. - Additional Detail: Fragmentation empowered Jotedars, who leased tiny plots at high rents, fueling 1859 revolts. - Middlemen Exploitation - Role: Moneylenders, gomasthas, sub-zamindars profited from revenue and crop sales. - Impact: Peasants faced usurious loans (20-100% interest); ~25% of Bengal’s farmland mortgaged by 1880s. - Additional Detail: The 1875 Deccan riots targeted moneylenders’ debt records, reflecting widespread anger. - Famines and Distress - Frequency: Major famines—1770 Bengal (10 million deaths), 1876-78 Deccan (5 million), 1896-97 North India (5 million), 1943 Bengal (2-3 million)—killed ~30 million total. - Causes: Revenue pressures, cash crops, British inaction (e.g., Churchill’s 1943 rice exports). - Additional Detail: Lytton’s 1878 famine policy prioritized exports over relief, sparking nationalist critiques. - Trade Imbalance - Shift: From 18th-century textile surplus to 19th-century raw material exports and British imports. - Impact: India’s global trade share fell from 15% (1700) to 2% (1900), per Paul Bairoch. - Additional Detail: Opium exports (£10 million/year by 1850s) balanced Britain’s China trade, tying India to colonial drug networks. - Social Polarization - Outcome: Absentee landlordism and urban migration widened gaps. Calcutta’s bhadralok contrasted with indebted ryots. - Additional Detail: The 1905 Bengal Partition protests reflected economic divides, uniting elites and peasants against British policies. - Economic Legacies in Independent India - Legacy of Poverty - Scale: At independence (1947), ~70% of Indians lived below poverty, with per capita income at Rs. 250/year (~$50), per Planning Commission data. - Causes - Colonial stagnation left India’s GDP growth at 0.5% annually (1870-1947), vs. 2% pre-1750. - Landlessness (40% of rural households) and low wages persisted, hampering savings. - Famines eroded human capital; 1943 Bengal famine’s orphans swelled urban slums. - Impact - Post-1947, India faced food shortages (e.g., 1950s PL-480 imports) and low literacy (18% in 1951), delaying development. - Poverty fueled social unrest, like Telangana peasant revolts (1946-51), demanding land reform. - Additional Detail - Nehru’s 1950s Five-Year Plans prioritized industry to counter poverty, but rural neglect sparked critiques from Ambedkar, who linked caste to economic exclusion. - Agrarian Imbalances - Issue: Colonial revenue systems left fragmented holdings (average 1.5 acres by 1950) and unequal ownership; 10% of landlords held 50% of land, per 1951 census. - Impact - Zamindari abolition (1950s) redistributed land slowly; tenant exploitation persisted. - Green Revolution (1960s) benefited Punjab but bypassed eastern India, deepening regional disparities. - Additional Detail - Bihar’s 1970s land reform failures, rooted in Jotedar resistance, fueled Naxalite movements, reflecting colonial legacies. - Industrial Underdevelopment - Issue: Deindustrialization left India with ~1% of global manufacturing by 1947, vs. 15% in 1700, per Bairoch. - Impact - Weak industrial base forced reliance on imports; India’s steel output was 1 million tons (1947) vs. Britain’s 13 million. - Post-1947 public sector (e.g., SAIL, BHEL) aimed to rebuild industry, but faced capital shortages. - Additional Detail - TISCO (1907), a rare colonial-era Indian firm, inspired Swadeshi but couldn’t scale without state support, a gap addressed by Nehru’s plans. - Infrastructural Bias - Issue: Colonial railways (54,000 km by 1947) and ports served extraction, not integration; rural roads covered <5% of villages. - Impact - Post-1947, India invested heavily in roads (PMGSY, 2000s) and irrigation to counter urban bias. - Uneven growth favored Bombay, Calcutta over interior regions like Odisha. - Additional Detail - The 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution prioritized balanced growth, but colonial port-centric trade delayed hinterland development. - Fiscal and Trade Constraints - Issue: Colonial drain left India with £1 billion debt (1947) and a weak rupee, devalued 30% in 1949. - Impact - Foreign exchange shortages forced import controls (1950s), delaying industrialization. - Export reliance on tea, jute persisted, limiting diversification until 1980s reforms. - Additional Detail - The 1991 liberalization traced roots to colonial trade imbalances, as India sought global integration to overcome inherited deficits. - Social and Economic Inequality - Issue: Colonial policies entrenched landlordism, caste hierarchies, and urban-rural divides. - Impact - Post-1947, affirmative action (e.g., reservations) tackled caste disparities, but rural poverty (50% below poverty line, 1970s) lingered. - Women’s low workforce participation (15% in 1951) reflected colonial neglect of education. - Additional Detail - Ambedkar’s 1948 Constitution drafting emphasized economic justice to counter colonial-era inequities, shaping India’s welfare policies. - Broader Perspectives - Global Context - India’s economic decline mirrored other colonies (e.g., China’s opium trade), but its drain was unique, funding Britain’s Industrial Revolution, per Immanuel Wallerstein’s world-systems theory. - India’s 2% global GDP share by 1947 contrasted with rising powers like the US (25%), underscoring colonial exploitation’s scale. - Environmental Impact - Colonial forest laws (1878, 1927) and cash crop monocultures degraded soil; ~30% of India’s forests were cleared by 1900, per Ramachandra Guha. - Post-1947, India faced desertification and water shortages, addressed by 1970s afforestation programs. - Cultural Shifts - Deindustrialization eroded artisanal pride, weakening guild traditions; Swadeshi revived khadi to restore dignity, per Gandhi’s 1920s campaigns. - Colonial education prioritized clerks over technicians, delaying scientific growth until IITs (1950s). - Resistance and Agency - Economic exploitation fueled revolts (1857, 1859 Indigo, 1875 Deccan) and Swadeshi, shaping nationalist economics. - Post-1947, India’s mixed economy balanced colonial critiques (socialism) with global integration, per Manmohan Singh’s 1991 reforms. - Additional Detail - The colonial legacy’s complexity—exploitation alongside railways, English education—sparked debates; historians like Amiya Bagchi see it as deliberate underdevelopment, while Niall Ferguson credits infrastructure, reflecting polarized views. - Socio-Religious Reform Movements - Understanding Socio-Religious Reform Movements - Aim - To transform society and religion by addressing social evils and promoting enlightenment for overall improvement. - Key Issues Addressed - Women's Emancipation (liberation): - Abolition of practices like sati, infanticide, and child marriage, alongside advocacy for widow remarriage. - Caste Reform: - Eradication of caste discrimination and untouchability to promote social equality. - Promotion of Education: - Fostered (encouraged) societal enlightenment through widespread education initiatives. - Religious Reforms: - Combated idolatry and polytheism, and countered exploitation by priests to purify religious practices. - Factors Leading to Socio-Religious Reforms - Contact with the West: - Exposure to modern ideas of liberty, equality, and democracy influenced India's emerging middle class. - Christian Missionary Efforts: - The Charter Act of 1813 permitted missionaries to critique Indian religious practices, sparking reformist responses. - Education: - Indian and European scholars fostered pride in India's heritage, empowering reform movements through knowledge and awareness. - Reform Strategies and Approaches - Reforms from Within: - Advocated self-initiated changes through raising societal awareness. - Reforms through Legislation: - Sought legal solutions to social issues, though colonial support was often limited. - Reforms through Symbols of Change: - Employed radical actions, such as those by the Derozians, to symbolize transformation. - Reforms through Social Work: - Combined practical efforts with intellectual endeavors to effect change. - Types of Reformers - Revivalists: - Aimed to restore religion to its original greatness, exemplified by movements like Wahabi and Deobandi. - Reformists: - Reshaped society with modern ideas, as seen in organizations like Brahmo Samaj and the Aligarh movement. - Eastern India - Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Brahmo Samaj - Known as the Father of Modern India for his pioneering reform efforts. - Key Contributions - Authored “Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin” (A Gift to Monotheists) in Persian in 1805, promoting monotheistic ideas. - Founded Atmiya Sabha in 1815 to critique idolatry and polytheism, advocating monotheism and rational thought. - Established the Calcutta Unitarian Committee in 1823 with Dwarka Nath Tagore, uniting prominent Brahmins and European residents to promote Hindu social reforms. - Influenced the abolition of sati in 1829 with Governor-General William Bentinck's support, drawing on Dayabhaga and Mitakshara legal schools, and championed widow rights and women's education. - Supported the establishment of Hindu College in 1817 to advance education. - Founded Vedanta College in 1825 to blend Western and Indian sciences for a holistic education. - Translated Vedas and Upanishads into accessible languages and published Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) and Mirat-ul-Akbar (Persian) to spread reformist ideas. - Brahmo Samaj (1828) - Focused on monotheism, social equality, and human dignity as core principles. - Evolution of Brahmo Samaj After Raja Ram Mohan Roy - After Roy's death in 1833, leadership passed to Debendranath Tagore, father of Rabindranath Tagore. - Debendranath Tagore's Contributions - Founded Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839 to promote rationalism, focusing on India's history and indigenous languages, continuing Roy's legacy. - Worked to reform Hinduism internally by eliminating idolatry and irrational customs, while resisting Christian missionaries' critiques and conversion efforts. - Expanded Brahmo Samaj's influence beyond Bengal to regions like the United Provinces, Punjab, Bombay, and Madras. - Keshab Chandra Sen's Role - A prominent reformer who joined Brahmo Samaj in the mid-19th century, bringing new directions. - Established the Tabernacle of New Dispensation in 1867 to integrate Hinduism, Islam, and Christianity into a unified spiritual framework. - Founded the Indian Reform Association in 1870 to address women's rights, caste discrimination, and education. - His radical ideas, including support for inter-caste marriages and teachings from all religions, led to a split in 1866: Brahmo Samaj of India (led by Keshab Chandra Sen) and Adi Brahmo Samaj (led by Debendranath Tagore). - Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) - Emerged after Keshab Chandra Sen conducted his underage daughter's marriage using orthodox rituals, contradicting reformist principles. - Disgruntled members formed this group, focusing on original Brahmo ideals: faith in a singular supreme being, emphasis on reason and morality, and opposition to orthodox practices. - - Henry Vivian Derozio and Young Bengal Movement - Derozio: An Anglo-Indian radical thinker and professor at Hindu College, Kolkata, who founded the Academic Association and championed free thought, liberty, equality, and fraternity. - Young Bengal Movement: Influenced by Western thinkers, it promoted Raja Ram Mohan Roy's ideas, emphasizing education, press freedom, and justice. - Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar - Key Contributions - Reformed Sanskrit education by admitting non-Brahmins to Sanskrit College in 1851. - Led the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 to legalize widow remarriage. - Advocated women's education and established schools for girls. - Authored Barna Parichay, a foundational text for modern Bengali grammar, significantly contributing to societal reform. - Western India - Balshastri Jambhekar - Known as the "Father of Marathi Journalism" for his pioneering media work. - Key Contributions: Founded Darpan, the first Marathi newspaper, in 1832. - Social Reforms: Opposed caste discrimination, sati, and child marriage, while advocating women's education and widow remarriage. - Manav Dharma Sabha - Founded in Surat in 1844 by Durgaram Manchharam, Dadoba Pandurang, and Dalpatram Bhagubai. - Focus: Challenged caste systems and societal superstitions through weekly meetings discussing rationalism and equality. - Paramahansa Mandali - Established in Bombay in 1849 by Ram Bal Krishna Jayakar and Dadoba Pandurang as a radical socio-religious group. - Teachings: Advocated monotheism and morality over rituals, opposed caste discrimination, and supported widow remarriage and women's education. - Prarthana Samaj - Founded by Atmaram Pandurang in Bombay in 1867, influenced by Brahmo Samaj ideals. - Goals: Promoted women's education and the abolition of caste discrimination. - Jyotirao Phule and the Satyashodhak Samaj - Jyotirao Phule: Criticized orthodox Brahmins and caste dominance, advocating education for women and lower castes, earning the title “Mahatma” for his social reform works. Published Gulamgiri and other equality-focused writings. - Savitribai Phule (Wife): Opened India's first school for girls in 1851 and founded Mahila Seva Mandal in 1852. - Satyashodhak Samaj (1873): Promoted inter-caste marriages, elimination of child marriage, widow remarriage, and education for marginalized sections to achieve societal equality. - Gopal Hari Deshmukh (Lokhitwadi) - A prominent social reformer and writer from Maharashtra. - Key Contributions: Advocated modern human values and criticized social evils through his journal Prabhakar (1848-1889), supported the Swadeshi movement for self-reliance, and championed women's education while opposing caste discrimination and untouchability. - Gopal Ganesh Agarkar - Co-founded New English School (1880) in Poona, Deccan Education Society (1884), and Fergusson College (1885). - Advocated for the Age of Consent Act (1891) to raise the legal marriage age, worked for women's rights, opposed child marriage, and supported legislative reforms over traditional methods. - Maharshi Dhondo Keshav Karve - Known as a pioneer for widow remarriage and women's education. - Key Achievements: Founded Vidhwa Vivah Uttejak Mandali (1893) to encourage widow remarriage, Hindu Widows Home Association (1896) for shelter and education, and SNDT Women's University (1916), India's first women's university in Maharashtra. Advocated women's self-reliance through education and vocational training, married a widow after his first wife's death as an example, and was honored with the Bharat Ratna in 1958. - Servants of India Society - Founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in 1905 at Poona. - Core Ideals: Promoted selfless service to the underprivileged, rural communities, and tribal populations, focusing on education, sanitation, and health care reforms. - Gopal Krishna Gokhale: Leader of the moderate Indian National Congress faction, mentored Mahatma Gandhi, coined the phrase “What Bengal thinks today, India thinks tomorrow,” and published The Hitavada (Nagpur, 1911) to spread reformist ideas. - Behramji Malabari - A Parsi social reformer focused on women's rights. - Key Contributions: Advocated for the Age of Consent Act (1891) to raise the marriageable age, founded Seva Sadan (1908) for shelter, education, and vocational training for destitute women, and inspired change through writings like The Indian Muse in English Garb. - Pandita Ramabai - First Indian woman awarded “Pandita” and “Saraswati” titles by the University of Calcutta for her scholarship. - Reforms and Contributions: Founded Sharada Sadan (Bombay) for widows and Mukti Mission (1890s) in Pune as a Christian charity for destitute women, toured the US to raise funds for widows, authored Stri Dharma Niti (Morals for Women) in 1882 and The High-Caste Hindu Woman critiquing child marriage and widow exploitation, and received the Kaisar-i-Hind Medal in 1919. - Rukhmabai Case - Rukhmabai (1864-1955): A physician and feminist, one of India's first women doctors. - Legal Battle: Fought against child marriage in Rukhmabai vs. Dadaji Bhikaji (1885), refusing to live with her husband, resulting in a landmark verdict questioning child marriage legality and highlighting women's rights. - Social Service League - Founded by N.M. Joshi in Bombay in 1911 to promote social welfare. - Vishnushastri Chiplunkar - Co-founded Mahratta and Kesari newspapers with Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Gopal Ganesh Agarkar to advocate reform and nationalism. - Pan India - Ramakrishna Movement - Founded by Ramakrishna Paramahansa (1834-1886). - Core Teachings: All religions lead to the same goal, emphasizing spiritual equality and service to mankind as service to God. - Objectives: Establish a monastic order for spiritual pursuit and engage in philanthropic and charitable works across caste, color, and creed. - Paramahansa's disciples, led by Vivekananda, formed Ramakrishna Math in 1887 and Ramakrishna Mission in 1897, headquartered at Belur near Calcutta. - Swami Vivekananda (Narendra Nath Dutta) - Disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahansa and key Vedantic philosophy proponent. - Key Contributions: Represented Hinduism at the World Parliament of Religions (1893) in Chicago, elevating India's spiritual legacy, founded Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for education, health care, and social welfare, established Belur Math as its headquarters, and published Prabuddha Bharata (monthly in English) and Udbodhan (fortnightly in Bengali). - Swami Dayanand Saraswati and Arya Samaj - Founder: Swami Dayananda Saraswati (originally Mool Shankar Tiwari), established Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875 with the slogan “Go Back to the Vedas.” - Ideology: Opposed idolatry, ritualism, and priesthood, advocated returning to Vedic principles as ultimate truth, opposed child marriages, and encouraged widow remarriage. - Key Contributions: Authored Satyarth Prakash (The Light of Truth), coined “India for Indians” in 1876 (known as Martin Luther of India), wrote Veda Bhasya and Veda Bhasya Bhumika, introduced the Shuddhi Movement for reconversion of Hindus (Ghar Wapsi), and promoted cow protection via Gokarunanidhi. - Post-Dayananda Era - Divisions: College Party (led by Lala Hansraj, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Lala Lal Chand) focused on modern education through DAV schools and colleges (e.g., DAV College, Lahore); Mahatma Party (later Gurukul Party, led by Swami Shraddhanand and Guru Datta Vidyarthi) emphasized Sanskrit and Vedic education via Kanya Mahavidyalaya for widows and Gurukuls. - Arya Mahila Samaj (Arya Women Society): Founded by Pandita Ramabai in 1882. - Indian Social Conference - Founded in 1887 by M.G. Ranade and Raghunath Rao as the social reform cell of the Indian National Congress, addressing caste discrimination and women's rights. - The Theosophical Society - Founded in 1875 in New York by Madame Helena Blavatsky and Colonel H.S. Olcott, shifted headquarters to Adyar, Madras, in 1882. - Key Tenets: Promoted brotherhood without distinction of race, creed, or gender, studied religion and philosophy concurrently, and investigated nature's hidden laws and mysticism. - Social Reform Work: Advocated caste abolition and untouchability eradication, founded Central Hindu School (1898) in Varanasi, which evolved into Banaras Hindu University led by Madan Mohan Malviya. - Radha Swami Satsang - Founded in 1861 by Shiv Dayal Saheb, emphasizing belief in one supreme being, spiritual equality, rejection of idol worship, and focus on moral living and ethical practices. - Dev Samaj - Founded by Shiv Narayan Agnihotri in 1887, focused on caste integration, women's education, and moral reform, with teachings compiled in Dev Shastra. - Bharat Dharma Mahamandal - Founded in 1902 in Varanasi to unify organizations like Sanatana Dharma Sabha and Dharma Maha Parishad, defending Hinduism against reformist movements like Arya Samaj and Theosophists. - Caste Reform Movements - Causes for the Rise of Caste Movements - Grievances of Educated Men: - Discrimination by upper castes and challenges to centuries-old caste-based inequality. - Social Mobility Aspirations: - Lower castes sought upward movement through Sanskritization, adopting upper-caste customs, manners, and taboos. - Radical Leaders: - Figures like Jyotirao Phule and Periyar opposed Brahminical dominance. - British Interventions: - The 1901 Census categorized castes hierarchically, reinforcing rigid social divisions. - Caste Reform Movements in South India - Ayya Vaikundar (Tamil Nadu) - Advocated equality and fraternity, abolishing caste-based discrimination. - Contributions: Simplified marriage customs without Sanskrit rituals, organized Sampanthi Bhojana (community meals) for diverse castes, dug common wells for lower castes, and inspired priests to apply sacred paste to all regardless of caste. - Ezhava Movement (Kerala) - Founder: Sree Narayana Guru Swamy among the Ezhava community. - Actions: Installed a Shivalinga in 1888 to challenge higher-caste monopoly, led Aruvippuram Kshetra Yogam (1889) for temple entry, education, and government representation for Ezhavas. - Legacy: Formed SNDP (Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam) for rights to school admission, government jobs, road access, temple entry, and political representation. - Palli Movement (Tamil Nadu) - Focused on lower-caste Pallis adopting Kshatriya customs for social upliftment. - Vokkaliga Sangha (Mysore Region) - Founded in 1905 as an anti-Brahmin movement, promoting social, cultural, and educational upliftment of the Vokkaliga community. - Nadar Movement (Tamil Nadu) - Focused on toddy-tappers achieving Kshatriya status, established Nadar Mahajana Sangam in 1910. - Justice Movement (Madras) - Leaders: C.N. Mudaliar, T.M. Nair, P. Tyagaraja Chetti. - Demands: Greater representation in government services and politics for intermediate castes. - Self-Respect Movement (E.V. Ramaswamy Periyar) - Advocated weddings without Brahmin priests, forcible temple entry, and rejection of Manusmriti. - Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker) - Tamil Nadu - Ideology: Rejected Brahminical culture and superstitions, promoted Dravidian leadership via Dravida Kazhagam, and advocated atheism, education, and anti-caste reforms. - Symbolism: Used black shirts and flags to protest caste hierarchies. - Vaikom Satyagraha (1924) (Kerala) - Leaders: K.P. Kesava, Sree Narayana Guru, T.K. Madhavan. - Objectives: Demanded temple entry for Dalits, supported by Gandhi, leading to state-managed temples opening to all in 1936. - Caste Reform Movements in Rest of India - Gopal Baba Walangkar (Maharashtra) - Founded Anarya Dosh-Parihar Mandali in 1886, challenged untouchability and caste oppression through writings like Vital Viddhwansak. - Kisan Faghu Bansode (Maharashtra) - Founded Antyaj Samaj for Dalit education, wrote plays, poems, and articles advocating emancipation. - Shivram Janba Kamble (Maharashtra) - Edited Somvanshiya Mitra, focusing on the Dalit cause, and organized India's first Dalit conference. - Maharshi Vitthal Ramji Shinde (Maharashtra) - Founded India Depressed Classes Mission in 1906, advocated untouchability eradication and Dalit upliftment, established the “All India Untouchability League.” - Mahad Movement - Led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in March 1927, targeting caste-based Hindu traditions. Earlier, in 1924, he founded Bahishkrit Hitkarini Sabha to voice Dalit challenges, guided by the principle “Educate, Agitate, and Organize.” - Parsi Reform Movements - Rahnomae Mazdayasanan Sabha (1851) - Focused on restoring Zoroastrian religion, led by Naoroji Furdonji and Dadabhai Naoroji (Rast Goftar). - Muslim Reform Movements - Wahhabi Movement (Revivalist) - Founder: Syed Ahmad Barelvi. - Advocated unity in Islamic interpretation and resistance against British rule and Sikh authority. - Fairaizi Movement (Revivalist) - Founder: Haji Shariatullah. - Aimed to protest un-Islamic practices among Muslims, influenced by the Wahhabi Movement. - Ahmadiyya Movement (Punjab) (Reformist) - Founder: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad in 1889, promoted universal brotherhood, Western liberal education, and religious tolerance. - Syed Ahmed Khan (Reformist) - Established Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1875 (later Aligarh Muslim University), founded the Scientific Society of Aligarh modeled on the Royal Society of London, and sought British support to modernize Muslim society through education and employment post-revolt politics. - Sikh Reform Movements - Nirankari Movement - Founder: Baba Dayal Das (1783-1855). - Rejected idol worship, emphasized Guru Nanak's teachings, and opposed evils like meat-eating and liquor consumption. - Namdhari Movement - Founder: Baba Ram Singh (1816-1885). - Objectives: Revitalized Sikhism and enforced strict vegetarianism. - Singh Sabha Movement (1873) - Led by Thakur Singh Sandhawalia and Giani Gian Singh, established Singh Sabha of Amritsar to counter Christian and Muslim conversion efforts, promote Gurumukhi and Punjabi literature, and founded Khalsa College in Amritsar in 1892. - Akali Movement - Targeted corrupt Mahants managing Sikh gurdwaras and aimed to restore control of Khalsa College to the Sikh community, supported the Non-Cooperation Movement, and resulted in the Sikh Gurdwara Act of 1925 for democratic management. - People's Resistance Against British Rule - Meaning of People's Resistance - Definition - The term "people" refers to diverse segments of Indian society adversely affected by foreign domination, including peasants, artisans, tribals, ruling classes (both active and dispossessed), military personnel (serving under the Company or demobilized from ex-rulers' armies), and religious leaders (both Hindu and Muslim). - Purpose of Resistance - To safeguard their interests, these groups fought both independently and in collaboration with others against British rule. - Factors for People's Uprisings Against the British - Economic and Social Grievances - Collapse of indigenous industries due to British economic policies. - Exploitation by non-tribal people like moneylenders and traders. - Discontent stemming from oppressive land policies. - Impact of East India Company's Rule - Resentment from zamindars and artisans over lost privileges and livelihoods. - Erosion of traditional rights and ownership systems under Company governance. - Cultural Factors - Desire for autonomy within the Indian cultural and political framework. - Resistance to imposed cultural influences like Sanskritization, which threatened local identities. - Civil and Peasant Uprisings During British Rule (Pre-1857) - Sanyasi Revolt (1760s-1800) - Nature of Revolt - An uprising by Hindu Sanyasis and Muslim Fakirs in Eastern India, supported by rural impoverished communities and minor zamindars. - Causes - Religious Restrictions: British restrictions on pilgrimage and taxes on religious donations angered spiritual leaders. - Economic Hardship: The Bengal Famine of 1770 worsened conditions, fueling rebellion. - Major Areas - Purnea, Malda, Dhaka, Rangpur, Cooch Behar, and Murshidabad in Bengal Province. - Notable Leaders and Activities - Leaders included Bhawani Pathak, Majnu Shah, Chirag Ali, and Musa Shah, who launched surprise raids on British outposts, treasuries, and factories. - Outcome - Eventually suppressed after a prolonged struggle by British forces. - Significance - Inspired literary works like "Devi Chaudhurani" and "Anandamath" by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, reflecting its cultural legacy. - Rangpur Dhing (1783) - Area of Revolt - Rangpur District of Bengal in 1783. - Nature of Revolt - A protest by peasants and zamindars against excessive revenue demands under the Ijaradari System (land auctioned to the highest bidder). - Leader - Kena Sarkar. - Outcome - Highlighted flaws in the Ijaradari System, contributing to reforms like the Permanent Settlement. - Paika Rebellion (1817) - Location - Odisha. - Causes - Resistance against British policies, particularly high land revenue demands. - Leaders - Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar and Mukunda Deva. - Outcome - Suppressed by 1818 but led to governance changes, including large remission of arrears, reduced assessments, and a new settlement on fixed tenures. - Additional Fact - In 2017, Odisha urged recognition as the First War of Independence, though the Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR) disagreed. - Who Were Paikas? - Paikas were foot soldiers recruited since the 16th century by Odisha kings for martial services in exchange for hereditary rent-free lands. - Mysore Rebellion (1830) - Location - Mysore (Nagar District). - Causes - Exploitative taxation after the Wodeyar dynasty's reinstatement and enforcement of subsidiary alliances, burdening peasants and lower societal sections. - Leader - Sardar Malla. - Outcome - Resulted in direct British administration of the region. - Kuka Movement (1840-1850) - Nature - Also known as the Namdhari Movement, it aimed at religious purification and political resistance against British rule. - Founder - Bhagat JawaharMal. - Leader - Baba Ram Singh, who emphasized military training and structured resistance; Kukas boycotted British goods, institutions, and laws. - Outcome - Suppressed by the British; Baba Ram Singh was deported to Rangoon. - Peasant Movements with Religious Overtones - Narkelberia Uprising (1830s) - Leader - Syed Mir Nisar Ali (Titu Mir). - Nature - Muslim tenants rose against Hindu landlords and British indigo planters imposing a bread tax on Faraizi Muslims; initially economic, it merged into the Wahabi movement with religious overtones. - The Pagal Panthis (1825-1833) - Nature - Peasant uprisings led by a religious sect in present-day Bangladesh, initiated by Karam Shah as a religious movement, later turned political under his son Tipu with local tribes. - Activities - Directed against zamindar oppression, refusing excessive rent and attacking their houses. - Outcome - Suppressed by British large-scale military operations. - Faraizi Revolt (1818-1857) - Leaders - Haji Shariatullah, later Dudu Mian of the Faraizi sect. - Nature - Sought to cleanse Islam and support tenants' rights against zamindars; many Faraizis joined the Wahhabi Movement. - - Tribal Uprisings During British Rule - Overview - Tribes in the 18th century lived in isolation with distinct agricultural methods, traditions, and societal structures, mainly in forested lands encroached upon by the British, leading to recurrent uprisings. - - Understanding the Evolution of Tribal Movements Under British Rule - First Phase (1795-1860) - Rise of the British Empire; leadership from traditional sections like zamindars whose privileges were undermined. - Second Phase (1860-1920) - Intensive colonialism and mercantilism impacted tribal economy, land, and forests; leadership emerged from lower tribal ranks. - Third Phase (1920-1947) - Tribals engaged in nationalist, agrarian, and separatist movements; leadership from educated tribal leaders and outsiders. - - Plight of the Tribals Under Colonial Rule - Key Issues - Debt Spirals and Outsider Dominance - Traders and moneylenders offered loans for non-local goods, leading to dependency, high interest rates, and debt cycles. - Eroded Chieftaincy (From Leaders to Enforcers) - Tribal leaders reduced to enforcers of British policies, losing respect among their people. - The Agrarian Dilemma (Forced Settlements and Fallow Fields) - Forced settlement and farming under unsuitable conditions increased hardships. - Forests Under Siege (Land Now State Property of British) - Forest laws restricted access, impacting livelihoods, forcing relocation, and reducing autonomy. - Labour Traps (Plantations and Mines) - Recruitment for tea plantations and mining led to loss of mobility and freedom. - Indian Forest Act - Background - A key conflict source due to timber demand in the 1850s for railways (fuel and sleepers) and shipbuilding (Indian teak for British naval dominance). - Forest Policy (1864) - Established by Lord Dalhousie, declaring forests state property and enabling British control over tree-containing land. - Forest Act of 1878 - Divided forests into Reserved (fully government-controlled for heavy commercial use), Protected (partly government-controlled), and Village Forests (controlled by nearby villages); tribes lost traditional rights like grazing and agriculture, receiving only limited privileges. - Forest Act of 1927 - Did not acknowledge community rights; individuals or communities had to claim rights before a Forest Officer; traditional practices like shifting agriculture and collecting forest produce were made illegal. - Revolt by Mainland Indian Tribes - Pahariyas' Rebellion (1778) - Area - Rajmahal Hills (Jharkhand). - Cause - Protest against British disruption of their lifestyle. - Main Tactic - Engaged British in guerrilla warfare. - Result - British declared the Pahariya region “Daman-i-Koh” (forbidden territory), agreeing not to extend administration further. - Chuar Uprising (1798-1799) - Area - Midnapore and Bankura districts of Bengal. - Cause - Protest against British revenue policies. - Activities - Multiple waves between 1766 and 1798, led by Durjan Singh, a deprived zamindar; also known as the Revolt of Jungle Mahal; brutally suppressed by British. - Kol Revolt (1831) - Location - Chotanagpur. - Cause - Against land transfers to non-tribal settlers and oppressive British colonial policies. - Leader - Budho Bhagat, under whom rebels killed about a thousand perceived oppressors. - Outcome - Suppressed with large-scale military operations. - Ho and Munda Uprisings (1820-1837) - Location - Singhbhum and broader Chotanagpur region. - Cause - Resistance to British revenue systems and Bengali settlers. - Leadership - Raja of Parahat. - Activities - Ho Revolt persisted until 1827 when Ho tribals surrendered; in 1831, they rebelled again with Mundas, subdued by 1837. - Koli Uprising (1822-1829) - Location - Maharashtra (particularly Akola hills). - Cause - British interventions in tribal rights and exploitation by moneylenders and zamindars. - Leader - Ramji Bhangre. - Activities - Rebels targeted Baniya moneylenders, attacking and looting financial documents; British responded with military force. - Ramosi Uprisings (1820s-1830s) - Location - Western Ghats. - Cause - Protest against livelihood loss after Maratha territory annexation. - Leaders - Chittur Singh and Umaji Naik. - Activities - Armed attacks on British establishments; brutally suppressed by British. - Santhal Rebellion (1855-1856) - Area - Santhal Pargana (Jharkhand and West Bengal). - Causes - Encroachment by outsiders (Dikus) invading land rights, economic exploitation by zamindars, and loss of traditional lifestyle. - Leaders - Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, who rallied Santhals, believing they were divinely chosen to end oppression and restore their way of life. - Tactics - Armed insurrection with traditional weapons. - Outcome - Suppressed by British; Santhal Pargana created as an administrative district in 1855 for some autonomy; the 1876 Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act prohibited land transfer to non-tribals. - Khond Uprisings (1837-1856) - Causes - Resentment against British control, cultural disruption, loss of territorial rights, abolition of the Meriah System (human sacrifices for fertility), and economic exploitation via taxes and moneylenders. - Regions - Hilly tracts of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. - Leader - Chakra Bisoi, uniting tribes like Ghumusar and Kalahandi against British policies. - Methods - Used traditional weapons like tangi (axes), bows, arrows, and swords. - Outcome - Suppressed due to superior British military strength. - Koya Revolts (1803-1886) - Causes - Oppression by police and moneylenders, exploitation under British forest laws. - Notable Leaders - Tomma Sora (1879-1880 rebellion) and Raja Anantayyar. - Methods - Guerrilla tactics exploiting terrain. - Outcome - Suppressed by British forces. - Bhil Revolts - Causes - Famine, economic hardship, and British misgovernance, with revolts in 1817, 1825, 1831, 1846, and 1913. - Regions - Western Ghats, southern Rajasthan (Banswara district), and Dhule district (Maharashtra), strategically linking central India to the western coast. - Notable Events - Sindwa Treasury Loot (1857): Around 500 Bhils, led by Kazi Singh, plundered the treasury. - Mangarh Massacre (1913) (Adivasi Jallianwala): Bhils, inspired by Govind Guru, protested peacefully for land and rights; British killed over 1,500, including women and children. - Methods - Guerrilla warfare and exploitation of mountainous terrain for plundering state treasures. - Outcome - Revolts suppressed by British. - Munda Rebellion (1899-1900) (Ulgulan, meaning Uprising) - Region - Chotanagpur region (Jharkhand). - Causes - Loss of tribal lands under the Khuntkatti System (collective ownership), seized by non-tribal settlers (Dikus) becoming jagirdars and zamindars, forcing Mundas into landless labor; protected forests deprived forest rights; exploitation via beth begari (forced labor) and missionary interference. - Leader - Birsa Munda, who declared himself a messenger of God, started the Birsait faith, blending Hindu-Christian elements into Munda ideology. - Methods - Transformed into the “Sardari Fight,” a political and religious campaign to establish Munda Raj. - Outcome - Birsa's arrest and death in 1900 ended the movement; the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) recognized Khuntkatti rights, banned begari, and restricted land transfer to non-tribals. - Tribal Uprisings of North East - Ahom Revolt (1828) - Causes - British refusal to leave Assam after the 1826 Treaty of Yandaboo, contrary to promises post-Anglo-Burmese War. - Regions - Sibsagar district, Assam. - Leaders - Gomadhar Konwar and Dhanjay Borgohain. - Outcome - Suppressed by British; leaders executed. - Anglo-Khasi War (1829-1833) - Causes - Khasi resistance to British colonization. - Leader - Tirath Singh, who organized an armed revolt. - Outcome - Tirath Singh captured and exiled to Dhaka. - Singhpo Rebellions (1830, 1843) - Regions - Arunachal Pradesh. - Leaders - Bom Singhpo (1830): Attacked British armory but was captured. - Beesa Gaum (1843): Led armed resistance but sentenced to life imprisonment. - Tai Khamti Resistance (1839-1844) - Location - Arunachal Pradesh. - Causes - Fear of British-imposed taxes. - Leader - Chow Rang Pha Gohain. - Outcome - British defeated the Khamtis and asserted control over Arunachal Pradesh. - Military Mutinies During British Rule - Overview - Military mutinies in British India, primarily by Indian sepoys, were significant acts of resistance against colonial authority, driven by cultural, economic, and political grievances.
