Q8: His principal forte was social and religious reform. He relied upon legislation to do away with social ills and worked unceasingly for the eradication of child marriage and the purdah system. To encourage consideration of social problems on a national scale, he inaugurated the Indian National Social Conference, which for many years met for its annual session alongside the Indian National Congress. The reference in this passage is to: - Options: (a) Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (b) Behramji Merwanji Malabari (c) Mahadev Govind Ranade (d) B.R. Ambedkar - Answer: (c) Mahadev Govind Ranade - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Mahadev Govind Ranade (1842-1901), a prominent social reformer and judge, was a leading figure in 19th-century India’s social reform movement, particularly in Maharashtra. - He founded the Indian National Social Conference in 1887 to address social issues like child marriage, purdah, and widow remarriage, holding sessions alongside the Indian National Congress to promote national discourse. - Ranade advocated legislative reforms, notably supporting the Age of Consent Act, 1891, which raised the marriageable age for girls, and worked through organizations like the Prarthana Samaj to challenge orthodox practices. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: - Incorrect—Vidyasagar focused on widow remarriage (Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act, 1856) and education but did not found the Indian National Social Conference. - (b) Behramji Merwanji Malabari: - Incorrect—Malabari campaigned against child marriage and supported the Age of Consent Act, but he was not associated with founding the Social Conference. - (d) B.R. Ambedkar: - Incorrect—Ambedkar focused on Dalit rights and constitutional reforms in the 20th century, not 19th-century social conferences or child marriage legislation. - Other Relevant Reform Movements: - Brahmo Samaj: - Founded by Raja Rammohan Roy, addressed similar issues like sati and child marriage. - Arya Samaj: - Led by Dayananda Saraswati, promoted Vedic revivalism and opposed purdah. - Widow Remarriage Association: - Supported by Vidyasagar, focused on legalizing widow remarriage. - Significance of Ranade’s Reforms: - Ranade’s legislative approach bridged traditional and modern values, influencing later reformers and shaping India’s social reform landscape. - The Indian National Social Conference provided a platform for reformers, fostering unity across regions on social issues, though it faced orthodox resistance. - Related Figures: - Raja Rammohan Roy: - Pioneer of social reform, influenced Ranade through the Brahmo Samaj. - Gopal Krishna Gokhale: - Ranade’s disciple, carried forward his reformist legacy via the Servants of India Society. - Kandukuri Veeresalingam: - South Indian reformer, paralleled Ranade’s efforts in Andhra Pradesh. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on social reform movements (e.g., Q33 [2004] on 19th-century reforms), women’s rights (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Age of Consent Act), or nationalism (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Congress history). - Reflects the interplay of social and political reform in colonial India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Ranade’s establishment of the Indian National Social Conference and legislative advocacy marked a pivotal moment in India’s social reform movement, fostering national dialogue on critical issues. - Q9: The following advertisement: THE MARVEL OF THE CENTURY, THE WONDER OF THE WORLD, LIVING PHOTOGRAPHIC PICTURES IN LIFE-SIZED REPRODUCTIONS BY MESSERS LUMIERE BROTHERS CINEMATOGRAPHIE, A FEW EXHIBITIONS WILL BE GIVEN AT WATSON’S HOTEL TONIGHT Appeared in the Times of India dated 7th August: - Options: (a) 1931 (b) 1929 (c) 1921 (d) 1896 - Answer: (d) 1896 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Lumière Brothers, Auguste and Louis, pioneered cinematography, introducing their Cinematographe to India in 1896. - On July 7, 1896, the first film screening in India took place at Watson’s Hotel (now Esplanade Mansion) in Bombay, advertised in the Times of India, marking the advent of cinema in the subcontinent. - The event showcased short films like “Arrival of a Train” and “Leaving the Factory,” captivating colonial and Indian audiences. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1931: - Incorrect—By 1931, Indian cinema had evolved, with the first talkie, Alam Ara, released, far beyond the Lumière Brothers’ initial screenings. - (b) 1929: - Incorrect—Silent films were dominant in 1929, but the Lumière screenings were much earlier. - (c) 1921: - Incorrect—Indian filmmakers like Dadasaheb Phalke were active by 1921 (e.g., Raja Harishchandra, 1913), postdating the 1896 event. - Other Relevant Early Cinema Events: - Dadasaheb Phalke’s Films: - Raja Harishchandra (1913), India’s first feature film, built on the Lumière legacy. - H.S. Bhatavdekar: - Filmed “The Wrestlers” (1899), one of India’s earliest short films, inspired by Lumière screenings. - Bioscope Shows: - Traveling cinema exhibitions in the early 1900s, popularizing films in rural India. - Significance of the 1896 Screening: - The Lumière Brothers’ exhibition introduced motion pictures to India, sparking interest among Indian filmmakers and laying the foundation for Bollywood. - Held at Watson’s Hotel, a colonial hub, it symbolized the intersection of Western technology and Indian cultural adaptation. - Related Figures: - Lumière Brothers: - Innovators of the Cinematographe, globalized early cinema. - Dadasaheb Phalke: - Father of Indian cinema, inspired by early screenings to create indigenous films. - Hiralal Sen: - Early Indian filmmaker, active in Calcutta post-1896, producing short films. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on cultural history (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Indian cinema), colonial influences (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on technology transfers), or media history (e.g., Q76 [2006] on print media). - Reflects the global spread of cinema as a cultural phenomenon in the late 19th century. - Key Takeaway: - The 1896 Lumière screening at Watson’s Hotel marked the birth of cinema in India, catalyzing the development of a vibrant film industry. - Q10: Who among the following was the first European to initiate the policy of taking part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories? - Options: (a) Clive (b) Dupleix (c) Albuquerque (d) Warren Hastings - Answer: (b) Dupleix - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Joseph François Dupleix, French Governor-General of Pondicherry (1742-1754), was the first European to systematically intervene in Indian princely disputes to expand French influence. - During the Carnatic Wars (1740s-1750s), Dupleix supported local rulers (e.g., Chanda Sahib in Arcot) against British-backed rivals, aiming to establish French dominance in South India. - His policy of manipulating succession disputes and offering military aid set a precedent for European territorial expansion, later adopted by the British. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Clive: - Incorrect—Robert Clive (active 1740s-1760s) built on Dupleix’s strategies, notably at Plassey (1757), but was not the first to initiate this policy. - (c) Albuquerque: - Incorrect—Afonso de Albuquerque (early 16th century) focused on Portuguese maritime dominance, capturing ports like Goa, not princely disputes. - (d) Warren Hastings: - Incorrect—Hastings (Governor-General, 1773-1785) expanded British territories, but Dupleix’s earlier interventions predated him. - Other Relevant European Strategies: - Subsidiary Alliance: - Later British policy under Wellesley, formalizing control over Indian states, inspired by Dupleix’s tactics. - Doctrine of Lapse: - Dalhousie’s policy (1848-1856), annexing princely states without heirs, a later evolution of territorial acquisition. - Portuguese Factories: - Albuquerque’s trade-focused approach, distinct from Dupleix’s political interventions. - Significance of Dupleix’s Policy: - Dupleix’s interventions marked a shift from trade to political dominance, escalating Anglo-French rivalry and shaping colonial India’s trajectory. - His recall in 1754 due to French government disapproval allowed the British to capitalize on his strategies, notably under Clive. - Related Figures: - Robert Clive: - Adopted Dupleix’s tactics, securing Bengal at Plassey. - Chanda Sahib: - Dupleix’s ally in the Carnatic, illustrating his princely alliances. - Anwaruddin Khan: - British-backed Nawab of Arcot, opposed Dupleix’s schemes. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on European colonialism (e.g., Q83 [2010-I] on Anglo-French rivalry), Carnatic Wars (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on British expansion), or territorial policies (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Plassey). - Reflects the broader European scramble for influence in 18th-century India. - Key Takeaway: - Dupleix’s pioneering policy of intervening in Indian princely disputes set the stage for European territorial expansion, profoundly influencing colonial India’s history. - Q11: Consider the following landmarks in Indian education: - List: 1. Hindu College, Calcutta 2. University of Calcutta 3. Adam’s Report 4. Wood’s Despatch - The correct chronological order of these landmarks is: - Options: (a) 1, 3, 4, 2 (b) 1, 4, 3, 2 (c) 3, 1, 4, 2 (d) 3, 2, 4, 1 - Answer: (a) 1, 3, 4, 2 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The 19th century saw significant developments in Indian education under British rule, transitioning from traditional to Western systems. - Correct chronological order: - 1. Hindu College, Calcutta (1817): Founded by Raja Rammohan Roy and others, introduced Western education for Indians. - 3. Adam’s Report (1835-1838): William Adam’s survey of indigenous education, informing British policy. - 4. Wood’s Despatch (1854): “Magna Carta of Indian Education,” advocating universities and vernacular education. - 2. (c) 3, 1, 4, 2: - Incorrect—Adam’s Report (1835-1838) follows Hindu College (1817). - (d) 3, 2, 4, 1: - Incorrect—University of Calcutta (1857) and Wood’s Despatch (1854) precede Hindu College (1817). - Other Relevant Educational Landmarks: - Serampore College (1818): - Founded by missionaries, promoted Western and Christian education. - Macaulay’s Minute (1835): - Advocated English education, influencing Wood’s Despatch. - Adam’s Report highlighted indigenous education’s strengths, shaping balanced policies. - Wood’s Despatch laid the foundation for modern education, leading to universities like Calcutta. - The University of Calcutta standardized higher education, producing India’s early modern intellectuals. - Related Figures: - Raja Rammohan Roy: - Co-founder of Hindu College, championed Western education. - William Adam: - Authored reports on indigenous education, influencing policy. - Charles Wood: - Architect of the 1854 Despatch, shaping colonial education. - Alexander Duff: - Missionary educator, supported Western education initiatives. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial education (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Wood’s Despatch), social reform (e.g., Q33 [2004] on educational reforms), or cultural history (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Bengal Renaissance). - Reflects the colonial project of reshaping Indian society through education, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The chronological sequence of Hindu College, Adam’s Report, Wood’s Despatch, and the University of Calcutta traces the evolution of modern education in colonial India, blending Indian and British initiatives. - Q12: Which one of the following is an important historical novel written during the latter half of the nineteenth century? - Options: (a) Rast Goftar (b) Durgesh Nandini (c) Maratha (d) Nibandhamala - Answer: (b) Durgesh Nandini - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Durgesh Nandini (1865), written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, is considered one of India’s first historical novels, published in Bengali during the Bengal Renaissance. - Set in 16th-century Bengal, it fictionalizes the conflict between Mughal and Pathan forces, blending romance and patriotism, and is notable for its literary style and historical backdrop. - The novel marked the rise of vernacular literature, influencing nationalist sentiments in colonial India. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Rast Goftar: - Incorrect—A Gujarati newspaper founded by Dadabhai Naoroji in 1851, not a novel. - (c) Maratha: - Incorrect—A newspaper associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, not a historical novel. - (d) Nibandhamala: - Incorrect—A collection of essays by Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, not a novel. - Other Relevant 19th-Century Literary Works: - Anandamath (1882): - Another Bankim Chandra novel, famous for “Vande Mataram,” with nationalist themes. - Rajmohan’s Wife (1864): - Bankim’s first English novel, a precursor to Durgesh Nandini. - Neel Darpan (1860): - Dinabandhu Mitra’s play on indigo planters’ oppression, reflecting social issues. - Significance of Durgesh Nandini: - As India’s first major historical novel, it popularized the genre, blending historical accuracy with fictional narrative, inspiring later writers. - Its patriotic undertones contributed to the cultural awakening of the Bengal Renaissance, influencing the Indian National Congress’s early nationalism. - Related Figures: - Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay: - Pioneer of Bengali literature, shaped nationalist consciousness. - Bhudev Mukhopadhyay: - Contemporary writer, explored historical themes in essays. - Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: - Literary reformer, supported vernacular literature development. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Bengal Renaissance (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Bankim Chandra), vernacular literature (e.g., Q76 [2006] on nationalist literature), or cultural history (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 19th-century reforms). - Reflects the role of literature in fostering national identity under colonial rule. - Key Takeaway: - Durgesh Nandini’s status as a pioneering historical novel underscores Bankim Chandra’s role in shaping modern Indian literature and nationalist thought during the 19th century. - [1997] - Q13: Who among the following was associated with suppression of thugs? - Options: (a) General Henry Prendergast (b) Captain Sleeman (c) Alexander Burres (d) Captain Robert Pemberton - Answer: (b) Captain Sleeman - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Thuggee was a notorious system of organized robbery and murder by groups called Thugs, primarily in Central and North India, active from medieval times into the 19th century. - Captain (later Major-General) William Henry Sleeman led the British campaign to suppress Thuggee in the 1830s, establishing the Thuggee and Dacoity Department in 1835. - Sleeman’s efforts involved intelligence-gathering, informant networks, and trials, resulting in the arrest and conviction of thousands of Thugs, significantly reducing their activities by the 1840s. - Why Not Others?: - (a) General Henry Prendergast: - Incorrect—Prendergast was a British military officer involved in the Third Anglo-Burman War (1885), not Thuggee suppression. - (c) Alexander Burres: - Incorrect—No historical record links Alexander Burres to Thuggee; this appears to be a fictitious or misnamed figure. - (d) Captain Robert Pemberton: - Incorrect—Pemberton was involved in Northeast India and Burma surveys (1830s), not Thuggee suppression. - Other Relevant Anti-Crime Campaigns: - Dacoity Suppression: - Post-Thuggee, Sleeman’s department targeted dacoits (armed robbers), expanding British law enforcement. - Pindari Suppression: - Early 19th-century campaign against Pindari bandits, led by Lord Hastings, preceding Thuggee efforts. - Criminal Tribes Act, 1871: - Later British policy targeting nomadic groups, influenced by Thuggee suppression tactics. - Significance of Thuggee Suppression: - Sleeman’s campaign strengthened British colonial control by enforcing law and order, portraying the British as protectors against indigenous criminality. - It introduced modern policing methods, including informant networks and centralized departments, shaping colonial governance. - Related Figures: - William Sleeman: - Authored “Rambles and Recollections of an Indian Official,” documenting Thuggee practices. - Lord William Bentinck: - Governor-General (1828-1835), supported Sleeman’s anti-Thuggee operations. - James Outram: - Assisted Sleeman in intelligence operations against Thugs. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British colonial administration (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Bentinck’s reforms), law enforcement (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on colonial policies), or social history (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on colonial interventions). - Reflects the British narrative of “civilizing” India, a key theme in colonial historiography. - Key Takeaway: - Sleeman’s suppression of Thuggee marked a significant British effort to impose law and order, enhancing colonial authority while shaping modern policing in India. - Q14: What is the correct chronological sequence of the following? - List: 1. Wood’s Despatch laid the foundation for modern universities (e.g., Calcutta, 1857). - Hunter Commission expanded access to primary education, addressing rural needs. - Sargent Report envisioned universal education, shaping India’s post-1947 system. - Led the 1882 Commission, focusing on vernacular education. - John Sargent: - Authored the 1944 Report, influencing independent India’s education. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial education (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Wood’s Despatch), social reform (e.g., Q33 [2004] on educational reforms), or nationalism (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Bengal Renaissance). - Reflects the colonial agenda of cultural transformation, countered by nationalist education movements. - Key Takeaway: - The sequence of Macaulay’s Minute, Wood’s Despatch, Hunter Commission, and Sargent Report traces the evolution of British educational policy, shaping modern India’s education system. - Pabna Revolt (1873-1876, Bengal): Peasants protested against zamindari oppression and high rents. - C. Birsa Munda Revolt (1899-1900, Bihar): Tribal rebellion led by Birsa Munda against British land policies and missionary activities in Chotanagpur. - Why Not Others?: - (b) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1: - Incorrect—Moplah Revolt was in Kerala, not Bihar; Birsa Munda Revolt was in Bihar, not Kerala. - (c) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4: - Incorrect—Pabna was in Bengal, not Bihar; Eka was in Awadh, not Bengal; Birsa Munda was in Bihar, not Awadh. - (d) A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2: - Incorrect—Moplah was in Kerala, not Bengal; Pabna was in Bengal, not Awadh; Eka was in Awadh, not Kerala. - Other Relevant Peasant/Tribal Revolts: - Santhal Rebellion (1855-1856, Bihar): - Led by Sidhu and Kanhu, against zamindars and British revenue policies. - Indigo Revolt (1859-1860, Bengal): - Peasants protested forced indigo cultivation, a precursor to Pabna. - Kuka Movement (1870s, Punjab): - Sikh peasant uprising against British rule, with agrarian grievances. - Significance of These Revolts: - Moplah Revolt highlighted communal tensions and anti-colonial sentiment, influencing the Khilafat Movement. - Pabna Revolt showcased peasant agency, leading to tenancy reforms like the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885. - Eka Movement reflected Gandhian influence, aligning with the Non-Cooperation Movement. - Birsa Munda Revolt symbolized tribal resistance, inspiring later Adivasi movements. - Related Figures: - Variyamkunnath Kunjahmed Haji: - Leader of the Moplah Revolt, blended anti-landlord and anti-British goals. - Ishan Chandra Roy: - Key organizer in the Pabna Revolt, mobilized peasants. - Madari Pasi: - Eka Movement leader, united peasants in Awadh. - Birsa Munda: - “Bhagwan Birsa,” led the Ulgulan revolt, a tribal icon. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on peasant movements (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on tribal revolts), colonial policies (e.g., Q76 [2006] on land revenue), or nationalism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Non-Cooperation). - Reflects the socio-economic grievances fueling India’s anti-colonial struggle. - Key Takeaway: - The Moplah, Pabna, Eka, and Birsa Munda revolts highlight diverse regional responses to colonial exploitation, shaping India’s resistance movements. - [1998] - Q16: The educated middle class in India: - Options: (a) opposed the revolt of 1857 (b) supported the revolt of 1857 (c) remained neutral to the revolt of 1857 (d) fought against native rulers - Answer: (c) remained neutral to the revolt of 1857 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Revolt of 1857, also known as the First War of Independence, was a widespread uprising against British rule, involving sepoys, princes, and peasants, primarily in North and Central India. - The educated middle class, emerging in urban centers like Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras, consisted of professionals (e.g., lawyers, teachers) educated in Western institutions like Hindu College (1817). - This class, influenced by British education and reforms, largely remained neutral during the 1857 Revolt, as their interests aligned with colonial stability and opportunities, though some sympathized with the rebels’ cause. - Why Not Others?: - (a) opposed the revolt of 1857: - Incorrect—While some middle-class individuals (e.g., in Calcutta) benefited from British rule, active opposition was minimal; neutrality was more common. - (b) supported the revolt of 1857: - Incorrect—Support was rare, as the middle class lacked the organization or ideological drive to join the revolt, unlike later nationalists. - (d) fought against native rulers: - Incorrect—The middle class did not engage in conflicts against native rulers during 1857; their focus was on reform and professional advancement. - Other Relevant Middle-Class Responses: - Bengal Renaissance: - Middle-class intellectuals like Raja Rammohan Roy (pre-1857) focused on social reform, not rebellion. - Young Bengal Movement: - Led by Henry Derozio, this group critiqued orthodoxy but remained aloof from 1857’s violence. - Post-1857 Nationalism: - The middle class later formed groups like the Indian National Congress (1885), reflecting a shift to political activism. - Significance of Neutrality: - The middle class’s neutrality preserved their socio-economic status under British rule, enabling them to later lead nationalist movements. - It highlighted the disconnect between urban elites and rural rebels, a recurring theme in India’s anti-colonial struggle. - Related Figures: - Raja Rammohan Roy: - Pre-1857 reformer, shaped middle-class reformist ideology, though deceased by 1857. - Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: - Middle-class leader, focused on education and widow remarriage, neutral in 1857. - Dadabhai Naoroji: - Emerging middle-class figure, later nationalist, uninvolved in 1857. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on the 1857 Revolt (e.g., Q76 [2006] on its causes), middle-class nationalism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Congress formation), or social reform (e.g., Q33 [2004] on Bengal Renaissance). - Reflects the complex socio-political dynamics of colonial India, with the middle class as a bridge between tradition and modernity. - Key Takeaway: - The educated middle class’s neutrality in 1857 underscores their early reformist focus and socio-economic dependence on British rule, setting the stage for their later nationalist leadership. - [1999] - Q17: The paintings of Abanindranath Tagore are classified as: - Options: (a) realistic (b) socialistic (c) revivalistic (d) impressionistic - Answer: (c) revivalistic - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Abanindranath Tagore (1871-1951), a key figure in the Bengal School of Art, pioneered a revivalistic approach in the early 20th century, emphasizing Indian cultural and artistic traditions. - His paintings, such as “Bharat Mata” (1905) and “The Passing of Shah Jahan,” drew inspiration from Mughal miniatures, Rajput art, and Ajanta frescoes, countering Western academic realism. - As a leader of the Bengal Renaissance, Abanindranath sought to revive indigenous aesthetics, aligning with the Swadeshi movement’s nationalist ideals. - Why Not Others?: - (a) realistic: - Incorrect—Realism, associated with European academic art, was rejected by Abanindranath in favor of stylized Indian forms. - (b) socialistic: - Incorrect—Socialistic art, linked to Soviet-inspired realism, was unrelated to Abanindranath’s focus on cultural revival. - (d) impressionistic: - Incorrect—Impressionism, a French movement emphasizing light and color, differed from Abanindranath’s narrative and symbolic style. - Other Relevant Art Movements: - Company School: - Hybrid Indo-European style of the 18th-19th centuries, contrasting with Abanindranath’s anti-colonial revivalism. - Progressive Artists’ Group: - Post-independence modernist movement (1947), diverging from the Bengal School’s traditionalism. - Kalighat Paintings: - 19th-century Bengali folk art, influencing Abanindranath’s use of local idioms. - Significance of Revivalistic Art: - Abanindranath’s work fostered a national artistic identity, challenging colonial cultural dominance and inspiring artists like Nandalal Bose. - It aligned with Swadeshi ideology, promoting self-reliance in art and culture during India’s freedom struggle. - Related Figures: - Abanindranath Tagore: - Founder of the Bengal School, mentored artists like Gaganendranath Tagore. - E.B. Havell: - British art historian, supported Abanindranath’s revival of Indian art traditions. - Rabindranath Tagore: - Abanindranath’s uncle, influenced his cultural nationalism through Visva-Bharati. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Indian art (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Bengal School), Swadeshi movement (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on nationalism), or cultural history (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Bengal Renaissance). - Reflects the broader theme of cultural nationalism in colonial India. - Key Takeaway: - Abanindranath Tagore’s revivalistic paintings, rooted in Indian traditions, played a pivotal role in fostering national identity through art during the Swadeshi era. - Q18: There was no independent development of industries in India during British rule because of the: - Options: (a) absence of heavy industries (b) scarcity of foreign capital (c) scarcity of natural resources (d) preference of the rich to invest in land - Answer: (a) absence of heavy industries - Analysis: - Historical Context: - During British rule (1757-1947), India’s industrial development was severely constrained due to the absence of a foundation for heavy industries. - The colonial government focused on exploiting India as a market for British finished goods and a source of raw materials. - Industrial growth, especially in core sectors like iron, steel, and machinery, was minimal before independence, impeding forward and backward linkages for broader industrialization. - Why Not Others?: - (b) scarcity of foreign capital: - Incorrect—Foreign capital did flow into India but was primarily invested in British-controlled sectors like railways, plantations, and trade, not indigenous industries. - (c) scarcity of natural resources: - Incorrect—India had abundant natural resources (e.g., coal, iron ore), but these were exploited for British benefit and not used for domestic industrial development. - (d) preference of the rich to invest in land: - Incorrect—While investment in land was common, it was a symptom of the lack of industrial infrastructure and incentives, not the primary reason for the absence of industrial development. - Other Relevant Colonial Economic Policies: - Deindustrialization: - Traditional industries like textiles declined due to British imports and policy bias against local manufacturing. - Railways and Infrastructure: - Built primarily to aid resource extraction and export, not internal industrial connectivity. - Fiscal Policy: - High taxation and the “Drain of Wealth” restricted capital accumulation within India. - Significance of Lack of Heavy Industries: - Without core industries, India lacked the industrial base necessary for self-sustained growth, delaying economic transformation. - This structural deficiency was only addressed in the post-independence period through state-led industrialization (e.g., Five-Year Plans). - Related Figures: - Dadabhai Naoroji: - Criticized colonial policies in “Poverty and Un-British Rule in India,” highlighting economic drain. - R.C. Dutt: - Documented the economic consequences of colonialism in “Economic History of India.” - Jamsetji Tata: - Pioneered industrial development with Tata Steel (1907), despite lack of state support. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on deindustrialization (e.g., Q110 [2014-I]), railways and colonial economy (e.g., Q78 [2011-I]), and post-independence industrial policy (e.g., Q150 [2024-I]). - Reflects larger themes of economic stagnation and colonial underdevelopment. - Key Takeaway: - The absence of heavy industries, a direct result of colonial priorities, was the principal barrier to independent industrial development in India under British rule. - Q19: The first feature film (talkie) to be produced in India was: - Options: (a) Hatimtai (b) Alam Ara (c) Pundalik (d) Raja Harishchandra - Answer: (b) Alam Ara - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Alam Ara, directed by Ardeshir Irani and released on March 14, 1931, was India’s first feature-length talkie (sound film), produced by Imperial Movietone in Bombay. - A Hindi-Urdu musical, it marked the transition from silent films to sound cinema, featuring songs and dialogue, and was a commercial success. - Its release at Majestic Cinema, Bombay, capitalized on the global advent of sound technology post-The Jazz Singer (1927, USA). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Hatimtai: - Incorrect—Hatimtai (1929) was a silent film, not a talkie, directed by Prafulla Ghosh. - (c) Pundalik: - Incorrect—Pundalik (1912), by R.G. Torney, was a silent film, often debated as an early feature but not a talkie. - (d) Raja Harishchandra: - Incorrect—Raja Harishchandra (1913), by Dadasaheb Phalke, was India’s first silent feature film, not a talkie. - Other Relevant Early Indian Films: - Raja Harishchandra (1913): - First Indian silent feature, foundational to Indian cinema. - Shirin Farhad (1931): - Another early talkie, released soon after Alam Ara, also by Irani. - Kalidas (1931): - First Tamil talkie, marking regional cinema’s sound era. - Significance of Alam Ara: - Alam Ara’s success popularized talkies, shaping Bollywood’s musical narrative style and establishing Hindi cinema’s dominance. - It marked a technological and cultural milestone, integrating sound to reflect India’s oral traditions. - Related Figures: - Ardeshir Irani: - Director of Alam Ara, pioneered sound in Indian cinema. - Dadasaheb Phalke: - Father of Indian cinema, laid the groundwork with silent films. - H.M. Reddy: - Directed Kalidas, expanding talkies to South India. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Indian cinema (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on film history), cultural history (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on technological advances), or colonial media (e.g., Q76 [2006] on cultural shifts). - Reflects the global spread of sound cinema and its localization in India. - Key Takeaway: - Alam Ara, as India’s first talkie, revolutionized Indian cinema, blending technology and cultural storytelling to lay the foundation for Bollywood. - Q20: The Governor-General who followed a spirited “Forward” policy towards Afghanistan was: - Options: (a) Minto (b) Dufferin (c) Elgin (d) Lytton - Answer: (d) Lytton - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Lord Lytton (Governor-General, 1876-1880) pursued the “Forward Policy” to counter perceived Russian threats in Central Asia during the Great Game, focusing on Afghanistan. - His aggressive stance led to the Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878-1880), aiming to install a pro-British ruler and secure India’s northwest frontier. - The policy involved military intervention and diplomacy, culminating in the Treaty of Gandamak (1879), though it faced resistance from Afghan tribes. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Minto: - Incorrect—Minto (1905-1910) focused on reforms (Morley-Minto Reforms, 1909), not Afghanistan. - (b) Dufferin: - Incorrect—Dufferin (1884-1888) dealt with Burma (Third Anglo-Burmese War), not a forward policy in Afghanistan. - (c) Elgin: - Incorrect—Elgin (1894-1899) managed frontier issues but did not initiate the Forward Policy. - Other Relevant Frontier Policies: - Masterly Inactivity: - John Lawrence’s (1864-1869) policy of non-intervention in Afghanistan, contrasting Lytton’s approach. - Close Border Policy: - Post-Lytton, a defensive strategy to secure frontiers without direct intervention. - Durand Line (1893): - Agreement defining the Afghan-India border, influenced by Lytton’s frontier focus. - Significance of the Forward Policy: - Lytton’s policy escalated Anglo-Russian tensions, shaping British India’s foreign policy and frontier administration. - The Second Anglo-Afghan War’s mixed outcomes highlighted the challenges of controlling Afghanistan, influencing later British restraint. - Related Figures: - Lord Lytton: - Architect of the Forward Policy, also known for controversial Vernacular Press Act (1878). - Sher Ali Khan: - Afghan Emir, resisted British influence, triggering the war. - John Lawrence: - Advocated Masterly Inactivity, Lytton’s predecessor in frontier policy. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British foreign policy (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Anglo-Afghan Wars), colonial administration (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on frontier policies), or Great Game (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on geopolitics). - Reflects the imperial rivalries of the 19th century, with India as a strategic hub. - Key Takeaway: - Lytton’s Forward Policy towards Afghanistan, culminating in the Second Anglo-Afghan War, underscored British imperial ambitions and the complexities of frontier governance. - Q21: At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors-General kept the British flag flying high in India? - Options: (a) Warren Hastings (b) Lord Cornwallis (c) Lord Wellesley (d) Lord Hastings - Answer: (d) Lord Hastings - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Napoleonic Wars (1790s-1815) disrupted European empires, including Britain’s continental influence. - Lord Hastings (Governor-General, 1813–1823) assumed office as the Napoleonic threat waned in Europe but continued its geopolitical implications globally. - He maintained and extended British supremacy in India through decisive wars and expansionist policies, ensuring stability when British focus was divided between Europe and the colonies. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Warren Hastings: - Incorrect—Served earlier (1773–1785), focused on administrative consolidation, unrelated to Napoleonic threats. - (b) Lord Cornwallis: - Incorrect—Governor-General (1786–1793), engaged in the Third Anglo-Mysore War, prior to Napoleon’s major European influence. - (c) Lord Wellesley: - Incorrect—Wellesley (1798–1805) countered French influence via Tipu Sultan but his tenure ended before the peak European collapse caused by Napoleon. - Major Actions under Lord Hastings: - Defeated the Pindaris and curbed Maratha power in the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818), consolidating British control. - Led the Anglo-Nepalese War (1814–1816), securing British territorial interests in the Himalayas. - Reformed administration and improved civil-military integration, asserting central authority. - Significance of Hastings’ Tenure: - Stabilized and expanded British India during a time of shifting European dynamics post-Napoleon. - His campaigns completed the process of subjugating major Indian powers, laying groundwork for future British dominance. - Related Figures: - Lord Hastings: - Key figure in the final consolidation phase of Company rule; aggressive militarist and reformer. - Pindaris: - Irregular warriors raiding British territories, crushed under Hastings. - Maratha Confederacy: - Major Indian power decisively weakened by Hastings’ military campaigns. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British consolidation (e.g., Q95 [2017-I] on Anglo-Maratha Wars), post-Napoleonic expansion (e.g., Q134 [2019-I] on Pindaris), and military policy (e.g., Q121 [2022-I]). - Reflects the continuity of imperial expansion despite European distractions, highlighting India's strategic value. - Key Takeaway: - Lord Hastings ensured British supremacy in India during a critical transitional period in global politics, effectively keeping the British flag flying high as empires in Europe faltered after Napoleon. - Q22: Which one of the following statements is not correct? - Options: (a) ‘Neel Darpan’ was a play based on the exploitation of the Indigo farmers (b) The author of the play ‘Ghashiram Kotwal’ is Vijay Tendulkar (c) The play ‘Navann’ by Nabin Chandra Das was based on the famine of Bengal (d) Urdu theatre used to depend heavily on Parsi theatre - Answer: (c) The play ‘Navann’ by Nabin Chandra Das was based on the famine of Bengal - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Neel Darpan (1860), by Dinabandhu Mitra, is a Bengali play portraying the indigo farmers' exploitation, sparking social consciousness. - Ghashiram Kotwal (1972), by Vijay Tendulkar, is a noted Marathi play criticizing power abuse. - Urdu theatre in the late 19th and early 20th century adopted the stylized, melodramatic format of Parsi theatre. - However, there is no evidence of a play called “Navann” by Nabin Chandra Das based on the Bengal famine—this statement is factually incorrect. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct—Neel Darpan is indeed a play (not a novel), depicting the Indigo Revolt; often confused in UPSC exams to mislead candidates. - (b) Correct—Tendulkar’s Ghashiram Kotwal is a landmark modern Indian play exploring despotism and morality. - (d) Correct—Parsi theatre influenced the development of Urdu theatre through format, themes, and presentation styles. - Other Relevant Indian Plays: - Nil Darpan (1860): - Inspired public sympathy for indigo cultivators and shaped socio-political theatre. - Ghashiram Kotwal: - Satirical, rooted in 18th-century Pune politics, criticized Brahminical power structures. - Inder Sabha (1853): - Early Urdu play, showcasing Parsi theatre’s influence. - Significance of Theatre in Social Reform: - Indian theatre evolved as a vehicle of critique and resistance, addressing colonial exploitation, social injustices, and power hierarchies. - Plays like Neel Darpan and Ghashiram Kotwal helped politicize theatre and shape public discourse. - Related Figures: - Dinabandhu Mitra: - Pioneer in vernacular social theatre with Neel Darpan. - Vijay Tendulkar: - Revived Marathi theatre, emphasized political and moral dilemmas. - Agha Hashr Kashmiri: - Urdu dramatist who blended Parsi techniques with indigenous themes. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on socio-political consciousness through art (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Indigo Revolt), theatre and cultural history (e.g., Q150 [2024-I]), and Bengal Renaissance movements. - Reinforces how drama reflected and shaped resistance and reform in colonial India. - Key Takeaway: - The incorrect attribution of “Navann” to Nabin Chandra Das exposes factual inaccuracies, emphasizing the importance of precise cultural knowledge in UPSC questions. - Q25: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: - List-I (Year): A. 1775 B. 1780 C. 1824 D. 1838 - List-II (Event): 1.
