Lord Auckland: - Initiated First Anglo-Afghan War, faced backlash for its failure. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British expansion (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Anglo-Maratha Wars), colonial wars (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Mysore Wars), or frontier policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Afghan conflicts). - Reflects Britain’s imperial strategy to secure India against regional powers and European rivals. - Key Takeaway: - The correct matching of these wars with their years highlights the phased expansion of British colonial power, shaping India’s geopolitical landscape. - [2000] - Q26: The last major extension of British Indian territory took place during the time of: - Options: (a) Dufferin (b) Dalhousie (c) Lytton (d) Curzon - Answer: (b) Dalhousie - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General, 1848-1856) pursued an aggressive expansionist policy, significantly extending British Indian territory through annexations. - Key annexations included Punjab (1849, Second Anglo-Sikh War), Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Nagpur and Jhansi (1853-1854) via the Doctrine of Lapse, and Awadh (1856) on grounds of misgovernance. - These were the last major territorial expansions before the 1857 Revolt, after which the British Crown assumed direct control (1858), focusing on consolidation rather than further annexations. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Dufferin: - Incorrect—Dufferin (1884-1888) oversaw the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885), annexing Upper Burma, but this was a minor extension compared to Dalhousie’s widespread annexations. - (c) Lytton: - Incorrect—Lytton (1876-1880) focused on the Second Anglo-Afghan War, with no major territorial gains in India. - (d) Curzon: - Incorrect—Curzon (1899-1905) partitioned Bengal (1905) but did not annex new territories; his focus was administrative reorganization. - Other Relevant British Expansion Policies: - Doctrine of Lapse: - Dalhousie’s policy, annexing princely states without a natural heir, e.g., Satara, Nagpur. - Subsidiary Alliance: - Wellesley’s earlier policy, indirectly controlling states, precursor to Dalhousie’s annexations. - Misgovernance Clause: - Used to annex Awadh, reflecting Dalhousie’s pretext for expansion. - Significance of Dalhousie’s Annexations: - Dalhousie’s policies nearly doubled British-controlled territory, consolidating the British Empire in India but fueling discontent that contributed to the 1857 Revolt. - The shift to Crown rule post-1857 marked the end of large-scale annexations, focusing on princely state alliances. - Related Figures: - Lord Dalhousie: - Architect of the Doctrine of Lapse, modernized infrastructure but provoked unrest. - Ranjit Singh: - Sikh ruler whose death (1839) enabled Punjab’s annexation under Dalhousie. - Nana Saheb: - Adopted heir of Baji Rao II, resisted Dalhousie’s lapse policy in Kanpur (1857). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British expansion (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Doctrine of Lapse), 1857 Revolt (e.g., Q76 [2006] on causes), or colonial policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on princely states). - Reflects the peak of British territorial ambition, a key UPSC theme in colonial history. - Key Takeaway: - Dalhousie’s tenure marked the last major territorial expansion of British India, driven by policies like the Doctrine of Lapse, shaping the prelude to the 1857 Revolt. - Q27: Which one of the following statements is incorrect? - Options: (a) Goa attained full statehood in 1987 (b) Diu is an island in the Gulf of Khambhat (c) Daman and Diu were separated from Goa by the 56th Amendment of the Constitution of India (d) Dadra and Nagar Haveli were under French colonial rule till 1954 - Answer: (d) Dadra and Nagar Haveli were under French colonial rule till 1954 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - (a) Goa attained statehood in 1987 through the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, following liberation from Portuguese rule in 1961. - (b) Diu is an island off the southern coast of Saurashtra in the Arabian Sea. While some mistakenly place it in the Gulf of Khambhat, it is geographically located further west. - (c) The 56th Constitutional Amendment (1987) separated Daman and Diu from Goa, allowing Goa to become India’s 25th state while the others remained Union Territories. - Incorrect statement: - (d) Dadra and Nagar Haveli were under Portuguese rule, not French. They were liberated in 1954 by local forces and integrated into India formally in 1961. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct—Goa’s transition to statehood in 1987 is well documented. - (b) Not factually wrong enough—Though often confused geographically, Diu’s location in the Arabian Sea is technically not in the Gulf of Khambhat, but this is not as critical an error as misidentifying colonial rulers. - (c) Correct—The 56th Amendment did indeed restructure Goa, Daman, and Diu appropriately. - Other Relevant Post-Colonial Reorganizations: - Pondicherry’s Integration (1954–1962): - Former French territories merged with India in stages, providing contrast with Portuguese territories. - Liberation of Goa (1961): - Operation Vijay led to the integration of Portuguese territories into India. - Dadra and Nagar Haveli: - Liberated in 1954 by Indian nationalists and volunteers, administered by a local body before integration. - Significance of the Error: - Confusing French and Portuguese rule reflects a common pitfall in understanding colonial legacies. - UPSC often tests subtle distinctions between French, Portuguese, and British colonial footprints. - Related Figures: - K.G. Badlani: - IAS officer who acted as the first administrator of liberated Dadra and Nagar Haveli. - Jawaharlal Nehru: - Oversaw diplomatic decisions on Goa and Dadra-Nagar Haveli integration. - Broader Connection: - Relevant to themes of post-independence integration (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on statehood), colonial legacies (e.g., Q105 [2015-I]), and Indian geography. - Helps clarify the difference in timelines and actors involved in the liberation and reorganization of French vs Portuguese enclaves. - Key Takeaway: - The incorrect attribution of French rule to Dadra and Nagar Haveli underscores the importance of precisely distinguishing between different colonial powers in India—a subtle but high-yield topic for UPSC. - [2001] - Q28: Who among the following Indian rulers established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? - Options: (a) Haider Ali (b) Mir Qasim (c) Shah Alam II (d) Tipu Sultan - Answer: (d) Tipu Sultan - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Tipu Sultan (r. 1782-1799), ruler of Mysore, was a visionary leader who established diplomatic missions on modern lines, sending envoys to France, Ottoman Turkey, and Persia to secure alliances against the British. - In 1787, Tipu sent ambassadors to Versailles (France) to negotiate military support, and to Constantinople (Ottoman Empire) and Muscat, adopting structured diplomatic protocols akin to European models. - These missions aimed to counter British expansion and leverage global alliances, reflecting Tipu’s modernizing approach to statecraft. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Haider Ali: - Incorrect—Haider Ali (r. 1761-1782), Tipu’s father, focused on military campaigns against the British but did not establish formal embassies abroad. - (b) Mir Qasim: - Incorrect—Mir Qasim (Nawab of Bengal, 1760-1763) sought alliances with local powers but had no record of foreign embassies. - (c) Shah Alam II: - Incorrect—Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor, 1759-1806) was a nominal ruler under British influence, lacking the authority to establish foreign missions. - Other Relevant Diplomatic Efforts: - Maratha Diplomacy: - Peshwas sent envoys to regional courts but not abroad on modern lines. - Mughal Envoys: - Earlier Mughals (e.g., Jahangir) exchanged letters with Persia, but these were not structured embassies. - Ranjit Singh’s Diplomacy: - Sikh ruler engaged with British and Afghan leaders but focused on regional alliances. - Significance of Tipu’s Diplomacy: - Tipu’s embassies were pioneering, introducing modern diplomatic practices to Indian statecraft and challenging British dominance through global outreach. - Though unsuccessful due to European politics and British interception, they highlighted Tipu’s strategic foresight and anti-colonial stance. - Related Figures: - Tipu Sultan: - “Tiger of Mysore,” modernized Mysore’s administration and diplomacy. - Louis XVI: - French king, received Tipu’s envoys, though alliances faltered. - Hyder Ali: - Tipu’s father, laid the groundwork for Mysore’s resistance but not diplomacy. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on anti-colonial resistance (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Anglo-Mysore Wars), Tipu’s reforms (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Mysore), or global diplomacy (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Napoleonic era). - Reflects the intersection of Indian and global politics in the late 18th century. - Key Takeaway: - Tipu Sultan’s establishment of modern embassies abroad marked a pioneering effort in Indian diplomacy, aiming to counter British power through international alliances. - Q29: Which of the following pairs is not correctly matched? - Options: (a) India’s first technicolour film—Jhansi ki Rani (b) India’s first 3-D film—My dear Kuttichathan (c) India’s first insured film—Taal (d) India’s first actress to win the Bharat Ratna—Meena Kumari - Answer: (d) India’s first actress to win the Bharat Ratna—Meena Kumari - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct pairs: - (a) Jhansi ki Rani (1953), directed by Sohrab Modi, was India’s first technicolour film, a historical drama on Rani Lakshmibai. - (b) My Dear Kuttichathan (1984), a Malayalam film by Jijo Punnoose, was India’s first 3-D film, pioneering stereoscopic technology. - (c) Taal (1999), directed by Subhash Ghai, was India’s first insured film, introducing film insurance to mitigate production risks. - Incorrect pair: - (d) Meena Kumari, a legendary actress, never received the Bharat Ratna; Lata Mangeshkar (2001) was the first film personality (singer) to win it, and no actress has won it to date. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct—Jhansi ki Rani is recognized as India’s first technicolour film. - (b) Correct—My Dear Kuttichathan holds the distinction of India’s first 3-D film. - (c) Correct—Taal pioneered film insurance in India, a notable milestone. - Other Relevant Indian Cinema Milestones: - Alam Ara (1931): - First talkie, marking the sound era (Q19). - Kisan Kanya (1937): - Early colour film, though not fully technicolour like Jhansi ki Rani. - Chori Chori (1956): - Early insured film, but Taal is credited as the first formally insured. - Significance of These Milestones: - Jhansi ki Rani and My Dear Kuttichathan showcased India’s adoption of global cinematic technologies, enhancing visual storytelling. - Taal’s insurance model mitigated financial risks, professionalizing Bollywood. - The absence of a Bharat Ratna for actresses highlights the award’s limited scope in cinema, favoring other fields. - Related Figures: - Sohrab Modi: - Director of Jhansi ki Rani, a pioneer in historical epics. - Jijo Punnoose: - Directed My Dear Kuttichathan, introduced 3-D to India. - Subhash Ghai: - Directed Taal, innovated with film insurance. - Lata Mangeshkar: - First film personality to win Bharat Ratna, relevant to (d). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Indian cinema (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on film history), technological advances (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on media), or cultural awards (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Bharat Ratna). - Reflects India’s evolving film industry and its global integration. - Key Takeaway: - The incorrect pairing of Meena Kumari with the Bharat Ratna underscores the need for precise knowledge of Indian cinema milestones, with Jhansi ki Rani, My Dear Kuttichathan, and Taal marking key technological advancements. - Q30: Under the Permanent Settlement, 1793, the Zamindars were required to issue pattas to the farmers which were not issued by many of the Zamindars. The reason was: - Options: (a) the Zamindars were trusted by the farmers (b) there was no official check upon the Zamindars (c) it was the responsibility of the British government (d) the farmers were not interested in getting pattas - Answer: (b) there was no official check upon the Zamindars - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, fixed land revenue permanently, making zamindars hereditary landlords responsible for revenue collection. - Zamindars were required to issue pattas (land leases) to farmers, specifying rent and rights, to ensure transparency and protect tenants. - Many zamindars failed to issue pattas, exploiting tenants by demanding arbitrary rents, as there was no effective British oversight or enforcement mechanism. - Why Not Others?: - (a) the Zamindars were trusted by the farmers: - Incorrect—Zamindars often exploited farmers, leading to distrust, as seen in revolts like the Pabna Revolt (Q15). - (c) it was the responsibility of the British government: - Incorrect—The British delegated patta issuance to zamindars, not assuming direct responsibility. - (d) the farmers were not interested in getting pattas: - Incorrect—Farmers sought pattas for legal protection against exploitative rents, but zamindars withheld them. - Other Relevant Land Revenue Systems: - Ryotwari System: - Introduced in Madras and Bombay, dealt directly with farmers, avoiding zamindar intermediaries. - Mahalwari System: - In North India, revenue was fixed for village communities, differing from Permanent Settlement. - Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885: - Later reform addressing patta issues, prompted by tenant agitations. - Significance of Patta Non-Issuance: - The lack of oversight on zamindars led to tenant exploitation, fueling agrarian unrest and necessitating reforms like the Bengal Tenancy Act. - It highlighted the flaws of the Permanent Settlement, prioritizing revenue over tenant welfare. - Related Figures: - Lord Cornwallis: - Introduced the Permanent Settlement, shaping Bengal’s agrarian structure. - R.C. Dutt: - Critiqued the Settlement’s impact on farmers in “Economic History of India.” - Ishan Chandra Roy: - Pabna Revolt leader, protested zamindari abuses (Q15). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial land revenue (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Permanent Settlement), peasant revolts (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Pabna), or economic policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on agrarian issues). - Reflects the socio-economic tensions of colonial India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The non-issuance of pattas by zamindars, due to lack of official checks, exposed the exploitative nature of the Permanent Settlement, driving agrarian discontent. - Q31: Consider the following statements: - List: 1. Arya Samaj was founded in 1835 2. Lala Lajpat Rai opposed the appeal of Arya Samaj to the authority of Vedas in support of its social reform programme 3. Under Keshab Chandra Sen, the Brahmo Samaj campaigned for women’s education 4. Vinoba Bhave founded the Sarvodaya Samaj to work among refugees - Which of these statements are correct? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 and 3 (c) 2 and 4 (d) 3 and 4 - Answer: (d) 3 and 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - 3. Keshab Chandra Sen, a Brahmo Samaj leader (1860s-1880s), campaigned for women’s education, founding institutions like the Native Ladies Normal School and advocating widow remarriage. - 4. Vinoba Bhave founded the Sarvodaya Samaj in the 1940s to promote Gandhian principles, working among partition refugees through initiatives like the Bhoodan Movement. - Incorrect statements: - 1. Arya Samaj was founded in 1875 by Dayananda Saraswati, not 1835, which predates its formation. - 2. Lala Lajpat Rai, an Arya Samaj member, supported its Vedic-based reforms, not opposed them, promoting social changes like widow remarriage. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Both statements 1 and 2 are false. - (b) 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is false; only 3 is correct. - (c) 2 and 4: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is false; only 4 is correct. - Other Relevant Social Reform Movements: - Prarthana Samaj: - Founded in 1867, focused on monotheism and social reform, similar to Brahmo Samaj. - Ramakrishna Mission: - Established by Vivekananda (1897), promoted education and social service. - Bhoodan Movement: - Vinoba Bhave’s post-Sarvodaya initiative, redistributing land to the landless. - Significance of These Reforms: - Keshab Chandra Sen’s Brahmo Samaj advanced gender equality, influencing legislative reforms like the Age of Consent Act (1891). - Vinoba Bhave’s Sarvodaya Samaj addressed post-partition refugee crises, extending Gandhian ideals into social reconstruction. - Related Figures: - Keshab Chandra Sen: - Brahmo Samaj leader, pioneered women’s education reforms. - Vinoba Bhave: - Gandhian, founded Sarvodaya Samaj, led Bhoodan Movement. - Dayananda Saraswati: - Founded Arya Samaj (1875), relevant to statement 1’s correction. - Lala Lajpat Rai: - Arya Samaj nationalist, relevant to statement 2’s correction. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on social reforms (e.g., Q33 [2004] on Brahmo Samaj), Gandhian movements (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Sarvodaya), or partition (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on refugee rehabilitation). - Reflects the 19th-20th century reformist and humanitarian responses to colonial challenges. - Key Takeaway: - The correct statements about Keshab Chandra Sen’s Brahmo Samaj and Vinoba Bhave’s Sarvodaya Samaj highlight their contributions to education and refugee welfare, key aspects of India’s social reform landscape. - Q32: Who amongst the following Englishmen first translated Bhagavad-Gita into English? - Options: (a) William Jones (b) Charles Wilkins (c) Alexander Cunningham (d) John Marshall - Answer: (b) Charles Wilkins - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Charles Wilkins, a British Orientalist and East India Company official, published the first English translation of the Bhagavad-Gita in 1785, titled “The Bhagvat-Geeta, or Dialogues of Kreeshna and Arjoon.” - His work, supported by Warren Hastings, introduced Indian philosophy to the West, fostering cross-cultural understanding during the colonial period. - The translation was a landmark in Indology, published in London and praised for its fidelity to the original Sanskrit text. - Why Not Others?: - (a) William Jones: - Incorrect—Jones, founder of the Asiatic Society (1784), translated other texts like Shakuntala but not the Bhagavad-Gita. - (c) Alexander Cunningham: - Incorrect—Cunningham, an archaeologist, focused on Buddhist sites and epigraphy, not translations. - (d) John Marshall: - Incorrect—Marshall, an archaeologist, led Indus Valley excavations (1920s), unrelated to translations. - Other Relevant Indological Contributions: - Shakuntala (1789): - William Jones’ translation of Kalidasa’s play, a key Orientalist work. - Manusmriti (1794): - Translated by Jones, influenced colonial legal studies. - Upanishads (1801-1802): - Later translated by Henry Thomas Colebrooke, building on Wilkins’ work. - Significance of Wilkins’ Translation: - The 1785 Bhagavad-Gita translation bridged Indian and Western intellectual traditions, influencing thinkers like Emerson and Thoreau. - It marked the beginning of systematic British Indology, shaping colonial cultural policies and global interest in Indian spirituality. - Related Figures: - Charles Wilkins: - Pioneer of Sanskrit studies, first to translate the Bhagavad-Gita. - Warren Hastings: - Patron of Wilkins, promoted Orientalist scholarship. - William Jones: - Contemporary Orientalist, founded Asiatic Society, contextual to Wilkins’ work. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Indology (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Orientalist studies), colonial cultural policies (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Asiatic Society), or Indian philosophy (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Bhagavad-Gita). - Reflects the colonial era’s complex engagement with Indian heritage, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Charles Wilkins’ 1785 translation of the Bhagavad-Gita was a pioneering Indological effort, introducing Indian philosophy to the West and shaping cross-cultural exchanges. - [2002] - Q33: Which one of the following submitted in 1875 a petition to the House of Commons demanding India’s direct representation in the British parliament? - Options: (a) The Deccan Association (b) The Indian Association (c) The Madras Mahajan Sabha (d) The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha - Answer: (d) The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, founded in 1870 by Mahadev Govind Ranade and others, was among the earliest socio-political organizations in India. - In 1875, it submitted a historic petition to the British House of Commons, demanding direct Indian representation in the British Parliament. - This act was a landmark in the evolution of Indian constitutional agitation, highlighting a growing awareness among Indian elites of the need for political representation. - Why Not Others?: - (a) The Deccan Association: - No credible historical record exists of an organization with this name submitting a petition in 1875; likely a distractor. - (b) The Indian Association: - Incorrect—Though a major political body, it was founded in 1876, after the 1875 petition by the Poona Sabha. - (c) The Madras Mahajan Sabha: - Incorrect—Formed in 1884, well after the petition, with a focus on South Indian regional issues and moderate reform. - Other Relevant Early Nationalist Organizations: - East India Association (1866): - Founded by Dadabhai Naoroji in London, also aimed to influence British political opinion. - Bombay Association (1852): - A predecessor in Western India advocating legal and administrative reforms. - British Indian Association (1851): - Focused more on elite zamindar interests than on democratic representation. - Significance of the Petition: - The 1875 petition was one of the earliest formal attempts to demand constitutional reform within the framework of the British Empire. - It marked a shift from localized social reform to broader political engagement, influencing later formations like the Indian National Congress (1885). - Related Figures: - Mahadev Govind Ranade: - Key founder of the Sabha, promoted legal and constitutional reforms. - Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi: - Prominent member of the Sabha, represented it at the Delhi Durbar (1877) in a coat of coarse cloth, symbolizing Indian poverty. - Broader Connection: - Ties into early constitutionalism (e.g., Q76 [2006] on pre-INC politics), political awakening (e.g., Q150 [2024-I]), and proto-nationalism. - Demonstrates the early moderate phase of Indian nationalism, relying on petitions and legislative appeals. - Key Takeaway: - The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha’s 1875 petition to the British Parliament was a critical milestone in Indian political history—an early voice for representation, laying intellectual groundwork for the nationalist movement to come. - Q34: With which one of the following mountain tribes did the British first come into contact with after the grant of Diwani in the year 1765? - Options: (a) Garos (b) Khasis (c) Kukis (d) Tipperahs - Answer: (b) Khasis - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Grant of Diwani (1765) by Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II gave the East India Company revenue rights over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, prompting British expansion into frontier regions. - The Khasis, a matrilineal tribe in the Khasi Hills (present-day Meghalaya), were among the first mountain tribes the British contacted post-1765, as they sought to secure trade routes and control Northeast India. - Initial British-Khasi interactions occurred in the late 1760s-1770s, with formal engagements intensifying by the 1820s, culminating in the Anglo-Khasi War (1826-1828). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Garos: - Incorrect—The British contacted the Garos (Garo Hills) later, primarily in the 19th century, post-Khasi engagements. - (c) Kukis: - Incorrect—Kuki interactions began in the 19th century, notably during the Kuki Rebellion (1917-1919), much later than 1765. - (d) Tipperahs: - Incorrect—The Tipperahs (Tripura’s tribal groups) were contacted later, with significant British influence post-1800s. - Other Relevant Northeast Tribal Interactions: - Anglo-Garo Conflicts (1830s): - Followed Khasi engagements, aimed at securing frontier stability. - Anglo-Naga Relations (1830s-1840s): - British expansion into Naga Hills, post-Khasi contact. - Anglo-Mizo Wars (1870s-1890s): - Later frontier conflicts, reflecting British Northeast policy. - Significance of Khasi Contact: - Early British-Khasi interactions marked the beginning of colonial penetration into Northeast India, shaping frontier policies and trade networks. - The Khasi resistance, notably under leaders like Tirot Sing, highlighted tribal autonomy, influencing later British treaty-based approaches. - Related Figures: - Tirot Sing: - Khasi leader, resisted British expansion in the 1820s. - David Scott: - British administrator, negotiated early Khasi agreements in the Northeast. - Robert Lindsay: - Early British official in Sylhet, engaged with Khasis post-1765. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British frontier policies (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Northeast expansion), tribal resistance (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Khasi uprising), or colonial administration (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Diwani). - Reflects the British strategy of controlling strategic frontier regions post-Diwani. - Key Takeaway: - The British first contacted the Khasis post-1765 Diwani, initiating colonial expansion into Northeast India’s tribal regions, a pivotal step in frontier consolidation. - Q35: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: - List-I (Acts of Colonial Government of India): A. Charter Act, 1813 B. Regulating Act C. Act of 1858 D. Pitt’s India Act - List-II (Provisions): 1. Set up a Board of Control in Britain to fully regulate the East India Company’s trade 2. Company’s trade monopoly in India was ended 3. The power to govern was transferred from the East India Company to the British Crown 4. The Company’s directors were asked to present to the British government all correspondence and documents pertaining to the administration of the company - Options: (a) A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 (b) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2 (c) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1 (d) A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2 - Answer: (a) A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - British colonial governance in India evolved through key legislative acts, balancing East India Company autonomy with Crown oversight. - Correct matches: - A. Charter Act, 1813: Ended the Company’s trade monopoly in India (2), opening trade to private merchants, though retaining China trade rights. - B. Regulating Act, 1773: Required Company directors to submit all administrative correspondence to the British government (4), introducing oversight. - C. Act of 1858: Transferred governance from the Company to the British Crown (3), post-1857 Revolt, creating the Viceroy’s office. - D. Pitt’s India Act, 1784: Established a Board of Control in Britain to regulate the Company’s trade and administration (1), strengthening government control. - Why Not Others?: - (b) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2: - Incorrect—Charter Act did not set up the Board of Control; Regulating Act did not transfer governance; Pitt’s Act did not end the monopoly. - (c) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1: - Incorrect—Regulating Act did not transfer governance; Act of 1858 did not involve correspondence submission. - (d) A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2: - Incorrect—Charter Act ended the monopoly, not set up the Board; Pitt’s Act established the Board, not ended the monopoly. - Other Relevant Colonial Legislative Acts: - Charter Act, 1833: - Ended Company’s China trade monopoly, centralized Indian administration (Q7). - Indian Councils Act, 1861: - Expanded legislative councils, post-1858 governance changes. - Government of India Act, 1935: - Introduced provincial autonomy, building on 1858’s Crown control. - Significance of These Acts: - Regulating Act (1773) initiated British government oversight, curbing Company autonomy. - Pitt’s India Act (1784) formalized control, balancing commercial and political interests. - Charter Act (1813) liberalized trade, integrating India into global markets. - Act of 1858 marked direct Crown rule, reshaping India’s colonial administration post-1857. - Related Figures: - Warren Hastings: - First Governor-General under Regulating Act, faced its oversight. - William Pitt: - Architect of Pitt’s India Act, strengthened British control. - Lord Canning: - First Viceroy under Act of 1858, oversaw transition to Crown rule. - Lord Ellenborough: - Governor-General during Charter Act, 1813, navigated trade changes. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial governance (e.g., Q76 [2006] on 1858 Act), British administration (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Regulating Act), or economic policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on trade reforms). - Reflects the gradual shift from Company to Crown rule, a central UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The correct matching of these acts with their provisions traces the evolution of British colonial governance, from Company oversight to direct Crown control. - Q36: Which one of the following Acts of British India strengthened the Viceroy’s authority over his Executive Council by substituting “Portfolio” or departmental system for corporate functioning? - Options: (a) Indian Council Act, 1861 (b) Government of India Act, 1858 (c) Indian Council Act, 1892 (d) Indian Council Act, 1909 - Answer: (a) Indian Council Act, 1861 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Indian Council Act, 1861, introduced significant administrative reforms post-1857 Revolt, enhancing the Viceroy’s authority to streamline governance. - It replaced the Executive Council’s corporate (collective) decision-making with a “portfolio” or departmental system, assigning specific departments (e.g., finance, home) to individual council members, reporting directly to the Viceroy. - This reform, implemented under Lord Canning, centralized power, improving efficiency in colonial administration. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Government of India Act, 1858: - Incorrect—It transferred governance to the Crown and created the Viceroy’s office but did not reform the Executive Council’s functioning. - (c) Indian Council Act, 1892: - Incorrect—It expanded legislative councils and introduced indirect elections, not portfolio system reforms. - (d) Indian Council Act, 1909: - Incorrect—Known as Morley-Minto Reforms, it expanded councils and introduced separate electorates, not Executive Council restructuring. - Other Relevant Administrative Reforms: - Act of 1858: - Established the Viceroy and Secretary of State, setting the stage for 1861 reforms. - Government of India Act, 1919: - Introduced dyarchy, decentralizing some powers, contrasting 1861’s centralization. - Government of India Act, 1935: - Further restructured governance, building on earlier centralizing measures. - Significance of the Portfolio System: - The portfolio system enhanced the Viceroy’s control, enabling faster decision-making and specialization in colonial governance. - It modernized British administration, addressing post-1857 administrative challenges and setting a precedent for later bureaucratic reforms. - Related Figures: - Lord Canning: - First Viceroy, implemented the 1861 Act’s reforms. - Charles Wood: - Secretary of State for India, influenced the 1861 Act’s provisions. - James Wilson: - Finance member under the new portfolio system, introduced income tax. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial administration (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on 1861 Act), Viceroy’s powers (e.g., Q76 [2006] on post-1857 reforms), or governance reforms (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on British bureaucracy). - Reflects the British response to the 1857 Revolt, strengthening centralized control. - Key Takeaway: - The Indian Council Act, 1861, introduced the portfolio system, significantly strengthening the Viceroy’s authority and modernizing colonial governance post-1857. - [2003] - Q37: During the colonial period in India, what was the purpose of the Whitley Commission? - Options: (a) To review the fitness of India for further political reforms (b) To report on existing conditions of labour and to make recommendations (c) To draw up a plan for financial reforms for India (d) To develop a comprehensive scheme for Civil Services in India - Answer: (b) To report on existing conditions of labour and to make recommendations - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Whitley Commission, officially the Royal Commission on Labour in India, was appointed in 1929 under John Henry Whitley to investigate labour conditions in colonial India. - Its purpose was to examine issues like wages, working hours, and factory conditions, and to recommend improvements, addressing growing labour unrest and trade union activism. - The Commission’s 1931 report led to reforms like the Factories Act, 1934, improving worker protections and shaping India’s labour laws. - Why Not Others?: - (a) To review the fitness of India for further political reforms: - Incorrect—Political reforms were addressed by commissions like the Simon Commission (1927), not Whitley. - (c) To draw up a plan for financial reforms for India: - Incorrect—Financial reforms were handled by bodies like the Hilton Young Commission (1926), not Whitley. - (d) To develop a comprehensive scheme for Civil Services in India: - Incorrect—Civil Services were reformed via the Lee Commission (1923-1924), not Whitley. - Other Relevant Colonial Labour Reforms: - Trade Unions Act, 1926: - Legalized trade unions, preceding Whitley’s recommendations. - Factories Act, 1934: - Implemented Whitley’s suggestions, regulating factory conditions. - Payment of Wages Act, 1936: - Ensured timely wage payments, influenced by labour reforms. - Significance of the Whitley Commission: - The Commission’s findings highlighted the plight of Indian workers, fostering labour welfare policies and strengthening trade union movements. - It marked a shift towards recognizing labour rights in colonial policy, influenced by global labour standards and Indian nationalist demands. - Related Figures: - John Henry Whitley: - Chaired the Commission, applied his expertise from British labour reforms. - N.M. Joshi: - Indian labour leader, provided evidence to the Commission, advocated worker rights. - B.R. Ambedkar: - Engaged with labour issues, influenced post-Whitley reforms. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial labour policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on trade unions), social reforms (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on worker welfare), or economic history (e.g., Q76 [2006] on industrialization). - Reflects the colonial response to labour unrest, a key UPSC theme in modern Indian history. - Key Takeaway: - The Whitley Commission’s focus on labour conditions and recommendations shaped colonial India’s labour reforms, addressing worker exploitation and influencing post-independence policies. - Q38: With reference to the entry of European powers into India, which one of the following statements is not correct? - Options: (a) The Portuguese captured Goa in 1499 (b) The English opened their first factory in South India at Masulipatam (c) In Eastern India, the English Company opened its first factory in Orissa in 1633 (d) Under the leadership of Dupleix, the French occupied Madras in 1746 - Answer: (a) The Portuguese captured Goa in 1499 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - (b) The English established their first South Indian factory at Masulipatam (1611), a key trade hub in the Golconda Sultanate. - (c) The English opened their first factory in Eastern India at Hariharpur, Orissa, in 1633, marking early expansion in the region. - (d) Joseph François Dupleix, French Governor-General, occupied Madras in 1746 during the First Carnatic War, a move later reversed by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748). - Incorrect statement: - (a) The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 under Afonso de Albuquerque, not 1499, which predates their significant Indian conquests (Vasco da Gama’s arrival was 1498). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Correct—Masulipatam was the English East India Company’s first South Indian factory. - (c) Correct—Orissa’s 1633 factory marked English expansion in Eastern India. - (d) Correct—Dupleix’s capture of Madras in 1746 is historically accurate. - Other Relevant European Colonial Milestones: - Portuguese Capture of Diu (1535): - Strengthened Portuguese control after Goa. - English Factory at Surat (1612): - First major English factory in Western India, preceding Masulipatam. - French Establishment at Pondicherry (1674): - Dupleix’s later base, post-Madras occupation. - Significance of Portuguese Goa: - The incorrect 1499 date for Goa’s capture is a common UPSC trap; the correct 1510 conquest established Portugal as a maritime power in India, influencing later European entries. - Goa remained a Portuguese stronghold until India’s liberation in 1961 (Q27). - Related Figures: - Afonso de Albuquerque: - Portuguese governor, captured Goa in 1510. - Joseph François Dupleix: - French leader, key in Carnatic Wars, captured Madras (Q10). - Thomas Roe: - English envoy, secured Surat factory rights, contextual to English expansion. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on European colonialism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Portuguese), Carnatic Wars (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Dupleix), or trade networks (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on factories). - Reflects the competitive European scramble for Indian trade in the 16th-18th centuries. - Key Takeaway: - The incorrect claim of Goa’s capture in 1499 highlights the Portuguese establishment in 1510, a pivotal moment in European colonial entry into India. - Q39: In India, the first Dutch factory was established at: - Options: (a) Surat (b) Pulicat (c) Cochin (d) Cassimbazar - Answer: (b) Pulicat - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Dutch East India Company (VOC), formed in 1602, entered India to compete with the Portuguese and English, focusing on spice trade and textiles. - The Dutch established their first factory in India at Pulicat (Tamil Nadu) in 1610, a strategic port north of Madras, serving as their primary base until Fort Geldria was built. - Pulicat’s location facilitated trade with the Coromandel Coast and Southeast Asia, marking the Dutch’s early colonial presence. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Surat: - Incorrect—The Dutch established a factory at Surat in 1616, after Pulicat. - (c) Cochin: - Incorrect—Cochin became a Dutch base in 1663 after capturing it from the Portuguese, post-Pulicat. - (d) Cassimbazar: - Incorrect—Cassimbazar (West Bengal) was a later Dutch factory, established in the 1650s for Bengal trade. - Other Relevant Dutch Colonial Sites: - Negapatam (1658): - Captured from the Portuguese, a later Dutch stronghold. - Chinsura (1653): - Dutch Bengal factory, complementing Cassimbazar. - Sadras (1647): - Another Coromandel factory, post-Pulicat expansion. - Significance of Pulicat Factory: - Pulicat’s establishment marked the Dutch entry into Indian trade, challenging Portuguese dominance and setting the stage for Anglo-Dutch rivalry. - It facilitated Dutch control over Coromandel textiles, influencing global trade networks until their decline in the 18th century. - Related Figures: - Pieter van den Broecke: - Dutch merchant, instrumental in establishing Pulicat factory. - Francisco Pelsaert: - Dutch chronicler, documented early Dutch trade in India. - Afonso de Albuquerque: - Portuguese rival, whose Goa conquest (1510) preceded Dutch entry. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on European colonialism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Dutch trade), Coromandel Coast (e.g., Q76 [2006] on factories), or global trade (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on spice trade). - Reflects the competitive European mercantile expansion in India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Dutch establishment of their first factory at Pulicat in 1610 marked their entry into Indian trade, shaping colonial competition on the Coromandel Coast. - Q40: The aim of education as stated by the Wood’s Despatch of 1854 was: - Options: (a) the creation of employment opportunities for native Indians (b) the spread of western culture in India (c) the promotion of literacy among the people using English medium (d) the introduction of scientific research and rationalism in the traditional Indian education - Answer: (d) the introduction of scientific research and rationalism in the traditional Indian education - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Wood’s Despatch of 1854, drafted by Sir Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control, is often called the “Magna Carta of English Education in India.” It provided a comprehensive plan for education from primary to university level. - While creating a class of Indians for administrative support and spreading Western cultural values were underlying consequences and likely intents, a key *stated* aim was the diffusion of European knowledge, including improvements in Arts, Science, Philosophy, and Literature of Europe, to raise the intellectual level and moral character of Indians. - Why (d) is Correct: - The Despatch explicitly aimed to introduce Western knowledge systems. This included the empirical methods of scientific inquiry and the philosophical traditions emphasizing rationalism, contrasting with existing traditional Indian modes of learning. - The goal was to impart "useful and practical knowledge" suited for material prosperity and to foster intellectual development through subjects like European science and philosophy. Therefore, introducing scientific research (as a concept and body of knowledge) and rationalism (as a mode of thought intrinsic to Western philosophy/science of the time) into the educational system provided *to* Indians fits this objective. "Traditional Indian education" here likely refers to the existing landscape onto which this new system, infused with science and rationalism, was introduced. - Why Not Others?: - (a) the creation of employment opportunities for native Indians: While the system did produce clerks and administrative staff (a practical outcome desired by the British), generating employment was not the primary *stated educational aim* of the Despatch itself; it was more focused on intellectual and moral development (through Western knowledge) and practical skills. - (b) the spread of western culture in India: This was certainly a major *consequence* and arguably an underlying *goal* of introducing Western education. However, the *stated* aim in the Despatch was often framed more specifically in terms of imparting superior European knowledge (including science/rationalism) for intellectual and moral improvement, rather than just broadly stating "cultural spread." Option (d) focuses on the specific intellectual content intended. - (c) the promotion of literacy among the people using English medium: Incorrect because Wood's Despatch explicitly recommended using vernacular languages at the primary level and supported a grants-in-aid system for vernacular schools, although English was the medium for higher education. It did not aim *solely* for English-medium literacy. - Other Relevant Educational Policies: - Macaulay’s Minute (1835): Advocated English as the medium of instruction for higher education, influencing the Despatch's emphasis on English at the university level. - Hunter Commission (1882): Reviewed the progress of education since the Despatch, focusing particularly on primary and secondary education and the role of private enterprise. - Indian Universities Act, 1904: Aimed to reform university administration and raise academic standards, building upon the universities established following the Despatch's recommendations (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras in 1857). - Significance of Wood’s Despatch: - It laid the foundation for a structured, hierarchical education system in India (Primary -> Secondary -> University). - Led to the establishment of formal universities and promoted secular education. - While aiming to introduce Western science/rationalism, its implementation contributed significantly to creating an anglicized Indian middle class and had long-term effects on Indian society and culture. - Related Figures: - Charles Wood: President of the Board of Control, oversaw the drafting of the Despatch. - Thomas Macaulay: His earlier Minute strongly advocated for Western education through English, setting a precedent. - Lord Dalhousie: Governor-General when the Despatch was issued, responsible for its initial implementation steps. - Broader Connection: - Connects to themes of colonial education policy, the introduction of Western thought systems, the anglicization debate, and the formation of modern Indian intellectual traditions. - Understanding the *stated* aims versus the *actual impact* is crucial for analyzing colonial policies. - Key Takeaway: - Wood’s Despatch of 1854 formally aimed to establish a comprehensive education system diffusing European knowledge, including science and rational modes of thought, to improve the intellectual capacity and provide practical skills to Indians, using both vernacular languages and English at different levels. - Q41: Which one of the following statements is not correct? - Options: (a) Ali Mardan Khan introduced the system of revenue farming in Bengal (b) Maharaja Ranjit Singh set up modern foundries to manufacture cannons at Lahore (c) Sawai Jai Singh of Amber had Euclid’s Elements of Geometry translated into Sanskrit (d) Sultan Tipu of Mysore gave money for the construction of the idol of Goddess Sharda in the Shringeri temple - Answer: (a) Ali Mardan Khan introduced the system of revenue farming in Bengal - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - (b) Maharaja Ranjit Singh (r. 1801-1839) modernized the Sikh army, establishing foundries in Lahore to manufacture cannons, aided by European experts. - (c) Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber (r. 1699-1743), a scholar-king, commissioned the translation of Euclid’s Elements of Geometry into Sanskrit, reflecting his interest in astronomy and mathematics. - (d) Tipu Sultan (r. 1782-1799) donated funds for the Shringeri temple’s Goddess Sharda idol, showcasing his patronage of Hindu institutions despite his Islamic faith (Q28). - Incorrect statement: - (a) Ali Mardan Khan, a Mughal governor under Shah Jahan, was known for canal construction (e.g., in Punjab) and military campaigns, not introducing revenue farming in Bengal. Revenue farming was introduced later by Murshid Quli Khan in the early 18th century. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Correct—Ranjit Singh’s foundries modernized Sikh artillery, a historical fact. - (c) Correct—Jai Singh’s translation of Euclid reflects his scientific patronage. - (d) Correct—Tipu’s donation to Shringeri temple is well-documented, showing his religious inclusivity. - Other Relevant Pre-Colonial Contributions: - Murshid Quli Khan’s Revenue System: - Introduced revenue farming in Bengal, correcting statement (a). - Jaipur’s Jantar Mantar: - Jai Singh’s observatories, complementing his mathematical translations. - Tipu’s Rocket Technology: - Advanced Mysore’s military, paralleling Ranjit Singh’s foundries. - Significance of These Contributions: - Ranjit Singh’s foundries strengthened the Sikh Empire, resisting British expansion. - Jai Singh’s translations bridged Indian and Western knowledge, enriching Rajput scholarship. - Tipu’s temple patronage highlighted his pragmatic governance, fostering Hindu-Muslim unity. - The incorrect attribution to Ali Mardan Khan underscores the need for precise historical knowledge. - Related Figures: - Ali Mardan Khan: - Mughal governor, known for canals, not revenue farming. - Maharaja Ranjit Singh: - Sikh ruler, modernized military with European techniques. - Sawai Jai Singh II: - Rajput astronomer-king, patron of scientific translations. - Tipu Sultan: - Mysore ruler, supported diverse religious institutions. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on pre-colonial India (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Tipu), Sikh history (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Ranjit Singh), or Mughal administration (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on revenue systems). - Reflects the diverse contributions of Indian rulers before British dominance. - Key Takeaway: - The incorrect claim about Ali Mardan Khan’s revenue farming highlights the accurate contributions of Ranjit Singh, Jai Singh, and Tipu, showcasing pre-colonial India’s military, scientific, and cultural advancements. - Q42: Which one of the following provisions was not made in the Charter Act of 1833? - Options: (a) The trading activities of the East India Company were to be abolished (b) The designation of the supreme authority was to be changed as the Governor-General of India in Council (c) All law-making powers to be conferred on Governor-General in Council (d) An Indian was to be appointed as a Law Member in the Governor-General’s Council - Answer: (d) An Indian was to be appointed as a Law Member in the Governor-General’s Council - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Charter Act of 1833, enacted under Lord William Bentinck, reformed the East India Company’s structure, centralizing governance and ending its commercial role. - Correct provisions: - (a) Abolished the Company’s trading activities, transforming it into an administrative body. - (b) Changed the title from Governor-General of Bengal to Governor-General of India in Council, reflecting expanded authority (Q7). - (c) Conferred all law-making powers to the Governor-General in Council, creating a centralized legislative framework. - Incorrect provision: - (d) The Act appointed a Law Member (Macaulay as the first) to the Governor-General’s Council but did not mandate an Indian; Indian representation came later with the Indian Councils Act, 1861. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct—The Act ended the Company’s trade monopoly, a key reform. - (b) Correct—The redesignation to Governor-General of India formalized centralized rule. - (c) Correct—Law-making powers were centralized, strengthening colonial governance. - Other Relevant Provisions of 1833 Act: - Slavery Mitigation: - Declared slavery illegal, a social reform under Bentinck. - Education Funding: - Allocated funds for Indian education, influencing Wood’s Despatch (Q40). - Open Competition for Civil Services: - Proposed competitive exams, though implemented later. - Significance of the Charter Act, 1833: - The Act marked the transition of the Company from a commercial to an administrative entity, consolidating British rule in India. - Its exclusion of Indian representation highlighted the colonial focus on British control, sparking later nationalist demands for inclusion. - Related Figures: - Lord William Bentinck: - Governor-General, oversaw the Act’s implementation. - Thomas Macaulay: - First Law Member, shaped legal and educational policies. - Charles Trevelyan: - Supported administrative reforms under the Act. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial governance (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on 1833 Act), British administration (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Bentinck), or Indian representation (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on councils). - Reflects the shift towards centralized colonial rule, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Charter Act of 1833 did not mandate an Indian Law Member, focusing instead on ending Company trade, centralizing governance, and empowering the Governor-General, shaping colonial India’s administration. - Q43: With reference to colonial rule in India, what was sought by the Ilbert Bill in 1883? - Options: (a) To bring Indians and Europeans at par as far as the criminal jurisdiction of courts was concerned (b) To impose severe restrictions on the freedom of the native press as it was perceived to be hostile to colonial rulers (c) To encourage the native Indians to appear for civil service examinations by conducting them in India (d) To allow native Indians to possess arms by amending the Arms Act - Answer: (a) To bring Indians and Europeans at par as far as the criminal jurisdiction of courts was concerned - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Ilbert Bill, introduced in 1883 by Viceroy Lord Ripon and drafted by Courtenay Ilbert, aimed to allow Indian judges in the Bengal Presidency to try Europeans in criminal cases, aligning with judicial equality. - It sought to remove racial discrimination in criminal jurisdiction, where previously only European judges could try Europeans, reflecting Ripon’s liberal reforms. - The Bill faced fierce opposition from European planters and officials, leading to its dilution in 1884, allowing Europeans to demand jury trials. - Why Not Others?: - (b) To impose severe restrictions on the native press: - Incorrect—Press restrictions were imposed by the Vernacular Press Act, 1878, not the Ilbert Bill. - (c) To encourage the native Indians to appear for civil service examinations: - Incorrect—Civil service reforms were addressed by the Aitchison Commission (1886), not the Ilbert Bill. - (d) To allow native Indians to possess arms: - Incorrect—The Arms Act, 1878, restricted Indian arms possession; the Ilbert Bill was unrelated. - Other Relevant Colonial Judicial Reforms: - Indian High Courts Act, 1861: - Established High Courts, setting the stage for judicial debates like Ilbert’s. - Age of Consent Act, 1891: - Later liberal reform, influenced by Ripon’s progressive policies. - Jury System Expansion (1884): - Compromise post-Ilbert controversy, allowed European jury trials. - Significance of the Ilbert Bill: - The Bill exposed deep racial tensions in colonial India, galvanizing Indian nationalist sentiment and European opposition, notably from indigo planters. - Its failure highlighted the limits of liberal reforms under British rule, fueling demands for equality and self-governance. - Related Figures: - Lord Ripon: - Liberal Viceroy, championed the Ilbert Bill, faced European backlash. - Courtenay Ilbert: - Legal member, drafted the Bill, aimed for judicial equality. - Surendranath Banerjea: - Nationalist leader, supported the Bill, mobilized Indian opinion (Q33). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial reforms (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Ripon), racial discrimination (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Ilbert controversy), or nationalism (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on early protests). - Reflects the tensions between liberal reforms and colonial racism, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Ilbert Bill of 1883 sought judicial equality by allowing Indian judges to try Europeans, sparking a major controversy that highlighted colonial racial divides and fueled nationalist movements. - Q44: In India, the first Bank of limited liability managed by Indians and founded in 1881 was: - Options: (a) Hindustan Commercial Bank (b) Oudh Commercial Bank (c) Punjab National Bank (d) Punjab and Sind Bank - Answer: (b) Oudh Commercial Bank - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Oudh Commercial Bank, established in 1881 in Faizabad (Awadh), was the first bank of limited liability managed entirely by Indians, a significant step in indigenous banking during colonial India. - Founded by Indian merchants and professionals, it operated on modern banking principles, offering loans and savings accounts, reflecting the growing economic agency of the Indian middle class. - Limited liability protected shareholders from personal financial risk, a modern banking feature distinguishing it from earlier unregulated banks. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Hindustan Commercial Bank: - Incorrect—No historical record exists of a Hindustan Commercial Bank in 1881; likely a fictitious option. - (c) Punjab National Bank: - Incorrect—Founded in 1894 in Lahore, it was a later Indian-managed bank with limited liability. - (d) Punjab and Sind Bank: - Incorrect—Established in 1908, it postdates Oudh Commercial Bank. - Other Relevant Early Indian Banks: - Allahabad Bank (1865): - Early Indian bank, but initially British-managed, not fully Indian-run. - Bank of Bombay (1840): - Part of Presidency Banks, British-controlled, not Indian-managed. - Central Bank of India (1911): - Later Indian initiative, post-Oudh Commercial Bank. - Significance of Oudh Commercial Bank: - As the first Indian-managed bank with limited liability, it marked a milestone in economic self-reliance, challenging British-dominated banking like the Presidency Banks. - It paved the way for later Indian banks like Punjab National Bank, supporting nationalist economic aspirations. - Related Figures: - Lala Harkishen Lal: - Early Indian banker, associated with Punjab National Bank, contextual to Oudh’s era. - Rai Bahadur Lala Sohan Lal: - Influential Awadh merchant, likely involved in Oudh Commercial Bank’s founding. - Dadabhai Naoroji: - Advocated economic nationalism, indirectly supported indigenous banking. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on economic nationalism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Indian enterprises), colonial economy (e.g., Q76 [2006] on banking), or Swadeshi movement (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on indigenous industries). - Reflects the growing Indian economic agency under colonial constraints, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Oudh Commercial Bank, founded in 1881, was India’s first Indian-managed bank with limited liability, symbolizing early economic nationalism and modern banking initiatives. - [2004] - Q45: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched? - List: 1. AD 1767-69: First Anglo-Maratha War 2. AD 1790-92: Third Mysore War 3. AD 1824-26: First Anglo-Burmese War 4. AD 1845-46: Second Sikh War - Options: (a) 2 and 4 (b) 3 and 4 (c) 1 and 2 (d) 2 and 3 - Answer: (d) 2 and 3 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct pairs: - 2. Third Mysore War (1790-1792): Fought under Lord Cornwallis against Tipu Sultan, ended with the Treaty of Seringapatam, ceding half of Mysore’s territory. - 3. First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-1826): Led by Lord Amherst, resulted in British annexation of Assam, Manipur, and Arakan via the Treaty of Yandabo (Q25). - Incorrect pairs: - 1. First Anglo-Maratha War: Occurred in 1775-1782, not 1767-1769, under Warren Hastings, ended with the Treaty of Salbai (Q25). - 4. Second Sikh War: Took place in 1848-1849, not 1845-1846, under Lord Dalhousie, leading to Punjab’s annexation (Q26). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 2 and 4: - Incorrect—Pair 4 is wrong (Second Sikh War was 1848-1849). - (b) 3 and 4: - Incorrect—Pair 4 is wrong (Second Sikh War was 1848-1849). - (c) 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Pair 1 is wrong (First Anglo-Maratha War was 1775-1782). - Other Relevant Colonial Wars: - Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805): - Under Wellesley, expanded British control, post-First Maratha War. - Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799): - Defeated Tipu Sultan, followed Third Mysore War (Q21). - First Sikh War (1845-1846): - Preceded Second Sikh War, weakened Sikh power. - Significance of These Wars: - The Third Mysore War curtailed Tipu’s power, strengthening British dominance in South India. - The First Anglo-Burmese War expanded British territory in Northeast India, shaping regional geopolitics. - Correct dating is crucial for UPSC, as misattributions (e.g., Maratha, Sikh wars) are common traps. - Related Figures: - Lord Cornwallis: - Led Third Mysore War, secured British gains. - Lord Amherst: - Governor-General during First Anglo-Burmese War. - Warren Hastings: - Oversaw First Anglo-Maratha War, relevant to pair 1’s correction. - Lord Dalhousie: - Led Second Sikh War, relevant to pair 4’s correction. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on British expansion (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Anglo-Mysore Wars), colonial wars (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Sikh Wars), or frontier policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Burmese conflicts). - Reflects Britain’s phased conquest of India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Third Mysore War (1790-1792) and First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-1826) are correctly matched, highlighting British territorial expansion in South and Northeast India. - Q46: Which of the following pairs is not correctly matched? - Options: (a) Pitt’s India Act—Warren Hastings (b) Doctrine of Lapse—Dalhousie (c) Vernacular Press Act—Curzon (d) Ilbert Bill—Ripon - Answer: (c) Vernacular Press Act—Curzon - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct pairs: - (a) Pitt’s India Act (1784): Enacted during Warren Hastings’ tenure, established a Board of Control to regulate the East India Company (Q35). - (b) Doctrine of Lapse (1848-1856): Introduced by Lord Dalhousie, used to annex princely states like Satara and Jhansi (Q26). - (d) Ilbert Bill (1883): Proposed by Lord Ripon, aimed at judicial equality for Indians and Europeans, sparking controversy (Q43). - Incorrect pair: - (c) Vernacular Press Act (1878): Enacted under Lord Lytton, not Curzon, to curb the Indian press; Curzon (1899-1905) was associated with the Bengal Partition (1905). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct—Pitt’s India Act aligned with Hastings’ governorship, enhancing British oversight. - (b) Correct—Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse was a key annexation policy. - (d) Correct—Ripon’s Ilbert Bill was a landmark liberal reform. - Other Relevant Colonial Policies: - Regulating Act, 1773: - Preceded Pitt’s India Act, also under Hastings (Q35). - Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885: - Ripon’s reform, complemented Ilbert Bill’s liberal agenda. - Universities Act, 1904: - Curzon’s actual policy, contrasting with Vernacular Press Act. - Significance of the Vernacular Press Act: - The Act, wrongly attributed to Curzon, suppressed nationalist newspapers under Lytton, fueling Indian discontent and early nationalism. - Its misattribution to Curzon is a UPSC trap, testing precise knowledge of Viceroys’ tenures. - Related Figures: - Warren Hastings: - First Governor-General, governed under Pitt’s India Act. - Lord Dalhousie: - Architect of Doctrine of Lapse, expanded British India. - Lord Lytton: - Enacted Vernacular Press Act, not Curzon. - Lord Ripon: - Proposed Ilbert Bill, championed liberal reforms. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial governance (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Viceroys), press freedom (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Vernacular Press Act), or annexation policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Doctrine of Lapse). - Reflects the diverse strategies of British control, from censorship to territorial expansion. - Key Takeaway: - The Vernacular Press Act, incorrectly paired with Curzon, was Lytton’s 1878 policy, underscoring the need for accurate Viceroy-policy associations in colonial history. - Q47: Consider the following Viceroys of India during the British rule: - List: 1. Lord Curzon 2. Lord Chelmsford 3. Lord Hardinge 4. Lord Irwin - The correct chronological order of their tenure is: - Options: (a) 1, 3, 2, 4 (b) 2, 4, 1, 3 (c) 1, 4, 2, 3 (d) 2, 3, 1, 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 3, 2, 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct chronological order: - 1. Lord Curzon (1899-1905): Known for Bengal Partition and administrative reforms. - 3. Lord Hardinge (1910-1916): Oversaw Delhi Durbar (1911) and shifted capital to Delhi. - 2. Lord Chelmsford (1916-1921): Implemented Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919). - 4. Lord Irwin (1926-1931): Negotiated Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), faced Civil Disobedience. - Why Not Others?: - (b) 2, 4, 1, 3: - Incorrect—Chelmsford (1916-1921) and Irwin (1926-1931) postdate Curzon (1899-1905). - (c) 1, 4, 2, 3: - Incorrect—Irwin (1926-1931) follows Chelmsford (1916-1921), not precedes. - (d) 2, 3, 1, 4: - Incorrect—Chelmsford (1916-1921) follows Hardinge (1910-1916), not precedes. - Other Relevant Viceroys: - Lord Minto (1905-1910): - Preceded Hardinge, introduced Morley-Minto Reforms. - Lord Willingdon (1931-1936): - Followed Irwin, oversaw Government of India Act, 1935. - Lord Linlithgow (1936-1943): - Post-Irwin, managed early WWII challenges. - Significance of Their Tenures: - Curzon’s partition fueled nationalist unrest, shaping early 20th-century politics. - Hardinge’s capital shift and Delhi Durbar symbolized imperial consolidation. - Chelmsford’s reforms introduced limited self-governance, a precursor to later constitutional changes. - Irwin’s pact with Gandhi marked a turning point in British-Indian negotiations. - Related Figures: - Lord Curzon: - Partitioned Bengal, centralized administration. - Lord Hardinge: - Shifted capital to Delhi, faced nationalist protests. - Lord Chelmsford: - Co-authored 1919 reforms with Montagu. - Lord Irwin: - Engaged with Gandhi, navigated Civil Disobedience. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Viceroys (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Curzon), constitutional reforms (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Montagu-Chelmsford), or nationalist movements (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Gandhi-Irwin Pact). - Reflects the evolving British response to Indian nationalism, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The correct chronological order (Curzon, Hardinge, Chelmsford, Irwin) traces the progression of British Viceroys, each shaping colonial governance and nationalist responses. - Q48: Consider the following princely States of the British rule in India: - List: 1. Jhansi (1853): Annexed after Raja Gangadhar Rao’s death, rejecting the adopted heir Damodar Rao (Q26). - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1, 2, 3: - Incorrect—Jhansi (1853) was annexed after Satara (1848) and Sambalpur (1849). - (b) 1, 3, 2: - Incorrect—Jhansi (1853) follows Satara (1848) and Sambalpur (1849). - (d) 3, 1, 2: - Incorrect—Sambalpur (1849) precedes Jhansi (1853). - Other Relevant Annexations under Doctrine of Lapse: - Nagpur (1854): - Annexed post-Jhansi, under Dalhousie’s policy. - Jaitpur (1849): - Annexed alongside Sambalpur, due to lack of heirs. - Awadh (1856): - Annexed on grounds of misgovernance, not Doctrine of Lapse. - Significance of These Annexations: - Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse expanded British territory but provoked resentment among Indian rulers, contributing to the 1857 Revolt, notably in Jhansi under Rani Lakshmibai. - The annexations centralized British control, reducing princely autonomy and fueling nationalist sentiments. - Related Figures: - Lord Dalhousie: - Architect of Doctrine of Lapse, drove annexations. - Rani Lakshmibai: - Jhansi’s queen, led 1857 Revolt against annexation. - Appa Sahib: - Satara’s ruler, whose death triggered annexation. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Doctrine of Lapse (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Dalhousie), 1857 Revolt (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Jhansi), or princely states (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on annexations). - Reflects British territorial consolidation, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The correct annexation order (Satara, Sambalpur, Jhansi) under Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse highlights the aggressive British expansion that fueled the 1857 Revolt. - Q49: Consider the following statements: - List: 1.
