[2013] - Q83: The Ilbert Bill controversy was related to the: - Options: (a) imposition of certain restrictions to carry arms by the Indians (b) imposition of restrictions on newspapers and magazines published in Indian languages (c) removal of disqualifications imposed on the Indian magistrates with regard to the trial of the Europeans (d) removal of a duty on imported cotton cloth - Answer: (c) removal of disqualifications imposed on the Indian magistrates with regard to the trial of the Europeans - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Ilbert Bill, introduced in 1883 under Lord Ripon, aimed to allow Indian magistrates to try Europeans in criminal cases, removing racial disqualifications in the judicial system. - The bill sparked intense opposition from European communities in India, who feared losing racial privileges, leading to protests and its eventual dilution in 1884. - The controversy highlighted racial discrimination in colonial governance and galvanized Indian nationalist sentiments, aligning with Ripon’s liberal reforms (Q64). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—The Arms Act (1878) under Lytton restricted Indian arms possession, unrelated to the Ilbert Bill (Q53). - (b) Incorrect—Vernacular Press Act (1878) targeted Indian newspapers, not the Ilbert Bill (Q53). - (d) Incorrect—Cotton duties were economic issues, not judicial, addressed in later nationalist critiques (Q78). - Other Relevant Colonial Judicial Reforms: - Indian High Courts Act (1861): - Established High Courts, pre-dated Ilbert Bill. - Criminal Procedure Code (1898): - Standardized judicial processes, post-Ilbert controversy. - Jury System Expansion (1860s): - Limited Indian involvement, contextual to Ilbert’s aim. - Significance of the Ilbert Bill Controversy: - The controversy exposed colonial racial biases, uniting Indian intellectuals and early nationalists, including those educated in institutions like Hindu College (Q70), in demanding equality, as you’ve explored in nationalism’s roots (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It marked a turning point in Indian political consciousness, strengthening the Indian National Congress’s formation in 1885. - Related Figures: - Lord Ripon: - Introduced Ilbert Bill, championed liberal reforms (Q64). - Surendranath Banerjee: - Supported the bill, mobilized Indian opinion (Q33). - C.P. Ilbert: - Drafted the bill, legal advisor to Ripon. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial reforms (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Ripon), early nationalism (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Ilbert Bill), or racial policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on judicial equality). - Reflects the tensions of colonial governance, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Ilbert Bill controversy (1883) concerned allowing Indian magistrates to try Europeans, highlighting racial discrimination and fueling nationalism. - [2014] - Q84: The Radcliffe Committee was appointed to: - Options: (a) solve the problem of minorities in India (b) give effect to the Independence Bill (c) delimit the boundaries between India and Pakistan (d) enquire into the riots in East Bengal - Answer: (c) delimit the boundaries between India and Pakistan - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Radcliffe Committee, chaired by Sir Cyril Radcliffe, was appointed in June 1947 to demarcate the boundaries between India and Pakistan following the Indian Independence Act, 1947. - Radcliffe, with limited knowledge of India, drew the Radcliffe Line, dividing Punjab and Bengal, leading to contentious borders and mass migrations during Partition. - The committee’s work was critical to implementing the partition plan announced in the Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Minority issues were addressed by the Constituent Assembly and Liaquat-Nehru Pact (1950), not Radcliffe. - (b) Incorrect—The Independence Bill was enacted by British Parliament; Radcliffe’s role was boundary delimitation. - (d) Incorrect—East Bengal riots (e.g., Noakhali, 1946) were investigated separately, not by Radcliffe. - Other Relevant Partition-Related Events: - Mountbatten Plan (1947): - Outlined partition, necessitated Radcliffe’s work. - Cabinet Mission Plan (1946): - Proposed united India, failed, led to partition. - Direct Action Day (1946): - Muslim League’s protests, escalated partition tensions. - Significance of the Radcliffe Committee: - The Radcliffe Line shaped India-Pakistan borders, causing massive displacement and communal violence, with lasting geopolitical impacts like the Kashmir dispute. - Its hasty implementation reflects the chaotic end of British rule, a critical juncture in modern Indian history. - Related Figures: - Cyril Radcliffe: - Chaired the committee, drew the boundary line. - Lord Mountbatten: - Last Viceroy, oversaw partition (Q58). - Jawaharlal Nehru: - Congress leader, influenced partition negotiations. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on partition (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Radcliffe Line), independence (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Mountbatten), or communal issues (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 1947). - Reflects the complexities of India’s independence, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Radcliffe Committee (1947) was appointed to delimit India-Pakistan boundaries, shaping the contentious Radcliffe Line. - Q85: The Partition of Bengal made by Lord Curzon in 1905 lasted until: - Options: (a) the First World War when Indian troops were needed by the British and the partition was ended (b) King George V abrogated Curzon’s Act at the Royal Durbar in Delhi in 1911 (c) Gandhiji launched his Civil Disobedience Movement (d) the Partition of India in 1947 when East Bengal became East Pakistan - Answer: (b) King George V abrogated Curzon’s Act at the Royal Durbar in Delhi in 1911 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905, creating East Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority) and West Bengal (Hindu-majority), citing administrative efficiency but aiming to weaken nationalist unity. - The partition sparked the Swadeshi Movement (1905-1908), with widespread protests led by Congress and leaders like Surendranath Banerjee (Q33). - King George V announced the annulment of the partition at the Delhi Durbar in 1911 under Lord Hardinge, reuniting Bengal and shifting the capital to Delhi. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—The First World War (1914-1918) post-dated the annulment; troop needs did not influence the decision. - (c) Incorrect—The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930) was unrelated to Bengal’s partition. - (d) Incorrect—The 1947 partition created East Pakistan, distinct from the 1905 event. - Other Relevant Colonial Partitions: - Partition of Punjab (1947): - Part of India-Pakistan division, post-Radcliffe (Q84). - Assam Separation (1874): - Created separate province, pre-Curzon. - Bihar-Orissa Separation (1912): - Post-Bengal reunification, administrative reform. - Significance of Bengal Partition’s Reversal: - The 1911 annulment was a British concession to Indian nationalist agitation, strengthening the Swadeshi Movement’s legacy and Congress’s organizational base. - It marked a shift in colonial policy, acknowledging Indian political mobilization, a theme you’ve explored in nationalism’s growth (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Related Figures: - Lord Curzon: - Initiated 1905 partition, sparked protests. - Lord Hardinge: - Oversaw 1911 reunification, Delhi Durbar. - Surendranath Banerjee: - Led Swadeshi protests against partition (Q33). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Swadeshi Movement (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Bengal partition), early nationalism (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Curzon), or colonial policies (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 1911). - Reflects the rise of Indian nationalism, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The 1905 Bengal partition lasted until King George V abrogated it in 1911 at the Delhi Durbar, responding to nationalist protests. - Q86: What was/were the object/objects of Queen Victoria’s Proclamation (1858)? - List: 1. To disclaim any intention to annex Indian States 2. To place the Indian administration under the British Crown 3. To regulate East India Company’s trade with India - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - 1. Queen Victoria’s Proclamation (1858), announced by Lord Canning, assured Indian princely states that the British Crown would not annex them, aiming to secure their loyalty post-1857 Revolt (Q51). - 2. It transferred Indian administration from the East India Company to the British Crown, establishing direct rule under a Secretary of State for India (Q58). - Incorrect statement: - 3. The Proclamation did not address the Company’s trade regulation; the Company’s commercial role ended, and trade was managed separately. - The Proclamation was a response to the 1857 Revolt, promising reforms and religious neutrality to stabilize British rule. - Why Not Others?: - (b) 2 only: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is also correct. - (c) 1 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 3 is false. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 3 is false. - Other Relevant Post-1857 Reforms: - Government of India Act, 1858: - Formalized Crown rule, created India Office (Q58). - Indian Councils Act, 1861: - Expanded legislative councils, post-Proclamation. - Army Reorganization (1861): - Increased British troops, ensured loyalty post-Revolt. - Significance of Queen Victoria’s Proclamation: - The Proclamation stabilized British rule by reassuring princely states and formalizing Crown governance, addressing 1857 Revolt grievances while reinforcing colonial control. - It laid the foundation for centralized administration, influencing later nationalist demands for representation. - Related Figures: - Lord Canning: - Announced Proclamation, first Viceroy (Q61). - Lord Dalhousie: - Predecessor, his annexations fueled 1857 Revolt (Q48). - Bahadur Shah Zafar: - Mughal leader in 1857, contextual to Revolt (Q51). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on 1857 Revolt (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Proclamation), Crown rule (e.g., Q76 [2006] on 1858 Act), or princely states (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on annexation). - Reflects the transition to direct British rule, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Queen Victoria’s Proclamation (1858) aimed to prevent annexation of Indian states and establish Crown rule, but not to regulate Company trade, making 1 and 2 correct. - Q87: A community of people called Manganiyars is well-known for their: - Options: (a) martial arts in North-East India (b) musical tradition in North-West India (c) classical vocal music in South India (d) pietra dura tradition in Central India - Answer: (b) musical tradition in North-West India - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Manganiyars are a hereditary Muslim community in Rajasthan (North-West India), renowned for their folk and classical musical tradition, blending Sufi, Rajput, and devotional elements. - They perform ballads, devotional songs, and oral histories, often at royal courts and festivals, preserving Rajasthan’s cultural heritage through instruments like the kamaicha and dholak. - Their music gained global recognition in the 20th century, but their tradition dates back centuries, rooted in the Thar Desert region. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Martial arts like Gatka are associated with Sikhs (Punjab), not Manganiyars; North-East India has distinct traditions (e.g., Kalaripayattu). - (c) Incorrect—South Indian classical vocal music is Carnatic, unrelated to Manganiyars. - (d) Incorrect—Pietra dura (stone inlay) is a Mughal craft in Central India (e.g., Agra), not a Manganiyar tradition. - Other Relevant Indian Musical Traditions: - Baul Music: - Bengal’s mystic folk tradition, contrasts with Manganiyars. - Qawwali: - Sufi devotional music, North India, shares spiritual elements. - Dhrupad: - Hindustani classical style, performed by some Rajasthani musicians. - Significance of Manganiyar Tradition: - The Manganiyars’ music preserves Rajasthan’s oral history and cultural diversity, bridging Hindu-Muslim traditions and showcasing India’s syncretic heritage. - Their global performances highlight India’s soft power, a cultural dimension relevant to UPSC’s art and culture syllabus. - Related Figures: - Roopayan Sansthan: - Institution promoting Manganiyar music, founded by Komal Kothari. - Amad Khan: - Notable Manganiyar musician, modern exponent. - Tansen: - Mughal-era musician, contextual to North Indian music traditions. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Indian cultural traditions (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on folk music), Rajasthan’s heritage (e.g., Q76 [2006] on regional culture), or syncretic traditions (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Sufi music). - Reflects India’s cultural diversity, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Manganiyars are renowned for their musical tradition in North-West India, particularly Rajasthan’s folk and classical songs. - Q88: The Ghadr (Ghadar) was a: - Options: (a) revolutionary association of Indians with headquarters at San Francisco (b) nationalist organization operating from Singapore (c) militant organization with headquarters at Berlin (d) communist movement for India’s freedom with headquarters at Tashkent - Answer: (a) revolutionary association of Indians with headquarters at San Francisco - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Ghadr Movement, founded in 1913 in San Francisco by Indian immigrants (e.g., Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna), was a revolutionary organization aiming to overthrow British colonial rule through armed struggle. - Its newspaper, Ghadr, called for rebellion, inspiring actions like the Komagata Maru incident (1914) and the Ghadr Conspiracy (1915) to incite mutinies in India. - Operating from the U.S., it drew support from Indian diaspora, particularly Punjabi Sikhs, and collaborated with Germany during World War I. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect—No major nationalist organization operated from Singapore; Home Rule Leagues were India-based (Q79). - (c) Incorrect—The Berlin Committee (1914) was a distinct revolutionary group, not Ghadr, though Ghadr collaborated with it. - (d) Incorrect—Communist movements (e.g., CPI, 1925) were separate; Tashkent hosted early communist training, not Ghadr. - Other Relevant Revolutionary Movements: - Berlin Committee (1914): - Indian revolutionaries in Germany, allied with Ghadr. - Anushilan Samiti (1902): - Bengal-based revolutionary group, pre-dated Ghadr. - Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928): - Later revolutionary group, built on Ghadr’s legacy. - Significance of the Ghadr Movement: - The Ghadr Movement radicalized the Indian diaspora, contributing to global anti-colonial networks and inspiring later revolutionary activities, reflecting the militant strand of nationalism you’ve explored (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Its failure (e.g., 1915 conspiracy) highlighted the challenges of overseas revolutionary efforts but energized domestic resistance. - Related Figures: - Lala Har Dayal: - Founded Ghadr, key ideologue. - Sohan Singh Bhakna: - Ghadr president, organized diaspora. - Kartar Singh Sarabha: - Young revolutionary, led 1915 conspiracy. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on revolutionary nationalism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Ghadr), diaspora movements (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Komagata Maru), or anti-colonialism (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 1915 conspiracy). - Reflects the global dimension of India’s freedom struggle, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Ghadr was a revolutionary association headquartered in San Francisco, advocating armed struggle against British rule from 1913. - [2015] - Q89: With reference to Indian history, which of the following is/are the essential element/elements of the feudal system? - List: 1. Creation of lord-vassal relationship between the feudal lord and his overlord - Which of the statements given above is/are correct? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - 2. The feudal system in medieval India (e.g., under the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire) was characterized by an administrative structure based on land control, with land grants (jagirs, iqtas) assigned to nobles for revenue collection and governance. - 3. A lord-vassal relationship existed, where local lords (jagirdars, zamindars) owed allegiance to overlords (sultans, emperors), receiving land in exchange for military and administrative services, similar to European feudalism you’ve explored (April 06, 2025, 06:09). - Incorrect statement: - 1. Indian feudalism typically featured a decentralized structure, with strong provincial authorities (e.g., jagirdars, chieftains) under a relatively weaker central authority, unlike European centralized feudalism; the Mughal Empire’s centralization was partial and varied by ruler. - This system was evident in the iqta system (Sultanate) and jagirdari system (Mughals), shaping medieval Indian polity. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 2: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; central authority was not consistently strong. - (c) 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is also correct. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false. - Other Relevant Feudal Elements in India: - Iqta System (13th century): - Sultanate’s land grant system, precursor to jagirdari. - Mansabdari System (16th century): - Mughal administrative structure, integrated feudal elements. - Bhakti Movement’s Impact: - Challenged feudal hierarchies, promoted social mobility. - Significance of Indian Feudal System: - The land-based administration and lord-vassal relationships sustained medieval Indian states, but decentralization often led to regional autonomy, influencing Mughal decline and colonial interventions. - It contrasts with colonial land systems like Permanent Settlement, which altered feudal dynamics (Q76). - Related Figures: - Alauddin Khalji: - Strengthened iqta system, feudal administrator. - Akbar: - Reformed jagirdari via mansabdari, balanced feudal ties. - Todar Mal: - Mughal revenue minister, managed land grants. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on medieval polity (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on jagirdari), feudal structures (e.g., Q76 [2006] on iqta), or Mughal administration (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on land grants). - Reflects the socio-political organization of medieval India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The feudal system in India involved land-based administration and lord-vassal relationships, but not strong centralized authority, making statements 2 and 3 correct. - Q90: Who of the following was/were economic critic/critics of colonialism in India? - List: 1. Dutt were all economic critics of colonialism, highlighting exploitation and fueling nationalism. - Q91: The Government of India Act of 1919 clearly defined: - Options: (a) the separation of power between the judiciary and the legislature (b) the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments (c) the powers of the Secretary of State for India and the Viceroy (d) None of the above - Answer: (b) the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms), introduced dyarchy, clearly defining the jurisdiction of central and provincial governments by dividing subjects into “reserved” (central control, e.g., defense, foreign affairs) and “transferred” (provincial control, e.g., education, agriculture). - Enacted post-World War I to address Indian demands for self-governance, it expanded legislative councils and introduced partial provincial autonomy, a step toward responsible government. - The Act was a response to nationalist agitation, including the Home Rule Movement, but was criticized by Congress for limited reforms (Q79). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—The Act focused on executive-legislative relations, not judicial-legislative separation, which was addressed later (e.g., 1935 Act). - (c) Incorrect—The powers of the Secretary of State and Viceroy were outlined in earlier acts (e.g., 1858, 1861); the 1919 Act clarified central-provincial roles. - (d) Incorrect—Option (b) is correct; the Act defined jurisdictions. - Other Relevant Constitutional Reforms: - Government of India Act, 1858: - Transferred rule to Crown, centralized power (Q86). - Indian Councils Act, 1909: - Introduced Morley-Minto Reforms, expanded councils (Q58). - Government of India Act, 1935: - Expanded provincial autonomy, federal structure. - Significance of the 1919 Act: - The Act’s dyarchy marked a cautious step toward self-governance, shaping Indian political participation and nationalist strategies, reflecting your interest in colonial governance’s evolution (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Its limitations fueled further demands, leading to the Civil Disobedience Movement and subsequent reforms (Q85). - Related Figures: - Edwin Montagu: - Secretary of State, co-authored reforms. - Lord Chelmsford: - Viceroy, implemented 1919 Act. - Annie Besant: - Home Rule leader, contextual to reform demands (Q79). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on constitutional reforms (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on dyarchy), nationalist movements (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Montagu-Chelmsford), or colonial governance (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 1919 Act). - Reflects the gradual devolution of power in colonial India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Government of India Act, 1919, clearly defined central and provincial government jurisdictions through dyarchy, advancing limited self-governance. - [2016] - Q92: Satya Shodhak Samaj organized: - Options: (a) a movement for upliftment of tribals in Bihar (b) a temple-entry movement in Gujarat (c) an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra (d) a peasant movement in Punjab - Answer: (c) an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Satya Shodhak Samaj, founded by Jyotirao Phule in 1873 in Maharashtra, was an anti-caste movement aimed at uplifting lower castes (Shudras and Dalits) by challenging Brahminical dominance and caste oppression. - It promoted education, social equality, and rationalism, organizing non-Brahmin communities to resist caste hierarchies and advocate for social justice. - Phule’s works, like Gulamgiri (1873), critiqued caste and supported peasant rights, aligning with broader social reforms (Q81). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Tribal movements in Bihar (e.g., Munda Revolt, Q77) were distinct; Satya Shodhak focused on caste in Maharashtra. - (b) Incorrect—Temple-entry movements (e.g., Vaikom, 1924) were later and South India-based, not Gujarat or Satya Shodhak. - (d) Incorrect—Peasant movements in Punjab (e.g., Kisan Sabha, 1920s) were unrelated; Phule addressed peasants but focused on caste. - Other Relevant Anti-Caste Movements: - Self-Respect Movement (1925): - Periyar’s Tamil Nadu movement, echoed Phule’s ideas. - Justice Party (1916): - South India’s non-Brahmin movement, inspired by Phule. - Ambedkar’s Dalit Movement (1930s): - Built on Satya Shodhak’s anti-caste legacy. - Significance of Satya Shodhak Samaj: - The Samaj pioneered anti-caste activism, empowering marginalized communities and influencing later Dalit and non-Brahmin movements, contributing to India’s social reform landscape. - Its emphasis on education for lower castes aligns with your interest in education’s role in social change (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Related Figures: - Jyotirao Phule: - Founded Satya Shodhak, authored Gulamgiri. - Savitribai Phule: - Co-led Samaj, pioneered women’s education. - B.R. Ambedkar: - Later anti-caste leader, influenced by Phule. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on social reforms (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Phule), anti-caste movements (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Satya Shodhak), or Dalit upliftment (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on caste). - Reflects the fight against social inequalities in colonial India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Satya Shodhak Samaj, founded by Jyotirao Phule, organized an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra to uplift lower castes. - Q93: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to: - Options: (a) social reforms (b) educational reforms (c) reforms in police administration (d) constitutional reforms - Answer: (d) constitutional reforms - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals, announced in 1918 and enacted as the Government of India Act, 1919, were constitutional reforms introducing dyarchy, dividing subjects into central “reserved” and provincial “transferred” categories (Q91). - Proposed by Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy), they aimed to grant limited self-governance in response to nationalist demands post-World War I, expanding legislative councils. - The reforms disappointed Congress for their limited scope, fueling further agitation (Q85). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Social reforms (e.g., Sati abolition, Q52) were separate; the Proposals focused on governance. - (b) Incorrect—Educational reforms (e.g., Hunter Commission, 1882) were unrelated; the Act addressed political structure. - (c) Incorrect—Police reforms (e.g., 1902 Commission) were distinct; the Proposals targeted constitutional changes. - Other Relevant Constitutional Reforms: - Morley-Minto Reforms (1909): - Expanded councils, introduced communal electorates (Q58). - Government of India Act, 1935: - Built on 1919 Act, introduced provincial autonomy. - Cripps Mission (1942): - Later constitutional proposal, offered dominion status (Q96). - Significance of Montague-Chelmsford Reforms: - The reforms marked a step toward responsible government, shaping Indian political participation and nationalist strategies, a key aspect of colonial governance you’ve explored (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Their limitations spurred radical nationalism, influencing movements like Non-Cooperation (1920-22). - Related Figures: - Edwin Montagu: - Co-authored reforms, pushed gradual self-rule (Q91). - Lord Chelmsford: - Viceroy, implemented 1919 Act (Q91). - Bal Gangadhar Tilak: - Home Rule leader, contextual to reform demands. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on dyarchy (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on 1919 Act), constitutional reforms (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Montagu-Chelmsford), or nationalism (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on reforms). - Reflects the evolution of colonial governance, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals (1918) were constitutional reforms, introducing dyarchy via the 1919 Act. - Q94: Consider the following: - List: 1. Calcutta Unitarian Committee 2. Tabernacle of New Dispensation 3. Indian Reform Association - Keshab Chandra Sen is associated with the establishment of which of the above? - Options: (a) 1 and 3 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - 2. Keshab Chandra Sen founded the Tabernacle of New Dispensation in 1880, a syncretic religious movement blending Brahmo Samaj principles with Christian and Vaishnava elements, emphasizing universal spirituality. - 3. He established the Indian Reform Association in 1870 to promote social reforms, including women’s education and charity, reflecting his Brahmo activism (Q81). - Incorrect statement: - 1. The Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1820s) was linked to Raja Rammohan Roy and William Adam, promoting Unitarianism, not founded by Sen, though he was influenced by Roy’s Brahmo Samaj (Q70). - Sen’s work advanced the Bengal Renaissance, focusing on social and religious reform. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false; Sen did not found the Unitarian Committee. - (c) 3 only: - Incorrect—Statement 2 is also correct. - (d) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—Statement 1 is false. - Other Relevant Brahmo Samaj Initiatives: - Brahmo Samaj of India (1866): - Sen’s split from original Brahmo Samaj, led by Debendranath Tagore. - Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878): - Formed by Sen’s opponents, continued reform legacy. - Bethune School (1849): - Supported by Brahmo reformers, contextual to Sen’s education focus (Q52). - Significance of Keshab Chandra Sen’s Organizations: - The Tabernacle and Indian Reform Association promoted universal religion and social equity, influencing educated Indians and strengthening reformist nationalism, a theme you’ve explored in education’s role (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Sen’s syncretism bridged Indian and Western thought, shaping modern Indian identity. - Related Figures: - Keshab Chandra Sen: - Founded Tabernacle, Indian Reform Association (Q70). - Raja Rammohan Roy: - Brahmo Samaj founder, influenced Sen (Q70). - Debendranath Tagore: - Brahmo leader, split with Sen over reforms. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Bengal Renaissance (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Sen), social reforms (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Brahmo Samaj), or religious movements (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on syncretism). - Reflects the intellectual reformist movement, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Keshab Chandra Sen established the Tabernacle of New Dispensation and Indian Reform Association, but not the Calcutta Unitarian Committee, making 2 and 3 correct. - Q95: What was the main reason for the split in the Indian National Congress at Surat in 1907? - Options: (a) Introduction of communalism into Indian politics by Lord Minto (b) Extremists’ lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the British Government (c) Foundation of Muslim League (d) Aurobindo Ghosh’s inability to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress - Answer: (b) Extremists’ lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the British Government - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Surat Split of 1907 divided the Indian National Congress into Moderates (e.g., Gopal Krishna Gokhale) and Extremists (e.g., Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Aurobindo Ghosh) due to ideological differences. - Extremists, frustrated by the Moderates’ faith in constitutional methods (e.g., petitions), demanded aggressive tactics like Swadeshi and boycott, especially after the Bengal Partition (1905, Q85). - The split occurred at the Surat session when Moderates rejected Extremist demands, electing Rash Behari Ghosh over Tilak, leading to a formal divide. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Lord Minto’s communal electorates (1909, Morley-Minto Reforms) post-dated the split; communalism was not the main cause. - (c) Incorrect—The Muslim League’s formation (1906) was peripheral; the split was internal to Congress ideology. - (d) Incorrect—Aurobindo was not a candidate for president; the issue was broader ideological conflict, not his election. - Other Relevant Congress Developments: - Swadeshi Movement (1905-08): - Extremist-led, sparked by Bengal Partition (Q85). - Lucknow Pact (1916): - Reunited Moderates and Extremists, post-Surat. - Home Rule Movement (1916): - Tilak’s post-split initiative, sustained Extremist goals. - Significance of the Surat Split: - The split marked a turning point in Indian nationalism, highlighting ideological divides and strengthening Extremist influence, shaping mass movements like Non-Cooperation, a dynamic you’ve explored in nationalism’s growth (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It weakened Congress temporarily but catalyzed radical nationalism. - Related Figures: - Bal Gangadhar Tilak: - Extremist leader, pushed Swadeshi (Q33). - Gopal Krishna Gokhale: - Moderate leader, favored negotiations. - Aurobindo Ghosh: - Extremist, advocated militant nationalism. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on early nationalism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Surat Split), Swadeshi Movement (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Extremists), or Congress history (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 1907). - Reflects the evolution of nationalist strategies, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Surat Split (1907) resulted from Extremists’ distrust in Moderates’ negotiation tactics, dividing Congress ideologically. - Q96: The plan of Sir Stafford Cripps envisaged that after the Second World War: - Options: (a) India should be granted complete independence (b) India should be partitioned into two before granting independence (c) India should be made a republic with the condition that she will join the Commonwealth (d) India should be given Dominion status - Answer: (d) India should be given Dominion status - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Cripps Mission, led by Sir Stafford Cripps in March 1942, proposed a post-World War II framework for India, offering Dominion status with the right to secede from the British Commonwealth, subject to a constituent assembly and provincial opt-out clauses. - Aimed to secure Indian support for the war, the plan included a promise of self-governance but allowed provinces to form separate unions, implying potential partition. - Congress and Muslim League rejected it—Congress for not guaranteeing immediate independence, League for not explicitly ensuring Pakistan. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Complete independence was not offered; Dominion status was proposed. - (b) Incorrect—Partition was not mandated; provincial opt-outs were optional. - (c) Incorrect—Republic status was not mentioned; Commonwealth membership was voluntary. - Other Relevant Wartime Proposals: - August Offer (1940): - Earlier British proposal, offered limited self-rule. - Cabinet Mission Plan (1946): - Post-Cripps, proposed federal structure (Q84). - Mountbatten Plan (1947): - Culminated in partition and independence (Q84). - Significance of Cripps Mission: - The Cripps Plan was a failed attempt to resolve India’s constitutional deadlock, escalating nationalist demands and leading to the Quit India Movement (1942), a pivotal moment in the freedom struggle. - It reflects British wartime pressures and Indian political complexity, relevant to your focus on colonial governance (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - Related Figures: - Sir Stafford Cripps: - Led the mission, proposed Dominion status. - Mahatma Gandhi: - Rejected Cripps, launched Quit India. - Muhammad Ali Jinnah: - League leader, sought clearer partition terms. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on independence negotiations (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Cripps), Quit India (e.g., Q76 [2006] on 1942), or constitutional proposals (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Dominion status). - Reflects the endgame of British rule, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Cripps Plan (1942) envisaged Dominion status for India post-World War II, rejected for its limited concessions. - [2018] - Q97: With reference to cultural history of India, consider the following statements: - List: 1. Most of the Tyagaraja Kritis are devotional songs in praise of Lord Krishna 2. Tyagaraja created several new ragas 3. Annamacharya and Tyagaraja are contemporaries 4. Annamacharya kirtanas are devotional songs in praise of Lord Venkateshwara - Which of the statements given above are correct? - Options: (a) 1 and 3 only (b) 2 and 4 only (c) 1, 2 and 3 (d) 2, 3 and 4 - Answer: (b) 2 and 4 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statements: - 2. Tyagaraja (1767-1847), a Carnatic music trinity composer, created new ragas (e.g., Kharaharapriya variants), enriching South Indian classical music. - 4. Annamacharya (1408-1503), a 15th-century Telugu composer, wrote kirtanas primarily in praise of Lord Venkateshwara, the deity of Tirupati. - Incorrect statements: - 1. Most Tyagaraja Kritis are devoted to Lord Rama, not Krishna, reflecting his Vaishnava devotion. - 3. Annamacharya (15th century) and Tyagaraja (18th-19th century) were not contemporaries, separated by over 250 years. - Both composers shaped South Indian devotional music, integral to India’s cultural heritage. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1 and 3: - Incorrect—Both 1 and 3 are false. - (c) 1, 2 and 3: - Incorrect—1 and 3 are false; only 2 is correct. - (d) 2, 3 and 4: - Incorrect—3 is false; only 2 and 4 are correct. - Other Relevant South Indian Musical Traditions: - Purandara Dasa (1484-1564): - Father of Carnatic music, contemporary of Annamacharya. - Syama Sastri (1762-1827): - Carnatic trinity, Tyagaraja’s contemporary. - Muthuswami Dikshitar (1775-1835): - Carnatic trinity, composed in multiple deities’ praise. - Significance of Tyagaraja and Annamacharya: - Tyagaraja’s innovative ragas and Annamacharya’s Venkateshwara kirtanas enriched Carnatic music, preserving devotional traditions and influencing modern performances. - Their works reflect South India’s cultural syncretism, relevant to your interest in cultural heritage (April 06, 2025, 06:09). - Related Figures: - Tyagaraja: - Carnatic composer, created Rama-centric Kritis. - Annamacharya: - Telugu composer, devoted to Venkateshwara. - Purandara Dasa: - Structured Carnatic music, contextual to both. - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on Carnatic music (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Tyagaraja), cultural heritage (e.g., Q76 [2006] on South Indian music), or devotional traditions (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on Bhakti). - Reflects India’s musical heritage, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Tyagaraja created new ragas, and Annamacharya’s kirtanas praised Venkateshwara, but Tyagaraja’s Kritis focused on Rama, and they were not contemporaries, making 2 and 4 correct. - Q98: The staple commodities of export by the English East India Company from Bengal in the middle of the 18th century were: - Options: (a) Raw cotton, oil-seeds and opium (b) Sugar, salt, zinc and lead (c) Copper, silver, gold, spices and tea (d) Cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium - Answer: (d) Cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the mid-18th century (post-Plassey, 1757), the English East India Company dominated Bengal’s trade, exporting: - Cotton: Bengal’s textiles (muslin, calico) were globally demanded. - Silk: Raw and woven silk, a high-value export. - Saltpetre: Used for gunpowder, critical for European wars. - Opium: Grown for export to China, fueling Company profits. - These commodities drove Bengal’s economic exploitation, contributing to the drain of wealth (Q78). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Raw cotton and opium were exported, but oil-seeds were not a staple export. - (b) Incorrect—Sugar and salt were minor; zinc and lead were not significant exports. - (c) Incorrect—Copper, silver, gold, spices, and tea were not Bengal’s primary exports; tea was later (19th century). - Other Relevant Colonial Exports: - Indigo: - Major 19th-century export, caused peasant unrest (Q69). - Jute: - Emerged later (19th century), Bengal’s key export. - Spices: - Exported from South India, not Bengal’s staple (Q82). - Significance of Bengal’s Exports: - The export of cotton, silk, saltpetre, and opium enriched the Company, deindustrialized Bengal’s textile economy, and fueled global trade, aligning with your interest in colonial economic policies (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It set the stage for economic critiques by Naoroji and Dutt (Q90). - Related Figures: - Robert Clive: - Secured Bengal post-Plassey, boosted trade (Q56). - Warren Hastings: - Expanded Company’s trade control (Q55). - Dadabhai Naoroji: - Critiqued export-driven exploitation (Q90). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial trade (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Bengal), economic exploitation (e.g., Q76 [2006] on opium), or drain of wealth (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on textiles). - Reflects colonial economic dominance, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The English East India Company exported cotton, silk, saltpetre, and opium from Bengal in the mid-18th century, driving colonial profits. - Q99: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley? - Options: (a) To maintain a large standing army at other’s expense (b) To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger (c) To secure a fixed income for the Company (d) To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States - Answer: (c) To secure a fixed income for the Company - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Subsidiary Alliance, introduced by Lord Wellesley (1798-1805), was a policy to expand British control over Indian states by: - (a) Maintaining a British-controlled army in the state, funded by the state, reducing its autonomy. - (b) Protecting India from French (Napoleonic) threats, as France allied with states like Mysore. - (d) Establishing British paramountcy, subordinating states (e.g., Hyderabad, 1798; Awadh, 1801) to Company authority. - Incorrect statement: - (c) The Alliance did not primarily aim to secure a fixed income; it focused on strategic control and military dominance, though states paid for troops, not as a fixed revenue stream. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct—States funded British troops, a core feature. - (b) Correct—Countering Napoleon was a strategic goal. - (d) Correct—Paramountcy was the ultimate aim. - Other Relevant Colonial Policies: - Doctrine of Lapse (1848): - Dalhousie’s annexation policy, post-Wellesley (Q48). - Permanent Settlement (1793): - Cornwallis’s revenue system, pre-Wellesley (Q76). - Ring-Fence Policy: - Warren Hastings’ earlier strategy, less aggressive. - Significance of Subsidiary Alliance: - The Alliance expanded British hegemony, weakening Indian states and paving the way for direct rule, a key colonial governance strategy you’ve explored (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It provoked resistance, contributing to the 1857 Revolt (Q51). - Related Figures: - Lord Wellesley: - Architect of Subsidiary Alliance, expanded Company power. - Tipu Sultan: - Resisted Alliance, fought Mysore Wars (Q38). - Lord Dalhousie: - Later annexed states, built on Wellesley’s policies (Q48). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial expansion (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Wellesley), paramountcy (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Alliance), or 1857 Revolt (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on state resistance). - Reflects British imperialism’s mechanisms, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - The Subsidiary Alliance aimed at military control, anti-Napoleonic defense, and paramountcy, but not primarily a fixed income, making (c) incorrect. - Q100: Economically, one of the results of the British rule in India in the 19th century was the: - Options: (a) increase in the export of Indian handicrafts (b) growth in the number of Indian owned factories (c) commercialization of Indian agriculture (d) rapid increase in the urban population - Answer: (c) commercialization of Indian agriculture - Analysis: - Historical Context: - British rule in the 19th century transformed Indian agriculture into a commercial system, with cash crops like indigo, opium, cotton, and jute grown for export to meet global demands (Q98). - Policies like Permanent Settlement (Q76) and Ryotwari (Q80) tied peasants to market-driven production, often at the expense of food crops, leading to famines and debt. - This commercialization enriched British trade but impoverished peasants, as critiqued by Naoroji and Dutt (Q90). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Handicraft exports (e.g., textiles) declined due to British competition and deindustrialization (Q90). - (b) Incorrect—Indian-owned factories emerged late (e.g., Tata, 1870s), not a widespread 19th-century trend. - (d) Incorrect—Urbanization was slow; rural agrarian distress dominated (Q77). - Other Relevant Economic Impacts: - Deindustrialization: - Decline of textiles, artisans, due to British imports (Q90). - Railway Expansion (1853): - Facilitated cash crop transport, boosted commercialization (Q71). - Drain of Wealth: - Export profits enriched Britain, not India (Q78). - Significance of Agricultural Commercialization: - Commercialization integrated India into the global economy but caused peasant exploitation, fueling unrest (e.g., Indigo Revolt, Q69) and nationalist economic critiques, a key colonial economic outcome you’ve explored (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It reshaped rural India, influencing tenancy reforms (e.g., Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885). - Related Figures: - Lord Cornwallis: - Permanent Settlement, spurred commercialization (Q76). - Dadabhai Naoroji: - Critiqued agricultural exploitation (Q90). - Lord Dalhousie: - Railways aided cash crop exports (Q71). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial economics (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on agriculture), peasant unrest (e.g., Q76 [2006] on commercialization), or nationalism (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on economic critique). - Reflects the economic restructuring under British rule, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - British rule in the 19th century commercialized Indian agriculture, prioritizing cash crops for export, transforming the rural economy. - Q101: Which among the following events happened earliest? - Options: (a) Swami Dayanand established Arya Samaj (b) Dinabandhu Mitra wrote Neeldarpan (c) Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Anandmath (d) Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to succeed in the Indian Civil Services Examination - Answer: (b) Dinabandhu Mitra wrote Neeldarpan - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Timelines: - (b) Dinabandhu Mitra wrote Neeldarpan in 1860, a play exposing indigo planters’ exploitation, sparking nationalist sentiment (Q69). - (a) Swami Dayanand established Arya Samaj in 1875, promoting Vedic reforms (Q81). - (d) Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian ICS officer in 1864, after passing the exam in 1863. - (c) Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Anandmath in 1882, a nationalist novel (Q69). - Neeldarpan (1860) is the earliest event, reflecting early resistance to colonial economic oppression. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 1875—Later than 1860. - (c) 1882—Later than 1860. - (d) 1863/64—Later than 1860. - Other Relevant 19th-Century Milestones: - Brahmo Samaj (1828): - Roy’s reform movement, pre-dates Neeldarpan (Q81). - Widow Remarriage Act (1856): - Social reform, pre-Neeldarpan (Q52). - Ilbert Bill (1883): - Judicial reform, post-Neeldarpan (Q83). - Significance of Neeldarpan: - Neeldarpan’s 1860 publication galvanized anti-colonial sentiment, highlighting economic exploitation and influencing literary nationalism, a precursor to later movements like Swadeshi (Q85). - Its early date underscores the rapid rise of resistance post-1857 Revolt (Q51). - Related Figures: - Dinabandhu Mitra: - Authored Neeldarpan, exposed indigo oppression (Q69). - Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay: - Wrote Anandmath, nationalist author (Q69). - Swami Dayanand: - Founded Arya Samaj, religious reformer (Q81). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on early nationalism (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on Neeldarpan), colonial exploitation (e.g., Q76 [2006] on indigo), or literary resistance (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on 1860s). - Reflects the emergence of anti-colonial consciousness, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Dinabandhu Mitra’s Neeldarpan (1860) was the earliest event, marking early literary resistance to colonial rule. - Q102: With reference to educational institutes during colonial rule in India, consider the following pairs of Institution vs Founder: - List: 1. Fort William College: Arthur Wellesley - Which of the pairs given above is/are correct? - Options: (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Correct statement: - 2. Wood’s Dispatch (1854), issued by Charles Wood, introduced the Grants-in-Aid system to fund private educational institutions, promoting mass education. - 2. [2020] - Q111: Indigo cultivation in India declined by the beginning of the 20th century because of: - Options: (a) Peasant resistance to the oppressive conduct of planters (b) Its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions (c) National leaders’ opposition to the cultivation of indigo (d) Government control over the planters - Answer: (b) Its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Indigo cultivation, a major colonial cash crop in Bengal and Bihar (Q100), declined by the early 20th century primarily due to the invention of synthetic dyes (e.g., aniline dyes) in Germany (1850s-1860s), which were cheaper and reduced global demand for natural indigo. - While peasant resistance (e.g., Indigo Revolt, 1859-60, Q69) and nationalist critiques (e.g., Gandhi’s Champaran Satyagraha, 1917) weakened the system, the decisive factor was economic unprofitability as synthetic dyes dominated world markets by the 1900s. - Government regulations (post-1860 reforms) existed but were secondary to market forces. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Peasant resistance (e.g., Neeldarpan, Q101) disrupted indigo cultivation but was not the primary cause of its decline; market forces were decisive. - (c) Incorrect—Nationalist opposition, notably Gandhi’s 1917 campaign, came later and was not the main reason for the early 20th-century decline. - (d) Incorrect—Government control (e.g., post-1859 reforms) was limited and not the primary driver; economic factors prevailed. - Other Relevant Colonial Agrarian Issues: - Indigo Revolt (1859-60): - Peasant uprising against planters, pre-dated decline (Q69). - Champaran Satyagraha (1917): - Gandhi’s campaign, post-dated main decline (Q110). - Deccan Riots (1875): - Peasant unrest over debt, unrelated to indigo (Q77). - Significance of Indigo’s Decline: - The shift to synthetic dyes reflects the global impact of industrialization on colonial economies, reducing India’s indigo exports and exacerbating rural distress, a theme you’ve explored in colonial economics (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It weakened planter power, paving the way for nationalist agrarian campaigns. - Related Figures: - Dinabandhu Mitra: - Authored Neeldarpan, exposed indigo oppression (Q101). - Mahatma Gandhi: - Led Champaran Satyagraha, later indigo critique (Q110). - Lord Cornwallis: - Early land policies enabled planter dominance (Q76). - Broader Connection: - Links to questions on colonial agriculture (e.g., Q105 [2015-I] on indigo), peasant movements (e.g., Q76 [2006] on Neeldarpan), or economic decline (e.g., Q150 [2024-I] on cash crops). - Reflects the impact of global markets on colonial India, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Indigo cultivation declined by the early 20th century due to its unprofitability in the world market, driven by synthetic dye inventions. - Q112: Wellesley established the Fort William College at Calcutta because: - Options: (a) He was asked by the Board of Directors at London to do so (b) He wanted to revive interest in oriental learning in India (c) He wanted to provide William Carey and his associates employment (d) He wanted to train British civilians for administrative purposes in India - Answer: (d) He wanted to train British civilians for administrative purposes in India - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Lord Wellesley established Fort William College in 1800 to train British East India Company civilians in Indian languages, laws, and customs, ensuring efficient colonial administration (Q102). - The college aimed to professionalize governance, addressing the need for culturally informed officials, contrasting with earlier ad-hoc systems under Hastings (Q102). - While oriental learning was part of the curriculum, the primary goal was administrative training, not revival of Indian traditions. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—No evidence suggests the Board of Directors mandated the college; it was Wellesley’s initiative. - (b) Incorrect—Oriental learning was a means, not the goal; administrative training was primary. - Hastings’ initiative for Muslim administrators (Q102). - Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791): - Duncan’s effort for Hindu learning (Q102). - Hindu College, Calcutta (1817): - Roy’s Western education hub, post-Wellesley (Q70). - Significance of Fort William College: - The college strengthened colonial governance by creating a cadre of trained administrators, fostering indirect control over Indian society, a theme you’ve explored in colonial governance (April 16, 2025, 01:25). - It influenced later education policies like Wood’s Dispatch (Q103). - Related Figures: - Lord Wellesley: - Founded Fort William College, expanded Company power (Q99). - Warren Hastings: - Early education efforts, contextual to Wellesley (Q102). - Reflects education’s role in colonial control, a key UPSC theme. - Key Takeaway: - Wellesley established Fort William College to train British civilians for administrative purposes in India. - Q113: Which of the following statements correctly explain the impact of the Industrial Revolution on India during the first half of the nineteenth century? - Answer: (a) Indian handicrafts were ruined - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Industrial Revolution (late 18th-early 19th century) in Britain led to mass-produced textiles flooding Indian markets, causing deindustrialization and ruining Indian handicrafts, especially cotton and silk textiles (Q98). - Q114: Vital-Vidhvansak, the first monthly journal to have the untouchable people as its target audience was published by: - Options: (a) Gopal Baba Walangkar (b) Jyotiba Phule (c) Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (d) Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar - Answer: (a) Gopal Baba Walangkar - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Vital-Vidhvansak (1888), the first monthly journal targeting untouchables (Dalits), was published by Gopal Baba Walangkar, a Dalit reformer and ex-soldier from Maharashtra, advocating against caste oppression and untouchability. - Walangkar’s work pre-dated Ambedkar’s Dalit movement, building on Phule’s anti-caste legacy (Q92) and influencing later reforms like Gandhi’s Harijan campaign (Q110). - The journal marked an early Dalit literary voice, addressing social exclusion. - Options: (a) The Regulating Act (b) The Pitt’s India Act (c) The Charter Act of 1793 (d) The Charter Act of 1833 - Answer: (d) The Charter Act of 1833 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Charter Act of 1833 centralized British administration in India by designating the Governor General of Bengal as the Governor General of India, with authority over all British territories, ending the Bengal-centric governance. - The First (November 1930–January 1931), Second (September–December 1931), and Third (November–December 1932) sessions were part of a continuous process, making the term “three conferences” misleading. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—While Congress boycotted the First and Third sessions, this does not negate the sessions being part of one conference process. - (b) Incorrect—Sectional interests of other parties (e.g., Muslim League) were present, but this is secondary to the structural issue of the sessions. - (c) Incorrect—British Labour Party’s stance did not alter the conference’s structure as a single entity with multiple sessions. - Other Relevant Constitutional Aspects: - Simon Commission (1927): - Preceded the conference, set reform context, boycotted by Congress (Q147 [2011-I]). - Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931): - Enabled Congress’s participation in the Second session (Q184 [2020-I]). - Communal Award (1932): - Outcome of the conference, led to Gandhi’s fast and Poona Pact (Q24 [1997]). - Government of India Act, 1935: - Resulted from conference discussions, implemented federal reforms (Q127 [2024]). - Cripps Mission (1942): - Later constitutional talks, post-conference (Q123 [2008]). - Significance: - The conference’s three-session structure shaped India’s constitutional trajectory, leading to the 1935 Act and influencing independence talks, despite Congress’s partial participation (Q127 [2024]). - Related Figures: - Mahatma Gandhi: - Attended Second session, represented Congress (Q184 [2020-I]). - B.R. - Options: - (a) Mahatma Gandhi - (b) Jawaharlal Nehru - (c) Sardar Patel - (d) Maulana Abul Kalam Azad - Answer: - (c) Sardar Patel - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Sardar Patel, a pragmatic Congress leader, was totally in favor of the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) for its federal structure, seeing it as a viable path to a united India while accepting its practical limitations, unlike Gandhi’s ambivalence, Nehru’s reservations, and Azad’s initial support tempered by concerns. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect—Gandhi was cautious, not fully committed to the plan. - (b) Incorrect—Nehru’s press conference in July 1946 questioned the plan’s grouping, undermining it. - (d) Incorrect—Azad supported the plan but expressed concerns over its implementation, less unequivocal than Patel. - Other Relevant Congress Responses: - Nehru’s Press Conference (1946): - Weakened the plan by questioning compulsory grouping (Q17 [1996]). - Muslim League Rejection (1946): - Jinnah withdrew support, demanding Pakistan. - Interim Government (1946): - Formed post-Mission, led by Nehru (Q44 [1999]). - Mountbatten Plan (1947): - Followed Mission’s failure, led to partition (Q38 [1998]). - Direct Action Day (1946): - Riots followed League’s rejection. - Significance: - Patel’s full support for the Cabinet Mission Plan reflected Congress’s pragmatic approach to unity, but its failure paved the way for partition (Q17 [1996]). - Related Figures: - Sardar Patel: - Key supporter, pragmatic leader (Q45 [1999]). - Maulana Azad: - Congress president, supported but less decisive (Q44 [1999]). - Jawaharlal Nehru: - Questioned plan, interim PM (Q16 [1996]). - Mahatma Gandhi: - Ambivalent, sought broader unity (Q45 [1999]). - Lord Wavell: - Viceroy, oversaw Mission (Q17 [1996]). - Broader Connection: - Links to Q17 [1996] on Cabinet Mission, Q44 [1999] on interim government, Q38 [1998] on Mountbatten, Q45 [1999] on partition, Q127 [2024] on independence.
